## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Buddhavamsa-Aṭṭhakathā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Ganthārambhakathā
I pay homage to the Buddha, who possesses infinite wisdom, who is the abode of great compassion, who has dispelled the sensual pleasures that are the basis of the stains of defilements, whose mind is well-concentrated, and who brings about the welfare of beings to be tamed. I pay homage to the sublime Dhamma, which protects one from falling into [lower] existences, and to the community of the Sangha, the source of virtues and free from the stains of defilements.

Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma and the foremost in wisdom among the disciples of the Buddha, asked a question to the Teacher, the Lord who has reached the further shore of Saṃsāra and is free from defilements, in the midst of his kinsmen.

That Tathāgata, who is of pure lineage, who is the Leader, who has destroyed the opportunity for [the results of] wholesome and unwholesome kamma, and who dwells in concentration, has clearly revealed this Buddhavamsa teaching, which is the excellent lineage of the Buddhas.

Until this very day, the noble sons of the Buddha (the monks) have well-preserved the sequence of the Pali, the meaning of the Pali, and the connection of the words, without letting them perish, just as they had heard them.
2:
This commentary, which is appropriately consistent with the lineage of that noble Buddha, which leads to Nibbāna—the deathless—whenever people hear it, and which generates devotion and wisdom, has come down in succession.

Having been requested for a very long time by the Elder Buddhasīha, who respectfully delights in the True Dhamma and is endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla), I shall begin the commentary on that Buddhavamsa teaching.

[I do this] for the long endurance of the Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana), which destroys the anger of people; for the increase of my own merit; and for the devotion of the great multitude of people.

Relying on the path of the Pali text descending from the Mahāvihāra, and being free from the faults of confusion, I shall write this Buddhavamsa commentary in a concise manner, capturing its essence.

There is no other speech in this world as worthy of hearing as this account of the Buddhavamsa, which generates devotion in those who delight in the virtues of the Buddha and washes away the great stains of evil and unwholesome deeds.

Therefore, being endowed with respectful concentration, having abandoned distraction and without letting the mind wander elsewhere, listen well to this sweet commentary while it is being explained, inclining your ear as if collecting gold.

Wise people should abandon all other duties and always respectfully listen to and speak this Buddhavamsa teaching; for this discourse is exceedingly rare to encounter.

In those introductory verses (Ganthārambhakathā), because it is said, "The commentary on the Buddhavamsa will be the essence"...
3:
In those introductory verses, because it was said, "The commentary on the Buddhavamsa will be the essence," the Buddhavamsa (Chronicle of Buddhas) should first be defined. In this regard, the definition is as follows: The discourse that expands upon the succession of the twenty-five Buddhas who appeared during the four incalculables and a hundred thousand eons prior to this [Bhadda] Kappa, by way of classifying the eons in which they appeared and so forth, is to be known as the "Buddhavamsa."

That Buddhavamsa is defined and categorized by these twenty-two classifications appearing in the Pali: classification of the eon, classification of the name, classification of the clan, classification of the caste, classification of the city, classification of the father, classification of the mother, classification of the Bodhi tree, classification of the place of turning the Wheel of Dhamma, classification of the realization of the Truths, classification of the assembly of disciples, classification of the chief disciples, classification of the attendant, classification of the chief female disciples, classification of the retinue of monks, classification of the radiance, classification of the physical stature, classification of the Bodhisatta's extraordinary aspiration, classification of the prophecy, classification of the Bodhisatta's practice of austerities, classification of the lifespan, and classification of the place of Parinibbāna.

Although not directly included in the Pali text, the Miscellaneous Section (Sambahulavāra) should also be brought in here. That Miscellaneous Section is defined in ten ways: the classification of living in the household, the classification of enjoying the three palaces, the classification of the dancing women, the classification of the chief queen, the classification of the son, the classification of the vehicle, the classification of the Great Renunciation, the classification of the practice of austerities, the classification of the attendant, and the classification of the monastery.

We shall proceed by showing that Miscellaneous Section,
In each respective place where it remains established,
Such as in the accounts of household life and so forth,
Only in a concise manner.

That Miscellaneous Section is to be defined thus:
Who taught this Buddhavamsa? Where was it taught?
For whose benefit was it taught?
At what time, for what purpose,
Whose word was received, and by whom was it brought forth?

Having first stated all these methods in brief,
I shall afterwards perform the explanation of the meaning of the Buddhavamsa.

In that verse, "By whom was this taught?" (kenāyaṃ desito) is a question asking who taught this Buddhavamsa. This Buddhavamsa [was taught by the Blessed One] who possesses unimpeded knowledge regarding all phenomena, who is endowed with the ten powers, and who is confident in the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa)...
4:
This Buddhavaṃsa discourse was preached by the Perfectly Enlightened One, the King of Dhamma, the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata who, like previous Buddhas, has come rightly, and the Knower of all things.

Where was it preached? It was preached while walking on the Jeweled Walkway (Ratana-caṅkama), which was the focus of the eyes of devas and humans and where He displayed supreme radiance, in the great Nigrodhārāma monastery in the great city of Kapilavatthu.

For whose benefit was it preached? It was preached for the benefit of eighty-two thousand relatives, as well as for the benefit of many crores of devas and humans.

For what purpose was it preached? It was preached for the purpose of enabling them to cross over the four floods (oghas) of saṃsāra.

When was it preached? For the first twenty years after His enlightenment, the Blessed One had no fixed residence and stayed wherever it was comfortable. How did He stay? Having turned the Wheel of Dhamma at the Isipatana Migadāya during the first rains retreat (vassa) and having given the drink of the Deathless to eighteen crores of Brahmas, He resided at the Isipatana Migadāya depending on the city of Bārāṇasī. During the second vassa, He resided at the great Veḷuvana monastery depending on Rājagaha. He stayed in that same place during the third and fourth vassas as well. During the fifth vassa, He resided at the Kūṭāgārasālā monastery in the Mahāvana forest depending on the city of Vesālī. During the sixth vassa, He resided at Makula Mountain. During the seventh vassa, He resided in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. During the eighth vassa, He resided at Bhesakaḷāvana near the city of Suṃsumāragiri in the Bhagga country. During the ninth vassa, He resided in Kosambī. During the tenth vassa, He resided in the Pālileyyaka forest. During the eleventh vassa, He resided in the Brahmin village of Nālā. During the twelfth vassa, He resided in the city of Verañjā. During the thirteenth vassa, He resided at Cāliya Mountain. During the fourteenth vassa, He resided at the great Jetavana monastery. During the fifteenth vassa, He resided in the great city of Kapilavatthu (in the nearby Mahāvana forest). During the sixteenth vassa, after taming the ogre Āḷavaka and giving the drink of the Deathless to eighty-four thousand beings, He resided in the city of Āḷavī. During the seventeenth vassa, He resided again in Rājagaha. During the eighteenth vassa, He resided again at Cāliya Mountain. Likewise, during the nineteenth vassa, He resided at Cāliya Mountain, but during the twentieth vassa, He resided again in Rājagaha. Therefore, it is said: "For the first twenty years after His enlightenment, the Blessed One had no fixed residence and stayed wherever it was comfortable." From that time onwards, depending on the city of Sāvatthī, He resided permanently at the great Jetavana monastery and the Pubbārāma monastery.

After becoming the Buddha and the Teacher of devas and humans, having spent the first vassa at Isipatana Migadāya in Bārāṇasī, and having performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony at the end of the vassa, He went to the Uruvela forest. While residing there for three months and taming the three hermit brothers, He set out for Rājagaha on the full moon day of Phussa (January) surrounded by a thousand monks, and resided in Rājagaha for two months. At that time, five months had passed since the Blessed One left Bārāṇasī. The entire winter season had also passed. About seven or eight days had passed since the arrival of the Elder Kāludāyī. On the full moon day of Phagguna (March), that Elder Kāludāyī thought: "The winter is over, the spring (Vasanta) has arrived. It is now time for the Tathāgata to go to the city of Kapilavatthu." Having thought thus, he praised the virtues of the journey in about sixty verses to invite the Buddha to the city of His relatives. Upon hearing the Elder's words, the Blessed One, wishing to favor His relatives, departed from Rājagaha surrounded by ten thousand Arahants who were noble sons of the Aṅga and Magadha countries, and ten thousand Arahants who were noble sons of Kapilavatthu, totaling twenty thousand Arahants. Traveling at the rate of one yojana per day, after two months He reached Kapilavatthu, which was sixty yojanas away from Rājagaha...
5:
The Blessed One, accompanied by His retinue, arrived at Rājagaha on the full moon day of Phussa and stayed there for two months. At that time, five months had passed since He left Bārāṇasī. The entire winter season had also passed. Seven or eight days after the arrival of the Elder Kāludāyī, on the full moon day of Phagguna, the Elder Kāludāyī thought: "The winter has passed, the spring has arrived; now is the time for the Tathāgata to go to the city of Kapila." Having thought thus, for the sake of the journey to the ancestral city, he praised the beauty of the journey with about sixty verses. Then the Teacher, hearing his words and desiring to show favor to His relatives, departed from Rājagaha surrounded by ten thousand noble sons of Aṅga and Magadha and ten thousand noble sons of Kapilavatthu—altogether twenty thousand Arahants (khīṇāsavas). Traveling one yojana each day, He reached the city of Kapilavatthu, sixty yojanas from Rājagaha, in two months. There, He performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) to make His relatives pay homage. It was at that time that this Buddhavaṃsa discourse was preached.

Whose word is it? It is the word of the Perfectly Enlightened One alone, not shared by disciples or Paccekabuddhas.

By whom was it brought? It was brought down through the lineage of teachers (ācariya-paramparā). Indeed, this Buddhavaṃsa discourse was brought down until the time of the Third Council by such elders as the Elder Sāriputta, Bhaddaji, Tissa, Sigjava the son of the Brahmin Kosiya, Moggaliputta Tissa the son of the Brahmin lady Moggali, Sudatta, Dhammika, Dāsaka, Soṇaka, and Revata. Furthermore, it was brought down from that time onwards by their pupils and grand-pupils. Thus, it should be understood that it has been brought down through the lineage of teachers until the present day.

By this much of the sequence of words:
"By whom was this preached, and where? For whose benefit was it preached?
For what purpose, when, whose word is it, and by whom was it brought?"
—the meaning of this verse has been explained.
6:
## Introduction
## External Background
The commentary on the meaning of this Buddhavamsa Pali, which has been brought forward in this way, now begins. This commentary is well-expounded only when it is explained by showing these three backgrounds: the Distant Background (Dūrenidāna), the Intermediate Background (Avidūrenidāna), and the Proximate Background (Santikenidāna). For those who hear this teaching, it will be well-understood because it is known from its origin. Therefore, I shall comment by showing those backgrounds.

Among those three backgrounds, the division of these backgrounds should be known from the beginning. To briefly explain the meaning among them: The account starting from the aspiration made by the Great Being at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, up to his passing away from the existence as King Vessantara and being reborn in the Tusita heaven, is called the Distant Background. The account starting from his passing away from the Tusita heaven until his attainment of Omniscience at the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhi-maṇḍa) is called the Intermediate Background. The Proximate Background should be known as the various places where the Blessed One stayed during the interval from his attainment of Omniscience at the Great Seat of Enlightenment until his Parinibbāna bed, such as: "At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery," and "He was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels' Feeding Place," and "He was staying at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall." With this brief explanation, the commentary on the External Background by way of the three backgrounds—Distant, Intermediate, and Proximate—is completed.

## Internal Background
## 1. Commentary on the Jewel Walk Section
Now, however—
"Sahampatī Brahmā, the lord of the world, with palms joined, requested the Peerless Buddha:
'There are beings here with little dust in their eyes;
Out of compassion for these beings, please teach the Dhamma.'"

In this way, the commentary on the meaning of the Internal Background, which proceeds in this manner, begins.
7:
In this context, why is the background stated in this way: "Sahampatī Brahmā, the lord of the world, with palms joined, requested the Peerless Buddha," instead of stating it in the manner of the Suttas such as: "At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels' Feeding Place," or "At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Monastery. Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One, and having approached, he asked the Blessed One about the Buddhavamsa"? It is said: It is stated to show the request of the Brahma for the teaching of the Dhamma, which is the cause for the Blessed One's teaching of all the Dhamma.

"When did the Brahma urge and request this Conqueror (Jina) to teach the Dhamma? When, where, and by whom was this verse spoken?"

It is said: After the Blessed One had become a Buddha, in the eighth week, Sahampatī Brahmā urged and requested him to teach the Dhamma. Regarding that request, this is the sequential account: It is said that the Great Being, having fulfilled his aspiration, on the day of the Great Renunciation, saw the dancing women sleeping in repulsive postures, which became clearly visible. Having become deeply disenchanted, he called the minister Channa, who was covered with a piece of cloth, and said, "Bring the noble horse named Kanthaka, who can overcome the host of enemies." Having had Kanthaka brought, he mounted the noble horse with Channa as his companion. As the deity guarding the city gate opened it, he departed from the city. Within the remainder of that night, he crossed three kingdoms. The One of Unfailing Effort (Anomasatta) stood on the bank of the river named Anomā and said to Channa: "Channa, take these ornaments of mine, which are not shared with others, and the noble horse Kanthaka, and return to Kapilavatthu." Thus, he sent Channa back.

With a sword like a black snake or a blue lotus, he cut off his topknot of hair and threw it into the sky. Taking the bowl and robes offered by Ghaṭikāra Brahma, he ordained himself. Gradually wandering on alms tour, he crossed the Ganges river, which was free from attachment and had waves rising due to the force of the wind. He entered the city named Rājagaha, which was illuminated by the net of rays from various gems. In that city of Rājagaha, as if mocking those intoxicated with the pride of power, as if shaming those of agitated appearance, as if binding the hearts of the citizens to himself with the beauty of his youth, as if robbing the eyes of all people with the splendor of his form radiant with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, as if he were a mass of merit walking with a physical form, like a mountain, unattached in his gait, with calmed faculties and a peaceful heart, looking only a yoke's length ahead, he wandered for alms in the city of Rājagaha. Having received just enough alms for sustenance, he left the city and sat on the side of Mount Paṇḍava, which was endowed with shade and water, pure and very delightful, and there he consumed the mixed alms-food through the power of reflection. As he proceeded to Mount Paṇḍava, King Bimbisāra, the ruler of Magadha, went to the Great Being, asked about his name and lineage, and with a joyful heart, invited him with the kingdom, saying, "Please take half of my kingdom." When thus invited, [the Great Being replied], "Great King, enough; I have no need for a kingdom. I have renounced kingship for the sake of the welfare of the world of beings, and for the sake of the work of meditation (padhāna)..."
8:
With a peaceful mind, looking only a yoke's length ahead, he wandered for alms in the city of Rājagaha. Having received just enough food for sustenance, he departed from the city and sat in a secluded, most delightful, and clean spot endowed with shade and water at the side of Mount Paṇḍava. After consuming the mixed alms-food through the power of reflection, King Bimbisāra, the lord of the Magadha kingdom, who had followed him to Mount Paṇḍava, approached the Great Being and asked for his name and lineage. With a joyful heart, the King invited him with the offer of his kingdom, saying, "Please take a portion of my kingdom." The Bodhisatta replied, "Enough, Great King, I have no need for a kingdom. I have renounced the kingship and come forth with the intention of striving for the benefit of the world, to become a Buddha who has removed the veil of defilements in the world."

King Bimbisāra then requested, "When you become a Buddha, please visit my kingdom first of all." Having given his promise to the King, saying "So be it," he approached the ascetics Āḷāra and Udaka. Finding no essence in their teachings, he departed from there and practiced the difficult austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for six years in the Uruvelā forest. However, unable to attain the Deathless Nibbāna, he nourished his body by consuming solid food.

At that time, in the village of Senānigama in the Uruvelā forest, a young woman named Sujātā, the daughter of the Senānigama landowner, having reached the age of maturity, made a vow at a banyan tree: "If I go to a house of equal status and obtain a son in my first pregnancy, I shall make an offering." Her vow was fulfilled. On the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha), thinking, "Today I shall make the offering," she prepared an extremely sweet milk-rice early in the morning without any difficulty.

The Bodhisatta, having performed his bodily ablutions on that very day, went early in the morning and sat at the foot of that banyan tree, awaiting the time for almsround. Then, a maid named Puṇṇာ (Puṇṇā), Sujātā's nurse, went to clean the foot of the tree and saw the Bodhisatta sitting there, looking towards the eastern world-element. His body possessed a beauty like the peak of a noble golden mountain tinged by the glow of twilight, dispelling the mass of darkness, like the sun that makes the lotus groves bloom, like the sun emerging from thick clouds, or like a Sage-sun who had approached the noble tree. Seeing the entire tree turned to a golden hue by the rays emanating from his body, Puṇṇā thought, "Today our tree deity has descended from the tree and is sitting there, wishing to accept the offering with his own hands." She went quickly and informed Sujātā of this matter.
9:
Then Sujātā, filled with intense faith, adorned herself with all kinds of ornaments, filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand with the most delicious milk-rice, covered it with another golden bowl, and carrying it on her head, went towards the Nigrodha (banyan) tree. While going, she saw from afar the Bodhisatta sitting there, looking like a tree deity, turning the entire tree into a golden color with the radiance of his body, appearing like a great heap of merit. Filled with joy and happiness, Sujātā, perceiving him as the "tree deity," approached him with a bowed body from the moment she saw him. Taking the golden bowl down from her head, she placed it in the hands of the Great Being, the Bodhisatta. After paying homage with the five-point prostration, she made a wish, saying, "Just as my heart's desire has been fulfilled, may your desire also be fulfilled," and then she departed.

The Bodhisatta then took the golden bowl and went to the banks of the Nerañjarā River. Placing the golden bowl at the bank near the ford named Suppatiṭṭhita, he bathed and, after coming out of the water, divided the milk-rice into forty-nine morsels and consumed them. Then he made a resolution: "If I am to become a Buddha today, may this golden bowl float upstream," and he cast it into the water. The bowl floated upstream and entered the realm of the Naga King named Kāla, where it struck the golden bowls of the three previous Buddhas and came to rest beneath them.

The Great Being spent the day in that forest grove and, in the evening, accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a grass-cutter named Sotthiya, who recognized the Great Being's noble appearance. He then ascended the Bodhi-maṇḍa (Seat of Enlightenment) and stood on the southern side. That spot trembled like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. The Great Man thought, "This spot is unable to support my virtues," and went to the western side. That spot also trembled in the same way. Again, he went to the northern side, and it also trembled. Finally, he went to the eastern side. There, the area the size of a throne remained firm and motionless. The Great Man decided, "This is the place for the destruction of defilements." Holding the grass by the tips, he scattered them, and they became like a soft cushion of cotton. The Bodhisatta made a firm resolution with fourfold effort: "I shall not break this cross-legged posture until I have attained Enlightenment." He sat down facing the east, with his back to the trunk of the Bodhi tree.

At that very moment, Māra created a thousand arms and, riding the elephant named Girimekhala which was one hundred and fifty leagues in size, approached like a great enemy, overwhelming the area with a thick army of Māra like a great mountain. Before the sun set, the Great Man conquered and defeated that extremely noisy army of Māra. Receiving the worship of the young Bodhi shoots which were like red coral, he attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa) in the first watch of the night. In the middle watch, he purified the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa). In the final watch, he reflected upon the Law of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) and, at dawn, became a Buddha who realized the Four Noble Truths.

## The House
"Through many births in saṃsāra, I have wandered, seeking but not finding the builder of this house. To be born again and again is painful. O house-builder, you are seen now! You shall not build the house again. All your rafters are broken, and the ridge-pole is destroyed. My mind has reached the unconditioned (Nibbāna). The end of craving has been attained."
10:
## Māra’s Attack and the Attainment of Buddhahood

At that very moment, Māra, the vanquisher of the whole world, created a thousand arms and, mounting the noble elephant named Girimekhala, which was one hundred and fifty leagues high and resembled a peak of the Himālaya mountains, approached the Bodhisatta like a great enemy, surrounded by a massive army of Māra’s forces equipped with weapons such as bows, swords, axes, arrows, and spears, spanning nine leagues and overwhelming like a great mountain from all four directions. The Great Being (Mahāpurisa), while the sun was still visible, blew away and dispelled the noisy army of Māra. As if being joyfully worshipped by the sprouts of the Bodhi tree, which were as beautiful as red coral buds falling upon his robes that resembled newly blossomed jasmine flowers, he attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives (Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa) in the first watch. In the middle watch, he purified the divine eye (Dibbacakkhuñāṇa). In the last watch, he applied his knowledge to Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), and while contemplating the round of rebirth and its cessation, he became the Buddha at dawn and uttered this inspired solemn utterance (Udāna):

“Through many births in saṃsāra have I wandered, seeking the builder of the house, but finding him not. Painful is repeated birth. O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build the house again. All your rafters are broken, the ridge-pole is shattered. My mind has reached the unconditioned (Nibbāna); it has attained the destruction of cravings.”

After uttering this Udāna, he remained for seven days experiencing the bliss of liberation (Vimuttisukha). On the eighth day, he emerged from the meditative attainment (Samāpatti) and, knowing the doubts of the devas, he rose into the air and performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) to dispel their doubts. After dispelling the doubts of the devas, he stood to the northeast of the throne (Pallanka) and remained for seven days gazing with unblinking eyes at the throne and the Bodhi tree, the place where he had attained the fruit of the perfections (Pāramīs) fulfilled for four incalculables (Asaṅkheyyas) and a hundred thousand aeons (Kappas), saying, “Indeed, upon this throne, I have realized Omniscience.” That place became known as the Animisa-cetiya.

Then, he spent seven days walking back and forth on the Jeweled Walkway (Ratana-caṅkama) that stretched east to west between the throne and the place where he had stood. That place became known as the Ratana-caṅkama-cetiya. After that, in the western direction, the devas created a Jeweled House (Ratana-ghara). Sitting there in a cross-legged posture, he spent seven days contemplating the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, especially the Paṭṭhāna of Infinite Methods. That place became known as the Ratana-ghara-cetiya. Thus, having spent four weeks (Sattāha) near the Bodhi tree, in the fifth week, he proceeded from the foot of the Bodhi tree to the Ajapāla Banyan tree. At that Ajapāla Banyan tree, he also spent seven days contemplating the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation.

Then, he sat for another seven days at the Mucalinda Lake. As soon as the Blessed One sat down, a great unseasonal storm arose, filling the entire world-system. At that time, Mucalinda the Naga King thought, “This great storm has arisen just as the Blessed One entered my abode; it is fitting to provide a dwelling for the Teacher to reside in.” Although that Naga King was capable of creating a celestial mansion made of the seven kinds of jewels, he thought, “By creating such a mansion, there will not be great merit for me; I shall personally serve the Blessed One.” Thus, he created a very large body, coiled around the Blessed One seven times, and stood with his great hood spread over him. At that time, the Blessed One resided within the Naga’s coils as if he were in a Gandhakuṭi chamber, scented with various fragrances and having a ceiling of various fragrant flower garlands hanging above a new throne made of all kinds of jewels in a large space. Thus, after the Blessed One had spent those seven days at the Mucalinda Lake, he went to another...
11:
Thus, having spent four weeks (28 days) near the Bodhi tree, in the fifth week, he approached the Ajapāla Banyan tree from the foot of the Bodhi tree. At that Ajapāla Banyan tree, he also spent seven days contemplating the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation.

In the same manner, he sat for another seven days at the Mucalinda Lake. Just as the Blessed One was sitting there, a great unseasonal storm arose, filling the entire world-system. When that unseasonal storm occurred, Mucalinda the Naga King thought, “This great storm has arisen just as the Buddha entered my abode; it is fitting to provide a dwelling for the Buddha to reside in.” Although that Naga King was capable of creating a celestial mansion similar to one made of the seven kinds of jewels, he thought, “By creating it in this way, there will not be great merit for me; I shall only perform personal service to the Blessed One.” Thus, he created a very large body, coiled around the Buddha seven times, and stood with his great hood spread over him. At that time, the Blessed One resided within the coils in a large space as if he were in a Gandhakuṭi chamber, scented with various fragrances and having a ceiling of various fragrant flower garlands hanging from above, upon a new throne made of all kinds of jewels. Thus, after the Blessed One had spent those seven days at that place, he sat for another seven days at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. At the foot of the Rājāyatana tree, he also experienced the bliss of liberation. With this, the seven weeks (Sattāha) were completed. During this period, the Blessed One spent his time in the bliss of meditative absorption (Jhāna) and the bliss of the fruition (Phala).

After that, when the seven weeks had passed, the thought arose, “I shall wash my face.” Sakka, the king of devas, brought and offered the medicinal myrobalan (Harītakī) which cures diseases. Furthermore, Sakka offered the Nāgalatā tooth-stick and water for washing the face. Then, the Blessed One chewed the tooth-stick, washed his face with water from Lake Anotatta, and sat at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. At that time, he accepted and consumed the parched grain and honey balls offered by the merchants Tapussa and Bhallika in the precious stone bowl presented by the Four Great Kings (Lokapāla), and then returned to sit at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree. While he was sitting at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree, as he was contemplating the profundity of the Dhamma he had realized, a reflection arose in the Blessed One—as is the custom of all Buddhas—inclining him not to teach the Dhamma to others: “This Dhamma I have realized is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.”
12:
Then, Brahma Sahampati, having known the thought of the Blessed One with his own mind, uttered these words: "Alas, the world is perishing! Alas, the world is truly being destroyed!" Accompanied by a host of Brahmas from ten thousand world systems, and followed by Sakka, Suyama, Santusita, and Paranimmitavasavatti devas, he arrived and appeared before the Blessed One. That Brahma Sahampati, having created ground for his standing, placed his right knee on the ground, and raising his joined palms—shining with ten fingernails like a red lotus bud free from impurities born in water—to his head, he entreated: "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma; let the Sugata teach the Dhamma. There are beings with little dust in their eyes; they are perishing through not hearing the Dhamma. There will be those who understand the Dhamma."

"In the past, there appeared in Magadha an impure Dhamma, devised by teachers together with defilements. Open the door to the Deathless; let them hear the Dhamma, the Noble Four Truths, realized by the Stainless One."

"Just as a man with sight standing on a rocky mountain peak might look out upon the people all around, even so, O Wise One, you who are endowed with the Eye of Omniscience and can see all around, ascend the palace of wisdom made of the supramundane Dhamma, which is like that mountain. Being yourself free from sorrow, look upon the people who are immersed in sorrow and overcome by birth and old age."

"Arise, O Hero, victor in battle, caravan leader who saves from the difficult journey, you who are free from the debt of defilements, wander through the world of beings. Let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma; there will be those who understand the Dhamma."

"Did you not [vow]: 'Having known the Four Truths myself, I will make others know them; having crossed the four floods myself, I will make others cross; having been liberated from defilements myself, I will liberate others'?"

"What is the use of my realizing the fruit of Arahantship and Nibbāna in an obscure form at the feet of this Buddha? Only after reaching Omniscience shall I save the world together with the devas," so...
13:
"What is the use of my realizing the fruit of Arahantship and Nibbāna in an obscure form at the feet of this Buddha? Only after reaching Omniscience shall I save the world together with the devas." Having made this aspiration and fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), he attained the state of Omniscience. Furthermore, he entreated the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma in many ways, such as: "If you do not teach the Dhamma, who else will teach it? For the world of beings, where else is there a refuge, a protection, a shelter, and a final resort?" Therefore, it is said: "In the eighth week after becoming a Buddha, the Teacher was entreated by the Brahma to teach the Dhamma."

Now, the opportunity has arrived to provide the answers to these questions: "When, where, and by whom was this verse uttered?" Among those questions, "When was it uttered?" means it was uttered at the time of the First Great Council. The First Great Council should be understood according to the method stated in the Saṅgītikhandhaka. As for "Where and by whom was it uttered?", it should be known that after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, at the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave on the side of Mount Vebhāra in the city of Rājagaha, in the pavilion built for the purpose of the Dhamma Council by King Ajātasattu of Magadha—who had conquered all enemies—a pavilion resembling the full moon and adorned with choice, essential timber, the Venerable Ānanda Thera, having taken the seat of Dhamma (dhammāsana), uttered this verse beginning with "Brahmā ca lokādhipatī." This is the connection (sambandha) of the verse in this context.

By this sequence of words: "When was the Victorious Buddha urged and entreated by the Brahma to teach the Dhamma? When, where, and by whom was this verse uttered?"—this verse also has its meaning already stated. Thus, I shall now provide the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) on the obscure terms of that verse uttered in this connection.

In that verse, "Brahmā" is so called because he is increased (brūhita) by various special qualities. This word "Brahma" is seen in the senses of Mahābrahmā, a Brahmin, the Tathāgata, parents, the highest, and so on. Indeed, in such passages as "Dvisahasso Brahmā," Mahābrahmā is intended. In this passage, "The Buddha, the dispeller of darkness... has been attended by me," a Brahmin is intended by "Brahmā." (Meaning of the verse: "O Brahma [Bāvarī Brahmin], I have attended that Blessed One who is truly named Buddha, who dispels the mass of darkness, who has the eye that sees all around, who has reached the end of the world, who has transcended all existence, who is free from cankers, and who has abandoned all suffering.") In the passage, "Monks, 'Brahma' is a name for the Tathāgata," the Buddha is intended by "Brahmā." In the passage, "Parents are said to be the first teachers, the Brahmas," parents are intended by "Brahmā." In the passage, "He sets in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma (Brahmacakka)," the highest is intended by "Brahmā." Alternatively, in this word "Brahmā," having developed the first jhāna which has great power...
14: "The Buddha, the dispeller of darkness, the one with all-seeing eyes, the one who has reached the end of the world, who has transcended all existence, who is free from taints, who has abandoned all suffering, and who is truly named 'Buddha'—I have attended upon him." (This is found in the Sutta Nipāta). In this Pali passage, the word 'Brahmā' refers to the Brahmin named Bāvarī. In the passage, "Monks, 'Brahmā' is a designation for the Tathāgata," it refers to the Tathāgata (the Buddha). In the passage, "Parents are called the first teachers, the 'Brahmās'," it refers to parents. In the passage, "He turns the supreme Wheel of Dhamma," it refers to the most excellent. However, in this context, it refers to Mahābrahmā, who, having developed the sublime first jhāna, was reborn in the realm of the first jhāna with a lifespan of an aeon. The word 'ca' (and) has the sense of inclusion, meaning Brahmā and other Brahmas from the ten thousand world systems, or it is merely a verse filler. Regarding the term 'Lokādhipati' (Lord of the World), there are three types of worlds: the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka), the world of beings (sattaloka), and the world of space (okāsaloka). Here, the world of beings is intended. He is called 'Lokādhipati' because he is the lord or ruler of that world of beings. Just like 'Devādhipati' (Lord of Devas) or 'Narādhipati' (Lord of Men), one who rules even a part of the world is called 'Lokādhipati'. Regarding 'Sahampati', it is heard that this Brahma was formerly a senior monk named Sahaka during the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa. Having attained the first jhāna and not having lost it, at the end of his life, he was reborn as Mahābrahmā in the realm of the first jhāna with a lifespan of an aeon. In that realm, he is known as 'Sahampati Brahmā'. Instead of saying 'Sahakapati', they say 'Sahampati' by adding an anusvāra through traditional usage (ruḷhī). 'Katañjalī' means one who has performed the añjali, meaning placing the palms together at the head. 'Anadhivara' means one who has no one superior or more excellent than himself (the Peerless One). It refers to that Peerless Buddha whom he 'ayācatha' (entreated or requested). Now, to show the purpose for which that Brahma entreated the Blessed One, the words beginning with 'Santīdha sattā' were spoken. Therein, 'santi' means they exist or are found, meaning there are beings who come into the range of the Buddha-eye. The indeclinable 'idha' (here) is used to indicate a location. In some places, this word 'idha' is spoken in reference to the Dispensation (Sāsana). As evidence: "Monks, only in this Dispensation is there the first recluse (Sotāpanna), only here is the second recluse (Sakadāgāmī), only here is the third recluse (Anāgāmī), only here is the fourth recluse (Arahant). Other doctrines are empty of recluses..."
15: The word 'idha' is an indeclinable used to indicate a location. In some places, this indeclinable is used in reference to the Dispensation (Sāsana). As the Buddha said: "Monks, only in this Dispensation is there the first recluse (Sotāpanna), the second recluse (Sakadāgāmī), the third recluse (Anāgāmī), and the fourth recluse (Arahant). Other doctrines are empty of recluses." In some places, it refers to a physical location. For example: "Venerable Sir, staying in this very place, I who have become a deva have regained my life; please know this." In some places, it is used merely as a verse filler (without specific meaning). For example: "Monks, here I have finished my meal and am satisfied." In some places, it is used in reference to the world. For example: "In this world, the Tathāgata arises for the welfare and happiness of many." In this context as well, it should be understood that it is spoken in reference to the world. Therefore, it means 'in this world of beings'. Beings are called 'satta' because they are attached (satta), intensely attached (visatta), clung (āsatta), or stuck (lagga) to the five aggregates such as form (rūpa) through desire and lust. Living beings are called 'satta'. However, by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī), this term is also applied to those who are free from lust. 'Apparajakkhajātika' refers to those beings because the dust of lust, hatred, and delusion in their eye of wisdom is little or slight. Alternatively, those who have little dust such as lust are 'apparajakkha'; those of such a nature are 'apparajakkhajātika'—this is how the meaning should be understood. For those beings who are 'apparajakkhajātika', the meaning should be understood by changing the inflection of the word 'sattānaṃ' and connecting it with 'desehi dhammaṃ' (Teach the Dhamma). 'Desehi' is a word of entreaty, meaning 'please preach' or 'please point out'. Regarding 'Dhamma' in this context, the word 'Dhamma' is found with various meanings such as scriptural learning (pariyatti), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), nature (pakati), essence (sabhāva), emptiness (suññatā), merit (puñña), offense (āpatti), the knowable (ñeyya), and the Four Noble Truths. For instance, it is seen in the sense of scriptural learning in passages such as: "Here, a monk learns the Dhamma: Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa... Vedalla." It is seen in the sense of concentration in passages such as: "Those Blessed Ones were of such a Dhamma (concentration)." In the verse: "O King of Monkeys, he who possesses these four qualities (dhamma) as you do—truth, wisdom (dhamma), fortitude (dhiti), and generosity (cāga)—surmounts the enemy he sees," it is seen in the sense of wisdom.
16:
In verses such as, “O Lord of Monkeys, for whomsoever these four qualities (dhamma) exist—truthfulness (sacca), wisdom (paññā), courage (dhiti), and generosity (cāga)—as they do in you, he transcends his enemies,” the word *dhamma* refers to wisdom (*paññā*). In passages such as, “Subject to birth, subject to aging, and also subject to death,” it refers to nature (*pakati*). In passages such as, “Wholesome states (dhammā), unwholesome states, indeterminate states,” it refers to ultimate reality (*sabhāva*). In passages such as, “At that time, there are states (dhammā), there are aggregates (khandhā),” it refers to the nature of emptiness (*suññatā*). In passages such as, “The Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness,” it refers to merit (*puñña*). In passages such as, “There are two indefinite offenses (dhammā),” it refers to an offense (*āpatti*). In passages such as, “All knowable things (dhammā) in every aspect come into the range of the knowledge of the Blessed Buddha,” it refers to knowable objects (*ñeyya*). In passages such as, “One who has seen the Dhamma, reached the Dhamma, known the Dhamma,” it refers to the Four Noble Truths. Here also, the word *dhamma* should be understood as the Four Noble Truths.

*Anukampā* means to show compassion and kindness. By the word *imaṃ* (this), the Buddha refers to the assembly of beings. *Pajā* (progeny/beings) is so called because they are born (*pajātattā*); the meaning is, “Please liberate this assembly of beings from the suffering of saṃsāra.” Some teachers, however, recite:

“The Blessed One is the Lord of the World, the Supreme among Men,
Requested by the hosts of Brahmas with joined palms.”

By this much, the meaning of this verse is entirely complete.

Then, the Blessed One, having heard the words of request from Sahampati Brahma—the One whose power of compassion had arisen over an immeasurable time, the One of Ten Powers, the One whose wisdom is skillful in acting for the welfare of others—Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) arose within Him toward all beings, merely by granting the opportunity (to teach). The Elders who performed the Recitation (Saṅgīti), wishing to show the arising of the Buddha’s compassion, placed this verse at the time of the Council:

“To the One endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Such One (Tādi),
To the Bearer of Radiance, the One wearing His final body,
To the Tathāgata, the Peerless Person,
Compassion arose toward all beings.”

In that verse, regarding the term *sampannavijjācaraṇassa*, the word *sampanna* (endowed/perfected) is of three kinds: by way of being complete (*paripuṇṇa*), being possessed of (*samaṅgī*), and being sweet/rich (*madhura*). Among those three—
17:
“O Kosiya, the shali rice field is perfected (*sampannaṃ*). The parrots eat that shali rice. I inform you, O Brahmin; I am not able to restrain them.” The meaning in this verse is “perfected in completeness” (*paripuṇṇa-sampanna*).

“He is endowed (*upeto*), fully endowed (*samupeto*), possessed of (*upagato*), fully possessed of (*samupagato*), perfected (*sampanno*), and possessed of (*samannāgato*) this Pātimokkha restraint virtue.” This passage is called “perfected by possession” (*samaṅgī-sampanna*).

“Venerable Sir, the lower surface of this great earth is rich (*sampannaṃ*); just as pure honey from small bees is delicious, so is its taste.” This passage is called “perfected in sweetness” (*madhura-sampanna*). In this context of *sampannavijjācaraṇassa*, both the meanings of “perfected in completeness” and “perfected by possession” are appropriate.

*Vijjā* (knowledge) is so called because it pierces through opposing states, because it makes things known, and because it is that which should be attained. Those knowledges are the three knowledges (*tevijjā*) and also the eight knowledges (*aṭṭhavijjā*). The three knowledges should be understood as they appear in the Bhayabherava Sutta, and the eight knowledges as in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. In that Ambaṭṭha Sutta, the eight knowledges are stated by including insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and the mind-made power (*manomayiddhi*) along with the six higher powers (*abhiññā*).

*Caraṇa* (conduct) should be understood as these fifteen states: restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*), guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, faith, shame, fear of wrongdoing, great learning, energy, mindfulness, being endowed with wisdom, and the four fine-material jhānas. These fifteen states are called *caraṇa* because by means of them, the noble disciple walks (*carati*) or goes to the deathless direction (Nibbāna). As it is said: “Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is virtuous.” Everything should be understood according to the method stated in the Majjhima-paṇṇāsa.

Knowledge and conduct are *vijjācaraṇa*. He whose knowledge and conduct are complete (*paripuṇṇa*) is *sampannavijjācaraṇa*. Alternatively, He who is endowed with or possessed of knowledge and conduct is *sampannavijjācaraṇa*. In both ways, the meaning is appropriate.

*Tādino* (The Such One) means *Tādi* because He possesses the characteristics of *Tādi* as mentioned in the Mahāniddesa, such as “He is such (*tādi*) in the face of the desirable, and such in the face of the undesirable.” The meaning is: He who is unchanging amidst the desirable and undesirable.

*Jutindharassa* means the radiant one; it means the bearer of the mass of radiance of the body, which is more glorious than the sun that has risen over Mount Yugandhara during the autumn season (*sarada*). Or, it is also appropriate to say, “The bearer of the light of wisdom.” For this was said by the Blessed One in the Saṃyutta Nikāya:

“There are four lights in the world,
A fifth light is not found here.
The sun shines by day,
The moon glows by night.
Furthermore, fire shines here and there,
Both by day and by night.
But the Buddha is the best of those that shine,
This light is supreme and peerless.”
18:
There are four lights in the world; a fifth is not found here. The sun shines by day, the moon glows by night. Furthermore, fire blazes here and there both by day and by night. The Fully Enlightened One is the best of those who shine; this radiance of the Buddha is supreme and unsurpassed. (Saṃ. Ni. 1.26, 85). Therefore, in both ways, it means the Blessed One who bears the excellent radiance of both the physical body and wisdom (Jutindhara). Antimadehadhārī means one who bears the very last body of all existences, for whom there is no further rebirth.

In the term 'Tathāgata', the Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata' for eight reasons. What are the eight? He is Tathāgata because he has come in that way (Tathā āgato); he is Tathāgata because he has gone in that way (Tathā gato); he is Tathāgata because he has arrived at the true characteristics (Tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato); he is Tathāgata because he has fully awakened to the true Dhamma as it really is (Tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho); he is Tathāgata because of seeing truly (Tathadassitāya); he is Tathāgata because of speaking truly (Tathavāditāya); he is Tathāgata because of acting accordingly (Tathākāritāya); and he is Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming all (Abhibhavanaṭṭhena).

How is the Blessed One 'Tathāgata' because he has come in that way (Tathā āgato)? Just as the previous Fully Enlightened Ones such as Vipassī and others came—having fulfilled the ten perfections (Pāramīs), the ten higher perfections (Upapāramīs), and the ten ultimate perfections (Paramatthapāramīs), thus completing the thirty perfections through the same aspiration and exertion, and having made the five great sacrifices (Maha-pariccāga) consisting of the sacrifice of limbs, life, wealth, kingdom, and children and wife—so too our Blessed One has come. Thus, he is called 'Tathāgata'. As it is said:

'Just as the Sages such as Vipassī and others came to this world to attain Omniscience, so too has this Sakyan Sage come; therefore, the One with Five Eyes is called Tathāgata.'

How is he 'Tathāgata' because he has gone in that way (Tathā gato)? Just as the previous Buddhas such as Vipassī and others, immediately after being born, stood on the earth with level feet and went seven steps facing the north, so too our Blessed One went. Thus, he is called 'Tathāgata'. As it is said:
19:
'Just as a bull, immediately after birth, touches the earth with level feet, so the Bodhisatta Gotama, immediately after birth, stepped upon the earth with level feet and walked seven steps. The Devas and Brahmas followed, holding the white umbrella.

Having gone seven steps, Gotama looked equally at all directions. He uttered a voice endowed with eight qualities, like a lion standing on a mountain peak.'

How is he 'Tathāgata' because he has arrived at the true characteristics (Tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato)? He has arrived at the specific characteristics and general characteristics of all mental and material phenomena truly and unerringly through his knowledge; he has attained them without fail and understood them in order. Therefore, he is called 'Tathāgata'.

'Because he has arrived truly at the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, the Teacher is called Tathāgata.'

How is he 'Tathāgata' because he has fully awakened to the true Dhamma as it really is (Tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho)? True Dhamma refers to the Four Noble Truths. As the Blessed One taught in detail: 'Monks, these four things are true, unerring, and not otherwise. What four? "This is suffering (Dukkha)", monks, this is true, this is unerring, this is not otherwise.' Because he has fully awakened to those truths as taught, he is called 'Tathāgata'. In this context, the word 'gata' means 'fully awakened' (abhisambuddha).

'The Leader fully awakened to the truths named "Tatha" (True); therefore, because of his awakening to the true truths, he is called Tathāgata.'

How is he 'Tathāgata' because of seeing truly (Tathadassitāya)? The Tathāgata knows and sees in every way the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects that come into range at the six doors of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind of immeasurable beings in immeasurable world systems. Thus, he is Tathāgata because of seeing truly. Alternatively, whatever nature is true in the world, he shows that nature to the people of the world exactly as it is true. For that reason also, the Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata'. In this context, the formation of the term 'Tathāgata' should be understood in the sense of 'seeing truly'.
20:
The Buddha knows the Dhamma in that true manner; he contemplates them repeatedly as impermanent and so forth. Because he is accustomed to seeing according to the truth, that Sammāsambuddha is called 'Tathāgata'.

How is he a 'Tathāgata' because of speaking the truth (tathavāditā)? From the time the Buddha attained enlightenment until he entered Parinibbāna, during the period of forty-five years, whatever Dhamma he preached or spoke that is comprised within the nine-fold limbs of the scriptures such as Sutta, all that speech is just as if weighed with a single scale; it is only true and unerring. Therefore, it was said:

'Cunda, from the night the Tathāgata attained the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment until the night he passed away into the Nibbāna element without remainder, whatever he speaks, utters, or points out in this interval, all that is just so and not otherwise. Therefore, he is called "Tathāgata".'

In this context, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'gada' (speech). Thus, he is a Tathāgata because he speaks the truth. Uttering (āgadana) is called 'āgada', which means speech (vacana). Because that Buddha has a true and non-perverted utterance, he is called 'Tathāgata'. It is said by changing the letter 'da' to 'ta'.

'Because the Victorious One (Jina) speaks the truth,
Because he reveals the true Dhamma,
And because he has such true utterance,
The Buddha is therefore called Tathāgata.'

How is he a 'Tathāgata' because of acting according to his speech (tathākāritā)? Whatever words the Buddha speaks, he acts accordingly with his body. His body conforms to his speech, and his speech conforms to his body. Therefore, it was said:

'Monks, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks... Therefore, he is called "Tathāgata".'

As the speech has gone, so the body has gone; as the body has gone, so the speech has gone. Thus, he is a Tathāgata because of acting according to his speech.

'As his speech has gone, 
So his body has gone accordingly.
Because of speaking the truth in this way,
The Sammāsambuddha, the Teacher, is therefore called Tathāgata.'

How is he a 'Tathāgata' in the sense of overcoming (abhibhavanaṭṭhena)? Defining the limit from the highest point of existence (Bhavagga) above to Avīci below, and across the infinite world systems, he overcomes all beings through virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana).
21:
For that Buddha, there is no comparison or measure. Indeed, he is incomparable, immeasurable, and unsurpassed. Therefore, the Buddha said: 

"Monks, in the world with its devas... the Tathāgata is the conqueror, the unvanquished, the all-seeing, the wielder of power. Therefore, he is called 'Tathāgata'."

The derivation of the word 'Tathāgata' should be understood in this way: he is called 'Agada' because he is like a medicine (agada) that cures diseases. What is that? It is the elegance of his teaching (desanāvilāsa) and his accumulation of merit (puññussaya). For by these, just as a physician of great power overcomes snakes with divine medicine, the Buddha overcomes all those of opposing views and the world with its devas. Because he can thus overcome the entire world, his non-perverted elegance of teaching and accumulation of merit are his medicine (agada). Because he possesses that 'agada', the letter 'da' is changed to 'ta', and he should be known as 'Tathāgata'. Thus, he is a Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming.

"For that Teacher who possesses the true and non-perverted medicine-like Dhamma,
Because he is the wielder of power, that Teacher is called Tathāgata."

'Appaṭipuggala' means one who is without a rival. Because there is no other person capable of making the claim, "I am the Buddha," he is 'Appaṭipuggala'. For that Buddha who is the peerless person. 'Uppajjī' means has arisen or has become manifest. 'Kāruññatā' is the state of compassion (karuṇā). 'Sabba-satte' is a term encompassing all beings without exception, meaning in the entire assembly of beings. By this much, the meaning of this verse has been stated.

Then the Buddha, having been requested by Brahma Sahampati to teach the Dhamma, and having aroused compassion for beings, wishing to teach the Dhamma, addressed the Great Brahma with a verse:

"Brahma, I have opened the doors to the Deathless (the Noble Path) for them.
Let those who have ears release their faith.
Thinking that it would only be wearisome to preach the sublime Dhamma to humans,
I did not speak this well-mastered Dhamma."
22:
Then, Sahampati Brahma, knowing that "I have received the opportunity from the Blessed One for the teaching of the Dhamma," placed his joined palms, shining with the meeting of his ten fingernails, upon his head, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated Him, and departed surrounded by the host of Brahmas.

Then the Blessed One, having given His promise to Sahampati Brahma, thought: "To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?" and the thought arose: "The ascetic Āḷāra is wise; he will quickly understand this Dhamma." Reflecting further, He realized that Āḷāra had passed away seven days ago. He also realized that the ascetic Uddaka had passed away at midnight the previous night. Again, He reflected: "Where are the group of five bhikkhus living now?" and realized: "They are living in the Deer Park at Isipatana near the city of Bārāṇasī." When the night of the full moon of Āsāḷha had turned to dawn, He took His bowl and robes early in the morning and set out on the journey of eighteen yojanas. On the way, He saw an Ajivaka named Upaka and revealed His Buddhahood to him. On that very day, in the evening, He arrived at Isipatana. There, He made His Buddhahood known to the group of five bhikkhus, took His place on the noble Buddha-seat that had been prepared, called the group of five bhikkhus, and preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta.

Among those five, the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, sending forth his wisdom according to the sequence of the teaching, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) along with eighteen crores of Brahmas at the conclusion of the Sutta. The Blessed One entered the rains-retreat (vassa) right there, and on the following day, He established the Elder Vappa in the fruit of Stream-entry. In this manner, He established all those Elders in the fruit of Stream-entry. Then, on the fifth day of the waning fortnight, He assembled all five Elders and preached the Anattalakkhana Sutta. At the conclusion of the teaching, all five Elders were established in Arahantship.

Then the Blessed One, seeing the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of a young man of good family named Yasa at that very place, and seeing him leaving home, called out: "Come, Yasa!" He established him in the fruit of Stream-entry that very night, and on the following day, established him in Arahantship. He also ordained fifty-four other friends of Yasa with the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination and established them in Arahantship. Thus, when sixty-one Arahants had appeared in the world, the Blessed One, having completed the rains-retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, addressed the bhikkhus and said:

"O bhikkhus, performing the welfare of others and your own welfare, wander through this earth preaching the word of Dhamma to humanity.

Constantly revealing my Sublime Dhamma to the people of the world, dwell in secluded mountains and in forests."
23:
"O bhikkhus, performing the welfare of others and your own welfare on this earth, practice the Dhamma while preaching the word of Dhamma to humanity.

Constantly revealing my Sublime Dhamma to the people of the world, dwell in secluded mountains and in forests.

O bhikkhus, for the sake of the peace and happiness (Nibbāna) of beings, you who are of good conduct, perform the duty of a messenger of Dhamma and my word, and make the Dhamma known.

You who are free from taints (anāsava), close all the doors to the woeful states; open the door to the peerless path of heaven and Nibbāna.

Being the abode of virtues such as great compassion, increase the wisdom and faith of the people of the world in every way through the preaching of Dhamma and the practice of virtue.

To those people who constantly assist you with material offerings (āmisa-dāna), make a return of gratitude through the gift of Dhamma (dhamma-dāna).

Wearing the robes which are like the banner of the sages, preach the Sublime Dhamma and strive well. You who have completed the task of the Path, practice for the welfare of others."

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One sent those bhikkhus to various directions. While He Himself was traveling to the Uruvela forest, He disciplined the thirty princes of the Bhaddavaggiya group in the Kappāsika woodland on the way. Among those princes, the youngest became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and the eldest became a Non-returner (Anāgāmī); not a single one remained an Arahant or an ordinary worldling (puthujjana). Having ordained all of them with the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination and sent them to various directions, He Himself went to the Uruvela forest. There, He performed three thousand five hundred miracles and disciplined the three ascetic brothers, including Uruvela Kassapa, along with their thousand ascetic followers. Having ordained them as 'Ehi Bhikkhus' and having them stay at Gayāsīsa, He established them in Arahantship through the preaching of the Ādittapariyāya Sutta.

Surrounded by those thousand Arahants, the Blessed One, thinking "I shall fulfill the promise given to King Bimbisāra," went to the palm grove garden named Laṭṭhivana near the city of Rājagaha. Then the park keeper informed the King. When the King heard that "The Teacher has arrived," he approached the Blessed One, surrounded by one hundred and twenty thousand brahmins and householders. The Blessed One appeared like the sun emerging from behind a mass of clouds, or like the sun of the noble monks beautifying the forest. The King bowed his head, which shone with the radiance of the gems in his crown, at the lotus-like soft feet of the Buddha, which were adorned with the mark of the wheel and free from defilement, and sat down in a suitable place with his retinue. At that time, a thought arose among those brahmins and householders: "How is it? Does the Great Monk practice the holy life under Uruvela Kassapa?"
24: Approaching the Blessed One, who was like the sun that had reached the interior of the forest, and like the sun that is the Noble Sage, they bowed their heads—shining with the brilliance of the gems in their crest-crowns—at the feet of the Ten-Powered One, which were adorned with the wheel-treasure and soft like a pure lotus grown in water, and sat down at one side with their retinue. Then, a thought occurred to those brahmins and householders: “Does the Great Ascetic (the Blessed One) practice the holy life under Uruvela Kassapa, or does Uruvela Kassapa practice the holy life under the Great Ascetic?” Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in their minds, addressed the Elder in verse: “Kassapa, who dwells in the Uruvela forest and admonishes lean ascetics, what benefit have you seen that you have abandoned the fire-sacrifice? I ask you this matter, Kassapa: why have you abandoned your fire-sacrifice?” The Elder, knowing the Blessed One's intention, replied: “Sacrifices are said to bring about the attainment of forms, sounds, tastes, and women for sensual enjoyment. Knowing these sensual pleasures to be merely defilements among the acquisitions (upadhi) of the aggregates, I no longer delight in great sacrifices or daily small offerings.” Having spoken this verse, to manifest his status as a disciple, he bowed his head at the feet of the Buddha and said, “Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am the disciple.” Then, rising into the air to the height of one palm tree, two palm trees... up to seven palm trees, he performed a miracle seven times, descended from the sky, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat at one side. Then the great multitude, seeing that miracle, said, “How wonderful are the Buddhas! How great is their power! Even Uruvela Kassapa, who held such firm wrong views and thought of himself as an Arahant, has had the net of his wrong views destroyed and been tamed by the Tathāgata,” and they spoke of the virtues of the Ten-Powered One. Hearing this, the Teacher said, “I have not tamed this Uruvela Kassapa only now; in the past too, he was tamed by me.” Then the great multitude rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and with hands joined in reverence above their heads, said, “Venerable Sir, now we have seen this Uruvela Kassapa being tamed. How did you tame him in the past?” Being thus requested by the multitude, the Blessed One related the Mahā-Nārada-Kassapa Jātaka, which was hidden by another birth, and revealed the Four Noble Truths. Upon hearing that Dhamma, King Bimbisāra, together with 110,000 brahmins and householders, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. 10,000 brahmins and householders attained the status of lay followers. King Bimbisāra, having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, invited the Blessed One along with the Saṅgha of monks for the next day, circumambulated him, paid homage, and departed. On the following day, the Blessed One, surrounded by a thousand monks, entered the city of Rājagaha like the King of Devas surrounded by a host of deities, or like Mahābrahmā surrounded by a host of Brahmas. King Bimbisāra, having offered alms-food to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, at the conclusion of the meal, addressed the Blessed One with these words:
25:
“We have now seen with our own eyes that this Uruvela Kassapa has been tamed; but how, Venerable Sir, did the Blessed One tame him in the past?” (the people asked). Then the Blessed One, being requested by the multitude, related the Mahā-Nārada-Kassapa Jātaka, which was hidden by another birth, and clearly revealed the Four Noble Truths.

Upon hearing that Dhamma discourse of the Blessed One, King Bimbisāra, together with 110,000 brahmins and householders, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry; 10,000 brahmins and householders realized the status of lay followers. The King, having taken refuge, invited the Blessed One along with the Saṅgha of monks for the next day, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, paid homage, and departed.

On the following day, the Blessed One, surrounded by a thousand monks, entered the city of Rājagaha like the thousand-eyed King of Devas surrounded by a host of deities, or like Mahābrahmā surrounded by a host of Brahmas. The King, having offered a gift to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, at the conclusion of the meal, addressed the Blessed One as follows: “Venerable Sir, I cannot live apart from the Triple Gem; whether at the proper time or not, I shall come to the presence of the Blessed One. The palm grove garden called Laṭṭhivana is very far; but this garden of ours called Veluvana is, for those desiring seclusion, neither too far from the city nor too near, and is easy of access. It is free from the crowding of people, possessing the bliss of seclusion, endowed with shade and water, and adorned with cool stone slabs. It has a most delightful ground and is continuously filled with fragrant flowering trees. It is adorned with delightful mansions, palatial houses, monasteries, and pavilions. Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept this garden out of compassion for me.” Having said this, he took a golden pitcher, which had the appearance of fresh embers, containing water scented with fragrant flowers and having the color of gems, and while dedicating the Veluvana Monastery, he poured the water of donation onto the hand of the Blessed One.

When that monastery was accepted, this great earth quaked as if dancing, moved by the power of joy, thinking, “The roots of the Buddha’s Dispensation have now descended.” In Jambudīpa, except for the Veluvana Mahāvihāra, there has never been an instance where the earth quaked upon the acceptance of another dwelling. Thereafter, the Blessed One, having accepted the Veluvana Monastery, performed the appreciation (anumodanā) for the King’s gift of the monastery:

“Who indeed is capable of describing the benefits of giving a dwelling, except for the Buddhas, the Lords of the World, even if one were endowed with a hundred billion mouths?

He who gives a monastery to the Saṅgha is said to give life, beauty, happiness, strength, and quick-wittedness—blessings that are noble and praised by the virtuous.” Thus it was spoken in detail.
26:
Whoever offers a monastery to the Saṅgha is said to give long life, beauty, happiness, strength, and analytical insight, which are noble and praised by the virtuous.

The virtuous declare that one who offers a dwelling that wards off cold and other dangers to life is a giver of life, because such a dwelling can protect the life of the donor.

Strength, beauty, and analytical insight can arise in one who resides in a dwelling during seasons of extreme heat or cold; therefore, the donor of a monastery is indeed a giver of strength, beauty, and analytical insight.

In this world, a donor who constantly offers a monastery provides happiness, as it wards off cold, heat, snakes, scorpions, and lice, as well as the various sufferings arising from wind and sun.

Because the donor of a monastery wards off the suffering caused by cold, heat, wind, sun, gadflies, mosquitoes, rain, and snakes, scorpions, lice, wild beasts, and deer, that donor experiences happiness in the afterlife.

With a clear mind and joy, whoever offers a delightful monastery—the cause of prosperity in life—to those endowed with virtues such as morality, is called a giver of everything.

Having discarded the stain of stinginess along with greed, one who gives a dwelling to those who are the abode of all virtues will be born in heaven, free from sorrow, as if being transported and placed there by others.
27:
“A person should build noble, excellent, and beautiful monasteries like the color of gold, and cause the monks to reside there. With a clear mind, one should always respectfully offer them food, drinks, and robes.

Great King, therefore, having repeatedly enjoyed delightful pleasures in the realms of existence, may you attain the peaceful and sorrowless bliss of Nibbāna through the merit of offering a monastery,” the Buddha said.

Thus, the Buddha, the King of Monks, having given the blessing for the monastery donation to King Bimbisāra, rose from his seat. Surrounded by the Saṅgha, he entered the Veḷuvana Mahāvihāra with incomparable Buddha-grace and infinite glory, making the city, forests, and mansions shine like ornaments drenched in liquid gold with the radiance of his exceptionally beautiful body.

“The wise Tathāgata, looking out for the welfare and happiness of those to be tamed, resided in that delightful Veḷuvana monastery, which is not a place of play, in various postures.”

While the Blessed One was residing there, King Suddhodana heard: “My son, after practicing austerities for six years and attaining supreme enlightenment, has set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, reached Rājagaha, and is staying at the Veḷuvana Mahāvihāra.” Upon hearing this, he called a high minister and said: “Come, man, go to Rājagaha with a thousand followers and say in my name, ‘Your father, King Suddhodana, wishes to see you,’ and bring my son back.” The minister agreed, saying, “Very well, your majesty,” and traveled the sixty-yojana journey with a thousand followers, entering the monastery while the Buddha was preaching. He thought, “Let the King’s message wait for a moment,” and stood at the edge of the assembly. Upon hearing the Buddha’s sermon, he attained Arahantship right where he stood along with the thousand men and requested ordination. The Blessed One stretched out his hand and said, “Come, monks (Ehi Bhikkhu).” Instantly, they were endowed with miraculous bowls and robes, appearing like elders of sixty years’ standing with graceful appearance, and surrounded the Blessed One.

The King, thinking “The one who went has not returned, nor is there any news,” sent ministers nine times in the same manner. Among those nine thousand men, not a single one reported back or sent news to the King; all attained Arahantship and became monks. Then the King, wondering “Who will obey my word?”, looked at his officials and saw the minister Kāḷudāyī. The minister Kāḷudāyī was a highly trusted inner secretary who accomplished all the King’s affairs. He was born on the same day as the Bodhisatta and was a childhood playmate. Then King Suddhodana said to the minister Kāḷudāyī: “Friend Udāyī, I have sent nine thousand men because I wish to see my son. Not even one man has returned, not even a word of news...”
28:
Thinking, "Those who go do not return, and no news is heard," the King sent ministers nine times in that same manner. Among those nine thousand men, not even one reported back to the King, nor did they send any news. All of them, having attained Arahantship, simply entered the monkhood.

Then the King thought, "Who will obey my word?" Looking over all the royal forces, he saw the minister Udāyī. That minister Kāḷudāyī was one who accomplished all the King's affairs, an internal secretary, and a very intimate confidant. He was born on the same day as the Bodhisatta and was a childhood friend who played in the dust together. Then the King addressed that minister, "Dear Udāyī, I wish to see my son and have sent nine thousand men; not even one man has returned to report even a bit of news. The danger to my life is hard to know; I wish to see my son while I am still alive. Can you show my son to me?" The minister replied, "Great King, I can show him if I am allowed to ordain." The King said, "Dear son, whether you ordain or not, show my son to me."

The minister, saying "Very well, your Majesty," took the King's message and went to the city of Rājagaha. Having heard the Buddha's Dhamma teaching, he attained Arahantship along with a thousand men and was established in the state of an 'Ehi Bhikkhu'. On the full moon day of Phagguna, he thought, "Winter has passed; the season of spring has arrived. The forest groves are in full bloom; the path is suitable for travel. It is time for the Blessed One to show favor to his relatives." Thinking thus, he approached the Blessed One and, with sixty verses, praised the beauty of the journey for the Blessed One to travel to his ancestral city:

"Lord, now the trees, seeking fruit, have cast off their coverings (old leaves) and possess a glow like glowing embers. O Great Hero, born of the Angīrasa lineage, it is time to travel to the city of your kinsmen."
29:
There are trees that are wonderful with red sprouts and young shoots, very beautiful, and resembling pavilions shining with jewels. O Great Hero, the Buddha, who is endowed with the radiance emanating from your body, it is time to travel to the royal city of Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

Trees, well-bloomed to their tips, adorned with flowers, delightful, and possessing a pure, fine fragrance, are beautiful on both sides of the road. O Great Hero, the Buddha, who is endowed with the radiance emanating from your body, it is time to travel to the royal city of Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

Wonderful trees, abundant with many fruits, can dispel hunger and thirst on both sides of the road. O Great Hero, the Buddha, who is endowed with the radiance emanating from your body, it is time to travel to the royal city of Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

Trees with wonderful flowers, well-arranged with pure young leaves and shoots, resembling the plumage of a peacock, are beautiful on both sides of the road. O Great Hero, the Buddha, who is endowed with the radiance emanating from your body, it is time to travel to the royal city of Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

Trees that are like permanent dwellings, beautiful with fruit-bearing young leaves and well-arranged, delight the beings weary from a long journey. O Great Hero, the Buddha, who is endowed with the radiance emanating from your body, it is time to travel to the royal city of Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

Many vines, with well-bloomed tips, clinging to the forest thickets and very beautiful, delight all beings like a ruby pavilion. O Great Hero, the Buddha, who is endowed with the radiance emanating from your body, it is time to travel to the royal city of Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

Many vines clinging to the trees, possessing an excellent fragrance, are alluring like a daughter-in-law with her loved ones. O Great Hero, the Buddha, who is endowed with the radiance emanating from your body, it is time to travel to the royal city of Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.
30:
Birds of various beautiful colors, such as dark blue, chirping all around, delight with their sweet voices. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is time for you to journey to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

Deer of various beautiful forms, with upright ears and lovely eyes, run about in all directions. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is time for you to journey to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

The earth all around is beautiful, covered with lush green grass; trees in full bloom are like ornaments on a crest, making the ground delightful. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is time for you to journey to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

The well-arranged sands, appearing as if made of strings of pearls, are well-situated and pleasant to the touch, beautifying all directions. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is time for you to journey to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

The ground is even, pleasant to the touch, and pure, scented with the fragrance of blooming flowers, shining with pure beauty. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is time for you to journey to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

The forest is well-prepared like the Nandana grove, adorned with various beautiful thickets of trees, fragrant and very delightful. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is time for you to journey to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

The lakes are various, wonderful, and heart-pleasing, well-adorned with lotuses and white lilies, full of clear, cool, and beautiful water. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is time for you to journey to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.
31:
Shining with various well-bloomed lotuses, their pure fragrances especially delight humans and gods. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.

Those birds, perched upon well-bloomed lotuses, make the surroundings echo and rejoice together with their mates. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.

Bees, taking pollen from well-bloomed flowers, fly about humming loudly. The fragrance of honey wafts through the directions. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.
