Elephants, intoxicated with rut, make unbroken, powerful sounds. Streams of water flow from the mountains, and the rivers flow most beautifully. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.

The mountains all around appear dark blue like the necks of peacocks. The directions shine and are beautiful. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.

Flocks of peacocks dance upon the mountain peaks together with the peahens. They cry out with various sweet voices. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.

Many delightful birds, such as parrots, shining with their colorful wings, stay upon the mountains and make them echo. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.

The mountains, spread with well-bloomed flowers and adorned with various fragrances, are beautiful in all directions. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.
32:
The mountains, mingled with well-bloomed Karama flowers and adorned with various fragrant petals, beautify the directions all around. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.

The rivers, possessing many extremely sweet fragrances like the lakes in the garden of the Asura king, flow most beautifully. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.

Adorned with wonderful landing places, the rivers where various delightful deer and birds gather flow well and are beautiful. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.

On both sides of the lakes, beautiful and fragrant trees in full bloom are adorned at their tops like celestial maidens. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.

The forest, filled with a network of various fragrant trees, heart-delighting and wonderful like the Nandana grove of the gods, is ever present on the path of the virtuous. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.

In the villages along the way, various pure and abundant foods, drinks, and savories are easily obtained, and the curries are full of delicious flavors. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.

The earth all around is especially beautiful; with its wonderful colors like those of flowers, it is as if adorned with Indagopaka insects. O Great Hero, O Aṅgīrasa, it is the season for you to go to the city of Kapilavatthu.
33:
Many people, endowed with virtues such as pure faith, are greatly longing for the Buddha-King and are devoted only to Him. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come (to journey to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen).

There are ponds covered with various kinds of lotuses in the exquisite groves. A scent like the taste of milk wafts from the lotus stalks and roots. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come.

There are delightful trees adorned with dark-colored foliage, growing well on both sides, serving as a gathering place for living beings. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come.

The forest is long like a wondrous dark cloud, like the Nandana grove in the realm of the king of gods; it is filled with fragrant flowers that bloom in all seasons. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come.

There are beautiful and pleasant roads at every yojana. There are delightful villages, crowded with people, where alms-food and drinks are easily obtained. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come.

There are many spacious rest houses and assembly halls, pleasant with abundant shade and water, providing all kinds of happiness to the residents. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come.

There are ponds covered with five kinds of lotuses and delightful gardens, adorned with various exquisite groves of trees. There are also well-created, pleasant fragrances. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come.
34:
The wind blowing gently is soft, cool, and pleasant; the surrounding sky is clear of clouds; and all directions are beautiful. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time is favorable (to journey to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen).

To prevent dust from rising on the road, a light drizzle falls at night; in the sky, the sun’s heat is mild and gentle. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time is favorable.

Herds of intoxicated elephants play joyfully with herds of female elephants; they run about in all directions, trumpeting loudly. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time is favorable.

The great forest, far from the haunts of men, is very dark green and lovely to behold; it is as delightful as the peak of a dark cloud, and truly wondrous to those who look upon it. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time is favorable.

The clouds are very pure, and the sky is exceedingly delightful, as if adorned equally with precious gems; it makes all directions shine brilliantly. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time is favorable.

Gandhabbas, Vijjādharas, and Kinnaras wander within that most delightful great forest, singing beautifully with sweet voices. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time is favorable.

There is a forest region filled with monasteries and groves, constantly frequented by groups of ascetics who fear the mass of defilements. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time is favorable.
35:
The forest edges, filled with various fruits, are peaceful and always delightful to the heart; they especially increase the joy of concentration. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come to journey to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

There is a great forest constantly frequented by many flocks of birds. In that region, there are people living in villages that are continuously connected to one another; there are also noble villages from ancient times. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come.

In that place, many people are well-provided with clothing, alms-food, drinks, lodgings, scents, flowers, and fragrant ointments. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come.

At that time, due to the power of their merit, people who have attained all kinds of fame and retinue live in various ways, being happy, prosperous, and possessing great wealth. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come.

In the sky and in all directions, the clouds have a very pure color. The moon also shines most beautifully. At night, the wind is soft, gentle, and cool. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come.

When the moon rises, all the people are joyful; they speak of wondrous things in their courtyards and rejoice greatly with their loved ones. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come.

The sky is beautiful with the rays of the moon. The earth is pure and has a color that is pleasing to the heart. All directions have a pure appearance. O Great Hero, descendant of Aṅgīrasa, the time has come.
36:
On the ground, for those who desire the quality of fragrance from all around, the flowers have bloomed upon seeing the noble moonlight even from afar. It is time, O Great Hero, Angīrasa, to travel to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

As if the earth were anointed with the rays of the moon, and adorned with flowers from all around, the earth shines like a young woman fully adorned with flowers on all her limbs. It is time, O Great Hero, Angīrasa, to travel to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

Elephants, intoxicated with rut, make their sounds. Birds with variegated plumage are all around. They raise their voices in the most delightful forest. It is time, O Great Hero, Angīrasa, to travel to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

The entire path is fit for travel. The kingdom is prosperous, with wealth and enjoyments. The praise of all brings happiness to all beings. It is time, O Great Hero, Angīrasa, to travel to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

The entire forest is of most variegated form. It is like the well-created Nandana grove of the gods. It constantly generates joy for the ascetics. It is time, O Great Hero, Angīrasa, to travel to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

The glorious city of your kinsmen, named Kapilavatthu, is here, delightful like an adorned city of the gods. It is time, O Great Hero, Angīrasa, to travel to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.

The city of Kapilavatthu is most delightful, with variegated and pleasant watchtowers, adorned with clusters of well-bloomed lotuses, and with variegated moats. It is time, O Great Hero, Angīrasa, to travel to Kapilavatthu, the city of your kinsmen.
37:
It is time, O Great Hero, Angīrasa, to go to the city of Kapilavatthu, which has variegated walls and gates, beautiful courtyards like the dwellings of the gods, and delightful streets resembling the heavenly world.

The Sakyan princes, adorned with noble ornaments, are shining and radiant like the sons of gods in the world of the Lord of Devas. It is time, O Great Hero, Angīrasa.

O Lord of Sages, King Suddhodana has sent ten groups of ministers' sons along with a great army to behold the Noble Sage. It is time, O Great Hero, Angīrasa.

Not one of those sent ministers is seen returning, nor is any word of news heard. That Great King, the leader of men, is being overcome and oppressed by grief. I wish to delight that lord of men. It is time, O Great Hero, Angīrasa.

O Lord of Sages, foremost in virtue, please delight that lord of men, the lord of bipeds, who is looking forward with a mass of wonderful joy at the sight of you. It is time, O Great Hero, Angīrasa.

With hope, the farmer plows the field; with hope, the seed is sown. With hope for wealth, merchants travel across the ocean. May that hope of mine, for which I stand, be fulfilled.

It is neither too cold nor too hot; there is no fear of famine or hunger. The ground is green with young grass. This is the time, O Great Sage.

Then the Teacher said to that elder, "Udāyi, why do you praise the virtues of traveling?" "Venerable Sir, your father, King Suddhodana, greatly desires to see you. Please show favor to your kinsmen." "Very well, Udāyi, I shall show favor to my kinsmen. Therefore, inform the community of monks; we shall fulfill the duties of one about to travel (gamiyavatta)." "Very well, Venerable Sir," replied the Venerable Kāludāyi, and he informed the community of monks.

Accompanied by twenty thousand Arahants in total—ten thousand noble sons from the regions of Anga and Magadha, and ten thousand noble sons from the city of Kapilavatthu—the Blessed One departed from the city of Rājagaha, traveling one league each day...
38:
The Blessed One said, "Kāḷudāyī, inform the Saṅgha of monks; they shall fulfill the duties of those who are to travel." "Very well, Bhante," the Elder replied and informed the Saṅgha of monks.

The Teacher, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahant monks—ten thousand noble sons who were residents of Aṅga and Magadha, and ten thousand who were residents of Kapilavatthu—departed from Rājagaha. Traveling at the rate of one yojana per day, he reached the city of Kapilavatthu in two months. When the Blessed One arrived, the Sakyans, thinking, "We shall see our noblest relative," searched for a place for the Blessed One to reside. Observing that "the Nigrodha Sakyan’s park is delightful," they performed all the necessary preparations and went out to welcome him with perfumes and flowers in their hands. With their bodies adorned with all kinds of ornaments, they honored the Blessed One with perfumes, flowers, and scented powders, and placing him at the front, they proceeded to the Nigrodhārāma monastery.

There, the Blessed One sat on the prepared noble Buddha-seat, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants. However, the Sakyans, being proud by nature and stiff with pride, thought, "Prince Siddhattha is much younger than us; he is like a younger brother, a son, a nephew, or a grandson." They said to the very young princes, "You pay homage; we will sit behind you." While they were sitting in that manner, the Blessed One, perceiving their inclination, thought, "These relatives do not pay homage to me because of their vain seniority. They do not know what a Buddha is like, or what the power of a Buddha is like; they do not know that a Buddha is like this, or that the power of a Buddha is like this. Now, I shall perform a miracle, demonstrating my own Buddha-power and psychic power. Having created a jeweled walkway in the sky, extending across ten thousand world-systems, I will walk upon that walkway, and observing the inclination of the great multitude, I will preach the Dhamma." Therefore, the reciters (Saṅgītikārakas) said this to show the Blessed One's reflection:

These people, together with the devas, do not know what kind of person this Buddha, the Supreme Man, is.
They do not know what his psychic power and power of wisdom are like, nor what the power of the Buddha, who brings welfare to the world, is like.
39:
These people, together with the devas, do not know that this Buddha, the Supreme Man, is of such a nature. They do not know that the psychic power and power of wisdom of the Buddha, who brings welfare to the world, are like this, and that the power of the Buddha is like this.

"Now, I shall demonstrate the unsurpassed power of a Buddha; I shall create a walkway adorned with jewels in the sky."

In that verse, 'na hete jānanti' means these people truly do not know. The letter 'na' has the sense of negation. The letter 'hi' is an indeclinable used in the sense of cause. The meaning is: since these devas and humans, such as my relatives, do not know as long as I have not revealed the Buddha-power and psychic power, thinking "The Buddha is like this, the psychic power is like this," therefore, I shall demonstrate my Buddha-power and psychic power.

In the word 'sadevamanusā', 'deva' refers to devas by rebirth (upapatti-deva). 'Sadeva' means together with devas. Who are they? They are the humans; humans together with devas are 'sadevamanusā'. Alternatively, 'deva' refers to the conventional deity (sammuti-deva), King Suddhodana. 'Sadeva' means together with King Suddhodana. 'Mānusā' refers to the humans who are relatives. The relatives together with King Suddhodana are 'sadevamanusā'. The meaning is: these relatives of mine, together with the King, do not know my power. The remaining devas are also included here. All devas are called 'deva' because of the sense of 'devana' (playing/shining). 'Devana' is the meaning of the root, such as playing. Alternatively, devas and humans are 'devamānusā'; those together with devas and humans are 'sadevamanusā'. Who are they? The omitted word 'loka' (world) should be added and understood.

'Buddha' means one who has personally realized the Four Noble Truths and has made others realize them; thus, he is called 'Buddha'. Regarding this, it was said: "O Brahmin, that which should be known through higher knowledge has been known by me; that which should be developed has been developed; that which should be abandoned has been abandoned; therefore, I am the Buddha."

Here, the derivation of the word 'Buddha' in the agentive sense (kattu-kāraka) should be noted. Because he is known by devas and humans who have attained distinction as "The Blessed One is indeed the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha)," he is called 'Buddha'. Here, the derivation of the word 'Buddha' in the passive sense (kamma-kāraka) should be noted. Alternatively, he is 'Buddha' because he has the Truths that have been known; it means one who possesses the known Truths. All of that should be understood according to the science of grammar. 'Kīdisako' means what is his nature like? What is he similar to? What kind of appearance and shape does he have? Is he tall or short?
40:
Naruttama means the supreme, most excellent, and praiseworthy person among men or groups of men; thus, he is called Naruttama.

In this term 'Iddhibala', it is called 'Iddhi' because of the sense of completion (attainment) and the sense of acquisition (capability). Alternatively, it is called 'Iddhi' because by that quality, beings become accomplished, prosperous, and reach the pinnacle. That Iddhi is of ten kinds. As it is said: "There are ten kinds of Iddhi. Which ten? Adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi (success by determination), Vikubbana-iddhi (success by transformation), Manomaya-iddhi (mind-made success), Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi (success by diffusion of knowledge), Samādhivipphāra-iddhi (success by diffusion of concentration), Ariya-iddhi (noble success), Kammavipākaja-iddhi (success born of kamma-result), Puññavato-iddhi (success of the meritorious), Vijjāmaya-iddhi (success through science/arts), and Iddhi in the sense of completion due to right effort in various instances" (from the Paṭisambhidāmagga).

The distinction among these Iddhis should be understood thus: Being naturally one, he contemplates many. Having contemplated a hundred or a thousand, he determines with knowledge, "Let me be many." The Iddhi shown through such analysis is called Adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi because it is accomplished by the power of determination. The meaning of Adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi is: having entered the fourth jhāna which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), and having emerged from it, if he desires a hundred, he performs the preliminary work (parikamma) with sense-sphere preliminary consciousness (kāmāvacara-parikamma-citta) saying, "Let me be a hundred, let me be a hundred." Then, he again enters the fourth jhāna which is the basis for direct knowledge, emerges, contemplates again, and determines. Simultaneously with the consciousness of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-citta), he becomes a hundred. The same method applies to a thousand and so on.

In this process, the basis-jhāna consciousness (pādaka-jhāna-citta) has the sign (nimitta) as its object. The preliminary consciousnesses (parikamma-citta) have the hundred or the thousand, etc., as their object. Furthermore, those objects are perceived by way of appearance (vaṇṇa), not by way of concept (paññatti). The determination-consciousness also has the hundred as its object. That determination-consciousness, like absorption-consciousness (appanā-citta), arises immediately after the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), associated with the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere. That person who has attained direct knowledge, abandoning his natural appearance, displays the appearance of a youth, or an elephant, or a garuḍa... or various army arrays. The Iddhi that appears in this way is called Vikubbana-iddhi because it proceeds by way of transformation, abandoning the natural appearance.

"Here, a monk creates from this body another body, having form, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and parts, with unimpaired senses." The Iddhi that comes by this method is called Manomaya-iddhi because it proceeds by way of producing another mind-made body within the body itself.

Whether before the arising of knowledge, or after, or at the moment of its arising, that which is produced by the power of the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) to be attained in that very existence...
41:
...the distinction produced by the diffusion of knowledge is called ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi. The psychic power of the Venerable Bākula and the Venerable Saṅkicca due to the diffusion of knowledge is ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi, and their stories should be told here.

The distinction produced by the power of serenity (samatha) before, after, or at the moment of concentration is called samādhivipphāra-iddhi. The psychic powers of the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Sañjīva, the Venerable Khāṇukoṇḍañña, the laywoman Uttarā, and the laywoman Sāmāvatī due to the diffusion of concentration are instances where their stories should be told here; however, for fear of the text becoming too long, I shall not elaborate.

What is noble iddhi (ariya-iddhi)? Here, in this Dispensation, if a monk so desires, he dwells perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive. If he so desires, he dwells perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive... [Pe]... he dwells there equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. This is called ariya-iddhi because it occurs only in the Noble Ones who have attained mastery over the mind.

What is iddhi born of the result of kamma (kammavipākaja-iddhi)? The ability to travel through the air, etc., of all birds, all devas, the humans of the first aeon, and some vinipātika asuras is called kammavipākaja-iddhi. What is iddhi of the meritorious (puññavato-iddhi)? A Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) can travel through the air with his fourfold army. For the financier Jaṭila, a golden mountain eighty cubits high appeared. This is called puññavato-iddhi. For the financier Ghosaka, remaining healthy and unharmed despite attempts to kill him in seven places is puññavato-iddhi. For the financier Meṇḍaka, the appearance of goats made of the seven kinds of jewels in an area of about eight karīsas is called puññavato-iddhi.

What is iddhi made of vidyā (vijjāmaya-iddhi)? Masters of vidyā (vijjādhara), having recited their spells, can travel through the air. They can show the form of an elephant in the sky... [Pe]... they can show various military arrays. The psychic power occurring in such ways is called vijjāmaya-iddhi. Having performed various deeds...
42:
The distinction that arises with the meaning of fulfillment due to right effort is called 'success through the fulfillment of right effort' (sammāpayoga-paccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi). In various contexts, it is called iddhi in the sense of completion through right effort. The strength of these ten kinds of iddhi is called 'the power of success' (iddhibala). The meaning is: 'They do not know this power of success of mine.'

'The power of wisdom' (paññābala) refers to the power of the wisdom of the path of Arahatship, which bestows all mundane and supramundane special qualities. They do not know that power of wisdom either. Some teachers say, 'The power of wisdom is a designation for the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa).'

'The power of a Buddha' (buddhabala) here refers to the majesty of the Buddhas or the Ten Powers of Knowledge (dasabala-ñāṇa). Among them, the ten powers of knowledge are: the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna-ñāṇa); the knowledge of the results of past, future, and present actions; the knowledge of the practice leading to all destinations; the knowledge of the world with its many and various elements; the knowledge of the various dispositions of beings; the knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies; the knowledge of the corruption, purification, and emergence regarding the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; the knowledge of the recollection of past lives; the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings; and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. The designation for these ten knowledges is 'the power of a Buddha'. 'Edisaṃ' means having such a nature, or this is simply the reading.

'Handa' is an indeclinable in the sense of resolution. 'Ahaṃ' refers to oneself. What is meant? 'Since these relatives of mine do not know the power of a Buddha or the virtues of a Buddha, and based merely on their own vain seniority, they do not pay homage to me, the eldest and foremost in all the world, out of pride. Therefore, I shall display the power of a Buddha to break the banner of pride they possess and make them pay homage.' This is the meaning. 'Dassayissāmi' means 'I shall show'. There is also the reading 'dassessāmi', which has the same meaning. 'The power of a Buddha' (buddhabala) means the majesty of a Buddha or the special knowledge of a Buddha. 'Anuttara' means unsurpassed and noble. 'Caṅkama' refers to the place for walking. 'Māpayissāmi' means 'I shall create'. There is also the reading 'caṅkamanaṃ māpessāmi', which has the same meaning. 'Nabe' means in the sky. 'Sabba-ratana-maṇḍita' refers to the walkway adorned with the ten kinds of delightful jewels: pearls, emeralds, rubies, cat's eyes, conch shells, crystal, coral, silver, gold, spotted rubies, and red rubies. Some read it as 'nabe ratana-maṇḍitaṃ'.

Then, as soon as the Blessed One had this thought, the deities such as the earth-dwelling deities living in the ten thousand world systems, with joyful hearts, gave a cry of 'Sādhu'. The reciters (saṅgītikāraka), clarifying that matter, said:

The earth-dwelling deities, the deities of the Four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa deities, the Yāma, the Tusita, the Nimmānarati, the Paranimmitavasavatti deities, and those who belong to the retinue of Brahmā, being greatly delighted, made a resounding shout.

In that verse, 'Bhummā' refers to the earth-dwelling deities residing on rocky mountains, in forests, and on trees. 'Mahārājikā' refers to the deities who are followers of the four Great Kings. Hearing the shout of the earth-dwelling deities, the sky-dwelling deities also made a great sound. Then the Abbhavalāhaka deities, then the Uṇhavalāhaka deities...
43:
“The earth-dwelling deities, the deities of the Four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa deities, the Yāma, the Tusita, the Nimmānarati, the Paranimmitavasavatti deities, and those who belong to the retinue of Brahmā, being greatly delighted, made a resounding shout.” It should be understood that the teachers who performed the rehearsal (Saṅgītikārakas) placed these verses at the beginning.

In that verse, “Bhummā” refers to the earth-dwelling deities residing on rocky mountains, in forests, on trees, and so forth. “Mahārājikā” refers to the deities who are followers of the four Great Kings. Hearing the shout of the earth-dwelling deities, the sky-dwelling deities made a great sound; then the Abbhavalāhaka deities, the Uṇhavalāhaka deities, the Sītavalāhaka deities, the Vassavalāhaka deities, the Vātavalāhaka deities, the four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa, the Yāma, the Tusita, the Nimmānarati, the Paranimmitavasavatti, the Brahmakāyikā Brahmās, the Brahmapurohitā Brahmās, the Mahābrahmās, the Parittābhā Brahmās, the Appamāṇābhā Brahmās, the Ābhassarā Brahmās, the Parittasubhā Brahmās, the Appamāṇasubhā Brahmās, the Subhakiṇhā Brahmās, the Vehapphala Brahmās, the Avihā Brahmās, the Atappā Brahmās, the Sudassā Brahmās, the Sudassī Brahmās, and the Akaniṭṭha Brahmās, having heard the shout, made a great sound. Excluding the non-percipient beings and the formless beings, all deities, humans, nagas, and others in places where the ear-base (sotāyatana) can function, with hearts filled with joy and rapture, made a resounding shout. “Ānanditā” means having joyful hearts, having arisen with rapture and happiness. “Vipulaṃ” means extensive and vast.

Then, immediately after the Teacher had thought thus, he entered the white-kasina attainment (odāta-kasiṇa-samāpatti) and resolved: “Let there be light in the ten thousand world systems.” Simultaneously with that resolve, light appeared from the surface of the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha realm. Therefore, it is said:

“The earth together with the world of deities was illuminated, and the vast world-interspaces, which are without support below, were revealed;
then the dense darkness was destroyed;
the people together with the deities, having seen the wonderful miracle, were greatly delighted.”

In that verse, “Obhāsitā” means it has been clearly shown. In the word “Pathavī”, this earth is the harsh and solid earth (kakkhaḷa-pathavī), the composite earth as a structure (sasambhāra-pathavī), the sign-earth (nimitta-pathavī)...
44:
In that verse, *obhāsitā* means manifested (*pakāsitā*). Regarding the term *pathavī* (earth), there are four types: *kakkhaḷa-pathavī* (solid earth), *sasambhāra-pathavī* (composite earth), *nimitta-pathavī* (sign earth), and *sammuti-pathavī* (conventional earth). Among these four, the earth mentioned in passages such as, "Friends, what is the internal earth element? That which is internal, personal, hard, and has the nature of hardness," is called *kakkhaḷa-pathavī*. The earth mentioned in passages such as, "Whatever monk should dig the earth or have it dug," is called *sasambhāra-pathavī*. The twenty parts of the body, such as hair and so on, as well as external materials like iron and copper, along with their properties like color (*vaṇṇa*), are also called *sasambhāra-pathavī*. The earth mentioned in passages such as, "One perceives the earth-kasiṇa," is called *nimitta-pathavī*, and it is also referred to as *ārammaṇa-pathavī* (object-earth). A person who attains the earth-kasiṇa jhāna and is reborn in the celestial realm receives the name *Pathavī-deva* (Earth Deity) by virtue of that attainment. This earth, as mentioned in passages such as, "The Water Deities and the Earth Deities," should be understood as *sammuti-pathavī* or *paññatti-pathavī*. In this context, however, *sasambhāra-pathavī* is intended.

*Sadevakā* means together with the world of devas. If the reading were *sadevatā*, it would be even better; it means the human world together with the devas is illuminated. *Puthū* means many. *Lokantarikā* is a designation for the spaces between the world systems where asuras and hell-beings reside. One such *lokantarika* hell exists in the space between every three world systems (*cakka-vāḷas*). Like the empty space in the middle of three cartwheels touching each other, each *lokantarika* hell is eight thousand yojanas in extent. *Asaṃvutā* means having no support or foundation below. *Tamo* means darkness. *Tibbo* means thick or dense. Because there is no light from the moon or sun, it is always in total darkness. *Vihato* means destroyed or dispelled. *Tadā* (at that time) means when the Blessed One, out of compassion for beings, spread forth light to perform a miracle; at that time, the thick darkness in the *lokantarika* hells was dispelled and destroyed.

*Accherakaṃ* means worthy of snapping one's fingers, meaning it is so wonderful that it is fit to be applauded by snapping the fingers. *Pāṭihīraṃ* is called so because it removes (*harana*) opposing states (defilements). Or, it is *pāṭihīraṃ* because it removes the minds of beings that have fallen into wrong views and conceit. Or, it is *pāṭihīraṃ* because it brings back (*paṭi-āharati*) the faith of those who are not yet settled in faith. There is also a reading *pāṭiheraṃ*, which has the same meaning. In this context, it is a designation for the special creation of light. *Disvāna*...
45:
Regarding the phrase "a wonderful miracle" (*accherakaṃ pāṭihīraṃ*), the meaning should be understood by bringing in the explanation that devas, humans, and even the beings born in the *lokantarika* hells, upon seeing that miracle of the Blessed One, attained supreme joy and gladness (*pīti-somanassa*). Otherwise, the preceding and following statements would not be consistent with each other.

Now, to show that light exists not only in the human worlds but in all three worlds—namely the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*), the world of beings (*satta-loka*), and the world of space (*okāsa-loka*)—this verse was spoken:

"Together with devas, gandhabbas, humans, and rakkhasas,
An excellent and vast radiance was born;
In this world and in the other, in both,
Below, above, and across, it spread."

In that verse, *devā* includes all devas: conventional devas (*sammuti-deva*), devas by rebirth (*upapatti-deva*), and devas by purity (*visuddhi-deva*). Devas, gandhabbas, humans, and rakkhasas are called *deva-gandhabba-manussa-rakkhasa*. Because it is together with those devas, gandhabbas, humans, and rakkhasas, it is called *sadeva-gandhabba-manussa-rakkhasa*. What is that? It is the world; it means in the world together with devas, gandhabbas, humans, and rakkhasas. *Ābhā* means light. In the word *uḷārā*, this term *uḷāra* is found in the senses of sweet, excellent, vast, and so on. For instance, it is found in the sense of "sweet" in passages such as, "They eat and consume excellent (*uḷāra*) foods." It is found in the sense of "excellent" in passages such as, "The venerable Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with excellent (*uḷāra*) praise." It is found in the sense of "vast" in passages such as, "Surpassing the divine power of the devas, an immeasurable and vast (*uḷāra*) radiance appeared." Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of "excellent." *Vipulā* means immeasurable. *Ajāyatha* means arose, became manifest, or occurred. "In this world and in the other" means in this human world and in the other celestial world. "In both" means occurring in both, to be understood as in the case of "internal and external" and so on. "Below" means in the hells such as Avīci. "Above" means in the open space above the peak of existence (*bhavagga*). "Across" means across the ten thousand world systems. *Vitthataṃ* means spread out. Having dispelled the darkness, (the light) pervaded the world and the regions in the manner described.
46:
The meaning is that the light has arisen. Alternatively, the meaning is that the light spread and remained throughout a vast, immeasurable region, extending even horizontally.

Then the Blessed One, having spread light throughout the ten thousand world-systems, entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā). Emerging from that jhāna and reflecting, he ascended into the air by an act of resolve (adhiṭṭhāna), and as if sprinkling the dust of his feet upon the heads of his kinsmen, he performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) in the midst of a great assembly of devas and humans. This miracle should be understood as it appears in the Pali text:

What is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the Twin Miracle? Here, the Tathāgata performs the Twin Miracle, which is not shared with disciples. From the upper part of his body, a mass of fire issues forth; from the lower part, a stream of water issues forth. From the lower part of his body, a mass of fire issues forth; from the upper part, a stream of water issues forth. ... From the front of his body, a mass of fire issues forth; from the back, a stream of water issues forth. From the back of his body, a mass of fire issues forth; from the front, a stream of water issues forth. ... From the right eye, a mass of fire issues forth; from the left eye, a stream of water issues forth. From the left eye, a mass of fire issues forth; from the right eye, a stream of water issues forth. ... From the right ear, a mass of fire issues forth; from the left ear, a stream of water issues forth. From the left ear, a mass of fire issues forth; from the right ear, a stream of water issues forth. ... From the right nostril, a mass of fire issues forth; from the left nostril, a stream of water issues forth. From the left nostril, a mass of fire issues forth; from the right nostril, a stream of water issues forth. ... From the right shoulder, a mass of fire issues forth; from the left shoulder, a stream of water issues forth. From the left shoulder, a mass of fire issues forth; from the right shoulder, a stream of water issues forth. ... From the right hand, a mass of fire issues forth; from the left hand, a stream of water issues forth. From the left hand, a mass of fire issues forth; from the right hand, a stream of water issues forth. ... From the right side, a mass of fire issues forth; from the left side, a stream of water issues forth.
47:
From the left side, a mass of fire issues forth; from the right side, a stream of water issues forth. From the right ear, a mass of fire issues forth; from the left ear, a stream of water issues forth. From the right nostril, a mass of fire issues forth; from the left nostril, a stream of water issues forth. From the left nostril, a mass of fire issues forth; from the right nostril, a stream of water issues forth. From the right shoulder, a mass of fire issues forth; from the left shoulder, a stream of water issues forth. From the left shoulder, a mass of fire issues forth; from the right shoulder, a stream of water issues forth. From the right hand, a mass of fire issues forth; from the left hand, a stream of water issues forth. From the left hand, a mass of fire issues forth; from the right hand, a stream of water issues forth. From the right side, a mass of fire issues forth; from the left side, a stream of water issues forth. From the left side, a mass of fire issues forth; from the right side, a stream of water issues forth. From the right foot, a mass of fire issues forth; from the left foot, a stream of water issues forth. From the left foot, a mass of fire issues forth; from the right foot, a stream of water issues forth. From every finger, a mass of fire issues forth; from every interval between the fingers, a stream of water issues forth. From every interval between the fingers, a mass of fire issues forth; from every finger, a stream of water issues forth. From every single hair, a mass of fire issues forth; from every single hair, a stream of water issues forth. From every single pore, a mass of fire issues forth; from every single pore, a stream of water issues forth. The six-colored rays—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson (or reddish-brown), and brilliant—issue forth.

"The Blessed One walks; the created Buddha (nimmitabuddha) stands, sits, or lies down. The Blessed One stands; the created Buddha walks, sits, or lies down. The Blessed One sits; the created Buddha walks, stands, or lies down. The Blessed One lies down; the created Buddha walks, stands, or sits. The created Buddha walks; the Blessed One stands, sits, or lies down. The created Buddha stands; the Blessed One walks, sits, or lies down. The created Buddha sits; the Blessed One walks, stands, or lies down. The created Buddha lies down; the Blessed One walks, stands, or sits. This is to be known as the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the Twin Miracle."

By the power of the Blessed One's attainment of the fire-kasiṇa (tejo-kasiṇa), a mass of fire issues from the upper part of his body. By the power of the attainment of the water-kasiṇa (āpo-kasiṇa), a stream of water issues from the lower part of his body. Again, to show that a mass of fire issues from where the stream of water was, and a stream of water issues from where the mass of fire was, it was said: "From the lower part of the body, a mass of fire issues forth; from the upper part, a stream of water issues forth." This same method applies to the remaining parts. In this, the mass of fire does not mix with the stream of water. Likewise, the stream of water does not mix with the mass of fire. Among the rays, each subsequent ray issues forth simultaneously with the preceding one, like pairs. As for the simultaneous occurrence of two thoughts...
48:
There is no such thing as the simultaneous occurrence of two consciousnesses. However, for the Buddhas, due to the lightness and speed of the life-continuum's process and because of their mastery (*vasībhāva*) practiced in five ways, these rays appear as if they occur simultaneously. But the adverting, preliminary work, and determination for those rays are indeed separate. Truly, for the sake of the blue rays, the Blessed One attains the blue *kasiṇa*. For the sake of the golden rays and so on, He attains the yellow *kasiṇa* and so on.

Thus, while the Blessed One was performing the Twin Miracle (*yamaka-pāṭihīra*), the entire ten thousand world systems became like a time of being decorated. Therefore, it was said:

"The Supreme among beings, the Unsurpassed, the Leader,
The Teacher of gods and humans, the One honored by gods and humans,
The One of great power, possessing the marks born of a hundred merits,
Has shown the marvelous miracle."

In that verse, '*Sattuttamo*' means He is supreme, excellent, and best among all beings due to His attributes such as virtue (*sīla*); thus, He is called '*Sattuttama*'. Or He is supreme among beings; thus, '*Sattuttama*'. Indeed, '*Satta*' is a name for knowledge (*ñāṇa*). He is supreme and excellent because of that knowledge known as the Ten Powers (*dasabala*), the Fourfold Intrepidity (*catur-vesārajja*), and the Six Uncommon Knowledges (*cha-asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa*); thus, He is called '*Sattuttama*'. Or He is called '*Sattuttama*' because, by way of apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the being is supreme. If that were the case, it should be said '*Uttamasatto*', because there is a text placing the word '*Uttama*' at the beginning. However, this variation should be understood like the words *Naruttama*, *Purisuttama*, *Naravara*, etc., due to lack of fixed rule and frequent usage. Alternatively, He is called '*Sattuttama*' because He possesses supreme knowledge. Here too, the word '*Uttama*' is placed at the beginning. Since there is a text placing the qualifier (*visesana*) at the beginning, as in '*Uttamasatto*', just like in the words '*Cittagū*' and '*Paddhagū*', this occurrence is not a fault. Or it should be understood like the text '*Āhitaggi*' and so on, because both are qualifiers. '*Vināyako*' means He is called '*Vināyaka*' because He disciplines and tames beings through many methods of discipline. '*Satthā*' means He is called '*Satthā*' because He instructs beings according to their needs regarding the benefits of this life and the next. '*Ahū*' has the meaning 'has been' or 'occurred'. '*Devamanussapūjito*': they are called '*Deva*' (gods) because they play and enjoy themselves with the five divine cords of sensual pleasure. They are called '*Manussa*' (humans) because of the abundance of mind/thought. Both gods and humans are '*Devamanussa*'.
49: He is called 'Devamanussapūjito' because he is worshipped by gods and humans. It means he is worshipped and revered with offerings such as flowers and the four requisites. One might ask: Why are only gods and humans mentioned? Was the Blessed One not also worshipped by animals such as the Nāgas Āravāဠa and Kāဠāpalāla, the elephants Dhanapāla (Nāဠāgiri) and Pālileyyaka, and by beings of the fallen realms such as the Yakkhas Sātāgira, Āဠavaka, Hemavata, Sūciloma, and Kharaloma? Indeed, he was. However, it should be understood that this statement is made in terms of the highest distinction and the classification of all individuals. ## 'Mahānubhāvo' means being endowed with the great power of the Buddhas. 'Satapuññalakkhaṇo' means that if all beings in infinite world-systems were to perform a single meritorious deed a hundred times, the Bodhisatta himself alone performed such deeds a hundredfold (many times) to be born. Therefore, he is called 'Satapuññalakkhaṇo' (one who has marks produced by a hundred merits). Some teachers say, 'one who has each mark produced by a hundred meritorious deeds.' If that were so, any random person could become a Buddha; thus, this statement is rejected in the Commentaries. 'Dassesi' means he showed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya), which caused great wonder to all gods and humans. Then the Teacher, having performed the miracle in the sky and observed the mental disposition of the great multitude, desired to give a Dhamma discourse suited to their inclinations while walking. He created a jeweled walkway (ratana-caṅkama) made of all kinds of gems, extending across ten thousand world-systems in the sky. Therefore, it is said: 'Requested by the excellent Brahmā, the One with Eyes, the Supreme among Men, Having then considered the welfare [of beings], the Leader of the World, Created a well-constructed walkway fashioned from all kinds of jewels.' In that verse, 'So' refers to that Teacher. 'Yācito' means he was first requested to teach the Dhamma during the eighth week. 'Devavarena' refers to Sahampati Brahmā. In the term 'Cakkhumā,' it is called 'Cakkhu' (eye) because it sees; it means it clearly distinguishes between the even and the uneven. That eye is of two kinds: the eye of knowledge (ñāṇa-cakkhu) and the physical eye (maṃsa-cakkhu). Among them, the eye of knowledge is fivefold: the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the All-seeing eye, the Divine-eye, and the Wisdom-eye. Among these five, the knowledge of the inclinations and latent tendencies of beings (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of the maturity of the faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) are called the 'Buddha-eye,' as mentioned in the passage: 'Surveying the world with the Buddha-eye.' The three lower paths and the three lower fruits are called the 'Dhamma-eye,' as mentioned in the passage: 'The dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arose.' Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is called the 'All-seeing eye,' as mentioned in the passage: 'The wise Sumedha, the Buddha with the All-seeing eye, having ascended the palace made of wisdom which is like a mountain.' The knowledge associated with the supernormal powers (abhiññā) produced by developing the light-kasina is called the 'Divine-eye,' as mentioned in the passage: 'With the eye similar to the pure divine eye.' The Wisdom-eye is as in 'The eye (knowledge) arose'...
50:
The lower three paths and the lower three fruits, as mentioned in the passage "The dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma (Dhamma-cakkhu) arose," are called the Eye of Dhamma. Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), as mentioned in the passage "O wise one, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, like that, the All-seeing Eye (Samanta-cakkhu)," is called the All-seeing Eye. The knowledge associated with the mind of supernormal power (abhiññā) produced by the expansion of the light kasina is called the Divine Eye (Dibba-cakkhu); it is mentioned as "with the divine eye, purified." In this text, "The eye arose, the knowledge arose," the knowledge such as the recollection of past lives is called the Eye of Wisdom (Paññā-cakkhu).

In this text, "Dependent on the eye and forms," the sensitive physical eye (pasāda-maṃsa-cakkhu) is meant. That physical eye is of two kinds: the constituent eye (sasambhāra-cakkhu) and the sensitive eye (pasāda-cakkhu). Among these two, in the mass of flesh surrounded by eyelashes within the eye-socket, there are briefly 13 constituents (sambhāra): the four great elements, color, smell, taste, nutritive essence, sperm (sambhavo), life-faculty (jīvita), sex-faculty (bhāva), eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), and body-sensitivity (kāya-pasāda). In detail, the 36 types of matter produced from the four causes (catu-samuṭṭhāna) that arise, along with these four—life-faculty, sex-faculty, eye-sensitivity, and body-sensitivity—which are produced by kamma, are called the constituent eye (sasambhāra). This is known as the sasambhāra-cakkhu. The mere sensitive matter (pasāda-rūpa) situated in the center of the vision-circle, surrounded by the black circle which is further demarcated by the white circle, and which is capable of seeing forms, is called the sensitive eye (pasāda-cakkhu). All these eyes are of one kind in terms of being impermanent and conditioned; of two kinds in terms of being with taints (sāsava) and without taints (anāsava), or mundane and supramundane; of three kinds in terms of planes (bhūmi) or the triad of grasped-at (upādinnattika); of four kinds in terms of being exclusively limited, immeasurable, or having fixed objects; of five kinds in terms of having objects such as form, Nibbāna, formless, all objects, or no objects; and of six kinds by way of the Buddha-eye and so forth. Because the Blessed One possesses these various kinds of eyes as described, He is called "The One with Eyes" (Cakkhumā).

"Atthaṃ samekkhitvā" means having created the walkway (caṅkama) and having investigated and considered the welfare of devas and humans, which is the primary cause for the preaching of the Dhamma. "Māpayi" means He created or manifested. He is called the "Leader of the World" (Lokanāyaka) because He leads the world towards heaven and Nibbāna. "Suniṭṭhitaṃ" means well-finished or reached completion. "Sabba-ratana-nimmitaṃ" means made of the ten kinds of gems.
51:
Now, to show the Blessed One's endowment with the three kinds of miracles (pāṭihāriya):

"Psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction; the Blessed One possessed mastery in these three miracles. The Leader of the World created the well-finished walkway, manifested from all kinds of gems."

In that verse, 'Iddhi' refers to the miracle of psychic power (iddhi-pāṭihāriya) known as the various forms of psychic power. That miracle of power manifests in such ways as being one and becoming many, or being many and becoming one. 'Ādesanā' refers to the miracle of mind-reading (ādesanā-pāṭihāriya), which is the speaking after knowing the thoughts and mental processes of others. This miracle of mind-reading is the constant preaching of Dhamma by the disciples and the Buddhas. 'Anusāsanī' refers to the miracle of instruction (anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya), meaning the advice and admonition that accords with the respective inclinations and dispositions of individuals. Thus, these miracles are of three kinds.

Among these three kinds of miracles, the miracle of psychic power and the miracle of instruction were the habitual practice of the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna. The miracle of mind-reading and the miracle of instruction were the habitual practice of the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta. The miracle of instruction, however, is the constant preaching of Dhamma by the Buddhas. 'Ti-pāṭihīre' means in these three kinds of miracles. 'Bhagavā' is a respectful title for the Teacher who is distinguished by qualities, supreme among beings, and worthy of honor.

Regarding this, the ancient teachers said:
"The word 'Bhagavā' is excellent; the word 'Bhagavā' is supreme. He is endowed with qualities worthy of honor; therefore, He is called 'Bhagavā'."

'Vasī' means reaching mastery in these three kinds of miracles, meaning having practiced mastery. Masteries are fivefold: mastery in adverting (āvajjana), in attaining (samāpajjana), in resolving (adhiṭṭhāna), in emerging (vuṭṭhāna), and in reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa). Among these five, the ability to advert to whichever jhāna one wishes, wherever one wishes, for as long as one wishes, without sluggishness in adverting, being able to advert quickly, is called 'mastery in adverting' (āvajjana-vasī). Likewise, the ability to attain whichever jhāna one wishes... and so on... without sluggishness in attaining, being able to attain quickly, is called 'mastery in attaining' (samāpajjana-vasī). The ability to remain for a long time is called 'mastery in resolving' (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī). Likewise, the ability to emerge quickly is called 'mastery in emerging' (vuṭṭhāna-vasī).
52:
Mastery in reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-vasī) consists only of the reviewing impulsions (javanas). These arise immediately after the advertence (āvajjana), and thus are spoken of within the mastery of advertence (āvajjana-vasī). In this way, among these five masteries, the practiced proficiency is called mastery (vasī). Therefore, it was said: "In performing the Twin Miracle, the Blessed One possessed mastery."

## Now, to show the method of creating that Jewelled Walkway:

"In the ten-thousandfold world system, upon the noble Sineru mountains,
He showed them like pillars in a row, in the walkway made of jewels."

In that verse, "dasa-sahassī-lokadhātuyā" means in the ten thousand world systems. "Sineru-pabbatu-ttame" means on the noble mountains known as Mahāmeru. "Thambheva" means like pillars; having made the Sineru mountains in the ten thousand world systems like golden pillars standing in a row, He created and showed the walkway above those pillars. "Ratanāmaye" means made of jewels.

"Dasa-sahassī atikkamma" means that when the Blessed One created the Jewelled Walkway, He made one end reach the eastern rim of the world system and the other end extend beyond the western rim of the world system. Therefore, it was said:

"Transcending the ten-thousandfold [world system], the Victor (Jina) created the walkway;
All the sides were made of gold, in the walkway made of jewels."

In that verse, "Jino" means the Victor because of conquering the enemies of defilements. "Sabba-soṇṇamayā passe" means that on both sides of the walkway thus created, there were extremely delightful borders made of gold, while the middle was made of gems (emeralds/rubies). 

"Tulā-saṅghāṭā" means pairs of beams; it should be understood that these beams were made of various jewels. "Anuvaggā" means suitable (to the beams). "Sovaṇṇa-phalaka-tthata" means covered with golden planks; it means there was a golden plank-roofing above the pairs of beams. "Vedikā sabba-sovaṇṇā" means the railings (balustrades) were entirely made of gold; the railing that surrounded the walkway was made of pure gold, unmixed with other jewels. "Dubhato passesu nimmitā" means created on both sides. The letter "da" is a euphonic particle (sandhi-kara).
53:
“Maṇi-muttā-vālukā-kiṇṇā” means strewn with sand made of emeralds, rubies, and pearls. Alternatively, emeralds, rubies, pearls, and sand are called “maṇi-muttā-vālukā,” and because it was spread and strewn with these, it is called “maṇi-muttā-vālukā-kiṇṇā.” “Nimmito” means created or made in this manner. “Ratanāmayo” means the walkway was made of all kinds of jewels. “Obhāseti disā sabbā” means illuminating and making clear all ten directions. “Sata-raṃsīva” means like the sun possessing a thousand rays. “Uggato” means having arisen. Just as the rising sun illuminates all ten directions, so too does this walkway made of all jewels shine brilliantly.

Now, to show the Blessed One's activity upon the completion of the walkway:
“On that walkway, the Firm One, endowed with the thirty-two noble marks, the Fully Enlightened One, the Victor, paced back and forth, shining resplendently.”
“Divine Mandārava flowers, lotuses, and Pāricchattaka flowers, all the assembled devas scattered upon the walkway.”
“The hosts of devas from the ten-thousandfold world system see Him and rejoice; paying homage, they prostrate, delighted, thrilled, and joyful,” these are the verses spoken.

In those verses, “dhīro” means endowed with firm energy. “Dvattiṃsa-vara-lakkhaṇo” means endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, such as well-planted feet (suppatiṭṭhita-pādatala). “Dibbaṃ” means existing in the deva world. “Pāricchattakaṃ” means the Pāricchattaka tree, which is extremely beautiful and extends a hundred yojanas all around due to the power of the Kovīḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. When that tree blooms, the entire city of the devas is perfumed with its fragrance, and the new golden mansions, strewn with the pollen of those flowers, appear golden-yellow. The flower of this Pāricchattaka tree is also called “pāricchattaka.” “Caṅkame okiranti” means scattering upon that jewelled walkway. It means they worship the Blessed One as He paces on that walkway with the aforementioned flowers. “Sabbe devā” refers to the devas of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) and others. Therefore, it was said: “The hosts of devas see Him.” It means they see the Blessed One pacing on the jewelled walkway even from their own abodes. “Dasa-sahassī” is a nominative case used in the sense of the locative; it means the hosts of devas in the ten thousand world systems see Him. “Pamoditā” means greatly rejoiced.

“Nipatanti” means assembling or falling down together. “Tuṭṭha-haṭṭhā” means being delighted and thrilled due to the power of zest (pīti). “Pamoditā” should be connected with the joy shared with the devas of Tāvatiṃsa and so on, who will be mentioned later. Otherwise, it would not be free from the fault of redundancy (punarutti-dosa). Alternatively, it means they see the Buddha with joy, and being delighted and thrilled, they assemble in various places.

Now, to specifically show those who see and assemble:
“The Tāvatiṃsa devas, the Yāma devas, the Tusita devas, the Nimmānarati devas, and the Paranimmitavasavatti devas, with minds uplifted and joyful, see the Buddha, the Leader of the World,” these are the verses spoken.
54:
The word 'nipantanti' means they assemble, or it means they fall together in harmony. 'Tuṭṭhahaṭṭhā' means they are delighted and joyful through the power of zest (pīti). The term 'pamoditā' should be understood in connection with the Tāvatiṃsa and other deities who will be mentioned; otherwise, it would not be free from the fault of repetition (punaruṭṭhidosa). Alternatively, it means they behold the Blessed One with rejoicing; being delighted and joyful, they assemble in various places, or they fall together in harmony.

Now, to show specifically who saw Him and who assembled, these verses were spoken:

"The Tāvatiṃsa, Yāma, and Tusita deities, the Nimmānarati deities, and those deities known as Vasavatti, with uplifted and happy minds, behold the Leader of the World.

Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, and also Kinnaras, together with devas, gandhabbas, humans, and rakkhasas, behold Him who is compassionate for the welfare of the world, like the full moon risen high in the sky.

The deities of the Ābhassara, Subhakiṇha, Vehapphala, and Akanittha realms, wearing extremely pure white garments, stand with hands joined in salutation.

They release five-colored Mandārava flowers mixed with sandalwood powder, and they wave their garments in the sky, [exclaiming]: 'Oh, the Victor is compassionate for the welfare of the world!'"

In those verses, 'udaggacittā' means having uplifted minds through the power of zest and happiness (pīti-somanassa). 'Sumanā' means happy precisely because of those uplifted minds. 'Lokahitānukampaka' means both the welfare of the world and compassion for the world. Or, one who is compassionate through the welfare of the world is 'lokahitānukampaka.' In the phrase 'nabbheva accuggatacandamaṇḍalaṃ,' it means they behold [the Buddha] shining with the glory of a Buddha, delighting the eyes like the full moon in the autumn season, newly risen in the sky, full, and free from all disturbances.

The word 'Ābhassara' is spoken by way of the highest limit. It should be understood that it includes all those born in the second jhana, categorized as Parittābha, Appamāṇābha, and Ābhassara. The word 'Subhakiṇha' is also a reference to the highest limit. Therefore, it should be understood to include all those born in the third jhana, categorized as Parittasubha, Appamāṇasubha, and Subhakiṇha. 'Vehapphala' means extensive...
55:
...[extensive] fruit, thus it is called Vehapphala. These [beings] are born of the fourth jhana and dwell on the same level as the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta). Since the Brahmakāyika and others born of the first jhana were shown below (previously), they are not shown here. Because of the absence of the eye-faculty and ear-faculty, the non-percipient beings and the formless beings (arūpī) are not mentioned here. In the phrase 'Akaniṭṭhā ca devatā,' this too is spoken by way of the highest limit. Therefore, it should be understood that all five Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa)—known as Avihā, Atappa, Sudassa, Sudassī, and Akanittha—are included.

'Susuddhasukkavatthavasana' means those who have very pure and white garments. Because they have donned and wrapped themselves in very pure white garments, they are called 'susuddhasukkavatthavasana.' There is also a reading 'susuddhasukkavasanā.' 'Pañjalīkata' means having made the salutation; they stand with their hands joined in salutation like a lotus bud upon their heads.

'Muñcanti' means they scatter. 'Pupphaṃ pana' means 'as for the flowers.' There is also a reading 'pupphāni vā'; this should be seen as a grammatical variation in number, but the meaning is the same. 'Pañcavaṇṇika' means having five colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson. 'Mixed with sandalwood powder.' 'Bhamenti celāni' means they wave their garments. "Oh, the Victor over the five Maras is wonderful indeed! Oh, the Buddha who constantly protects the welfare of the world is wonderful indeed! Oh, He is the Great Compassionate One!"—uttering such words of praise, they scatter flowers and wave their garments.

Now, to show the words of praise employed by them, these verses were spoken:

"You are the Teacher, the Banner, the Flag, and the Sacrificial Post for living beings. You are the Refuge, the Support, the Lamp, and the Supreme among bipeds.

In the ten-thousandfold world system, the deities of great power, surrounding [You], worship with delight, joy, and rejoicing.

Devas and celestial maidens, with confident and joyful minds, honor the Bull among Men with five-colored flowers.

The hosts of deities, with confident and joyful minds, behold Him; they honor the Bull among Men with five-colored flowers."
56:
Oh, how wonderful it is in the world! How marvelous and hair-raising! I have never seen such a wonderful, hair-raising thing before.

Deities, sitting in their respective mansions, laugh a great laugh upon seeing the marvel in the sky.

Deities of the sky, the earth, and those dwelling in grass, reeds, and paths, being delighted and joyful, pay homage with joined palms.

Even the long-lived Nagas, meritorious and of great power, rejoice and pay homage to the Buddha, the Supreme Man.

Deities cause celestial dancers to dance in the sky, the path of the wind; they beat drums covered with skin upon seeing the marvel in the sky.

Upon seeing the marvel in the sky, they sound conchs, panava drums, and many dindima drums in the atmosphere.

Indeed, a marvelous, hair-raising event has arisen for us today; we shall surely obtain the fulfillment of our goals; the opportune moment has been attained by us.

Hearing the word 'Buddha', joy arose in those deities at that very moment; saying 'Buddha, Buddha', they stand with joined palms.

Various beings in the sky, with joined palms, produce sounds of 'Hiṃ', 'Sādhu', shouts of joy, and expressions of delight.

'O Great Hero, the wheel-marks on your feet, adorned with banners, thunderbolts, flags, finials, and goads, are truly beautiful,' they sing, whistle, play instruments, strike their arms, and dance. They scatter five-colored Mandārava flowers mixed with sandalwood powder.

In those words: He is called 'Satthā' (Teacher) because he instructs for the benefit of this world and the next. He is called 'Ketu' (Pinnacle) because he is like a pinnacle in the sense of being worthy of respect. He is called 'Dhaja' (Flag) because you, O Blessed One, are like a flag in the sense of being raised high and being beautiful to behold.
57:
Alternatively, just as in the world, by merely seeing someone's flag, it is known as 'This is the flag of so-and-so,' and the owner is recognized by the flag, so too, for the sake of attaining the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship and Nibbāna, by merely seeing the Blessed One, the attainment of Nibbāna becomes manifest. Therefore, it is said, 'You are the flag and the sacrificial post.' The meaning is that you are the sacrificial post (yūpa) erected for the purpose of performing all sacrifices, starting from generosity and ending with the knowledge of the destruction of taints, as taught in the Kūṭadanta Sutta. 'Parāyana' means refuge (final resort). 'Patiṭṭhā' means that just as the great earth is the support and foundation for all living beings, so too are you the foundation. 'Dīpa' means a lamp. Just as a lamp lit for beings in fourfold darkness can show forms, so too are you the lamp that shows the ultimate meaning to beings in the darkness of ignorance. Alternatively, just as an island in the great ocean is a refuge for beings whose ships are wrecked, so too are you called 'Dīpa' because you are like an island for beings sinking in the ocean of Saṃsāra where no support can be found.

'Dvipaduttama' means the supreme among bipeds. Here, since there is no characteristic of 'specification' (niddhāraṇa), there is no prohibition of the genitive tatpuruṣa compound; however, a compound with a genitive case having the characteristic of specification is prohibited. The Fully Enlightened One is indeed supreme among footless beings, bipeds, quadrupeds, many-footed beings, those with form, the formless, the conscious, the unconscious, and those neither-conscious-nor-unconscious. If it is asked, 'Why is he called "Dvipaduttama" here?' it is because of his superior excellence. For when the Supreme One arises in this world, he does not arise among footless, quadrupeds, or many-footed beings; he arises only among bipeds. Among which bipeds? Among humans and devas. When arising among humans, he is born as a Buddha capable of exercising authority over the three-thousandfold great-thousandfold world system. When arising among devas, he is born as a Mahābrahmā who rules over ten thousand world systems. That Mahābrahmā then becomes a provider of allowable items (kappiyakāraka) or a monastery attendant for the Buddha. Thus, because of his even greater excellence than those, he is called 'Dvipaduttama'.

'Dasasahassilokadhātu' means in the ten thousand world systems. 'Mahiddhika' means endowed with great psychic power, meaning of great majesty. 'Parivāretvā' means having surrounded the Blessed One on all sides. 'Pasannā' means those in whom faith has arisen. 'Narāsabha' means the supreme among men (the Buddha). In the phrase 'Aho acchariyaṃ', it is called 'acchariya' because it does not happen constantly, like a blind man climbing a mountain. Or, it is called 'acchariya' because it is associated with wonder. The meaning is that it is worthy of snapping one's fingers, thinking, 'Oh, this is a marvel!'
58: 'Abbhuta' is called 'Abhūta' because it has not happened before. Both 'Abbhuta' and 'Acchariya' are terms for what brings about wonder. 'Lomahaṃsana' means causing the hair to stand on end (horripilation). 'Na medisaṃ bhūtapubbaṃ' means 'I have never seen such a wonder before.' Here, the word 'diṭṭhaṃ' (seen) should be included in the meaning. 'Acchera' means wonderful. 'Sakasakambi bhavane' means in their respective abodes. 'Nisīditvāna' means staying close by. It should be understood that the word 'Devatā' is a common term for both gods and goddesses. 'Hasanti tā' means those deities laugh excessively. Due to the force of joy, their hearts are delighted, and they do not merely smile but laugh loudly. 'Nabe' means in the sky. 'Akāsaṭṭhā' refers to deities residing in celestial mansions and so on in the sky. The same method applies to the earth-dwelling deities (Bhūmaṭṭha). 'Tiṇapanthanivāsino' refers to deities living in grass thickets, bamboo groves, and along paths. Those deities possess great merit and great power. 'Saṅgītiyo pavattenti' means they perform the dances and songs of celestial performers; it means they strive to worship the Tathāgata. 'Ambare' means in the sky. 'Anilañjase' means in the path of the wind (the sky). Since the word 'Ambara' has many meanings, 'Anilañjase' is used, and it is a synonym for the previous term. 'Cammanaddhāni' refers to celestial drums covered with leather. 'Vādenti' means the deities play [the instruments]. 'Saṅkhā' refers to conch shells that are blown. 'Paṇavā' refers to specific medium-sized musical instruments. 'Diṇဍima' refers to small drums and hand-drums. 'Vajjanti' means playing [the instruments]. 'Abbhuto vata no' means 'How wonderful it is for us!' 'Uppajji' means has arisen. 'Lomahaṃsano' means that which causes horripilation. 'Dhuvaṃ' means that since this marvelous Teacher has appeared in the world, we will certainly and surely achieve our welfare; this is the intention. 'Labhāma' means we shall obtain. 'Khaṇo' refers to the ninth moment, the moment of a Buddha's arising (Buddhuppāda-khaṇa), which is free from the eight inopportune moments. 'No' means for us. 'Paṭipādito' means has been obtained. 'Buddhoti tesaṃ sutvāna' means that upon hearing the word 'Buddha,' fivefold joy arose in those deities. 'Tāvade' means at that time. 'Hiṅkārā' are the 'hiṃ-hiṃ' sounds that Yakkhas and others make when they are joyful. 'Sādhukārā' refers to the occurrence of shouts of 'Sādhu' (well done). 'Ukkuṭṭhī' means shouts of acclamation and echoing sounds. 'Pajā' refers to beings such as deities. Some teachers read it as 'various banners and flags are flying in the sky.' 'Gāyanti' means they sing songs connected with the qualities of the Buddha.
59: 'Seḷenti' means they make whistling sounds with their mouths. 'Vādayanti' means they play and employ various lutes such as the great Vipañcikā, those that arouse sensual desire, and other musical instruments to honor the Tathāgata. 'Bhujāni pothenti' means they slap their arms and shoulders (as in a challenge or celebration); here, the change of gender (liṅga-vipariyāsa) should be noted. 'Naccanti ca' means they make others dance and they themselves dance. In the phrase 'Just as there is the wheel-mark on Your feet, O Great Hero,' 'yathā' means 'in which manner.' He is called 'Mahāvīra' (Great Hero) because He is endowed with great energy (viriya). 'Pādesu cakkalakkhaṇaṃ' means that on both the soles of Your feet, the wheel-mark shines, complete with a thousand spokes, a rim, and a hub, and perfect in every aspect. This word 'cakka' (wheel) is seen in contexts such as sampatti-cakka (wheel of prosperity), rathaṅga-cakka (chariot wheel), iriyāpatha-cakka (wheel of postures), dāna-cakka (wheel of giving), ratana-cakka (wheel-treasure), dhamma-cakka (wheel of Dhamma), khura-cakka (razor-wheel/weapon), and lakkhaṇa-cakka (mark-wheel). In passages such as 'Monks, there are these four wheels endowed with which deities and humans [prosper]...', it is seen as sampatti-cakka. In 'As the chariot wheel follows the hoofprint of the ox...', it is seen as rathaṅga-cakka. In 'Four wheels, nine doors...', it is seen as iriyāpatha-cakka. In the Jātaka Pali, 'Give, enjoy, and be not negligent; set the wheel of giving in motion for all beings,' it is seen as dāna-cakka. In 'The divine wheel-treasure appeared,' it is seen as ratana-cakka. In 'The wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion by Me,' it is seen as dhamma-cakka. In the Jātaka Pali, 'On the head of the man smitten by desire, the razor-wheel spins,' it is seen as khura-cakka or weapon-wheel. In 'Wheel-marks were born on the soles of the feet,' it is seen as lakkhaṇa-cakka. Here too, it should be understood as the lakkhaṇa-cakka. 'Dhaja-vajira-paṭākā, vaḍḍhamānaṅkusācitaṃ' means the wheel-mark on the feet is adorned and surrounded by banners, thunderbolts, flags, auspicious vessels (or garlands), and goads. When the wheel-mark is mentioned, the remaining marks, the eighty minor marks, and the fathom-wide aura are also included. Therefore, the body of the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor marks, and the fathom-wide aura, is exceedingly beautiful, like a Pāricchattaka tree in full bloom, like a pond of blossoming lotuses, like a golden portal decorated with various jewels, or like the sky radiant with the light of stars, emitting the six-colored Buddha-rays that flicker and dart here and there. Now, to show the perfection of the Buddha's physical body (rūpa-kāya) and Dhamma-body (dhamma-kāya), the following verse is spoken: "The Buddha is incomparable in His form, in His virtue, in His concentration, and in His wisdom. He is equal only to the Buddhas who are incomparable in liberation and in the preaching of the Dhamma-cakka." In that verse, the word 'rūpa' is found in the sense of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), the realm of form (rūpabhava), the kasiṇa-sign, cause (paccaya), the physical body, color (vaṇṇa), and shape (saṇṭhāna). How did the Buddha preach, saying, 'All form—past, future, or present...'?
60:
Now, to demonstrate the perfection of the Blessed One's physical body (rūpakāya) and Dhamma body (dhammakāya), this verse was spoken:

“In physical form, in virtue, in concentration, and in wisdom, he is peerless; in the liberation [of fruition] and in the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, he is the equal of the unequaled.”

In that verse, the word ‘rūpe’ (in physical form) uses the term ‘rūpa’, which is found in the senses of the aggregate of form, form-existence, the kasina-sign, causal condition, the physical body, color, and shape/configuration. When the Buddha taught, “Whatever form—past, future, or present...” (M. Ni. 1.361, 3.86, 89; Vibh. 2; Mahāva. 22), it is found in the sense of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). When he taught, “He develops the path for rebirth in the form realm” (Dha. Sa. 160-161; Vibh. 624), it is found in the sense of form-existence (rūpabhava). When he taught, “Not perceiving form internally, he sees forms externally” (Dī. Ni. 3.338; Ma. Ni. 2.249; A. Ni. 1.435-442; Dha. Sa. 204-205), it is found in the sense of the kasina-sign (kasiṇanimitta). When he taught, “Monks, evil unwholesome states arise with a cause (sarūpā), not without a cause (no arūpā)” (A. Ni. 2.83), it is found in the sense of causal condition (paccaya). When he taught, “Space enclosed [by an appearance] is simply designated as form” (Ma. Ni. 1.306), it is found in the sense of the physical body (sarīra). When he taught, “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises” (Ma. Ni. 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425-426; Saṃ. Ni. 4.60; Kathā. 465), it is found in the sense of color (vaṇṇa). When he taught, “Measured by form, pleased by form” (A. Ni. 4.65), it is found in the sense of shape/configuration (saṇṭhāna). In this context also, it should be understood in the sense of shape/configuration (A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.1.1).

‘Sīle’ refers to the fourfold virtue. ‘Samādhimhi’ refers to the threefold concentration. ‘Paññāya’ refers to mundane and supramundane wisdom. ‘Asādiso’ means peerless or incomparable. ‘Vimuttiyā’ refers to the liberation of fruition (phalavimutti). ‘Asamasamo’ means that because he is equal in virtue and so on to the past Buddhas who are themselves unequaled (asama), he is called ‘equal to the unequaled’ (asamasamo). By this much, the perfection of the Blessed One's physical body has been shown.

Now, to show the Blessed One's physical strength (kāyabala) and so on, it was said:

“The strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is in your body, your natural strength; in the power of psychic potency and in the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, you are unequaled.”

In that verse, ‘dasanāgabalaṃ’ means the strength of ten Chaddanta elephants. Indeed, the strength of the Tathāgata is twofold: physical strength (kāyabala) and the strength of knowledge (ñāṇabala). Among these, physical strength should be understood according to the lineage of elephants. How?
61:
“The Kāḷāvaka lineage, the Gaṅgeyya lineage, the Paṇḍara, the Tamba, the Piṅgala, the Gandha, the Maṅgala, the Hema, the Uposatha, and the Chaddanta—these are the ten.” (Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.148; Saṃ. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.2.22; A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.10.21; Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.198; Vibh. Aṭṭha. 760; Udā. Aṭṭha. 75; Cūḷani. Aṭṭha. 81; Paṭi. Ma. Aṭṭha. 2.2.44).

These ten lineages of elephants should be known. Kāḷāvaka refers to the ordinary elephant lineage. The physical strength of ten men is equal to the strength of one Kāḷāvaka elephant. The strength of ten Kāḷāvaka elephants is equal to the strength of one Gaṅgeyya elephant. By this method, it should be traced up to the strength of a Chaddanta elephant. The strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is equal to one [unit of] the Tathāgata’s strength; this is called Nārāyaṇa strength or Vajira strength. In terms of ordinary elephants, that strength is equal to the strength of a thousand crores of elephants; in terms of men, it is equal to the strength of ten thousand crores of men. This is the natural physical strength (kāyabala) of the Tathāgata. As for the strength of knowledge (ñāṇabala), it is immeasurable. The Ten Powers of Knowledge (dasabalañāṇa), the Fourfold Intrepidity (catuvesārajjañāṇa), the unshakability in the eight assemblies, the knowledge of the four types of birth, the knowledge of the five destinations, and the fourteen types of Buddha-knowledge—these constitute the strength of knowledge. In this context, however, physical strength is intended. “Your natural strength is in your body” means that such natural strength exists in your physical body. Therefore, “dasanāgabala” means the strength of ten Chaddanta noble elephants.

Now, wishing to show the strength of knowledge, it was said: “In the power of psychic potency and in the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, you have no equal.” Therein, “no equal in the power of psychic potency” refers to being peerless and incomparable in psychic powers such as the power of transformation (vikubbaniddhi) and the power of determination (adhiṭṭhānaniddhi). “In the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma” means having no equal in the knowledge of teaching (desanāñāṇa).

Now, to show the exhortation to pay homage to the Tathāgata, saying, “Worship that Teacher who is endowed with such qualities, who is the sole leader of the entire world,” it was said:

“Worship the Great Sage, the Compassionate One,
The Protector of the World, who is thus endowed with all qualities,
And complete in all limbs.”

In that verse, the word “evaṃ” (thus) is a particle indicating the manner already described. In the word “sabbaguṇūpetaṃ,” the word “sabba” (all) signifies without remainder. The word “guṇa” is well-known in many meanings. Indeed, for that reason, this word ‘guṇa’ is evident in the sense of ‘layer’ in the Pali: “Monks, among new clothes, a double-layered (duguṇa) outer robe...” In the sense of periods of time such as morning, midday, evening...
62:
The word 'guṇa' is found in various senses. Indeed, in the passage, 'Monks, I allow a double-layered (diguṇa) outer robe for new cloths,' it is found in the sense of a layer or fold. In the passage, 'Times pass, nights fly by, the stages of life (vayoguṇa) desert one in succession,' it is found in the sense of a mass or aggregate. In the passage, 'A hundredfold (sataguṇa) benefit of a gift is to be expected,' it is found in the sense of benefit or blessing. In the passages, 'The large intestine and the intestinal membrane (antaguṇa)' and 'One should make many garlands (mālāguṇa),' it is found in the sense of a bond or string. In the passage, 'I have acquired the supernormal powers endowed with eightfold qualities (aṭṭhaguṇa),' it is found in the sense of attainment or excellence. In this context (sabbaguṇūpetaṃ) as well, it should be understood in the sense of attainment. Therefore, the meaning is: one who is endowed with and possessed of all mundane and supramundane qualities and all attainments.

'Sabbaṅgasamupāgataṃ' means being fully endowed with all the Buddha-qualities or the factors of virtue. 'Mahāmuni' means the Great Sage, so called because he is superior to other sages such as Paccekabuddhas. 'Kāruṇikaṃ' means the Compassionate One, because he is associated with the quality of great compassion. 'Lokanāthaṃ' means the sole Protector of the entire world. It means the Protector of the World because all beings in the world aspire, saying, 'May this Blessed One be the one who destroys and calms the oppression of our suffering.'

Now, to show that the Possessor of Ten Powers is worthy of all forms of respect, it is said:

'Salutation, praise in absence, 
Bowing and praise in presence, 
Anjali and offerings—all these 
You, O Lord, are worthy to receive.

Whatever beings in the world are worthy of honor, 
Those who deserve such salutation, 
You are the most excellent of them all, O Great Hero, 
There is no one equal to You.'

In those verses, 'Abhivādanaṃ' means causing others to salute oneself. 'Thomanaṃ' means praise in one's absence. 'Vandanaṃ' means bowing down. 'Pasaṃsanaṃ' means praise in one's presence. 'Namassanaṃ' means making the anjali (palms together) or salutation with the mind. 'Pūjanaṃ' means honoring with flowers, scents, unguents, and so on. 'Sabbā' means that You, O Lord, are worthy and fit to receive all those various kinds of special honors mentioned.
