'Ye keci loke vandaneyyā' refers to all those in the world who should be honored or are worthy of honor because they deserve salutation. 'Ye' means those who...
63:
...are worthy of salutation in the world. This is merely a synonym for the preceding term. 'Sabbaseṭṭho' means the most excellent or supreme among all of them. The meaning is: 'O Great Hero (Mahāvīra), there is no one in the world equal to You.'

Then, after the Blessed One displayed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) and created a jeweled walkway (ratanacaṅkama), while he was walking upon it, the Venerable Sāriputta was staying at Rajagaha on the Vulture Peak Mountain (Gijjhakūṭa) with five hundred attendant monks. Then the Elder, looking toward the Blessed One, saw him walking on the jeweled walkway in the sky at Kapilavatthu. Therefore, it is said:

'Sāriputta, of great wisdom, 
Skilled in concentration and absorption, 
Standing right there on Vulture Peak, 
Beholds the Leader of the World.'

In that verse, 'Sāriputto' means the son of the Brahmin woman named Rūpasārī. 'Mahāpañño' means one endowed with great sixteen-fold wisdom. In the term 'Samādhijjhānakovido,' 'Samādhi' means concentration, because it places the mind evenly and fixes it on an object. That concentration is of three types: with initial and sustained thought, with sustained thought only, and without both initial and sustained thought. 'Jhāna' refers to the first, second, third, and fourth jhānas. By these terms starting with the first jhāna, the jhānas of loving-kindness (mettā-jhāna) and others are also included. Jhāna is also of two kinds: 'Lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna' (meditation on characteristics) and 'Ārammaṇūpanijjhāna' (meditation on the object). Among them, the insight wisdom (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that closely contemplates characteristics such as impermanence is called 'Lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna.' The first jhāna and others are called 'Jhāna' because they closely contemplate the object or because they burn away the opposing hindrances (nīvaraṇa). One who is skilled and proficient in these concentrations and absorptions is 'Samādhijjhānakovido.' 'Gijjhakūṭe' means he beheld him while standing on the mountain of that name.

'Like a king of Sal trees in full bloom' means he beheld the Blessed One, the Possessor of Ten Powers, who is like a king of Sal trees—having a perfectly round trunk, branches adorned with well-emerged, abundant, and tender leaf-buds and sprouts, and being in full bloom all over. This is to be connected with the word 'beheld' (olokesi) as follows: with virtue as the root, the aggregate of concentration as the trunk, wisdom as the branches, supernormal powers as the flowers, and the fruit of Arahantship as the fruit. 'Like the moon in the sky' means he beheld the Buddha-moon, who, like the full moon in the autumn season, is free from the obstructions of clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rahu, is surrounded by a host of stars, dispels the darkness of defilements, and causes the white lotus-groves of beings to be tamed (veneyya) to bloom. This word 'yathā' (as/like)...
64:
It means that one beholds the moon-like noble Sage (Muni), who dispels the darkness of all defilements and causes the white lotus groves of veneyya beings (those to be tamed) to bloom. The word 'yathā' is merely a particle. 'Majjhanhikēva sūriyaṃ' means shining brightly like the sun with its circle of intense rays at midday. 'Narāsabhaṃ' refers to the Noble One among men (the Buddha).

It means one who is radiant, possessing a delightful facial complexion like the glory of the full moon in the autumn season (the month of Kattika), with a noble body adorned with the major and minor marks, and shining with the supreme glory of a Buddha. 'Dīparukkhaṃ vā' is like a lit lamp-stand. 'Taruṇasūriyaṃva uggataṃ' means shining with a cool nature like the rising young sun. The youthfulness of the sun is spoken of in reference to its rising. Unlike the moon, the sun has no waning or waxing. 'Byāmappabhānurañjitaṃ' means adorned with the fathom-wide radiance. 'Dhīraṃ passati lokanāyakaṃ' means one beholds the Lord of the World, who possesses incomparable and steadfast concentration (samādhi) in the entire world.

At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, while standing on Gijjhakūṭa Hill—whose peaks are touched by clusters of extremely cool clouds, perfumed by various fragrant trees and flowers, and are exceedingly beautiful and wonderful—saw the Blessed One walking on a cloister made of all kinds of jewels, surrounded by hosts of devas and brahmas from ten thousand world-systems, and endowed with the supreme glory of a Buddha and incomparable Buddha-grace. He thought, 'Now, I shall approach the Blessed One and request Him to teach the Buddhavamsa discourse, which illustrates the attributes of a Buddha.' Having thought thus, he assembled the five hundred monks who lived with him. Therefore, it is said:
'In an instant, he assembled five hundred monks, who had done what was to be done, who were endowed with the quality of Tādi, whose taints were exhausted, and who were stainless.'

In that verse, 'pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ' means five hundred monks; here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative case. 'Katakiccānaṃ' means those who have completed the sixteen functions of the path regarding the Four Noble Truths through full understanding (pariññā), abandonment (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriyā), and development (bhāvanā) by means of the four paths. 'Khīṇāsavānaṃ' refers to those whose four taints (āsava) are exhausted. 'Vimalānaṃ' means those who are free from stains, or it means those whose mental continuities are extremely pure because their taints are exhausted. 'Khaṇena' means in just a moment. 'Sannipātayī' means he assembled them.

Now, to show the reason for the gathering and the departure of those monks, the verses beginning with 'Lokappasādanaṃ' were spoken:
'The Buddha displayed the miracle named "Lokappasādana" (Gladdening the World). We too shall go there and pay homage to the Victorious One. Come, let us all go; we shall praise the Victorious One. By beholding the Lord of the World, we shall dispel our doubt.'
65: Now, to show the reason for the gathering and the departure of those monks—'He has shown the miracle named Lokappasādana, which gladdens the world; we too shall go there and pay homage to the Victorious One. Come, let us all go; we shall request the Victorious One; by beholding the Leader of the World, we shall dispel our doubt'—these verses were spoken. In those verses, 'lokappasādanaṃ nāma' is called the Lokappasādana miracle because it causes the gladdening of the world. There is also a reading 'ullokappasādanaṃ nāma', the meaning of which is the miracle of revealing the world. That miracle is described as the determination (adhiṭṭhāna) to create a single light in the interval from the Akaniṭṭha realm above down to the Avīci hell below, making all beings see one another. 'Nidassayī' means He showed. 'Amhepi' means we too. 'Tattha' means in the place where the Blessed One is. 'Vandissāma' means we shall pay homage to the Blessed One's feet with our heads. Here, of the two words 'amhepi' and 'mayaṃ', the former should be understood as connected with the action of going, and the latter with the action of paying homage. Otherwise, one cannot escape the fault of tautology (punarutti). 'Etha' means come. Regarding the phrase 'kaṅkhaṃ vinodayissāma'—it might be asked: 'Since Arahants have no doubt whatsoever, why did the Elder speak thus?' It is true that such doubt is entirely eradicated by the first path. As it is said: 'Which states are to be abandoned by vision (the path of stream-entry)? The four consciousnesses associated with wrong view, the consciousness accompanied by skeptical doubt, and the greed, hatred, delusion, and conceit that lead to the lower realms, as well as the defilements that stand in the same place as that wrong view and doubt.' Although the doubt known as skeptical doubt (vicikicchā) does not exist, there is still the 'not knowing of designations' (paññatti-ajānana). The Elder wished to ask the Blessed One about the Buddhavamsa; however, that is the domain of Buddhas alone, not the domain of Paccekabuddhas or disciples. Therefore, it should be understood that the Elder spoke thus because it was not their domain. 'Vinodayissāma' means we shall dispel.
66:
Then those five hundred monks, having heard the words of the Venerable Sāriputta, took their own bowls and triple robes. Like great elephants well-armored, they had destroyed the defilements in various ways, cut the bonds, had few wishes, were contented, secluded, and unentangled with people. Being endowed with virtue, concentration, wisdom, the fruit of Arahantship, and the knowledge and vision of the fruit of Arahantship, they assembled in haste. Therefore, it is said:

“Having accepted, saying ‘Sādhu’, being prudent and with restrained senses, taking their bowls and robes, they approached in haste.”

In that verse, the word “Sādhu” is seen in meanings such as request (āyācana), acceptance (sampaṭicchana), joy (sampahaṃsana), and goodness (sundara). This is true. Therefore, this word “Sādhu” is found in the sense of a request in such passages as: “Sādhu (Please), Bhante, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief.” It is found in the sense of acceptance in: “The monk, having rejoiced and approved of what the Blessed One said, saying ‘Sādhu (It is well), Bhante’.” It is found in the sense of joy in: “Sādhu, Sādhu (Well said, well said), Sāriputta.”

It is found in the sense of goodness in: “Sādhu (It is good) for a king to delight in the Dhamma; Sādhu (it is good) for a man to be wise; Sādhu (it is good) not to betray friends; not doing evil is a blessing.” In this context, however, it should be understood in the sense of acceptance. Therefore, it means accepting the Elder's words by saying “Sādhu, suṭṭhu” (It is well, it is good). “Nipaka” means those who are mature and wise. “Saṃvutindriya” means those whose sense-doors are guarded, those endowed with sense restraint. “Taramānā” means in haste. “Upāgamuṃ” means they approached the Elder.

50-1. Now, the Reciters (Sangītikārakas), wishing to show the circumstances of the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, spoke the verses beginning with “Khīṇāsavehi vimalehi”. In that verse, “dantehi” refers to those who are tamed in body and mind. “Uttame dame” refers to the fruit of Arahantship; it should be understood in the locative sense of cause. “Tehi bhikkhūhi” refers to those five hundred monks. “Mahāgaṇī” means one who has a great group (gaṇa) either by virtue (sīla) etc., or by way of number. Alternatively, “mahāgaṇa” means a group that is great in qualities like virtue through various terms, and one who possesses such a group is “mahāgaṇī”. “Laḷanto devova gagane” means he approached the Blessed One like a god sporting in the sky with the splendor of psychic power.
67:
He is thus called Mahāgaṇī. He approached the Blessed One, who was resplendent in the sky, like a god with the splendor of psychic power.

Now, for the purpose of showing the manner of their approach, saying “Those monks, being in such a state (or having reached such distinction), approached,” the passage beginning with “Ukkāsitañca khipitaṃ” was spoken. In that verse, “ukkāsitañca” refers to the sound of coughing, and “khipitaṃ” refers to the sound of sneezing. “Ajjhupekkhiyā” means disregarding, meaning not doing both of those. “Subbatā” means those who possess very pure ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa). “Sappatissā” means those who are respectful and humble in conduct.

“Sayambhūṃ” refers to the state of Buddhahood attained by fulfilling the perfections by oneself without the guidance of others. “Accuggataṃ” means newly risen. “Candaṃ vā” means like the moon. The connection of the words should be understood as: they saw the Blessed One shining in the sky like the moon in the sky. Here too, the word “yathā” is merely an indeclinable particle (nipāta) without a specific meaning.

“Vijjūṃ vā” means like a solid mass of lightning. It means having such a nature as if lightning were to remain for a long time. “Gagane yathā” means as in the sky. Here too, the word “yathā” is merely a particle. Hereafter, in such places, the word “yathā” should be understood as a mere particle.

“Rahadamiva vippasannaṃ” refers to water that is exceptionally clear and undisturbed, like a very deep and wide great lake. “Suphullaṃ padumaṃ yathā” should be understood as meaning like a lake with a well-bloomed forest of lotuses. There is also a reading “Suphullaṃ kamalaṃ yathā”, which means like a well-bloomed forest of lotuses because of its loveliness.

Then those monks, with the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, at their head, placed their joined palms on their heads and prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, which were adorned with the wheel marks. Therefore, the passage beginning with “Añjaliṃ paggahetvāna, tuṭṭhahaṭṭhā pamoditā” was spoken. In that verse, “nipatanti” means they prostrated or worshipped. “Cakkalakkhaṇe” means the foot which has the mark of a wheel; in that wheel-marked foot. Although it is said “at the foot” by way of class, it means they prostrated at the soles of the feet adorned with the Blessed One's wheel marks.

Now, wishing to show the names of some of those Elders, the verses beginning with “Sāriputto mahāpañño, koraṇḍasamasādiso” were spoken. In that verse, “koraṇḍasamasādiso” means having a color like the color of the Koraṇḍa flower (yellow amaranth). If this is the case, although one should say “koraṇḍasamo” or “koraṇḍasadiso”, why...
68:
## Sāriputta, of great wisdom, like a Koraṇḍa flower. Skilled in concentration and jhāna, he pays homage to the Leader of the World.

If it is asked regarding the double mention of "samasādiso" (like/similar), it is not a fault. He is of an appearance similar to the Koraṇḍa flower simply because of his likeness to it. The intention is not to use an exaggerated expression. In the term "samādhijjhānakusalo" (skilled in concentration and jhāna), this word "kusala" is first seen in the senses of health (ārogya), blamelessness (anavajja), skillfulness (cheka), and happy result (sukhavipāka), etc. This word "kusala" is seen in the sense of health in passages such as, "Is the venerable one healthy (kusala)? Is the venerable one free from ailment?" It is seen in the sense of blamelessness in passages such as, "Venerable Ānanda, what kind of bodily conduct of the Blessed One is wholesome (kusala)? Great King, that bodily conduct of the Blessed One which is blameless (anavajja) [is wholesome]." It is seen in the sense of skillfulness in passages such as, "You are skilled (kusala) in the various parts of a chariot." It is seen in the sense of happy result in passages such as, "Due to the performance and accumulation of wholesome (kusala) kamma [eye-consciousness arises]." Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of skillfulness. "Vandate" means he worshipped.

## Thundering like a dark cloud, like a blue lotus in hue. Unequaled in the power of psychic success, Moggallāna of great psychic power.

"Gajjitā" (thundering) is so called because of the act of thundering. "Kālamegho va" (like a dark cloud) means he thunders in the sphere of psychic power like a dark rain cloud carrying blue-black water. "Nīluppalasamasādiso" means having a color similar to a blue lotus. The meaning here should be understood in the same manner as mentioned below. "Moggallāno" is the Elder Kolita, who received this name by way of his lineage (gotta).

## And the Elder Mahākassapa too, resembling molten gold. Established as foremost in ascetic qualities, praised and extolled by the Teacher.

In the phrase "Mahākassapopi ca," he is called "Mahākassapa" because he is great (mahā) in comparison to the junior elders such as Uruvela-Kassapa, Nadī-Kassapa, Gayā-Kassapa, and Kumāra-Kassapa. The words "pi ca" serve the purpose of commendation and conjunction. "Uttattakanakasannibho" means having a complexion like polished gold. In the term "dhutaguṇe," the Dhamma is called "dhuta" because it shakes off (dhunana) defilements; "dhutaguṇa" refers to the "dhuta-dhamma" (ascetic practice). What is the "dhuta-dhamma"? The five qualities—fewness of wishes (appicchatā), contentment (santuṭṭhitā), effacement (sallekhatā), seclusion (pavivekatā), and specific purposefulness (idamaṭṭhikatā)—are called "dhuta-dhamma" according to the words "depending only on fewness of wishes," etc., because they are the attendants of the volition of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga-cetanā). Alternatively, wisdom (ñāṇa) is called "dhuta" because it shakes off defilements. In those ascetic qualities, "agganikkhitto" means one who is placed as the foremost, the best, or the pinnacle. The meaning is that he was placed in that specific position (ṭhānantara) by the words: "Monks, among my bhikkhu disciples who are speakers of ascetic practices (dhutavādānaṃ), Mahākassapa is the foremost (etadaggaṃ)." This word "agga" is seen in the senses of beginning (ādi), tip or end (koṭi), portion (koṭṭhāsa), and best (seṭṭha), etc.

To elaborate on that: It is seen in the sense of "beginning" in the words from the Upāli Sutta of the Gahapati-vagga, Majjhima-paṇṇāsa, Majjhima Nikāya: "Friend gatekeeper, from today onwards (ajjatagge), I close the door to Nigaṇṭha men and Nigaṇṭha women." It is seen in the sense of "tip or end" in such words as: "One should touch the tip of that finger only with the tip of that finger," "the tip of sugarcane," "the tip of bamboo." It is seen in the sense of "portion" in such words as: "the sour portion," "the sweet portion," and "Monks, I allow distribution by room-portion or by precinct-portion." It is seen in the sense of "best" in the words from the fourth sutta of the Cakka-vagga, Paṭhama-paṇṇāsa, Catukka-nipāta, Aṅguttara Nikāya: "Monks, among beings without feet, those with two feet, etc., the Tathāgata is said to be the foremost (agga) among those beings." Beings without feet are snakes, fish, etc. Beings with two feet are humans, birds, etc. Beings with four feet are elephants, horses, etc. Beings with many feet are centipedes, etc. Beings with form are also...
69:
"O gatekeeper, from today onwards I close the door to Nigaṇṭha men and Nigaṇṭha women," etc. In such passages (Majjhima Nikāya, Upāli Sutta), the word 'agga' is found in the sense of 'beginning' (ādi). "With that very finger-tip, one should touch that finger-tip," "the tip of sugarcane, the tip of bamboo," etc. In such terms, it is found in the sense of 'tip' or 'extremity' (koṭi). "A portion of sour taste or a portion of sweet taste," "Monks, I allow you to distribute by monastery-portion or by cell-portion," etc. In such terms, it is found in the sense of 'portion' or 'share' (koṭṭhāsa). "Monks, as far as there are beings, whether footless or two-footed... the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them," etc. In such terms, it is found in the sense of 'foremost' or 'best' (seṭṭha). In this context, 'agga' should be understood in the sense of 'best'. It also applies to the sense of 'pinnacle'. The Elder is both the best in his own field and has reached the pinnacle. Therefore, it is said, "agganikkhitto" (one who is placed as the foremost). 'Agga' means noble, or one who has reached the pinnacle. 'Thomita' means praised (pasaṃsita) by devas, humans, and others. 'Satthu vaṇṇita' means praised by the Teacher, as in: "Monks, Kassapa approaches families like the moon; he draws back his body and mind, is always a newcomer among families, and is not impudent," and other such various methods of the Suttas. It means that the Venerable Mahākassapa, who was thus praised and commended, also pays homage to the Blessed One.

The Venerable Anuruddha, who is the foremost among those possessing the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), who has a large following of monks, and who is a noble relative of the Blessed One, stays in the very presence of the Blessed One.

'Dibba-cakkhūnaṃ' means the foremost (seṭṭha) among the monks who possess the divine eye. As it was said: "Monks, among my monk disciples who possess the divine eye, the foremost is Anuruddha." The Elder Anuruddha was the son of the Sakyan King Amitodana, the younger brother of the Buddha's father; he was the younger brother of King Mahānāma, possessed great merit, and was extremely delicate. He renounced the world from the life of a householder to the homeless life as the seventh member of his group. The sequence of his ordination is mentioned in the Saṅghabhedaka Khandhaka. 'Avidūre' means in the very presence of the Blessed One.

The Venerable Upāli, who is skilled in offenses and non-offenses, and in curable and incurable offenses, who was appointed as the foremost in the field of Vinaya, and who was praised by the Blessed One, (pays homage to the Blessed One).

Skillfulness in offenses and non-offenses is called 'āpatti-anāpattiyā'. Skillfulness in curable (sappaṭikamma) and incurable (appaṭikamma) offenses is called 'satekicchāya'. Among them, curable offenses are of six kinds, and incurable offenses are the Pārājika offenses. There is also a reading "āpatti-anāpattiyā, satekicchāya kovido," which has the same meaning. 'Vinaye' refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka. 'Agganikkhitto' means, "Monks, among my monk disciples who are Vinaya-holders, the foremost is Upāli," and so forth...
70:
"...the foremost is Upāli" (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Etadagga Vagga). This means he was appointed to the position of the foremost. 'Upāli' refers to the Elder Upāli. 'Satthu vaṇṇita' means praised and commended by the Teacher. It is said that the Elder learned the Vinaya Piṭaka in the presence of the Tathāgata himself and resolved the three cases—the Bhārukaccha case, the Ajjuka case, and the Kumārakassapa case—by comparing and coordinating them with the Buddha's Omniscient Knowledge. Therefore, it is said that the Elder was praised by the Teacher in such ways as being the foremost among the Vinaya-holders.

'Sukhumanipuṇatthapaṭividdho' means one who has penetrated subtle and profound meanings, or one who possesses subtle meanings that are difficult to see. 'Kathikānaṃ pavaro' means the best among the preachers of Dhamma. Because he was placed in the Etadagga Pali as: "Monks, among my monk disciples who are Dhamma-preachers, the foremost is Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta," he is called 'kathikānaṃ pavaro'. 'Gaṇī' means one who has a group or a following of monks. It is said that there were five hundred noble sons who were ordained in the presence of the Elder. All of them were born in the birthplace of the Possessor of Ten Powers (the Buddha), were residents of the Sakyan kingdom, were all Arahants, and were all masters of the ten subjects of discourse (dasakathāvatthu). Therefore, he is called 'gaṇī'. 'Isi' is called such because he seeks (esati/gavesati) wholesome states. 'Mantāṇiyā putto' means the son of the Brahmin lady named Mantāṇī. 'Puṇṇa' is his name. 'Vissuto' means famous for his qualities such as fewness of wishes.

As for the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, after the Teacher attained Enlightenment and set the Noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, he came in due course to Kapilavatthu while the Buddha was residing near Rājagaha. He ordained his own nephew, the youth named Puṇṇa, and after paying homage and taking leave of the Blessed One, he himself went to Lake Chaddanta to reside. The Elder Puṇṇa, however, although he had come with the Elder (Koṇḍañña) to see the Blessed One, remained in Kapilavatthu, thinking, "I will go to the presence of the Possessor of Ten Powers only after bringing my task of monkhood to its completion (attaining Arahantship)." While practicing wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), he attained Arahantship before long and then approached the Blessed One. In this context, the two Elders, Anuruddha and Upāli, are presented as if they were ordained on the day the Buddha entered the city of Kapilavatthu and met his relatives. However, that presentation does not agree with the Khandhaka Pali and the Commentary. It should be accepted only after careful investigation.
71:
Then the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts of the five hundred monks led by the Venerable Sāriputta, strove to speak of his own virtues. Therefore, it is said:

“The Sage, skilled in similes, having known their thoughts, the Great Hero who cuts off doubt, spoke of his own virtues.”

In that verse, ‘Opammakusalo’ means skilled in similes. ‘Kaṅkhacchedo’ means the one who cuts off the doubts of all beings.

Now, as the Blessed One speaks of his own virtues, to show those virtues:

“There are four incalculables whose beginning or end is not known: the collection of beings, space, the infinite world-systems, and the immeasurable knowledge of the Buddha. These four incalculables cannot be known.”

In that verse, ‘Cattāro’ refers to the division of number. ‘Ete’ points to the meanings to be mentioned. ‘Asaṅkhyeyyā’ are called incalculable because they cannot be counted; the meaning is that they transcend the path of counting. ‘Koṭi’ is the limit, either the beginning or the end. ‘Yesaṃ’ means of those four incalculables. ‘Na nāyati’ means not known or not apparent. To show those four incalculables of the aforementioned types, he said ‘Sattakāyo’ and so on. ‘Sattakāyo’ means the collection of beings; the collection of beings is infinite, boundless, and immeasurable. Likewise, space has no end. Likewise, the world-systems are indeed infinite. The knowledge of the Buddha, which is the Knowledge of Omniscience (Sabbaññutañāṇa), is immeasurable. ‘Na sakkā ete vijānituṃ’ means that because these four incalculables are infinite, they cannot be known.

Now, the Blessed One, wishing to expand the Dhamma teaching to the multitude of devas and humans who were experiencing unprecedented wonder and amazement at his display of psychic power, said, “What is this wonder? There is a wonder and marvel even more distinguished and excellent than this. Listen to that teaching of mine,” and spoke the following verse:

“What is this wonder in the world, this display of my psychic power? There are many other wonders, marvelous and hair-raising.”
72:
## In that verse, the word ‘Kiṃ’ is a word of rejection. ‘Etaṃ’ is said with reference to this display of psychic power. The word ‘Yaṃ’ is seen in the accusative case (upayogavacana) in such Pali passages as ‘Yaṃ taṃ apucchimha...’. It is seen in the causal sense (kāraṇavacana) in such Pali passages as ‘Aṭṭhānametaṃ bhikkhave... yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā...’. It is seen in the locative case (bhumma) in the Pali ‘Yaṃ vipassī bhagavā kappe udapādi’. It is seen in the nominative case (paccattavacana) in such Pali passages as ‘Yaṃ kho me bhante devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sammukhā sutaṃ...’. Here also, it should be understood in the nominative sense. It is intended to show that not only is there such a display of psychic power in the Buddha, but there are also many other wonderful and extraordinary virtues.

Now, wishing to show those wonders, he spoke the verse beginning with: ‘Yadāhaṃ tusite kāye, santusito nāmahaṃ tadā, dasasahassī samāgamma, yācanti pañjalī mamaṃ.’

In that verse, ‘Yadā’ means at which time. ‘Ahaṃ’ is a reference to himself. ‘Tusite kāye’ means in the group of devas known as Tusita. When I, the Buddha, had fulfilled the thirty perfections, made the five great sacrifices, reached the pinnacle of the three modes of conduct—conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariya), conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariya), and conduct for the benefit of Buddhahood (buddhattha-cariya)—given the great gifts in sets of seven hundred, and shaken the earth seven times, I passed away from the life of King Vessantara and, in the second thought-moment, was reborn in the Tusita realm. At that time, I was the king of devas named Santusita. ‘Dasasahassī samāgamma’ means that the deities from ten thousand world-systems gathered. ‘Yācanti pañjalī mamaṃ’ means they approached me and entreated, “O Noble One, when you fulfilled the ten perfections, you did not fulfill them desiring the prosperity of Sakka, Māra, Brahmā, or a Universal Monarch. You fulfilled them desiring Buddhahood for the sake of delivering the world. O Noble One, now is the time for you to become a Buddha; the season has arrived for Buddhahood.” Therefore, he said: ‘ကာလော ခေါ တေ မဟာဝီရ၊ ဥပ္ပဇ္ဇ မာတုကုစ္ဆိယံ၊ သဒေဝကံ တာရယန္တော၊ ဗုဇ္ဈဿု အမတံ ပဒံ’.

In that verse, ‘Kālo te’ means it is time for you. ‘Uppajja’ means please take conception. ‘Sadevakaṃ’ means the world together with the devas. In the place of ‘Tārayanto’, it refers to the one who fulfilled the perfections, the one who brought the perfections to their pinnacle, the one who passed away from the life of King Vessantara and took conception in the Tusita heaven, staying there for five hundred and seventy-six million years, the one who, being entreated by the devas and Brahmās, made the five great observations and took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā, the one who stayed in the mother's womb for ten months, the one who lived in the palace for twenty-nine years, the one who, on the day Prince Rāhula was born, went forth into the homeless life riding the horse Kaṇṭhaka with the minister Channa, and having passed through three kingdoms, at the bank of the river named Anomā...
73:
In that verse, 'Kālo te' means "It is the right time for you to become a Buddha," or this very reading 'Kālo te' exists in some versions. 'Uppajja' means "Take rebirth," and there is also a reading 'Okkama'. 'Sadevakaṃ' means the world together with the devas.

Regarding the word 'Tārayanto' (saving/delivering): one who is fulfilling the perfections is said to be saving; one who is bringing the perfections to their peak is said to be saving; one who, after passing away from the life of King Vessantara, took rebirth in the Tusita heaven and remained there for fifty-seven crores and sixty million years is said to be saving; one who, being requested by the devas, made the five great observations and took rebirth in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā, and remained in the mother's womb for ten months is said to be saving; one who remained in the palace for twenty-nine years is said to be saving. One who, on the day Prince Rāhula was born, accompanied by the minister Channa, mounted the horse Kaṇṭhaka and went forth into the forest, and after crossing three kingdoms, became a monk on the bank of the river named Anomā is said to be saving; one who practiced austerities for six years, and on the full moon day of Vesākha (Kason), ascended the seat of enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa), defeated the army of Māra, recollected past lives in the first watch of the night, purified the divine eye in the middle watch, and in the last watch, contemplated the twelve links of Dependent Origination in forward and reverse order and realized the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga) is said to be saving; at the moment of the Fruit of Stream-entry, at the moment of the Path of Once-returning, at the moment of the Fruit of Once-returning, at the moment of the Path of Non-returning, at the moment of the Fruit of Non-returning, at the moment of the Path of Arahantship, and at the moment of the Fruit of Arahantship, he is said to be saving; when he gave the nectar of immortality to the group of five monks along with eighteen crores of devas and Brahmas, from that time onwards he is said to have saved. Therefore, it is said:

## “Sadevakaṃ tārayanto, bujjhassu amataṃ padaṃ.”

Then, although the Bodhisatta was requested by the devas and Brahmas, he did not yet give his consent to them, but made the five great observations regarding the time, the continent, the place, the family, and the limit of the mother's lifespan. Among those five, he first observed the time: "Is it now the right time to become a Buddha, or not?" There, a period when the lifespan is over one hundred thousand years is not the right time. Why? Because birth, aging, and death are not apparent to beings; and the Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas is never free from the three marks of existence. When those Buddhas preach about impermanence, suffering, and non-self, people do not believe, thinking, "What are these people talking about?" Therefore, the realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisamaya) does not occur. When there is no such realization, the Dispensation (Sāsana) is not a means of deliverance from the cycle of rebirth...
74:
...it is so. Therefore, that time of over one hundred thousand years is not the right time. A period when the lifespan is less than one hundred years is also not the right time. Why? Because at that time, beings have abundant defilements, and the advice given to beings with abundant defilements does not remain in the place of advice. Therefore, that time of less than one hundred years is also not the right time. The period when the lifespan is below one hundred thousand years and above one hundred years is called the right time. Seeing that humans now have a lifespan of one hundred years, the Bodhisatta perceived, "It is the time to be reborn."

Then, observing the continent, he saw the continent, thinking, "Buddhas are born only in Jambudīpa." Then, observing the place, thinking, "Jambudīpa is very vast, measuring ten thousand yojanas; in which region do Buddhas arise?" he saw the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). Then, observing the family, he saw the family, thinking, "Buddhas are born only in a noble family esteemed by the world. Now the warrior caste (Khattiya) is the family esteemed by the world. I shall be born in that family. King Suddhodana shall be my father." Then, observing the mother, he considered, "The mother of a Buddha is not flighty or a drunkard; she is one who keeps the five precepts unbroken. This Queen Mahāmāyā is of such nature. She shall be my mother. How long will this mother's life last?" and he saw that she would live for only seven days beyond the ten months of pregnancy.

Having thus observed with these five great observations, he gave his consent to the devas, saying, "Friends, it is the time for me to become a Buddha." After remaining in that Tusita heaven until the end of his lifespan, he passed away from there and took rebirth in the womb of Queen Māyā in the Sakyan royal family. Therefore, it is said:

"When he passed away from the Tusita heaven and entered the mother's womb,
The earth of the ten thousand world systems then trembled."

In that verse, "Okkami" means entered or descended. "Kucchiyaṃ" means in the mother's womb. "Dasa-sahassī lokadhātu kampittha" means that the Bodhisatta, being mindful and clearly comprehending, while descending into the mother's womb, took rebirth with a Great Resultant consciousness (Mahāvipāka citta) similar to the unprompted wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge and accompanied by joy, preceded by loving-kindness, among the nineteen types of rebirth-linking consciousness, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, in conjunction with the Uttarāsāḷha nakshatra. At that time, the ten thousand world systems...
75:
The entire ten thousand world systems shook; they moved up and down, trembled thoroughly, and quaked in all directions. It is called 'Dharaṇī' (the Earth) because it bears all things, both animate and inanimate.

In the phrase "Sampajānova nikkhami," it means: at the time when I, the Buddha, being mindful and clearly comprehending, came out from my mother's womb, I was like a Dhamma preacher descending from the Dhamma-seat, or like a man descending a ladder. I stood with both hands and feet stretched out, and emerged unstained by any impurity arising from the mother's womb. "Sādhukāraṃ pavattenti" means they uttered cries of "Sādhu" (well done); they gave applause. "Pakampittha" means it shook. It means that at the time of descending into the mother's womb and at the time of emerging from the womb, the ten thousand world systems shook.

Then the Blessed One, seeing no one equal to himself in matters such as conception, uttered this verse to show his own marvel in such events as conception:

Okkanti me samo natthi, jātito abhinikkhame.
Sambodhiyaṃ ahaṃ seṭṭho, dhammacakkappavattane.

In that verse, "Okkanti" refers to the descent into the womb. Here, the nominative case expresses the meaning of the locative case (in). It means "in the taking of conception." "Me" means "with me" (or "of mine"). "Samo" means there is no one equal. In the word "Jātito," the mother is called "Jāti" because she gives birth. "Jātito" means because of being born from that mother. "Abhinikkhame" means when there is the departure (birth) from the mother's womb. In the word "Sambodhiyaṃ," the praised and excellent Bodhi is called Sambodhi. This word "Bodhi" is found in contexts such as the Bodhi tree, the Path (Magga), Nibbāna, and Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). In the passages "Bodhirukkhamūle paṭhamābhisambuddho" and "Antarā ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhiṃ," the tree is called Bodhi. In the passage "Bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ," it refers to the Path. In the passage "Patvāna bodhiṃ amataṃ asaṅkhataṃ," it refers to Nibbāna. In the passage "Pappoti bodhiṃ varabhūrimedhaso," it refers to Omniscient Knowledge. Here, however, the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (Arahattamagga-ñāṇa) of the Blessed One is intended. Some teachers also say it is "Omniscient Knowledge." It means "In that Supreme Enlightenment, I am the foremost."

Why does the Blessed One praise himself with reference to Supreme Enlightenment? Because it bestows all qualities. The Supreme Enlightenment of the Blessed One bestows all qualities; it bestows all the qualities of a Buddha without exception.
76:
The Supreme Enlightenment (Sambodhi-ñāṇa) bestows the qualities of a Buddha, but the enlightenment of others does not. For some others, the Path of Arahatship gives only the Fruit of Arahatship; for some, the three knowledges (tisso vijjā); for some, the six higher powers (cha abhiññā); for some, the four analytical insights (catasso paṭisambhidā); for some, the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa). For Paccekabuddhas, it gives only the knowledge of a Silent Buddha's enlightenment (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa). But for the Buddhas, it gives the fulfillment of all qualities. Therefore, the Blessed One praises himself, saying, "In Supreme Enlightenment, I am the foremost," because it bestows all qualities. Alternatively, he says, "In Supreme Enlightenment, I am the foremost," because he reached Supreme Enlightenment by causing the earth to shake. In the phrase "Dhammacakkappavattane," the Wheel of Dhamma is of two kinds: penetrative knowledge (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and teaching knowledge (desanā-ñāṇa). Of these two, the knowledge produced by wisdom that brings about one's own Noble Fruit is penetrative knowledge. The knowledge produced by compassion that brings about the Noble Fruit for disciples is teaching knowledge. Penetrative knowledge is supramundane wholesome (lokuttara kusala), accompanied by equanimity, and is without initial and sustained application of thought (avitakka-avicāra). Teaching knowledge is mundane indeterminate (lokiya abyākata). Both of these are unique knowledges (asādhāraṇa) not shared with others. Here, however, teaching knowledge is intended.

Now, having heard of the occurrence of the earthquake and so on at the Blessed One's conception, the devas and brahmās uttered this verse: "How marvelous in the world!" In that verse, "Buddhānaṃ guṇamahantatā" means "Oh, how great are the qualities of the Buddhas! Oh, how great is the majesty of the Buddhas!" "Dasa-sahassī lokadhātu chappakāraṃ pakampatha" means that in the ten thousand world systems, the great earth shook and moved in six ways. How? It rises in the east and sinks in the west; it rises in the west and sinks in the east; it rises in the north and sinks in the south; it rises in the south and sinks in the north; it rises in the center and sinks at the edges; it rises at the edges and sinks in the center. In this way, in six ways, like a boat struck by waves moved by the force of the wind, this great earth—which is 240,000 yojanas thick and bounded by the water that supports the earth—though inanimate, shook as if it were animate and dancing with joy. "Obhāso ca mahā āsi" means a great light appeared, surpassing the majesty of the devas. "Accheraṃ lomahaṃsanaṃ" means it was marvelous and hair-raising.

Now, while these marvels such as the earthquake and the appearance of light were occurring, the verses beginning with "Bhagavā tamhi samaye" were spoken to show the Blessed One's state. In that verse, "Lokajeṭṭho" means the foremost in the world.
77:
"Sadevakaṃ" means "of the world together with the devas"; here, the second accusative case should be understood in the sense of the sixth genitive case (possession). "Dassayanto" means wishing to display miraculous powers.

"Caṅkamanto vā" means that He preached the Dhamma while walking to and fro on that walkway made of the ten kinds of jewels, which stood pervading the ten thousand world-systems. "Lokanāyako" means that the Teacher then preached the sweet Dhamma discourse—adorned with the Three Characteristics, connected with the Four Noble Truths, and diversified by various methods—with a Brahma-like voice that is pleasant to hear and delightful, endowed with the eight qualities, like a lion uttering a lion's roar on a cinnabar stone, like a heavy thundering rain, and like the celestial Ganges descending from the sky.

In the passage "Antarā na nivatteti, catuhatthe caṅkame yathā," one end of that jeweled walkway created by the Buddha was at the edge of the eastern world-system, and the other end was at the edge of the western world-system. While walking on that jeweled walkway, the Teacher turned back only upon reaching the two ends; He did not turn back in the middle before reaching the two ends. Just as one walking on a small walkway of four cubits turns back quickly upon reaching the two ends, so He did not turn back in the middle before reaching the ends of this great walkway. Did the Blessed One shorten the walkway, which was ten thousand yojanas in length, or did He create such a large body? He did neither. The power of the Buddhas is inconceivable. The region from the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm down to the Avīci hell became like a single courtyard. In breadth, the ten thousand world-systems also became like a single courtyard. Devas saw humans, and humans also saw devas. Just as all devas and humans see Him walking normally, so they saw the Blessed One walking on the walkway. The Blessed One preached the Dhamma while walking and also entered meditative attainments in between.

Then, Venerable Sāriputta saw the Blessed One, who was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and radiant with the eighty minor marks produced by the power of merit accumulated over an immeasurable time; whose noble body was like the full moon in the autumn season (the month of Kattika), or like a Pāricchattaka tree one hundred yojanas high in full bloom; who possessed the glory of being surrounded by a fathom-wide radiance, being eighteen cubits high; who was like a moving noble golden mountain, walking with incomparable Buddha-grace and incomparable Buddha-glory, surrounded by ten thousand groups of devas. Having seen Him...
78:
"The entire ten thousand world-systems have assembled; a great Dhamma teaching will surely take place in this assembly. The Buddhavaṃsa discourse is of great benefit and brings about faith in the Blessed One. It would be well if I were to ask about the Buddhavaṃsa, starting from the initial aspiration for Buddhahood of the Lord of Ten Powers." Having thought thus, he adjusted his robe over his left shoulder, approached the Blessed One, and placing his hands—which were bright with ten nails and resembled a pure, perfect lotus bud—upon his head, he asked the Blessed One: "Great Hero, what was Your aspiration like?" and so on. Referring to this questioning, it is said:

"Sāriputta, of great wisdom, skilled in concentration and jhāna,
Having reached the pinnacle of wisdom, asks the Leader of the World:
'Great Hero, Supreme among Men, what was Your aspiration like?
O Wise One, at what time did You aspire for the supreme Perfect Enlightenment?'"

What is the name of this connection (anusandhi)? It is called pucchānusandhi (connection by question). There are three types of connections: pucchānusandhi, ajjhāsayānusandhi (connection by disposition), and yathānusandhi (connection by natural sequence). Among these, pucchānusandhi should be understood through the suttas where the Blessed One answered those who asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the near shore, and what is the far shore?"

"Then, a thought arose in the mind of a certain monk: 'Friends, it is said that form is non-self, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-self. What self will the deeds performed by the non-self (five aggregates) touch?' Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in that monk's mind, addressed the monks: 'Monks, it is possible that some hollow man here, being ignorant and fallen into nescience, might think to overstep the Teacher's instruction with a mind dominated by craving, saying: "Form is non-self... what self will the deeds performed by the non-self touch?" ... Monks, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?'" Thus, ajjhāsayānusandhi should be understood through what the Blessed One spoke after knowing the inclinations of others.
79:
The connection (anusandhi) should be understood by the power of those discourses where the subsequent teaching arises in accordance with the teaching at the beginning, or by the power of rejection. Therefore, it is called "pucchā-anusandhi" (connection by question).

In that verse, "paññāya pāramippatto" means having reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). "Pucchati" means he asks. In this context, there are five types of questions (pucchā): (1) a question to illuminate what is not seen or known (adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā), (2) a question to compare or verify what is already known (diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā), (3) a question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanā-pucchā), (4) a question for approval, such as those asked by the Buddha to know the listeners' inclination (anumati-pucchā), and (5) a question asked out of a desire to speak or explain (kathetukamyatā-pucchā). Among these five, if one asks what type of question this is from the Venerable Sāriputta—since this Buddhavamsa teaching is not the domain of Paccekabuddhas, who accumulated merit for an incalculable period and a hundred thousand aeons, nor of the two Chief Disciples, nor of the remaining Great Disciples who accumulated merit for a hundred thousand aeons, but is the domain of the Omniscient Buddhas alone—it should be understood that the Venerable Sāriputta's question is an "adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā."

"Kīdiso" refers to the manner of questioning, meaning "of what nature?" "Te" means "yours." "Abhinīhāra" (aspiration) refers to the act of resolving the mind for the sake of Buddhahood and lying down with determined effort, thinking, "I shall not rise until I receive the prophecy of Buddhahood." Therefore, it is said: "O Great Hero (Mahāvīra), Best of Men (Naruṭṭama), of what nature was your aspiration (abhinīhāra)?"

"Kamhi kāle" means "at that time." "Patthitā" means greatly desired or longed for. It is a question asking when the aspiration for Buddhahood was made in such a way as: "Having understood the Four Noble Truths myself, may I make others understand; having been liberated from Saṃsāra, may I liberate others." "Bodhi" is a name for Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), which consists of the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (Arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) and Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). "Uttamā" is called supreme because it is more noble than the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvaka-bodhi) or the enlightenment of a private buddha (pacceka-bodhi). The letter "ma" between the two words "Bodhi" and "Uttama" is inserted for euphonic junction (sandhi).

Now, desiring to ask about the qualities that make one a Buddha, the Venerable Sāriputta said:

"Of what nature are generosity (dāna), virtue (sīla), renunciation (nekkhamma), wisdom (paññā), and energy (viriya)?
Of what nature are patience (khanti), truthfulness (sacca), resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), loving-kindness (mettā), and equanimity (upekkhā)?"

"O Leader of the World, O Wise One, how did You fulfill the ten perfections (pāramī)?
How were the secondary perfections (upapāramī) fulfilled? How were the ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramī) fulfilled?"

Among those ten perfections, I shall first speak of the answer regarding the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramī). The sacrifice of external goods is called Pāramī. The sacrifice of limbs such as hands, feet, ears, and nose is called Upapāramī. The sacrifice of one's own life...
80:
Among those ten perfections, in the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramī), first, the sacrifice of external goods is called Pāramī; the sacrifice of limbs such as hands, feet, ears, and nose is called Upapāramī; and the sacrifice of one's own life is called Paramatthapāramī. This same method applies to the remaining perfections as well. Thus, there are thirty perfections: ten Pāramīs, ten Upapāramīs, and ten Paramatthapāramīs.

Among those thirty perfections, there is no limit to the number of existences in which the Bodhisatta fulfilled the perfection of generosity. Specifically, in the Sasa-paṇḍita Jātaka, he said:

"Seeing a beggar (Sakka in the guise of a brahmin) approaching for food, I sacrificed myself.
In generosity, there is no one equal to me; this is my perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramī)."

In this way, the dāna-pāramī of the Bodhisatta who sacrifices his life for another becomes what is called Paramatthapāramī.

Likewise, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī). Specifically, in the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka, he said:

"Even when being pierced by stakes and struck by spears by the sons of hunters, I did not become angry with them.
This is my perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī)."

In this way, the sīla-pāramī of the Bodhisatta who sacrifices his life becomes what is called Paramatthapāramī.

Likewise, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī) by giving up a great kingdom. Specifically, in the Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka, he said:

"The great kingdom that had come into my hands, I discarded like a glob of spit without any regard.
As I renounced it, there was no attachment in me for that kingdom; this is my perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī)."

In this way, the nekkhamma-pāramī of the Bodhisatta who renounces his country and goes forth into the forest without attachment becomes what is called Paramatthapāramī.

Likewise, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī), such as when he was the wise Mahosadha. Specifically, in the Sattubhattaka Jātaka, he said:

"Investigating with wisdom, I liberated the old brahmin from suffering.
In wisdom, there is no one equal to me; this is my perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī)."
81:
The Perfection of Wisdom of the Bodhisatta, who showed the snake inside the leather bag (to the king and the assembly), is called the Ultimate Perfection of Wisdom.

Similarly, there is no limit to the number of lifetimes in which he fulfilled the Perfection of Energy. Indeed, in the Mahājanaka Jātaka:

"In the midst of the ocean, where the shore cannot be seen, all people have perished (due to dangers).
But in my mind, there is no deviation (from effort); this is my Perfection of Energy."

Thus, the Perfection of Energy of the Bodhisatta, who swam across the great ocean, is called the Ultimate Perfection of Energy.

Similarly, in the Khantivādī Jātaka:

"Even though the King of Kāsi has me cut with a sharp axe as if cutting a senseless log,
I do not get angry with him; this is my Perfection of Patience."

Thus, the Perfection of Patience of the Bodhisatta, who endured great suffering as if he were a senseless object, is called the Ultimate Perfection of Patience.

Similarly, in the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka:

"Sacrificing my own life and keeping my word of truth,
I have set free one hundred and one kings (from the fear of death); this is my Perfection of Truthfulness."

Thus, the Perfection of Truthfulness of the Bodhisatta, who protected the truth by sacrificing his life, is called the Ultimate Perfection of Truthfulness.

Similarly, in the Mūgapakkha Jātaka:

"It is not that I do not love my parents, nor that I do not love myself.
To me, omniscience alone is the most beloved; therefore, I have undertaken this practice (determination)."

Thus, the Perfection of Determination of the Bodhisatta, who undertook the practice even by sacrificing his life, is called the Ultimate Perfection of Determination.

Similarly, in the Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka:

"No one is afraid of me, nor am I afraid of anyone.
Supported by the power of loving-kindness, I then delighted in the forest."
82:
Thus, the Perfection of Loving-kindness of the Bodhisatta, who developed loving-kindness without even regarding his life, is called the Ultimate Perfection. 

Then, in the Lomahaṃsa Jātaka: "I made my bed in a cemetery, leaning against the bones of a corpse; village children approached me and showed many inappropriate gestures (such as spitting)." 

Thus, although the village children caused pleasure and pain through spitting and the like, or through offerings of flowers and scents and the like, the Perfection of Equanimity of the Bodhisatta, who did not overstep his equanimity, is called the Ultimate Perfection. This is only a brief summary here; the detailed account should be taken from the Cariyāpiṭaka.

Now, the Elders who were the Reciters (Saṅgītikāra), wishing to show the Blessed One's answer to the question asked by the Elder Sāriputta, said:

"The Blessed One, who has a voice as sweet as the Karavīka bird, being questioned by the Elder Sāriputta, answered him, cooling the heart and gladdening the world including the devas. He clearly revealed to the world including the devas the lineage of the Buddhas (Buddhavaṃsa), which was taught by past Buddhas, handed down through the succession of Buddhas, and is for the welfare of the world, by means of his knowledge that follows the sequence of past lives."

Among those verses, "tassa puṭṭho viyākāsi" means that being questioned by the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, he answered him; he taught the entire Chronicle of Buddhas (Buddhavaṃsa) starting from his initial resolution (abhinīhāra) up to the attainment of supreme enlightenment (abhisambodhi). 

"Karavīkamadhuragiro" means one who has a voice as sweet as the Karavīka bird; it refers to one whose voice is as sweet and melodious as that of the Karavīka bird. 

Regarding the sweetness of the Karavīka birds' voice: it is said that when the Karavīka birds peck at sweet, ripe mangoes with their beaks, drink the flowing juice, and then sing while flapping their wings, four-footed animals begin to frolic as if intoxicated. Even herds of animals engaged in seeking food drop the grass from their mouths and listen to that sound. Predatory beasts, while chasing small animals, stop like statues without even putting down their raised feet.
83:
Wild beasts stand as if they were statues, without lowering their raised feet. The hunted deer also stand, forgetting even the fear of death. The birds flying in the sky also stand with their wings outstretched. The fish in the water also stand, listening to that sound without moving their gills. In this way, the Karavīka birds have a sweet voice. "Nibbāpayanto hadayaṃ" means cooling the hearts of all beings who are intensely burning with the fire of defilements (kilesa) with the stream of the ambrosia of the Dhamma discourse. "Hāsayanto" means causing delight. "Sadevakaṃ" refers to the world together with the devas.

"Atītabuddhānaṃ" means of the past Buddhas. Before our Blessed One's aspiration for Buddhahood, four Buddhas—Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara—appeared in a single aeon (kappa). After those Buddhas, twenty-three Buddhas beginning with Koṇḍañña appeared. Thus, the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara are intended here by "Atītabuddhā". It means "of those past Buddhas". "Jinānaṃ" is a synonym for that same "Atītabuddhānaṃ". "Desitaṃ" means that which was taught. It refers to the Dhamma discourse connected with the Four Noble Truths of the twenty-four Buddhas. "Nikīlitaṃ" refers to the conduct (biography) of those Buddhas. The details of the aeon, birth, caste, lineage, lifespan, Bodhi tree, assembly of disciples, attendant, parents, son, wife, and so on are called "Nikīlita". "Buddhaparamparāgataṃ" means the teaching or conduct handed down through the succession of Buddhas, starting from Dīpaṅkara Buddha up to Kassapa Buddha. "Pubbenivāsānugatāya buddhiyā" means by the knowledge that follows the previous existence, which is the sequence of aggregates (khandha) lived in the past, analyzed as one birth, two births, and so on; it means by the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa). "Pakāsayī" means he revealed (or answered). "Lokahitaṃ" refers to the Buddhavaṃsa, which is for the benefit of the whole world. "Sadevake" means in the world together with the devas.

Then the Blessed One, with a heart cooled by compassion, wishing to urge the world together with the devas to listen to the Dhamma, spoke the verse beginning with "Pītipāmojjajananaṃ":

Generating joy and happiness,
Dispelling the dart of sorrow,
Leading to the attainment of all prosperity,
Listen to the Buddhavaṃsa from me with respect.

In that verse, "Pītipāmojjajananaṃ" means causing joy and happiness; it means generating happiness, which is the precursor to joy, and the five kinds of joy (pīti). "Sokasal-lavinodanaṃ" means dispelling or destroying the darts known as sorrow. "Sabbasampattipaṭilābhaṃ" means it is called "Sabbasampattipaṭilābha" because one can attain all forms of prosperity, such as the prosperity of devas and humans, through this Buddhavaṃsa teaching. It means the Buddhavaṃsa teaching that causes the attainment of all those prosperities. "Cittīkatvā" means performing it by placing the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati) at the forefront of the mind.
84:
"Cittīkatvā" means having made it in the mind, having placed the recollection of the Buddha at the forefront. "Suṇātha" means listen, understand. "Me" means from me.

"Madanimmadana" means that which causes the crushing of all intoxications, such as the intoxication of birth (caste). "Sokanuda": sorrow (soka) is the mental burning of a being affected by the loss of relatives and so on. Although in essence it is just mental unpleasantness (domanassa), it has the characteristic of internal burning, the function of consuming the mind, and manifests as repeated grieving. Because it dispels that sorrow, it is called "Sokanuda". "Saṃsārapari-mocana" means that which effects liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra. There is also a reading "Saṃsārasamatikkamaṃ", which means that which effects the transcending of saṃsāra.

In the term "Sabbadukkhakkhaya", the word "dukkha" is found in meanings such as painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā), the basis of suffering (dukkha-vatthu), the object of suffering (dukkha-ārammaṇa), the cause of suffering (dukkha-paccaya), and the place of suffering (dukkha-ṭṭhāna). This word "dukkha" is found in the sense of painful feeling in passages such as "Dukkhassa ca pahānā". It is found in the sense of the basis of suffering in passages such as "Jātipi dukkhā jarāpi dukkhā". It is found in the sense of the object of suffering in passages such as "Yasmā ca kho Mahāli rūpaṃ dukkhaṃ". It is found in the sense of the cause of suffering in passages such as "Dukkho pāpassa uccayo". It is found in the sense of the place of suffering in passages such as "Yāva dukkhā nirayā". Here, however, this word "dukkha" should be understood in the senses of the basis of suffering and the cause of suffering. Therefore, it means that which effects the end of all suffering, such as birth. "Magga" (the path) refers to the Buddhavaṃsa teaching, either because it is sought by those desiring merit (kusala) or because it goes along killing the defilements. It means the Buddhavaṃsa teaching which is the path to Nibbāna. "Sakkaccaṃ" means having attended to it respectfully, having lent an ear. "Paṭipajjatha" means establish yourselves firmly, listen. Alternatively, having heard this Buddhavaṃsa teaching which generates joy and happiness, dispels the dart of sorrow, and is the cause for attaining all prosperity, now practice the path to Buddhahood which brings the special qualities such as the crushing of intoxication and is the end of all suffering. Thus, he inspires the effort of all devas and humans by aiming for Buddhahood. The remaining words here are clear.

## Thus ends the explanation of the Ratanacaṅkamanakaṇḍa
## in the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary named Madhuratthavilāsinī.
## The explanation of the meaning of the internal prologue (Abbhantaranidāna) is also complete in every respect.
85:
## 2. Commentary on the Aspiration of the Bodhisatta Sumedha

Now—
1-2. "A hundred thousand aeons and four incalculables ago, there was a city named Amara, beautiful and delightful to behold.

That city was abundant in food and drink. It was never silent, resounded by the ten sounds: the sounds of elephants, horses, drums, conchs, and chariots, as well as the cries related to food and drink, such as 'Eat! Drink!'" The time has now arrived to comment on the Buddhavamsa, which begins in this manner. Since this commentary on the Buddhavamsa becomes clear only after examining the *sutta-nikkhepa* (the occasions for teaching the Suttas), the examination of the *sutta-nikkhepa* should first be understood.

There are four types of *sutta-nikkhepa*: *attajjhāsaya* (by one's own inclination), *parajjhāsaya* (by the inclination of others), *pucchāvasika* (by way of a question), and *atthuppattika* (due to a specific event). Among these four, the Suttas taught by the Blessed One solely by His own volition without being urged by others—such as the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta and the Vattha Sutta—are called *attajjhāsaya-nikkhepa*.

Alternatively, when the Buddha observes the inclination, disposition, mind, and capacity for understanding of others, such as thinking, "The factors for the ripening of Rāhula's liberation have matured; what if I were to lead Rāhula further to the destruction of the taints (the fruit of Arahantship)?" and teaches accordingly—such as the Rāhulovāda Sutta and the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta—these are called *parajjhāsaya-nikkhepa*.

Various devas and humans approach the Blessed One and ask questions. The Suttas taught by the Blessed One when thus questioned—such as the Devatā Saṃyutta and the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta—are called *pucchāvasika-nikkhepa*.

Alternatively, the Suttas taught based on a specific cause or event that has arisen—such as the Dhammadāyāda Sutta and the Puttamaṃsūpama Sutta—are called *atthuppattika-nikkhepa*. Thus, among these four types of *sutta-nikkhepa*, this Buddhavamsa teaching is *pucchāvasika-nikkhepa*. This is because the Blessed One taught this discourse in response to a question. In response to whose question was it taught? It was in response to the question of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta. Indeed, it was stated in this very prologue (Nidāna):

"Sāriputta, of great wisdom, skilled in concentration and jhāna,
Who has reached the pinnacle of wisdom, asks the Leader of the World:
'O Great Hero, Supreme among Men,
What was the nature of Your aspiration (abhinīhāra)?'"

Therefore, it should be understood that this Buddhavamsa teaching is *pucchāvasika-nikkhepa*.

In that verse, regarding the words "kappe ca satasahasse," the word "kappa" is found in the senses of great conviction, decision, designation of time, cutting, deliberation, a small hint, surrounding entirety, life-span (āyukappa), great aeon (mahākappa), and so on. This is true. In the Mahāsaccaka Sutta of the Mahāyamakavagga, Mūlapaṇṇāsa, Majjhima Nikāya, it is found in the sense of great conviction in such passages as: "This word of the Venerable Gotama is worthy of conviction, as is fitting for an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One like the Venerable Gotama."
86:
"Sāriputta, of great wisdom, skilled in concentration and jhāna, who has reached the pinnacle of wisdom, asks the Leader of the World: 'O Great Hero, Supreme among Men, what was the nature of Your aspiration (abhinīhāra)?'" (Bu. Va. 1.74-75). Thus, it should be understood that this Buddhavamsa teaching is *pucchāvasika*.

In that verse, regarding the words "kappe ca satasahasse," the word "kappa" is evident in the senses of great conviction, usage (vohāra), time (kāla), designation, cutting, special deliberation (vikappa), a small hint (lesa), surrounding entirety, life-span (āyukappa), great aeon (mahākappa), and so on. This is true. To elaborate: it is evident in the sense of great conviction in such passages as: "This word of the Venerable Gotama is worthy of conviction, as is fitting for a Perfectly Enlightened One worthy of offerings."

It is evident in the sense of usage (vohāra) in such passages as: "Monks, I allow you to consume fruit through the five types of ascetic usage (samaṇakappa)."

It is evident in the sense of time (kāla) in such passages as: "By which (attainment of fruition) I always (niccakappaṃ) dwell."

It is evident in the sense of designation (paññatti) in such passages as: "Venerable Kappa," and "The Blessed One has designated the name of that brahmin monk as Nigrodhakappa."

It is evident in the sense of cutting (chedana) in such passages as: "Adorned, with hair and beard trimmed (kappita)."

It is evident in the sense of deliberation/option (vikappa) in such passages as: "The two-finger-breadth rule (dvaṅgulakappa) is allowable (after noon)."

It is evident in the sense of a hint (lesa) in such passages as: "There is a small opportunity (kappa) to lie down."

It is evident in the sense of surrounding entirety (samantabhāva) in such passages as: "Illuminating the entire (kevalakappaṃ) Jetavana monastery."

It is evident in the sense of life-span (āyukappa) in this passage: "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One remain for a kappa; let the Sugata remain for a kappa."

It is evident in the sense of a great aeon (mahākappa) in this passage: "Venerable Sir, how long is a kappa?"

By the word "ādi" (and so on), it is evident in the sense of similarity (paṭibhāga) in this passage: "Friends, while we were consulting with a disciple who is like the Teacher (satthukappa), we did not realize it was Sāriputta."

It is evident in the sense of a Vinaya procedure (vinayakappa) in this passage: "The smudge (kappabindu) is destroyed; the place where the smudge was made is worn out."

In this context, however, the word "kappa" should be understood in the sense of a great aeon (mahākappa). Therefore, "kappe ca satasahasse" means at the end of a hundred thousand great aeons. In the phrase "caturo ca asaṅkhiye," the remaining words "at the end of four incalculables" should be added to complete the meaning. Thus, it means at the end of four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. "Amaram nāma nagaram" means there was a city named "Amara" or "Amaravatī." Some teachers, in this passage, by another method...
87:
That city was named "Amaravatī." Some teachers praise it in other ways in this context; what is the use of their words? This name is merely the name of that city. It was lovely (dassanīya) because it was adorned with well-proportioned and wonderful crossroads, gates, squares, junctions, walls, enclosures, palaces, mansions, and residences. It was called "Manorama" (Delightful) because it had level, clean, and extremely pleasant grounds, was endowed with shade and water, had easily obtainable food, was equipped with all necessities, and was prosperous, thus delighting the minds of gods and humans.

It was a city not devoid of the ten sounds: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of drums, the sound of conchs, the sound of mridangams, the sound of lutes, the sound of singing, the sound of cymbals, and the tenth sound, "Eat, drink, and chew!" This means that at all times, incomparable festivals were held where dancers played and enjoyed themselves. It was called "Annapānasamayuta" because it was well-endowed with the four types of food and drinks. This expression shows the abundance of almsfood (subhikkha). It means being endowed with plenty of food and drink.

Now, to show those ten sounds by way of substance:
"With the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, drums, conchs, and chariots;
And with 'chew and drink,' it was proclaimed with food and drink."

In that verse, "hatthisaddaṃ" means with a sound like the trumpeting (koñcanāda) of elephants; here, the accusative case should be understood in the sense of the instrumental. This method applies to the remaining terms as well. "Bherisaṅkharathāni ca" means with the sound of drums, the sound of conchs, and the sound of chariots. It is spoken with a change of gender. "Khādatha pivatha" and so on means it was proclaimed (abhinādita) with sounds connected to food and drink. Here, one might ask: "Is only a part of those sounds shown, and not the whole?" No, it is not just a part; all ten kinds of sounds are indeed shown. How? The sound of drums includes the sound of mridangams; the sound of conchs includes the sounds of lutes, singing, and cymbals. Thus, all ten are shown.

Having thus praised the prosperity of the city in one way, again to show that same prosperity:
"The city of Amaravatī is complete in all parts, endowed with all works,
Endowed with the seven gems, and crowded with various kinds of people.
Prosperous like the city of the gods, it is the abode of those of meritorious deeds."

In that verse, "sabbangasampannaṃ" means being complete in all parts of a city, such as walls, gates, and watchtowers. Or it means being full of all wealth, necessities, riches, grain, grass, wood, and water. "Sabbakammupāgataṃ" means endowed with all desired objects, animate or inanimate, or endowed with all sensual pleasures.
88:
"The city is complete in all parts, endowed with all works, endowed with the seven gems, crowded with various kinds of people, prosperous like the city of the gods, the abode of those of meritorious deeds." - So it was said.

Therein, "sabbangasampannaṃ" means complete with all city components like walls, gate-towers, and watchtowers; or it means full of all wealth, equipment, riches, grain, grass, wood, and water. "Sabbakammupāgataṃ" means reached by all works, meaning all works are fully accomplished. "Sattaratanasampannaṃ" means full of the seven gems such as pearls, etc., or endowed with the seven treasures of a Wheel-turning Monarch, such as the elephant-treasure, etc. "Nānājanasamākulaṃ" means crowded with people from various regions and speaking various languages. "Samiddhaṃ" means prosperous and wealthy with all necessities for human enjoyment. "Devanagaraṃ va" means prosperous like the celestial city Alakamandā or the celestial Amaravatī. "Āvāsaṃ puññakammīနံ" means it is called "āvāsa" (abode) because meritorious people dwell there. It should be understood that "āvāsaṃ" is used with a change of gender instead of "āvāso." It is called "puñña" (merit) because it makes one known (paññāyati) through family, appearance, great wealth, and sovereignty. Or it is called "puñña" because it purifies (punāti), as it washes away the dust and stains of all unwholesome states. Those who have such meritorious deeds are "puññakammī," and it is the abode of those meritorious ones.

In that city of Amaravatī, there lived a brahmin named Sumedha. He was well-born on both the mother's and father's side, of pure descent as far back as seven generations, irreproachable and beyond reproach in terms of birth. He was handsome, pleasant to look at, inspiring, and possessed of the highest beauty of complexion. He was a master of the three Vedas, along with the Nighaṇḍu, Keṭubha, Akkharappabheda, and the Itihāsas as the fifth; he was a scholar of the words (padaka), a grammarian (veyyākaraṇa), and perfect in Lokāyata and the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa). While he was still young, his parents passed away. Then the minister in charge of the wealth brought the account books, opened the storerooms filled with various gems like gold, silver, rubies, and pearls, and said: "Young man, this much is your mother's property, this much is your father's, and this much belongs to your grandfathers and great-grandfathers," pointing out the wealth of seven generations. He handed it over, saying, "Take charge of this." Sumedha accepted it, saying "Very well," and lived in the household life performing meritorious deeds. Therefore, it was said:

## In the city of Amaravatī, the brahmin named Sumedha had accumulated many crores of wealth. He was endowed with much property, wealth, and provisions. He was a reciter and bearer of the Vedas, having reached the end of the three Vedas. He was a master of the science of marks, the Itihāsas, and his own Vedic arts.

In those verses, "nagere amaravatiyā" means in the city called Amaravatī. In the phrase "sumedho nāma", wisdom is called "medhā". Because that brahmin possessed excellent wisdom, he was known as "Sumedha." "Brāhmaṇo" means he is a brahmin because he recites and studies the Vedic texts. Scholars of phonetics say he is a "brahmin" because he is a son of Brahmā. Alternatively, Noble Ones (Ariyas) are called "brahmins" because they have discarded evil. "Anekakoṭisannicayo" means he had accumulated many crores of wealth. For that brahmin Sumedha, the accumulation of not just one but many crores...
89:
In the city of Amaravatī, there was a Brahmin named Sumedha. This Brahmin had accumulated many crores of wealth and was endowed with abundant riches and grain.
He was a reciter of the Vedas, a bearer of the mantras, and one who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas. He had attained perfection in the science of signs (Lakkhaṇa), history (Itihāsa), and his own traditional laws.

In those verses, "nagare Amaravatiyā" means in the city known as Amaravatī. In the phrase "Sumedho nāma," "medhā" refers to wisdom. Because he possessed that beautiful and praised wisdom, he was known as Sumedha. "Brāhmaṇa" means one who recites or studies the sacred texts (brahma), meaning he chants the mantras. However, grammarians (akkharacintakā) say "Brāhmaṇa" because he is a descendant of Brahmā. The Noble Ones (Ariyas), however, call one a Brāhmaṇa because they have barred (bāhita) evil. "Anekakoṭisannicayo" means one who has an accumulation of many crores; it implies one who has gathered many crores of wealth. "Pahūtadhanadhaññavā" means one who has much wealth and grain. It should be understood that the word "dhana" mentioned previously refers to wealth and grain buried in the ground or kept in storehouses, while the word "dhaññavā" here refers to wealth and grain for daily use.

"Ajjhāyaka" means one who does not meditate (na jhāyati), implying one devoid of meditative absorption (jhāna-bhāvanā). Regarding this, the Buddha taught: "Vāseṭṭha, now these people do not meditate; therefore, the designation 'Ajjhāyaka, Ajjhāyaka' arose." Thus, in the beginning of the world-cycle, this arose as a term of reproach for Brahmins devoid of meditation. Nowadays, however, they are called "Ajjhāyaka" because they recite the Vedas; they use it as a term of praise in the sense of one who repeatedly recites the Vedas. He is called "Mantadharo" because he bears the mantras. "Tiṇṇam vedānam" refers to the three Vedas: the Iruveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda. This word "Veda" is found in the senses of knowledge (ñāṇa), joy (somanassa), and scriptures (gantha). In passages such as "Yam brāhmaṇam vedagumābhijaññā, akiñcanam kāmabhave asattam," it is found in the sense of knowledge. In "Ye vedajātā vicaranti loke," it is found in the sense of joy. In "Tiṇṇam vedānam pāragū sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānam," it is found in the sense of scriptures. Here too, the sense of scriptures should be taken. "Pāragū" means one who has reached the end of the three Vedas merely by oral mastery. "Lakkhaṇe" refers to the science of signs, such as the signs of women, the signs of men, and the signs of a Great Man. "Itihāse" means "thus it has been, thus it has been"...
90:
...a special class of scripture consisting of ancient stories related to the saying "So it has been, so it has been." "Sadhamme" refers to the brahmins' own law or their teachers' tradition. "Pāramiṃ gato" means he had reached the further shore, meaning he had become a world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha).

Then one day, that wise Sumedha, who was delighted by a multitude of ten qualities, went into seclusion on the magnificent upper terrace of his palace. Sitting cross-legged, he reflected: "Rebirth in a new existence is indeed suffering. Likewise, the breaking up of the body in every place of birth is suffering. I am subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to sickness, and subject to death. Being such, I should seek Nibbāna—the unborn, unaging, healthy, deathless, true happiness, and peace. Surely there must be a single path leading to Nibbāna, escaping from the prison of existence."

Therefore, it was said:

"Then, having gone into seclusion and sat down, I thought thus:
Rebirth is indeed suffering, as is the breaking up of the body.

At that time, being subject to birth, aging, and sickness,
I shall seek the peace of Nibbāna, which is free from aging, death, and danger.

What if I were to discard this putrid body, filled with various kinds of corpses,
and depart without longing or need?

That path for liberation from existence must surely exist.
It cannot be that it does not exist; I shall seek that path for liberation from existence."

Here, we shall proceed after explaining the connection of the verses and the meaning of the obscure terms. In those verses, "rahogato" means gone to a private place, or sitting in a secluded spot. "Evaṃ cintesahaṃ" means "I thought thus." The word "evaṃ" shows the manner of his thinking. "Tadā" refers to the time when he was the wise Sumedha. By saying "evaṃ cintesahaṃ," the Buddha identifies himself with the wise Sumedha as one and the same. Therefore, to make it clear that "the Sumedha of that time was I myself," the Buddha spoke in the first person (uttamapurisa), saying "evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā." "Jātidhammo" means having the nature of being reborn. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Nibbutiṃ" refers to Nibbāna.
91:
"Yaṃ nūna" is a particle used in the sense of reflection; it means "If I were to...". "Pūtikāya" refers to the foul body. "Nānākuṇapapūrita" means being filled with many impurities such as urine, feces, pus, blood, bile, phlegm, saliva, and snot. "Anapekkha" means being without attachment. "Atthi" means it certainly exists (it is attainable). "Hehiti" means it will be; this is a word of reflection. "Na so sakkā na hetuye" means that by that path, it cannot not be; it means that path is not not a cause, but is indeed the cause. "Bhavato parimuttiyā" means for liberation from the bond of existence.

Now, to fulfill the meaning he had reflected upon, he spoke the words beginning with "Yathāpi". Just as in the world there is what is called happiness, which is the opposite of suffering, so when there is existence (bhava), there must also be non-existence (vibhava), which is its opposite.
