Just as when there is heat, there is also cold, which is its quenching, so when there are the fires of lust and so on, there must be Nibbāna, which is their quenching. Just as there is wholesome, faultless Dhamma, which is the opposite of evil, base Dhamma, so too, when there is base birth (jāti), there must certainly be Nibbāna, called non-birth (ajātī), which brings all birth to an end. Therefore, it was said:

"Just as when suffering exists, what is called happiness also exists; even so, when existence exists, non-existence (Nibbāna) should also be sought."

"Just as when heat exists, there exists another, which is cold; even so, when the three fires exist, Nibbāna should be sought."

"Just as when evil exists, the wholesome also exists; even so, when birth exists, non-birth (Nibbāna) should also be sought."

In those verses, "Yathāpi" is a particle used in the sense of a simile. "Sukha" is the happiness of both body and mind; it is called happiness because it thoroughly destroys (digs out) suffering. "Bhava" occurs in the sense of arising (janana). "Vibhava" is non-arising (ajanana); when there is arising, the nature of non-arising should also be sought. "Tividhaggi vijjante" means when the three fires of lust and so on exist. "Nibbāna" means the quenching and calming of those three fires of lust and so on; Nibbāna should be sought. "Pāpa" occurs in the sense of base unwholesome states. "Kalyāṇa" refers to the wholesome. "Evameva" means in this very way. Birth...
92:
"Vijjante" means when birth (jāti) exists. It is spoken by making a change of gender and elision of the case ending. "Ajāti" means that Nibbāna, which is the absence of birth and brings birth to an end, should also be sought.

Then I reflected further: "For example, a man submerged in a heap of dung, seeing from afar a lake of clear water adorned with clusters of red, blue, and white lotuses, should seek that lake, thinking, 'By which path should I go there?' If that man does not seek it, the fault is not that of the lake, but only of that man. In the same way, while there exists the great lake of the Deathless (Amata), which can wash away the impurities of defilements, if one does not seek it, the fault is not that of the great lake of Nibbāna, called the Deathless, but only of that man. For example, if a man surrounded by enemies does not flee even though there is an escape route, the fault is not that of the path, but only of that man. In the same way, for a man who is surrounded and captured by the thieves of defilements, when there is a great, safe path leading to the great city of Nibbāna, not seeking that path is not the fault of the path, but only of that man. For example, if a man afflicted by disease does not seek a physician who can treat the disease even though such a physician exists, the fault is not that of the physician, but only of that man. In the same way, if one who is afflicted by the disease of defilements does not seek a teacher who exists and is skilled in the path to quench defilements, the fault is his alone, not the fault of the teacher who can remove the disease of defilements." Thus I reflected. Therefore, he said:

"A man fallen into dung, seeing a lake full of water, if he does not seek that lake, the fault is not that of the lake."

"In the same way, while the lake of the Deathless exists to wash away the impurities of defilements, if one does not seek that lake, the fault is not that of the lake of the Deathless."

"When there is a path to go while surrounded by enemies, if that man does not flee, the fault is not that of the path."

"In the same way, while there is a safe path while surrounded by defilements, if one does not seek that path, the fault is not that of the safe path."

In those verses, "Gūthagato" means one who has fallen into a pit of dung or is smeared with dung. "Kilesamaladhovaṃ" is a word in the nominative case with the meaning of cleansing the impurities of defilements. "Amatantaḷe" should be understood as the use of the locative case in the sense of the genitive, meaning 'of the lake of the Deathless Nibbāna'...
93:
For example, just as a man who is ill does not have his illness treated even though a doctor is available, and that lack of treatment is not the fault of the doctor but only the fault of the patient; in the same way, a person who is afflicted and oppressed by the diseases of defilements but does not seek out a teacher who can give guidance—that failure to seek is not the fault of the teacher who gives guidance.

In those verses, 'gūthagato' means one who has fallen into a cesspool or one who is smeared with dung. 'Kilesamaladhovaṃ' means cleansing the impurities of defilements; here the nominative case is used in the sense of the locative. 'Amatantaḷe' means the lake of the Deathless; it should be understood that the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive, and it is spoken with the addition of the niggahīta. 'Arīhi' means by enemies. 'Pariruddho' means surrounded or blocked from all sides. 'Gamanampathe' means on the path of travel; it is spoken with the addition of the niggahīta to preserve the meter. 'Na palāyati' means if he does not flee. 'So puriso' refers to that man who is surrounded and blocked by thieves. 'Añjasassa' means of the path. There are many names for a path: magga, pantha, patha, pajja, añjasa, vaṭuma, ayana, nāvā (waterway), uttarasetu (bridge), kulla (raft), bhisi, and saṅkama. Here, it is referred to by the name 'añjasa'. 'Sive' means a place where all dangers are absent, hence a place of peace. 'Sivamañjase' means of the path that is peaceful. 'Tikicchake' refers to a doctor. 'Na tikicchāpeti' means he would not have himself treated. 'Na doso so tikicchake' means there is no fault in the doctor; the fault lies only with the sick person. 'Dukkhito' refers to one in whom physical and mental suffering has arisen. 'Ācariyaṃ' refers to the teacher of the path to Nibbāna. 'Vināyake' has the meaning of teacher.

After I had reflected thus, I further reflected: "For example, just as a man who is fond of ornaments would discard a carcass clinging to his neck and go happily; in the same way, I too should discard this foul body and enter the great city of Nibbāna without any lingering concern. For example, just as men and women, after passing excrement and urine at a place for easing oneself, do not take that excrement and urine away in their laps or by wrapping it in the hem of their clothes, but rather, being disgusted and not even wishing to look at it, they discard it without concern and go away; in the same way, I too should discard this foul body without concern and enter the city of Nibbāna, which is free from death. For example, just as sailors abandon a dilapidated boat that is taking on water and go away without concern; in the same way, I too, discarding this body that leaks from nine wound-like openings, shall enter the great city of Nibbāna without concern."
94:
I shall enter (Nibbāna). Just as a man carrying various jewels such as pearls, emeralds, and lapis lazuli, while traveling with thieves, abandons those thieves and takes a safe path out of fear that his jewels might be destroyed or lost; in the same way, this foul body is like a thief who robs and destroys jewels. If I were to cherish craving for this body, my jewels of wholesome states, namely the Noble Path, would perish. Therefore, I should discard this physical body (karajakāya), which is like a great thief, and enter the great city of Nibbāna." Therefore, (the Buddha) said:

"Just as a man who likes ornaments, having released a disgusting carcass tied to his neck, would go happily, freely, and as his own master.

"Even so, I should discard this foul body, a collection of various carcasses, and go without concern or need for it.

"Just as men and women, at a place of excrement, discard the dung and go without concern or need for it.

"Even so, I shall discard this body, filled with various carcasses, and go, just as one leaves a latrine after easing oneself.

"Just as owners abandon a dilapidated, broken boat that is taking on water and go without concern or need for it.

"Even so, I shall discard this body with nine openings that is constantly leaking, just as owners abandon an old boat.

"Just as a man traveling with thieves while carrying goods, seeing the danger of his goods being stolen, discards (the thieves) and goes.

"Even so, I shall go, abandoning this body which is like a great thief, for fear of losing my wholesome states."

In those verses, "Yathāpi kuṇapaṃ puriso" means: just as a young, youthful man who is fond of ornaments, being oppressed, ashamed, and disgusted by a snake carcass, a dog carcass, or a human carcass clinging to his neck, would release that carcass and go.
95:
It is like releasing [a rotting corpse] and going away. "Sukhī" means one who has attained happiness or one who possesses happiness. "Serī" means one who dwells according to their own will or one who has a body under their own control. "Nānākuṇapasañcayaṃ" means being a heap of various kinds of corpses. In some versions, the reading is "Nānākuṇapapūritaṃ."

"Uccāraṭṭhānaṃ" means: in this place, they void excrement (uccāra); therefore, it is called uccāra. Since it is both excrement and the place [of voiding], it is called uccāraṭṭhāna (the place of excrement). Alternatively, it is called ussāsa because it flows; this is a name for excrement. The place of that excrement is ussāsaṭṭhāna. "In that ussāsaṭṭhāna" means in the place of excrement. It means just as men and women void excrement and then leave the latrine (vacca-kuṭi).

"Jajjaraṃ" means decayed, worn out, and old. "Paluggaṃ" means breaking down, meaning being scattered in disorder. "Udagāhiniṃ" means [a boat] that takes in water. "Sāmī" means the owners of the boat. "Navacchiddaṃ": Because it is associated with holes and openings through the nine wound-mouths such as the eyes, ears, etc., it is called navacchidda (the body with nine openings). "Dhuva-ssavaṃ" means constant flowing; it means an impure thing that flows constantly.

"Bhaṇḍamādīya" means taking some property such as jewels, etc. "Bhaṇḍacchedabhayaṃ" means seeing the danger of the property being snatched away or destroyed. "Evameva" means being like that man who goes taking the property. "Ayaṃ kāyo": This body is called kāya because it is the place of origin (āya) of things that are extremely loathsome. "Āya" means the place of occurrence. Since loathsome things like hair, etc., arise from it, it is called āya. Thus, it is called kāya as the place of origin for loathsome hair and so on. "Mahācorasamamo viya": Like a great thief, through the power of intense attachment and so on to pleasant forms and so on via the eyes and so on, one becomes a thief of life-taking, taking what is not given, and so on, and plunders all wholesome states; thus, it is like a great thief. Therefore, just as a man carrying a treasure of jewels who is traveling with thieves abandons those thieves and goes, in the same way, I too shall abandon this body which is like a great thief and go to seek the Path (Magga) that brings about my own safety and happiness—this is how the connection of meaning should be understood. "Kusalacchedanabhayā" means because of the danger of wholesome states being plundered and destroyed.

Then the wise Sumedha, having reflected on the reasons for renunciation (nekkhamma) through various metaphors, reflected again: "My father, grandfather, and others who accumulated this great mass of wealth could not take even a single kahāpaṇa when they went to the next world. I, however, should act in a way that I can take it with me." Having thought thus, he went to the King...
96:
The wise Sumedha informed the King: "Great King, my heart is oppressed by the dangers of birth, aging, and so on. I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness. I have wealth amounting to many hundreds of thousands of crores. May Your Majesty take charge of it." The King said: "I have no need for your wealth; do as you wish."

And he, saying "Very well, Your Majesty," had the drum sounded throughout the city. Having given gifts to the great multitude and abandoned both sensual objects (vatthu-kāma) and sensual defilements (kilesa-kāma), he departed from the city of Amaravatī, which is like the city of the gods. Alone, he went to the Himalayas (Himavanta), where there are various herds of wild animals. Depending on the mountain named Dhammika, he built a hermitage. There, he built a leaf-hut, created a walking path (caṅkama) free from five defects, and to acquire the power of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā) endowed with eight qualities, he abandoned his cloth garment which had nine defects, put on a bark-garment (vākacīra) endowed with twelve qualities, and went forth as an ascetic. Having thus gone forth, he abandoned the leaf-hut crowded with eight defects, approached the foot of a tree endowed with ten qualities, abandoned all kinds of grain, and lived eating only naturally fallen fruits. Striving hard through sitting, standing, and walking, within seven days he became an attainer of the eight attainments (samāpatti) and five supernormal knowledges (abhiññā). Regarding this, it was said:

"Having reflected thus, I gave away wealth of many hundreds of crores to those with and without protectors, and I approached the Himalayas."

"Near the Himalayas is a mountain named Dhammika. There, a hermitage was well-prepared by me, and a leaf-hut was well-created."

"There, I created a walking path free from five defects. I acquired the power of supernormal knowledge endowed with eight qualities."

"There, I abandoned the cloth garment which had nine defects and put on a bark-garment endowed with twelve qualities."

"I abandoned the leaf-hut crowded with eight defects and approached the foot of a tree endowed with ten qualities."

"I abandoned sown and planted grain entirely and took up naturally fallen fruits endowed with many qualities."

In those verses, "Evāhaṃ" means "I, having reflected as mentioned above." "Nāthānāthānaṃ" means "to those with protectors and without, the wealthy and the poor," saying "Let those who want it take it," and giving it away along with the granaries and treasuries. "Himavantassāvidūre" means "near the king of mountains, the Himavanta." "Dhammiko nāma pabbato" means "there is a mountain named Dhammika." Why is this mountain called Dhammika? Usually, Bodhisattas become ascetics and, depending on that mountain, develop supernormal knowledges and practice the recluse's Dhamma (samaṇadhamma)...
97:
## 
Sāriputta, in that hermitage, I exerted effort (in the form of abandoning unwholesome states and developing wholesome states) in the postures of sitting, standing, and walking. Within only seven days, I attained the power of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā).

In that verse, "Evāhaṃ" means "Thus I, having thought in the manner mentioned above." "Nāthānāthānaṃ" means giving to those with protectors and those without, to the wealthy and the poor, saying, "Let those in need take," and donating along with the granaries and treasuries. "Himavantassāvidūre" means near the king of mountains, the Himavantā. "Dhammiko nāma pabbato" means there is a mountain named Dhammika. Why is that mountain called Dhammika? Because generally, Bodhisattas, having gone forth as ascetics, depended on that mountain, developed supernormal knowledges, and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse; because it was the support for the practice of a recluse, it became famous as "Dhammika."

Although it is said as if the wise Sumedha created the hermitage, the leaf-hut, and the walking path with his own hands, in reality, they were not created by his own hands but were fashioned by the celestial son Vissakamma, sent by Sakka, the king of devas. The Blessed One, referring to that accomplishment which arose due to the power of his own merit at that time, said: "Sāriputta, on that mountain, I have well-prepared a hermitage, I have well-fashioned a leaf-hut, and there I have fashioned a walking path free from the five defects," and so on.

In that verse, "paṇṇasālā" means a hut roofed with leaves. "Tattha" means in that hermitage site. "Pañcadosavivajjitaṃ" means being free from the five defects of a walking path. The five defects of a walking path are: the ground being hard and uneven, having trees inside, being overgrown with thickets, being too narrow, and being too wide. It refers to a walking path that is, at its best dimension, sixty cubits in length and one and a half cubits in width. Alternatively, "free from the five defects" means being free from the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and this should be understood in connection with the subsequent phrase "attained the power of supernormal knowledge."

"Aṭṭhaguṇasamupetaṃ" means having attained the power of supernormal knowledge endowed with the eight qualities, namely: "Thus the mind is concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, free from defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability." Some teachers, however, say that the 'eight qualities' refer to being endowed with the eight comforts of a recluse. Those eight comforts of a recluse are: having no hoarding of wealth and grain, seeking blameless alms, consuming alms in peace, having no distress from the oppression of taxes, being free from attachment to requisites, being free from the danger of thieves, having no association with kings and ministers, and the four...
98:
## 
Some teachers say, "Thus I fashioned a hermitage endowed with the eight comforts of a recluse; those comforts of a recluse are: having no hoarding of wealth and grain, seeking blameless alms, consuming alms in peace, having no mental distress caused by the oppression of the country even when royal officers oppress the kingdom to take wealth and grain, having desire and lust removed regarding buildings and requisites, having no fear caused by the plundering of thieves, having no association with kings and great ministers of kings, and being unhindered in the four directions. I fashioned a hermitage well-endowed with these eight comforts of a recluse," thus connecting it with the hermitage. Such a statement does not agree with the Pali text.

"Sāṭaka" means a cloth garment. "Tattha" means in that hermitage. It means, "Sāriputta, while living in that hermitage, I abandoned and gave up the expensive cloth that I wore and used." In abandoning the cloth, it is shown that it was abandoned upon seeing the nine defects in that cloth. For those who have gone forth as ascetics, the nine defects in a layman's cloth are clearly shown. What are those nine? The cloth being expensive, being dependent on others, becoming dirty quickly through use, needing to be washed and dyed again when dirty, wearing out through use, needing to be sewn or patched again when worn out, being difficult to obtain when seeking it again, being unsuitable for the state of an ascetic, being shared with enemies (having to guard it securely so that enemies cannot take it), being a basis for decoration (beautification) for the wearer, and causing great desire in the one who takes it away. It is shown that, having abandoned the cloth associated with these nine defects, he wore a bark-fiber robe.

"Vākacīra" means taking a bark-fiber robe made by shredding munja grass into strips and knotting them, for the purpose of wearing and covering. "Dvādasaguṇamupāgataṃ" means being endowed with twelve kinds of benefits. Here, the word "guṇa" expresses the meaning of benefit. It is like in the Pali, "A gift with a hundredfold benefit (guṇa) is to be expected." The letter "ma" is inserted for euphonic junction (padasandhi). There are twelve benefits in a bark-fiber robe. What are those benefits? Being inexpensive, not being dependent on others, being able to be made with one's own hands, having no need for sewing even when worn out through use, having no fear of thieves, being easy to make for the one seeking it, being suitable for the state of an ascetic, not being a basis for decoration for the one using it, having fewness of wishes regarding the robe requisite, being comfortable (easy) in use, the bark and fiber being easy to obtain, and even if the bark-fiber robe is lost...
99:
It is endowed with these twelve qualities: fewness of wishes, happiness in usage, ease of obtaining bark-fiber, and lack of concern even if the bark-garment is lost.

Then, the wise Sumedha, while residing in that leaf-hut, arose at dawn and reflected on the reason for his renunciation, thinking: "I have abandoned the household life, which is delightful to householders with the sweet sounds of laughter and conversation mingled with the tinkling of new golden bracelets and anklets, and which is resplendent with great wealth and resembles the mansions of the chief deities. I have cast it away like a glob of spit and entered the Tapovana forest, which washes away the evils of all people because of its delight in solitude. Yet, my living here in this leaf-hut is like a second household life. Now, I shall live at the foot of a tree." Therefore, he said: "I abandoned the leaf-hut, which is filled with eight defects."

In that verse, "filled with eight defects" means being associated with eight faults. What are the eight? They are: the necessity of being constructed with great effort; the need for constant maintenance with grass, leaves, and clay; the fact that a dwelling is suitable for elders, so one who is untimely evicted cannot achieve one-pointedness of mind; the softening of the body by warding off cold and heat; the ability to hide blameworthy acts since one who enters a house can commit any evil; the sense of possession, thinking "this is mine"; the fact that having a house is like living with a companion; and being shared with many creatures such as lice, bedbugs, and house lizards. Seeing these eight disadvantages, the Great Being (Mahāsatta) abandoned the leaf-hut.

"Endowed with ten qualities" means rejecting the roofed shelter and approaching the foot of a tree endowed with ten qualities. What are the ten? They are: little effort in preparation; being easily obtained without fault just by approaching; the arising of the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā) by constantly seeing the changes in the tree's leaves; the absence of stinginess regarding the dwelling; the unsuitability for doing evil because one who does evil there feels ashamed; the absence of a sense of possession; living with deities; the rejection of a roofed shelter; happiness in usage; and the lack of concern because a tree-root dwelling is easily found wherever one goes. Seeing these ten qualities, he said he approached the foot of a tree. The Elder Buddhaghosa said in the Visuddhimagga Commentary:

"Where can there be a dwelling for one who desires solitude, equal to the foot of a tree, which was praised by the Buddha and taught as a support (nissaya) for the monkhood?"

"A virtuous person living at a secluded tree-root, which removes stinginess regarding dwellings and is protected by deities—"

"While looking at the fallen leaves of the tree—those that are very red, green, or yellow—he dispels the perception of permanence."
100:
“Where can there be a secluded place equal to the foot of a tree for a yogi who desires solitude, which was praised by the Buddha and taught as a ‘nissaya’ (support) for the monkhood?

“A virtuous yogi living at a secluded tree-root, which removes stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsamacchera) and is protected by tree-deities—

“While looking at the leaves of the tree—which are reddish when young, dark green when mature, and turn yellow and fall from the stalk when ripe—he can dispel the perception of permanence (niccasaññā) that thinks things are ‘permanent’.

“Therefore, a wise person should not despise the secluded tree-root, which is the inheritance of the Buddha and the dwelling of those who delight in meditation (bhāvanā).” (Visuddhimagga 1.32)

Then, the wise Sumedha, having seen the defects in the leaf-hut and having obtained the benefits of the tree-root dwelling, reflected further while residing there: “For me, going to the village for food and the hardship of seeking food is a great suffering. I did not renounce and become a monk for the sake of food due to some misfortune. There is no limit to the suffering caused by the pursuit of food. It would be good if I could subsist only on fallen fruits.” To show this special meaning—

32-33. “I abandoned the sown and planted crops entirely, and took only the fallen fruits which are endowed with many qualities.” Thus he said.

In that verse, ‘wāpita’ means that which is produced by sowing. ‘ropita’ means that which is produced by planting. The production of crops is only of two kinds: sowing and planting. Because of his fewness of wishes, he abandoned both kinds and subsisted on fallen fruits. ‘Pavattaphala’ means fruits that have fallen by themselves. ‘Ādiyi’ means consumed.

“A sage who is content with fallen fruits, who does not depend on others for his livelihood, and who is free from greed for food, can travel without hindrance in the four directions.

“He can abandon the craving for taste, and his livelihood is pure. Therefore, one should not despise the consumption of fallen fruits.” (Somewhat similar to Visuddhimagga 1.26) —

The wise Sumedha, living and practicing in this way, soon attained the eight attainments (samāpatti) and the five higher knowledges (abhiññā) within seven days. To manifest this meaning, the Buddha—
101:
In that (Padhāna Sutta), it is said: "In that hermitage, I exerted effort," and so forth. There, "tattha" means in that hermitage. "Padhāna" means energy (vīriya); it is called "padhāna" because it should be exerted or because it performs the function of spiritual exertion. "Padahiṃ" means "I exerted effort." "Nisajjaṭṭhānacaṅkame" means (exertion) through sitting, standing, and walking.

The wise Sumedha, having rejected sleep, passed the nights and days only through sitting, standing, and walking, and within just seven days, he attained the power of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā). While the ascetic Sumedha, having thus attained the power of supernormal knowledge, was passing the time in the bliss of meditative attainment (samāpatti), at that time, the Teacher named Dīpaṅkara appeared in the world—he who benefits all people, who causes fear to the forces of Māra, and who acts as the lamp of omniscience.

To speak briefly of the successive account of that Buddha: This Great Being named Dīpaṅkara, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and remaining in a state of existence similar to that of King Vessantara, gave great gifts such as those that cause the earth to tremble. At the end of his life, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Having stayed there for the full lifespan, the deities and Brahmās from the ten thousand world-systems assembled and requested:

"O Great Hero, the time has come for you;
Be conceived in the mother's womb.
Saving the world together with the devas,
Realize the deathless state (Nibbāna)."

Then, having heard the words of the deities and having performed the five great observations, the Bodhisatta passed away from that Tusita heaven and was conceived in the womb of Queen Sumedhā, in the family of King Sudeva—who was powerful with his retinue and fame and had conquered his enemies—in the city of Rammavatī, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha under the constellation of Uttarāsāḷha. Being protected by a great retinue, he stayed in the womb of the Great Queen for ten months without being smeared by any impurity, like a jeweled pinnacle, and then emerged from the Queen's womb like the autumn moon emerging from behind a cloud.

## The Thirty-Two Omens (Dvattiṃsa Pubbanimittāni)

At the moment of Prince Dīpaṅkara's conception and at the moment of his birth, the thirty-two omens and miracles became manifest. (These thirty-two omens occur) when all Omniscient Bodhisattas descend into their mother's womb, when they emerge from the mother's womb, when they realize the Four Noble Truths, and when they turn the Wheel of Dhamma.
102: In these four occasions (conception, birth, enlightenment, and preaching), the thirty-two miracles always occur. Therefore, to make it clear, I have shown (the miracles that occurred) at the birth of Prince Dīpaṅkara as follows: When the Bodhisatta Prince named Dīpaṅkara, who brings beauty, happiness, and peace, was born, at that time, the ten thousand world systems all around shook and trembled violently. The deities from ten thousand world systems assembled together in a single world system at that time. As soon as the Great Being, the Bodhisatta, was born, the deities first received him, and afterwards, human beings received him. Drums covered with leather and lutes with fine sounding-boards, though not played by anyone, and ornaments, though not struck, all around produced sweet sounds at that moment. In all places, bonds were broken, and all diseases were spontaneously cured. Those blind from birth saw forms, and the deaf all around heard sounds. People who were dull-witted from birth gained mindfulness. The lame gained the means of travel as if they could walk on foot. Ships traveling to other lands reached their ports quickly and spontaneously. All jewels situated in the sky and on the earth shone beautifully all around of their own accord. The fire in the terrible hells was extinguished, and the water in the rivers stopped flowing.
103: Even in the Lokantarika hell, where suffering is incessant, a great and vast light appeared. Similarly, at that time, this great ocean had calm waves and its water became sweet. No harsh or rough wind blew, and the trees were covered with well-bloomed flowers. The moon shone exceedingly bright along with the stars, and the sun was not hot. Birds from the sky and from the trees descended joyfully to the ground below. A great cloud reaching all four great islands rained down sweet water all around. The deities, staying in their own celestial mansions with clear minds, danced, sang, played music, shouted in praise, and made merry. It is said that the great door-leaves opened spontaneously at that very moment. Hunger and thirst did not oppress the multitude of people in the world even slightly. All creatures who were habitual enemies felt supreme loving-kindness. Crows wandered together with owls, and "saung-hto-tan" birds played with wild boars. Fierce poisonous snakes and faceless snakes played as they wished with mongooses. Even house mice, with trusting hearts, searched for lice on the heads of cats.
104:
Beings in the realm of spirits (pisāca-loka) who had not obtained water for the entire interval between two Buddhas became free from thirst. 
Those who were hunchbacked became straight-bodied, endowed with a pleasing and steady appearance. 
Those who were mute also spoke sweet words.

All beings with clear and faithful minds spoke affectionately to one another. 
Horses neighed with joyful hearts. 
Even the noble elephants in rut trumpeted.

The ten-thousandfold world system was filled all around with fragrant sandalwood powder; 
It was redolent with the scents of flowers, garlands, and kunkuma incense; 
It was adorned with various beautiful and great rows of banners.

In those verses, the trembling of the ten-thousandfold world system was the premonitory sign of the Bodhisatta's attainment of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). The gathering of deities in a single world system was the premonitory sign of their gathering to receive the Dhamma at the time of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana). The initial reception by the deities was the premonitory sign of the attainment of the four fine-material sphere jhānas (rūpāvacara-jhāna). The subsequent reception by humans was the premonitory sign of the attainment of the four immaterial sphere jhānas (arūpāvacara-jhāna). The spontaneous sounding of leather-bound drums was the premonitory sign of the proclamation of the great drum of Dhamma. The spontaneous sounding of lutes and ornaments was the premonitory sign of the attainment of the successive meditative attainments (anupubba-vihāra). The spontaneous breaking of bonds was the premonitory sign of the total cutting off of the conceit 'I am' (asmi-māna). The curing of all diseases of the great multitude was the premonitory sign of the attainment of the Four Truths and their Fruits. The sight of forms by those blind from birth was the premonitory sign of the attainment of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). The hearing of sounds by the deaf was the premonitory sign of the attainment of the divine ear (dibba-sota).

The recovery of memory by those mute from birth was the premonitory sign of the attainment of the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). The ability of the lame to walk on foot was the premonitory sign of the attainment of the four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda). The safe arrival at port of ships traveling to other lands was the premonitory sign of the attainment of the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The spontaneous radiance of gems was the premonitory sign of the attainment of the light of Dhamma. The extinguishing of hell-fires in the hells was the premonitory sign of the extinguishing of the eleven fires. The stopping of the flow of water in rivers was the premonitory sign of the attainment of the four grounds of self-confidence (vesārajja-ñāṇa). The appearance of light in the Lokantarika hell was the premonitory sign of the vision of the light of knowledge after dispelling the darkness of ignorance (avijjā).
105:
The ocean water becoming sweet was the premonitory sign of the single nature of the taste of Nibbāna (the task of calming defilements). The absence of strong winds was the premonitory sign of the destruction of the sixty-two types of wrong views. The blooming of trees was the premonitory sign of blooming with the flowers of the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala).

The moon's extreme radiance was the premonitory sign of being beloved by the great multitude. The sun's lack of excessive heat and its clarity was the premonitory sign of the arising of physical and mental happiness. The birds descending from mountains and such to the ground was the premonitory sign of the great multitude taking refuge for life after hearing the admonition. The falling of great rain over the four continents was the premonitory sign of the falling of the great rain of Dhamma. The deities dancing and playing while staying in their respective celestial mansions was the premonitory sign of the uttering of joyful exclamations (udāna) upon reaching Buddhahood. The spontaneous opening of door-leaves was the premonitory sign of the opening of the door of the Noble Eightfold Path. The absence of the oppression of hunger was the premonitory sign of being happy through the bliss of liberation (vimutti-sukha). Enemies gaining minds of loving-kindness was the premonitory sign of the attainment of the four divine abodes (brahma-vihāra). The continuous row of banners throughout the ten-thousandfold world system was the premonitory sign of being adorned with the banners of the Noble Ones (ariya-dhaja). Other extraordinary signs should be understood as premonitory signs of the attainment of the remaining qualities of a Buddha.

At that time, Prince Dīpaṅkara, enjoying great prosperity and in due course reaching the prime of youth, experienced royal splendor like that of the celestial realm in three palaces suited for the three seasons. While going out for enjoyment in the park, he successively saw the three divine messengers—an old man, a sick man, and a dead man. Filled with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he turned back and entered the city named Rammavatī, which possessed wealth and beauty like the city of Sudassana. After entering the city, on the fourth occasion, he called the elephant trainer and said, "Friend trainer, I wish to go out to see the park; prepare the elephant vehicles." The trainer replied, "Very well, my Lord," and had eighty-four thousand elephants prepared.

Then, a deity named Vissakamma adorned the Bodhisatta by dressing him in garments of various colors, decorating him with strings of pearls and armlets, providing him with pleasing golden bracelets, a diadem, and earrings, and adorning his hair with extremely fragrant flowers. Then Prince Dīpaṅkara, like a celestial youth, surrounded by eighty-four thousand elephants, mounted upon a noble elephant's back. Surrounded by a great army, he entered the delightful park. Dismounting from the elephant's back, he wandered through the park and sat upon a most beautiful stone slab that cooled his heart, and turned his mind toward renunciation...
106: (Prince Dīpaṅkara) gave rise to the intention to ordain. At that very moment, a Mahābrahmā, an Arahant from the Suddhāvāsa realm, brought the eight requisites of a monk and appeared before the Great Being. Seeing them, the Great Being asked, "What is this?" and hearing "They are the requisites of a monk," he removed his ornaments and handed them to the treasurer. Taking his auspicious sword, he cut his hair along with the crown and threw them into the sky. Then Sakka, the king of devas, received the hair and crown in a golden casket and established the Makuṭa Cetiya, three yojanas in height and made of sapphire, on the summit of Mount Sineru. Then the Great Being donned the saffron robes, the banner of Arahantship offered by the Mahābrahmā, and threw his pair of garments into the sky. The Brahmā received them and built a cetiya twelve yojanas high, made of all kinds of jewels, in the Brahma realm. When Prince Dīpaṅkara ordained, ten million people followed him into the monkhood. Surrounded by that assembly, the Bodhisatta practiced austerities for ten months. Then, on the full moon day of Visākha, he entered a certain city for alms. In that city on that day, people were cooking pure milk-rice (pāyāsa) to offer to the deities. They offered it to the Bodhisatta who had entered for alms with his followers. That milk-rice was sufficient for all ten million monks. Furthermore, the deities infused divine essence (ojā) into the Great Being's bowl. Having partaken of that food, he spent the day in that Sal grove. In the evening, rising from his solitary seclusion and dismissing the group, he took eight handfuls of grass offered by an ascetic named Sunanda and went to the foot of the Pipphali Bodhi tree. Spreading the grass mat and leaning his back against the ninety-cubit trunk of the Pipphali Bodhi tree, he sat cross-legged, established a fourfold resolution, and remained at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Then, having defeated the host of Māra, he attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa) in the first watch of the night. In the middle watch, he purified the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). In the last watch, he contemplated dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in forward and reverse order and entered the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna). Emerging from that jhāna, he directed his mind to the five aggregates, saw the fifty characteristics by way of arising and passing away, and developed insight up to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). At dawn, through the Noble Path, he realized all the qualities of a Buddha and uttered the lion's roar of a Buddha. He spent seven weeks (forty-nine days) near the Bodhi tree. Accepting the request of the Brahmā to teach the Dhamma, he turned the Wheel of Dhamma at Sunandārāma. He gave the nectar of Dhamma to a billion devas and humans, causing the rain of Dhamma to fall like a great cloud over the four great islands, liberating the people from the bonds of defilements, and wandering through the countryside. At that time, the wise Sumedha, spending his time in the bliss of meditative attainment, did not notice the shaking of the earth. Not seeing those great omens, it is said: "Thus, while I had attained psychic powers and mastery in the Dispensation, the Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, arose." "Thus, while I had attained psychic powers and mastery in the Dispensation, the Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, arose."
107: Causing the rain of Dhamma to fall and liberating the multitude from the bonds of defilements, he wandered through the countryside. At that time, the wise Sumedha, passing the time in the bliss of meditative attainment, did not see the shaking of the earth nor those great omens. Therefore, it was said: "Thus, when I had reached the perfection of psychic powers and attained mastery in the Dispensation, the Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, arose in the world. I did not see the four omens that occurred at the time of his conception, his birth, his awakening to the Four Noble Truths, and the preaching of the Wheel of Dhamma, as I was absorbed in the delight of jhāna." In that verse, 'evaṃ' (thus) indicates the matter to be explained. 'me' means 'my' or 'I'. 'siddhippattassa' means having reached the perfection of the five mundane psychic powers. 'vasībhūtassa' means having attained mastery through practice. 'sāsane' means in the dispensation of those with secluded minds (referring to jhāna and psychic powers); here the genitive case should be understood in the sense of disregard (anādara). 'jino' (Conqueror) is so called because of conquering the enemies of defilements. 'uppajjante' refers to the taking of conception. 'jāyante' refers to the birth from the mother's womb. 'bujjhante' refers to the realization of the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. 'dhammadessane' refers to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma. 'caturo nimitte' refers to the four omens. It means the omens such as the shaking of the ten thousand world systems that occurred at the four occasions of the Dīpaṅkara Buddha's conception, birth, enlightenment, and turning of the Wheel of Dhamma. Here, one might ask: 'Since there are many such omens, why is it said "four omens"? Is it not inappropriate?' It is not inappropriate; it is appropriate. Although there are many omens, they are called 'the four omens' because they occurred on four occasions. 'nāddasaṃ' means 'I did not see'. Now, to show the reason for not seeing those four omens, he said 'absorbed in the delight of jhāna'. 'jhānaratī' is a synonym for the bliss of meditative attainment. Because he was endowed with the delight of jhāna, he did not see those omens. At that time, the Dīpaṅkara Buddha, surrounded by four hundred thousand Arahants, wandering in due course, reached the delightful city named Ramma and stayed at the Sudassana Great Monastery. The citizens of Ramma, hearing that 'the Dīpaṅkara Buddha, having attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and turned the noble Wheel of Dhamma, has reached the city of Ramma in his travels and is staying at the Sudassana Great Monastery,' took medicines such as ghee, and after their morning meal, dressed in clean upper garments and carrying flowers and perfumes, approached the Buddha. Having approached and paid homage to the Buddha, they honored him with flowers and perfumes and sat in suitable places. Having heard the extremely sweet Dhamma, they invited the Buddha for the next day to increase their meritorious joy and rose from their seats.
108:
At that time, the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, accompanied by four hundred thousand Arahants, while wandering on a journey in due course, arrived at the city of Rammavatī and stayed at the Sudassana Mahāvihāra monastery. The citizens of Rammavatī heard: "The Blessed One Dīpaṅkara has attained the peerless Supreme Enlightenment, has turned the noble Wheel of Dhamma, and while wandering on a journey in due course, has now arrived at Rammavatī and is staying at the Sudassana Mahāvihāra monastery." They took medicines such as ghee and others, and after eating their morning meal, dressed in clean upper robes, carrying flowers, incense, and perfumes in their hands, approached the place where the Buddha was. Having approached, they paid homage to the Teacher, made offerings with flowers and so on, sat in a suitable place, and listened to the extremely sweet discourse on the Dhamma. After inviting the Blessed One for the following day, they rose from their seats, circumambulated the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala) to the right, and departed.

On the following day, they prepared an incomparable great offering, had a pavilion constructed, covered it with stainless and tender blue lotuses, and decorated it with the four kinds of perfumes. They scattered parched rice and fragrant flowers, placed pots filled with cool, sweet water at the four corners of the pavilion, and covered them with banana leaves. Above the pavilion, they fastened a most beautiful cloth canopy resembling the jasmine flower, and decorated it with stars of gold, gems, and silver. In that pavilion, they hung garlands of perfume, flowers, leaves, and jewels, and made it like a cloudy sky with incense. They swept the entire beautiful city of Rammavatī, placed banana trees with fruit and full water pots decorated with flowers, and hoisted banners and flags of various colors. They enclosed both sides of the main road with curtains and screens, and while decorating the path by which the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara would come, they filled in the places eroded by water with earth, leveled the uneven muddy ground, and made it even. They scattered white sand resembling pearls, scattered parched rice and flowers, and planted banana buds with fruit.

At that time, the hermit Sumedha, rising from his hermitage and traveling through the sky above those people of Rammavatī, saw those people who were exceedingly joyful, clearing and decorating the road. Thinking, "What could be the reason?", he descended from the sky in the sight of everyone, stood at one side, and asked those people: "Friends, for whose sake are you clearing this road?" This matter is stated in the Pāḷi:

"In the border region, having invited the Tathāgata, they clear the path of his coming with joyful hearts."

"At that time, I, having departed from my hermitage, shaking my bark-garments, was then traveling through the sky."

"Seeing the people filled with joy, glad and delighted, I descended from the sky and then asked the people."

"O joyful, glad, and delighted people, for whom is this road being cleared—this straight path (añjasa), this track (vaṭuma), this way (ayana)?"
109:
Seeing the people filled with joy, glad and delighted, I descended from the sky and then asked the people.
"O joyful, glad, and delighted people, for whom is this road being cleared—this straight path, this track, this way?"

In that (verse), 'paccantadesavisaye' means in a province known as the border region on one side of the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). 'Tassa āgamanaṃ maggaṃ' means the path by which that Buddha would come. 'Ahaṃ tena samayena' means I at that time; here the instrumental case should be understood in the sense of the locative. 'Sakassamā' means having departed from his own hermitage. 'Dhunanto' means shaking out (the bark-garments). It should be understood that these two words 'tena samayena' and 'tadā' have the same meaning, so the former is connected with the action of departing and the latter with the action of going; otherwise, the fault of tautology (punarutti-dosa) cannot be avoided. 'Tadā' means at that time.

'Vedajātaṃ' means the arising of joy (somanassa). These three words 'tuṭṭhahaṭṭhaṃ pamoditaṃ' are synonyms of each other and clarify each other's meaning. Alternatively, 'tuṭṭha' means pleased by happiness, 'haṭṭha' means gladdened by rapture (pīti), and 'pamudita' means delighted by joy (pāmojja). 'Orohitvāna' means having descended. 'Mānuse pucchi' means he asked the humans. There is also a variant reading 'mānuse pucchi'. 'Tāvade' means at that time, at that very moment. Now, wishing to show the meaning of what was asked, the words beginning with 'tuṭṭhahaṭṭho pamudito' were spoken. Therein, this great multitude of people, having hearts that are pleased, gladdened, and delighted, are clearing the road; for what reason are they clearing it, or for whose sake are they clearing it? Thus, the word 'sodheti' (clears) should be brought in to understand the meaning; otherwise, it is not appropriate. 'Sodhīyati' means it is being made clean. 'Maggo añjasaṃ vaṭumāyanaṃ' are simply synonyms for the road.

When thus asked by the hermit Sumedha, those people said: "Venerable Sumedha, do you not know? The Buddha named Dīpaṅkara, having attained the peerless Supreme Enlightenment and having set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, while wandering through the provinces, has arrived at our city in due course and is staying at the Sudassana Mahāvihāra monastery. We have invited that Blessed One and are clearing the path by which that Buddha, the Blessed One, will come." Hearing that, the wise Sumedha thought: "Even the sound 'Buddha' is rare to hear, let alone the arising of a Buddha. Therefore, it is proper for me also to clear the path of the coming of the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala) together with these people." Those people...
111:
Thus, the Blessed One, being himself free from lust, surrounded by monks free from lust; being himself free from hatred, surrounded by monks free from hatred; and being himself free from delusion, surrounded by monks free from delusion, shone exceedingly. Then the Teacher, surrounded by four hundred thousand cankerless Arahants possessed of great majesty and the six higher powers (abhiññā), set out upon that decorated and prepared path which was like the expanse of the sky. He appeared like the thousand-eyed Sakka surrounded by hosts of devas, or like the Mahābrahmā Hārita surrounded by hosts of Brahmas, or like the autumnal moon surrounded by hosts of stars, moving with the incomparable Buddha-grace generated by the power of merit accumulated over an immeasurable period.

"With a golden-hued radiance, the Wise One, making the trees along the path appear golden-hued and creating golden-hued flowers, the golden-hued Buddha set out upon the path."

Sumedha the hermit also opened his eyes and beheld the physical body of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, who was approaching along that decorated and prepared path. The Buddha was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, embellished with the eighty minor marks, surrounded by a fathom-wide radiance, full of glory, resembling a dark blue sapphire, and emitting the six-colored Buddha-rays like various streaks of lightning in the sky, having reached the pinnacle of physical beauty. Seeing this, Sumedha thought: "Today, it is proper for me to make the sacrifice of my life for the Possessor of Ten Powers. Let the Blessed One not tread upon the mud. Let him, along with the four hundred thousand cankerless Arahants, proceed by treading upon my back as if treading upon a bridge of jeweled planks. That will be for my long-lasting welfare and happiness." Thus, he loosened his hair, spread his antelope skin, matted hair, and bark garment over the black mud, and lay prostrate on his face upon that very mud. Referring to that event:

"Those people whom I asked replied to me: 'The Buddha, the unsurpassed in the world, the Conqueror (Jina) named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the World, has arisen. It is his path, called Añjasa, Vaṭuma, and Ayana, that is being cleared.'

As soon as I heard the word 'Buddha,' joy arose within me. Uttering 'Buddha, Buddha,' I experienced joyful happiness (somanassa)."
112:
Standing at the place where I descended from the sky, with a heart filled with joy and spiritual urgency, I thought: 'I shall plant the seeds of merit in this fertile field of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. Let not the ninth moment of the Buddha's appearance, which is so difficult to encounter, pass in vain.'

'O people, if you are clearing the path for the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, please give me a portion as well. I too wish to clear the straight path for the Buddha's arrival along with you.'

Then, those people gave me a portion (which was very difficult to clear) to prepare the path. At that time, I cleared the path while contemplating "Buddha, Buddha."

Before the portion I was clearing was finished, the Conqueror Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage who had overcome the five Maras, arrived on that decorated path, surrounded by four hundred thousand Arahants who possessed the six higher powers (abhiññā), the quality of steadfastness (tādi), and were pure and free from taints.

The citizens of Rammavatī came out to welcome him, and many drums were beaten. Both humans and devas were greatly delighted and uttered cries of "Sādhu, Sādhu!"

Devas saw humans, and humans saw devas. Both, with hands joined in reverence, followed the Tathāgata.

Devas with celestial instruments and humans with human instruments played music, and both followed the Tathāgata.

The devas traveling in the sky showered divine Mandārava flowers, Paduma lotuses, and Pārichattaka flowers in all directions as an offering.

The devas traveling in the sky showered divine sandalwood powder and various excellent perfumes in all directions as an offering.

The humans on the ground also threw and offered Campaka, Sarala, Nīpa, Nāga, Punnāga, and Ketaka flowers in all directions.

Then, I loosened my matted hair and spread my bark garment and deer skin over the mud, and lay face down.

'May the Buddha, together with his disciples, proceed by treading upon me; let him not tread upon the mud. Such treading upon me will be for my long-term benefit and happiness.'

In these verses, 'Viyākaṃsu' means they spoke. In some palm-leaf manuscripts, there is also the reading 'Dīpaṅkaro nāma jino, tassa sodhiyati patho.' 'Somanassaṃ pavedayi' means he experienced the feeling of joy. 'Tattha ṭhatvā' means standing in that place where he descended from the sky. 'Saṃviggamānaso' means having a heart amazed by rapture (pīti). 'Idha' means in this fertile field for planting seeds of merit, which is the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. 'Bījāni' means the seeds of merit (kusala). 'Ropissaṃ' means I shall plant the seeds. 'Khaṇo' refers to the ninth moment of the Buddha's appearance, which is free from the eight inopportune times (akkhaṇa) and is a very rare occasion. It means 'I have obtained that very rare ninth moment.' The word 've' is just a particle. 'Mā upaccagā' means let not that moment pass in vain without the task being completed. 'Dadātha' means please give. 'Te' refers to those people whom I asked. 'Sodhemahaṃ tadā' means at that time, I cleared (the path).
113: In these verses, 'Viyākaṃsu' means 'byākariṃsu' (they spoke). In some versions, there is also the reading 'Dīpaṅkaro nāma jino, tassa sodhīyati patho' (The Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, his path is being cleared). 'Somanassaṃ pavedayiṃ' means the feeling of joy was experienced. 'Tattha ṭhatvā' means standing right there in the place where he descended from the sky. 'Saṃviggamānaso' means having a heart amazed and entranced by rapture (pīti). 'Idha' means in this fertile field for planting seeds of merit, which is the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. 'Bījāni' refers to the seeds of merit (kusala). 'Ropissanti' means (the seeds) will be planted. 'Khaṇo' refers to the assembly of the ninth opportune moment (navama-khaṇa), which is free from the eight inopportune times (akkhaṇa). I have obtained that extremely rare opportune moment. The word 've' is just a particle. 'Mā upaccagā' means let not that opportune moment pass in vain, let it not be missed. 'Dadātha' means please give. 'Te' refers to those people whom I asked. 'Sodhemahaṃ tadā' means at that time, I cleared (the path). 'Aniṭṭhite' means before it was finished, while it was still in progress. 'Khīṇāsavehi'—here, there are four taints (āsava): the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), the taint of wrong view (diṭṭhāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). Those Arahants in whom these taints are exhausted, abandoned, cut off, calmed, incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship, are called 'Khīṇāsava' (taint-exhausted ones). It means 'together with those Arahants.' Because the four taints are exhausted, they are called 'Vimala' (stainless), free from impurities like lust. Regarding 'Devā manusse passanti' (Devas see humans), there is nothing special to say about devas seeing humans, but it means that just as humans standing here can see (devas) by the power of natural vision, so too devas see humans. 'Devatā' refers to the devas. 'Ubho pi' means both devas and humans. 'Pañjalikā' means with hands joined in reverence, placing both hands upon the head. 'Anuyanti Tathāgataṃ' means they followed behind the Buddha. According to the grammatical rule that the second accusative case (upayoga-vacana) can occur in the sense of the sixth genitive case when associated with the prefix 'anu', it is stated as 'Anuyanti Tathāgataṃ.' 'Vajjayantā' means while playing (musical instruments). 'Mandāravaṃ' refers to the divine Mandārava flower. 'Disodisaṃ' means in various directions. 'Okiranti' means they showered down. 'Ākāsanabhagatā' means those who have reached the sky known as 'nabha', or those who have gone to the sky, or those who have reached heaven. This is because the word 'nabha' also refers to heaven. 'Marū' refers to the devas. 'Saralaṃ' refers to the Sarala flower, 'Nīpaṃ' to the Kadamba flower, and 'Nāgapunnāgaketakaṃ' to the Nāga, Punnāga, and Ketaka flowers. 'Bhūmitalagatā' means those situated on the ground. 'Kese muñcitvāhaṃ' means I loosened my bound matted hair and spread it out disheveled. 'Tattha' means in the muddy portion given to me (by the people of Rammavatī). 'Cammakaṃ' refers to the hide of a black antelope. 'Kalale' means in the mud. 'Avakujjo' means being face down (prostrate). 'Nipajjahaṃ' means I lay down.
114:
I lay down. In this phrase 'mā naṃ', 'mā' is a particle in the sense of prohibition, and 'naṃ' is a particle used merely for completing the verse. The meaning is: "May the Buddha not step on the mud." The phrase 'hitāya me bhavissati' means that not being stepped on in the mud will be for my benefit for a long time. There is also a reading 'sukhāya me bhavissati' (it will be for my happiness).

Then the wise Sumedha, lying on the surface of the mud, thought thus: "If I so desired, I could burn away all defilements and enter the city of Rammā as the most junior monk in the Saṅgha. However, there is no need for me to attain Nibbāna by burning defilements in an unknown form. If I, like the Dīpaṅkara Ten-Powered One, reach the supreme Enlightenment, board the boat of Dhamma, and rescue the multitude from the ocean of Saṃsāra before attaining Parinibbāna, this would be appropriate for me." Then, combining the eight factors and making the formal aspiration (abhinīhāra) for Buddhahood, he lay down. Therefore, it was said:

"As I lay upon the earth, this thought occurred to me:
If I so wished today, I could burn away my defilements.

What use is there for me to realize the Dhamma here in an unknown form?
Having reached omniscience, I shall become a Buddha in the world including the devas.

What use is there for me, a man who sees his own strength, to cross over alone?
Having reached omniscience, I shall help the world including the devas to cross over.

By this extraordinary merit of mine performed towards the Supreme Man,
Having reached omniscience, I shall rescue the great multitude.

Cutting the stream of Saṃsāra, destroying the three realms of existence,
And boarding the boat of Dhamma, I shall help the world including the devas to cross over."

In those verses, 'pathaviyaṃ nipannassa' means of one lying on the ground. This reading itself is correct. 'Cetaso' means the thought of the mind occurred. There is also a reading 'evaṃ me āsi cetanā'. 'Icchamāno' means if one so desires. 'Kilese' refers to the ten defilements such as greed (rāga), which are called 'kilesa' because they defile and torment. 'Jhāpaye' means I shall burn; the meaning is "I shall burn my defilements."

'Kiṃ' is a word of rejection. 'Aññāta-vesena' means in an unmanifested form, in a hidden form without letting others know. Indeed, what is the use of effecting the destruction of taints (āsava) in this Dispensation like other monks? For the sake of Buddhahood...
115:
The meaning is: having fulfilled the perfections (pāramī) such as generosity (dāna) which produce Buddhahood, and having caused the great earth to tremble at the moments of conception, birth, enlightenment, and the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, may I be a Buddha who, having realized the truths, makes others realize them; who, having crossed over, makes others cross; who, having been freed, makes others free. 'Sadevake' means in the world including the devas.

'Thāmadassinā' means by one who sees his own strength and power. 'Santāressaṃ' means I shall help to cross over (santāressāmi). 'Sadevakaṃ' means either the assembly of beings including devas or the world including devas. 'Adhikārena' means by an extraordinary and superior act of merit; the meaning is by the extraordinary merit of sacrificing my life for the Buddha and lying down on the surface of the mud.

'Saṃsāra-sotaṃ': Saṃsāra is the wandering here and there through the modes of birth (yoni), destinations (gati), stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and the nine abodes of beings (navasattāvāsa) by the power of kamma and defilements. As it was said: 'The uninterrupted succession of the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and sense bases (āyatana) is called Saṃsāra.'

It is 'saṃsāra-sota' because it is both Saṃsāra and a stream; thus, 'that stream of Saṃsāra'. Alternatively, the stream of Saṃsāra is 'saṃsāra-sota'; the meaning is having cut the stream of craving (taṇhā) which is the cause of Saṃsāra. 'Tayo bhave' refers to the sense realm (kāma-bhava), the fine-material realm (rūpa-bhava), and the immaterial realm (arūpa-bhava). The three 'bhava' are intended as the kamma and defilements that cause rebirth in the three realms. 'Dhamma-nāvaṃ' refers to the Noble Eightfold Path. It is called the 'Boat of Dhamma' because it enables one to cross the four floods (ogha). 'Samāruyha' means having boarded. 'Santāressaṃ' means I shall help to cross over.

Because, for one who aspires for Buddhahood:
"Humanity, the male sex, the root cause, meeting the Teacher,
Renunciation, the attainment of virtues, an extraordinary act, and strong desire—
By the combination of these eight factors, the formal aspiration (abhinīhāra) succeeds."

Among those eight, 'manussattaṃ' means the aspiration of one who aspires for Buddhahood only while remaining in the state of a human succeeds; it does not succeed for those in the state of a Naga, etc. Why? Because they are rootless (ahetuka) beings.

'Liṅgasampatti' means even for one who is in the state of a human, the aspiration succeeds only for one who remains in the male sex; it does not succeed for a woman, a eunuch (paṇḍaka), a neuter (napuṃsaka), or a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka).
116:
(The aspiration) is fulfilled. Why? Because there is an absence of the fulfillment of the marks [of a Great Man] in women. For it has been said: "It is impossible, bhikkhus, it cannot happen, that a woman should be an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One"—this is explained in detail. Therefore, even for a human being, if one remains in the female form, the aspiration cannot be fulfilled.

'Hetu' (Cause) means: Even for a man, the aspiration is fulfilled only for one who is endowed with the cause to attain the fruit of Arahatship in that very existence, and not for any other.

'Satthāradassana' (Seeing the Teacher) means: The aspiration is fulfilled only if one makes the wish in the presence of a living Buddha. If one makes the wish after the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna—whether near a stupa, at the foot of a Bodhi tree, near a statue, or in the presence of a Paccekabuddha or a disciple of the Buddha—the aspiration is not fulfilled. Why? Because they are unable to give a prophecy by determining through the 'Knowledge of the Determination of the Results of Kamma' (Kamma-vipāka-paricchedaka-ñāṇa) after knowing who is capable and who is not. Therefore, the aspiration is fulfilled only in the presence of a Buddha.

'Pabbajjā' (Going Forth) means: Even for one who makes the aspiration in the presence of a Buddha, it is fulfilled only for one who has gone forth as an ascetic or a monk who teaches the efficacy of action (Kammakiriyavādī), and not for one remaining in the form of a householder. Why? Because Bodhisattas attain Supreme Enlightenment only after going forth, and not as householders. Therefore, even at the time of the initial aspiration, one must be a renunciant.

'Guṇasampatti' (Possession of Virtues) means: Even for a renunciant, it is fulfilled only for one who has attained the eight meditative attainments and the five supernormal powers, and not for one who is devoid of these virtues. Why? Because such [an aspiration] cannot occur for one without virtues.

'Adhikāra' (Dedication) means: Even for one endowed with virtues, it is fulfilled only for one who has dedicated his life to the Buddhas; for one endowed with such dedication, it is fulfilled, and not for any other.

'Chandatā' (Zeal) means: Even for one endowed with the preliminary aspiration (abhinīhāra), it is fulfilled only for one who has great desire, effort, zeal, and search for the qualities that make one a Buddha (Buddhakāra-dhamma), and not for any other. Here is an analogy for the greatness of this zeal: If there were a person capable of crossing the entire world-system filled with a single mass of water by the strength of his arms to reach the other shore, such a person could attain Buddhahood. If one does not consider this difficult and is endowed with such great zeal and effort, thinking, "I will cross this water and go to the other shore," then his aspiration is fulfilled, and not for any other.
117:
Only when the wise Sumedha combined these eight factors did he make the preliminary aspiration (abhinīhāra) to become a Buddha and lay down. The Blessed One Dīpaṅkara also came and stood near the head of the wise Sumedha. Seeing the ascetic Sumedha lying on the surface of the mud, He reflected by directing His 'Knowledge of the Future' (Anāgataṃsañāṇa): "This ascetic has made the preliminary aspiration for Buddhahood and is lying down. Will his aspiration be fulfilled or not?" Knowing that "After four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons from now, he will become a Buddha named Gotama," He stood in the midst of the assembly and proclaimed: "Do you see, bhikkhus, this ascetic of fierce austerity lying on the surface of the mud?" The monks replied, "Yes, Bhante." "This man has made the preliminary aspiration for Buddhahood and is lying down; the aspiration of this ascetic will be fulfilled. For at the end of four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world. In that existence, the city named Kapilavatthu will be his residence, Queen Mahāmāyā will be his mother, King Suddhodana will be his father, Upatissa and Kolita will be his two chief disciples, the monk named Ānanda will be his attendant, and Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā will be his two chief female disciples. Having matured his knowledge, he will depart on the Great Renunciation, practice the Great Striving, receive milk-rice offered by the young woman named Sujātā at the foot of a Nigrodha tree, eat it on the bank of the Nerañjarā river, ascend the Bodhimanda, and attain Supreme Enlightenment at the foot of an Assattha (Ficus religiosa) tree." Thus He gave the prophecy. Regarding this, it was said:

60. Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the Worlds, the Recipient of Offerings, stood near my head and spoke these words:

61. "Look at this ascetic with matted hair, of fierce austerity. In the Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon) beyond four incalculables from this aeon, he will become a Buddha in the world."

62. "Having departed from the pleasant city named Kapila, that Tathāgata, having practiced the [Great] Striving and performed difficult austerities (dukkaracariya),"

63. "That Tathāgata, having sat at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree and received milk-rice there, will go to the Nerañjarā river."

64. "That Conqueror (Jina), having eaten the milk-rice on the bank of the Nerañjarā river, will go to the foot of the Bodhi tree by the excellent prepared path."
118:
Then, that peerless Bodhisatta, possessed of great retinue and fame, having circumambulated the Bodhimaṇḍa clockwise, will attain enlightenment at the foot of the Assattha tree.

The mother who gives birth to this Bodhisatta will be named Māyā, the father will be named Suddhodana, and this Buddha will be named Gotama.

Koliṭa and Upatissa, who are free from taints (āsavas), free from lust, of peaceful mind, and concentrated heart, will be the chief disciples. The attendant named Ānanda will serve this Conqueror (Jina).

Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā, who are free from taints, free from lust, of peaceful mind, and concentrated heart, will be the chief female disciples.

The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Assattha tree. Citta the householder and Hatthāḷavaka will be the chief male lay attendants. Uttarā, the mother of Nanda, and Khujjuttarā will be the chief female lay attendants.

In those verses, 'Lokavidū' means one who knows the world in every way. Indeed, the Blessed One knew, understood, and penetrated the world in every way: by its nature, its origin (samudaya), its cessation (nirodha), and the path leading to its cessation (magga). Therefore, he is called 'Lokavidū'. As it is said:

'Therefore, indeed, the wise one who knows the world, who has reached the end of the world, who has lived the holy life, having known the end of the world (Nibbāna) and being at peace, does not long for this world or the next.'

Furthermore, there are three worlds: the world of formations (sankhāra-loka), the world of beings (satta-loka), and the world of space (okāsa-loka). Among them, the world of formations refers to phenomena such as the earth element, etc., which arise depending on causes. The world of beings refers to beings with perception, without perception, and with neither-perception-nor-non-perception. The world of space refers to the dwelling places of beings. Since the Blessed One knows all these three worlds according to their true nature, he is called 'Lokavidū'. 'Āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho' means being worthy of receiving offerings and gifts because of being one worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya); he is one who deserves to receive offerings brought from afar. 'Ussīsake maṃ ṭhatvānā' means standing near my head...
119:
Standing near my head means 'He spoke these words which should be spoken now.' 'Jaṭila' means one who has matted hair; it refers to that ascetic Sumedha. 'Uggatāpana' refers to the ascetic of fierce practice. 'Ahū' means in the days; 'Atha' means thereafter. Or, this reading 'Atha' is the original text. 'Kapilavhayā' means from the royal city named Kapilavatthu. 'Rammā' means because of being delightful. 'Padhānaṃ' refers to energetic effort (viriya). 'Ehiti' means will arrive. In the remaining verses, the meaning is clear.

Then the wise Sumedha, thinking 'My aspiration will surely be fulfilled,' felt great joy. The great multitude, hearing the words of the Dīpaṅkara Buddha of Ten Powers, were delighted, thinking 'The ascetic Sumedha is indeed the sprout of a Buddha.' This thought occurred to them: 'Just as a man crossing a river, if unable to cross at the straight landing-place, crosses at a lower landing-place, even so, if we do not attain the Path and Fruit in the dispensation of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, we may be able to realize the Path and Fruit in your presence when you become a Buddha in the future.' Thus they made their aspiration. Dīpaṅkara Buddha, having praised the Bodhisatta Mahāsatta, honored him with eight handfuls of flowers, circumambulated him clockwise, and departed. Those four hundred thousand Arahats also honored the Bodhisatta with flowers and perfumes, circumambulated him clockwise, and departed. Devas and humans likewise honored and paid homage to him and departed.

Then the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the illuminator of the wisdom of the entire world, surrounded by four hundred thousand Arahats, receiving the offerings of the citizens of Rammavatī and the homage of the devas, proceeded across the ground like a noble golden mountain peak tinged with the glow of twilight. While many miracles were occurring, he traveled along that decorated and prepared road and entered the city of Rammavatī, which was fragrant with various sweet-smelling flowers, scented with aromatic powders, adorned with hoisted flags and banners, where swarms of bees hummed as their hearts were drawn by the fragrance, darkened by the smoke of incense, and as beautiful and delightful as the city of the gods (Amarapura). Then, the Dīpaṅkara Buddha of Ten Powers sat upon the costly Buddha-seat prepared for him, like the autumn moon atop Mount Yugandhara, destroying the mass of darkness, causing the lotus groves to bloom, and acting like the sun of the day. The community of monks also sat in their respective seats in order. The lay devotees of Rammavatī, endowed with virtues such as faith, offered to the community of monks headed by the Buddha an incomparable alms-giving, the source of happiness, consisting of various foods, etc., complete in color, fragrance, and taste.
120:
Then the Bodhisatta, having heard the prophecy of the Buddha, the Possessor of Ten Powers, felt as if the state of Buddhahood were already within the palm of his hand. With a joyful heart, when everyone had departed, he rose from his place of rest and sat down cross-legged upon a heap of flowers, thinking, "I shall now investigate the Perfections."

While the Great Being was thus seated, the deities of the entire ten thousand world systems gave a shout of applause and praised the Bodhisatta in various ways, saying: "O Lord Sumedha the Hermit, those portents which appear when former Bodhisattas sit cross-legged, thinking, 'I shall investigate the Perfections,' have all appeared today. Without a doubt, you will become a Buddha; we know this. For he to whom these omens appear will certainly become a Buddha. Therefore, make your effort firm and exert yourself."

In reference to this, it was said:

"Hearing this word of the Incomparable Great Seer, humans and devas rejoiced, thinking, 'This is indeed a Buddha-seed.'

Shouts of applause are raised; they clap their hands and laugh. The ten thousand world systems, together with the devas, pay homage with joined palms.

'If we should fail to attain the Path and Fruit under the Dispensation of this Lord of the World, may we be in the presence of this person in the future.'

'Just as people crossing a river, if they miss the direct landing place, take a lower landing place and thus cross the great river,'

'Even so, if all of us should miss this Conqueror, may we be in the presence of this person in the future.'

Knowing the world and being the recipient of offerings, Dīpaṅkara the Buddha, having praised my deed, raised his right foot.

All the sons of the Conqueror who were there circumambulated me to the right. Devas, humans, and asuras, having paid homage, departed.

When the Leader of the World, together with the Saṅgha, had passed out of my sight, I then rose from my place of rest and sat down cross-legged."
121:
I attained happiness through the bliss born of hearing the prophecy that I would become a Buddha; my mind was gladdened with youthful joy, and my entire body was suffused with intense rapture. At that time, I sat in the cross-legged posture.

Sitting there cross-legged, I then reflected: I have attained mastery in the Jhanas, and I have reached the pinnacle of the supernormal knowledges (Abhiññās).

In the ten thousand world-elements, there are no hermits equal to me. I am peerless in the qualities of psychic power. I have obtained such happiness.

While I was sitting cross-legged, the deities dwelling in the ten thousand world systems raised a great shout, saying: "Lord Sumedha, you will surely and certainly become a Buddha."

Those omens which appeared when the Bodhisattas of the past sat in the noble cross-legged posture are appearing today.

Cold disappears and heat is calmed. These omens appear today; you will surely become a Buddha.

The ten thousand world-elements become silent and undisturbed. These omens appear today; you will surely become a Buddha.

The great winds do not blow, and the rivers stop their flow. These omens appear today; you will surely become a Buddha.

All flowers, both land-grown and water-grown, bloom at that moment. All those flowers are blooming today; you will surely become a Buddha.

All creepers and trees bear the weight of fruit at that moment. All those creepers and trees are bearing fruit today; you will surely become a Buddha.

Jewels situated in the sky and on the earth shine at that moment. Those jewels are shining today; you will surely become a Buddha.

Musical instruments of humans and devas sound of their own accord at that moment. Both of these are sounding melodiously today; you will surely become a Buddha.

Wonderful showers of flowers fall from the sky at that moment. Those showers of flowers are falling today; you will surely become a Buddha.
122:
The great ocean swirls, and the ten thousand world-elements tremble. Both the great ocean and the ten thousand worlds are roaring today; you will surely become a Buddha.

At the time when former Bodhisattas sat cross-legged, the fires in the hells within the ten thousand world systems were extinguished. Those fires are extinguished today; you will surely become a Buddha.

The sun is stainless, and all the stars are visible. All those stars are clearly seen today; you will surely become a Buddha.

At the time when former Bodhisattas sat cross-legged, water sprang from the earth without rain. That water is springing from the earth today; you will surely become a Buddha.

The hosts of stars and the constellations shine beautifully in the vault of the sky. The Visākhā constellation is joined with the full moon; you will surely become a Buddha.

Beings living in holes and caves come out of their dwellings. Those beings are coming out of their dwellings today; you will surely become a Buddha.

At the time when former Bodhisattas sat cross-legged, beings felt no discontent but were satisfied. All those beings are satisfied today; you will surely become a Buddha.

At that time, diseases are calmed for beings, and hunger is destroyed. That calming of disease and destruction of hunger are manifest today; you will surely become a Buddha.

At that time, lust becomes thin for beings, and hatred and delusion are destroyed. All those lusts, hatreds, and delusions have vanished today; you will surely become a Buddha.

At that time, fear does not arise; this absence of fear is manifest today. By that sign we know: you will surely become a Buddha.

Dust does not rise or fly into the upper sky; this absence of dust is manifest today. By that sign we know: you will surely become a Buddha.

Foul odors depart, and divine scents waft. That divine scent is wafting today; you will surely become a Buddha.
123:
“All the gods are visible, except for the formless ones. Today they are all visible; surely you will become a Buddha.

“All the places called hells are visible to that extent. Today they are all visible; surely you will become a Buddha.

“At that time, walls, doors, and rocks are no longer obstructions. Today they have become like open space; surely you will become a Buddha.
