“At that moment, there is no passing away or rebirth of beings. Today those signs are visible; surely you will become a Buddha.

“Firmly exert your energy; do not retreat, but advance. We also know this; surely you will become a Buddha” (thus said the assembly of gods and men).

In those verses, ‘having heard this word’ means because of hearing the words of the prophecy given by the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara to the Bodhisatta. ‘To the peerless one’ means the peerless one because of the absence of an equal. As it is said—

“I have no teacher, no one like me exists; in the world with its gods, I have no counterpart.”

‘To the Mahesī’ means he is called Mahesī because he seeks the great aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom; it refers to that Mahesī. ‘Men and gods’ means humans and deities; although this is an ‘excellent description’ (ukkaṭṭhaniddesa) pointing to the highest, all the Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, Yakkhas, and so on in the ten thousand world systems were also delighted. It means they were delighted, thinking, ‘This is indeed the sprout of a Buddha that has arisen.’

‘Sounds of shouting’ means echoing sounds are occurring. ‘They clap their hands’ means they strike their arms with their hands. ‘Ten thousand’ refers to the ten thousand world systems. ‘With the gods’ means the inhabitants of the ten thousand world systems along with the gods pay homage. ‘Yadimassa’ should be analyzed as ‘Yadi imassa’, or this is simply the reading. ‘We shall fail’ means if we cannot reach or attain (this Buddha’s dispensation). ‘In the future time’ means in the time to come. ‘We shall become’ means we shall become (those who meet the Buddha). ‘Face-to-face’ means those who behold him. ‘Imaṃ’ is the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive ‘imassa’ (of this one).
124:
“Nadiṃ tarantā” means those crossing the river. There is also a reading “Nadītarantā”. “Paṭititthaṃ” means the opposite landing place. “Virajjhiyā” means having failed or missed. “Yadi muñcāma” means if we miss the opportunity to see this Blessed One and depart without completing the task of the Path. “Mama kammaṃ pakittetvā” means having prophesied the result of my cultivated merit (of laying the bridge). “Dakkhiṇံ pādamuddharī” means he raised his right foot. There is also a reading “Katapadakkhiṇo”.

“Jinaputtā” are the disciples of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara. “Gods, humans, and asuras, having paid homage, departed” means all these beings, having circumambulated me three times to the right, honored me with flowers and scents, bowed with the five-fold prostration, and having turned back to look again and again, departed while praising me with various sweet words and meanings. There is also a reading “Nara nāgā ca gandhabbā, abhivādetvāna pakkamuṃ”.

“Dassanaṃ me atikkante” means when the Blessed One passed out of my sight. There is also a reading “Jahite dassanūpacāre”. “Sasaṅghe” means in that Sangha along with the community of monks. “Sayanā vuṭṭhahitvāna” means rising from the mud where he lay. “Pallankaṃ ābhujuṃ” means sitting on a heap of flowers in a cross-legged posture. There is also a reading “Haṭṭho haṭṭhena cittena, āsanā vuṭṭhahiṃ tadā”, which has a clear meaning.

“Pītiyā ca abhissanno” means the whole body was suffused with joy. “Vasībhūto” means having reached the state of mastery. “Jhāne” refers to the fine-material and immaterial sphere jhanas. “Sahassiyamhi” means in the ten thousand world systems. “Lokamhi” means in the world system. “Me samā” means there are no others like me. Having said generally “There is no one equal to me,” he now specifies for that hermit, “Asamo iddhidhammesu” (Peerless in psychic powers). There, “iddhidhammesu” means in the five psychic powers such as the supernormal powers. “Alabhiṃ” means I received. “Īdisaṃ sukhaṃ” means such joy and mental pleasure (from hearing about becoming a Buddha).

Then, Sumedha the Hermit, hearing the prophecy of the One of Ten Powers (Dīpaṅkara Buddha), felt as if Buddhahood had reached the palm of his hand. With a joyful heart, the Great Brahmas of the Pure Abodes in the ten thousand world systems, who had seen past Buddhas, manifested the miracles that occur during the prophecy of a definite Bodhisatta. To show that they were delighting Sumedha by declaring the truth of the Tathāgata’s words, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with “Pallankābhujane mayhaṃ” (When I was sitting cross-legged).
125:
In these verses, 'pallaṅkābhujane mayhaṃ' means "at the time of my sitting cross-legged (on the throne)." Alternatively, the reading 'pallaṅkābhujane mama' is the correct reading. 'Dasasahassādhivāsino' refers to the Suddhāvāsa Mahābrahmas who dwell in the ten thousand world systems. 'Yā pubbe' means "those signs which occurred in the presence of past Buddhas"; it should be understood that this is stated with the elision of the case ending. 'Pallaṅkavarama-ābhuje' means "when sitting cross-legged on the noble throne." 'Nimittāni padissanti' means "the signs appeared." Although the past tense should be used, the present tense is used here. Even though it is stated in the present tense, the meaning should be taken in the sense of the past. 'Tāni ajja padissare' means "those signs which arose when the Bodhisattas who had received the definite prophecy sat cross-legged in the presence of past Buddhas, those signs appear today." Therefore, it means "you will certainly become a Buddha." However, it should be understood that it is not those very same signs that arose, but because they are similar, it is said, "those signs appear today."

'Sītaṃ' means the state of being cold. 'Byapagataṃ' means gone away or disappeared. 'Tāni' refers to the disappearance of cold and the subsiding of heat. 'Nissaddā' means silent, without noise or shouting. 'Nirākulā' means free from disturbance or confusion; alternatively, the reading 'anākulā' is the correct reading. 'Na sandanti' means they do not flow or drift. 'Savantiyo' means rivers. 'Tāni' refers to the signs of the wind not blowing and the rivers not flowing. 'Thalajā' refers to flowers born on the ground, mountains, and trees. 'Dakajā' refers to flowers born in water. 'Pupphanti' means they bloomed in the presence of past Bodhisattas; the use of the present tense for the past meaning should be understood in the same way as mentioned above. 'Tepajja pupphitāni' means "those flowers bloom today."

'Phalabhārā' means the state of bearing fruit. 'Tepajjā' means "those (vines or trees) today"; it is stated as 'te pi' using the masculine gender because it refers to "vines or trees." 'Phalitā' means having produced fruit. 'Ākāsaṭṭhā ca bhūmaṭṭhā ca' refers to jewels such as pearls that are located in the sky and on the ground. 'Jotanti' means they shine or glow. 'Mānussakā' refers to musical instruments belonging to humans. 'Dibbā' refers to musical instruments belonging to devas. 'Turiyā' refers to the five types of musical instruments: ātata, vitata, ātatavitata, susira, and ghana. Among these five, ātata refers to one-sided instruments such as drums covered with skin on one side. Vitata refers to two-sided instruments. Ātatavitata refers to instruments covered with skin on all sides, such as a large lute (vīṇā). Susira refers to instruments such as flutes. Ghana refers to instruments such as gongs, bronze bells, and cymbals. 'Vajjanti' means they sounded by themselves, as mentioned above; it should be understood that the present tense is used for the past meaning. This same method should be applied to similar expressions hereafter. 'Abhiravanti' means they sound melodiously and resonantly, as if they were well-released, well-struck, and well-played by experts in various places.
126:
Variegated flowers of various scents and colors are called 'vicitrapupphā'. 'Abhivassanti' means they have rained down or fallen down. 'Tepi' means those variegated flower-rains are manifested as raining down; the meaning is that they are being scattered by the hosts of devas and Brahmās. 'Ābhujati' means it recedes (or coils). 'Tepajjubho' means today those two great oceans along with the ten thousand world systems; 'abhiravanti' means they roar spontaneously with a thunderous and earth-shaking sound. 'Niraye' means in the hells. 'Dasasahassā' means many ten thousand universes. 'Nibbanti' means they are extinguished or attain peace. 'Tārakā' means the clusters of stars and constellations. 'Tepi ajja padissanti' means that because of the sun's purity, those clusters of stars are seen even during the day today.

'Anovatthena' refers to the use of the instrumental case in the sense of the locative case, meaning 'when it does not rain'. Alternatively, 'anovatthe' means 'even though it does not rain'. The word 'nā' is merely a particle without specific meaning, as in 'sutvā na dūtavacanaṃ' and so on. 'Tampajjubbhijjate' means that water also springs up today; it means it rises up after springing forth. 'Mahiyā' is the ablative case meaning 'from the earth'. 'Tārāgaṇā' refers to all clusters of stars, including planets and constellations. 'Nakkhattā' refers to the twenty-seven lunar mansions. 'Gaganamandale' means they shine beautifully throughout the entire expanse of the sky. 'Bilāsayā' refers to burrow-dwelling creatures such as snakes, mongooses, crocodiles, and monitor lizards. 'Darīsayā' refers to creatures that live in chasms. This reading 'jharāsayā' is the correct reading. 'Nikkhamanti' means they have emerged. 'Sakāsayā' means from their own dwellings. There is also the reading 'tadāsayā', which means from their own burrows or dwellings at that time. 'Chuddhā' means they have emerged well or have reached maturity.

'Arati' means discontent (boredom). 'Santuṭṭhā' means they are contented with supreme contentment. 'Vinassati' means it disappears. 'Rāgo' refers to sensual lust (kāmarāga). 'Tadā tanu hoti' means at that time it becomes very slight; this indicates the absence of obsessive outbursts (pariyuṭṭhāna). 'Vihatā' means they are destroyed. 'Tadā' means in the past, at the time when the Bodhisattas sat in the cross-legged posture. 'Na bhavati' means it does not happen. 'Ajjapetam' means today, even when you, Sumedha, sit in the cross-legged posture, that danger certainly does not occur. 'Tena lingena jānāma' means by that sign or reason, we all know that you will become a Buddha.

'Anuddhaṃsati' means it does not rise or scatter. 'Aniṭṭhagandho' means an unpleasant odor (foul smell). 'Pakkamati' means it departs or disappears. 'Pavāyati' means it diffuses (is fragrant). 'Sopajjā' means today that divine scent also exists. 'Padissanti' means they have become manifest. 'Tepajjā' means today all those devas also exist. 'Yāvatā' is a particle indicating a limit or extent.
127:
The word 'yāvatā' is a particle used in the sense of a limit, meaning 'as many as'. 'Kuṭṭā' means walls. 'Na hontāvaraṇā' means they did not act as obstructions. 'Tadā' means in the past. 'Ākāsabhūtā' means those walls, doors, and mountains, being unable to act as obstructions or barriers, became like the open sky. 'Cuti' means death. 'Upapatti' means taking rebirth. 'Khaṇe' means at the moment when the Bodhisattas sat in the cross-legged posture in the past. 'Na vijjati' means it did not exist. 'Tānipajjā' means today those deaths and births also [do not exist]. 'Mā nivatti' means do not turn back. 'Abhikkamā' means strive forward. The remaining words in this verse are clear.

Then, the wise Sumedha, having heard the words of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara of Ten Powers and the words of the devas of the ten thousand universes, became possessed of even greater effort and reflected: 'Buddhas are those whose words are not in vain; there is no alteration in the speech of the Buddhas. For example, just as the falling of a stone thrown into the sky is certain, the death of one who is born is certain, the rising of the sun at dawn is certain, the roaring of a lion emerged from its lair is certain, and the delivery of a woman heavy with child is certain and inevitable; in this very same way, the word of the Buddhas is certain and not in vain. I shall surely become a Buddha.' Thus it was said:

'Having heard the word of the Buddha and of both [groups in] the ten thousand universes, I was then glad, happy, and joyful, and I reflected thus:

The Buddhas do not have double speech; the victorious Buddhas do not have words in vain. There is no falsehood in the Buddhas; I shall surely become a Buddha.

Just as a stone thrown into the sky certainly falls to the ground, even so the word of the Excellent Buddhas is certain and eternal. There is no falsehood in the Buddhas; I shall surely become a Buddha.

Just as the death of all beings is certain and eternal, even so the word of the Excellent Buddhas is certain and eternal. There is no falsehood in the Buddhas; I shall surely become a Buddha.

Just as the rising of the sun is certain when the night has ended, even so the word of the Excellent Buddhas is certain and eternal. There is no falsehood in the Buddhas; I shall surely become a Buddha.'
128:
“Just as the roar of a lion that has emerged from its lair is certain, so too the word of the most excellent Buddhas is certain and eternal. There is no falsehood in the Buddhas; I shall certainly become a Buddha.”

“Just as for pregnant women, the laying down of the burden (giving birth) is certain, so too the word of the most excellent Buddhas is certain and eternal. There is no falsehood in the Buddhas; I shall certainly become a Buddha.”

In those verses, ‘hearing the word of the Buddha and the ten thousand’ (buddhassa vacanaṃ sutvā, dasasahassī na cubhayaṃ) means hearing the words of the Dīpaṅkara Buddha and the deities of the ten thousand world-systems. ‘Both’ (ubhayaṃ) refers to the words of those two parties. ‘Thus I thought’ (evaṃ cintesahaṃ) means I reflected in this way.

‘Not having two words’ (advejjhavacana) means not having speech that occurs in two ways; it means having speech that is certain. There is also the reading ‘faultless speech’ (acchiddavacana), which means having speech that is beyond reproach. ‘Not-vain speech’ (amoghavacana) means having speech that does not fail. ‘Falsehood’ (vitathaṃ) means there is no false speech. ‘I shall certainly become a Buddha’ (dhuvaṃ buddho bhavāmahaṃ) should be understood as being stated in the present tense with the sense of absolute certainty and inevitability, meaning “I will surely become a Buddha.”

‘Sunrise’ (suriyuggamanaṃ) means the rising of the sun. ‘Certain and eternal’ (dhuvassassataṃ) means both certain to happen and permanent. ‘Of one who has emerged from the lair’ (nikkhantasayanassa) means of one who has come out from the place of sleep. ‘Of pregnant women’ (āpannasattānaṃ) means of those with heavy wombs, i.e., pregnant women. ‘Laying down the burden’ (bhāramoropanaṃ) means the laying down of the womb, i.e., giving birth. The letter ‘ma’ is a sandhi-maker (padasandhikara). The rest of the words here are clear.

After making the resolution, “I shall certainly become a Buddha,” in order to investigate the qualities that make one a Buddha (buddhakāraka dhammā), he searched through the entire Dhamma-element (dhammadhātu) in order—above, below, in the cardinal and intermediate directions—asking, “Where are the Buddha-making qualities?” He saw the first, the Perfection of Generosity (dāna pāramī), which had been practiced and cultivated by previous Bodhisattas, and he exhorted himself thus: “Wise Sumedha, from this day forward, you should fulfill the first Perfection of Generosity. Just as an overturned water pot pours out its water completely and does not take it back, even so, without looking back at wealth, fame, children, wife, or limbs, giving everything desired to all who ask, you will sit at the foot of the Bodhi tree and become a Buddha.” Thus, he firmly resolved upon the first Perfection of Generosity. Therefore, it is said:

115. “Now I shall search here and there for the qualities that make one a Buddha. I shall search above, below, in the ten directions, and as far as the Dhamma-element extends.”

116. “Sāriputta, then, as I was searching for the Buddha-making qualities, I saw the first Perfection of Generosity, the great path followed and practiced by previous Bodhisattas.”

117. “If you desire to reach Enlightenment (bodhi), undertake and fulfill this first Perfection of Generosity firmly.”
129:
“Now I shall search and investigate here and there for the qualities that make one a Buddha. I shall search above in the celestial realms, below in the human realm, in the ten directions, and as far as the Dhamma-element extends.

While searching and investigating thus, I saw the first Perfection of Generosity, the great path followed and practiced by previous Great Sages.

If you desire to reach Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa), first undertake this Perfection of Generosity firmly and fulfill it until you reach the perfection of giving.

Just as when someone overturns a pot full of water, the water is poured out completely without remainder, and that pot does not protect (retain) any of it,

Even so, when you see beggars—whether low, middle, or high—give the gift completely, like the overturned pot.”

In those verses, ‘Handa’ is an indeclinable (nipāta) in the sense of exertion. ‘Buddhakare dhamme’ means the qualities that make one a Buddha. The qualities that make one a Buddha are the ten qualities beginning with the Perfection of Generosity. ‘Vicināmi’ means I shall search, I shall test, I shall investigate. ‘Ito cito’ means here and there, or searching in various places. ‘Above’ (uddhaṃ) means in the celestial realms. ‘Below’ (adho) means in the human realm. ‘Ten directions’ (dasa disā) refers to searching for where the Buddha-making qualities are—above, below, across, in the cardinal and intermediate directions. In the phrase ‘yāvatā dhammadhātuya’, ‘yāvatā’ is a word defining the extent. ‘Dhammadhātuya’ should be understood by adding the remaining word ‘occurrence’ (pavatti) of the nature of things. What is meant? It means “I shall search as far as the occurrence of natural phenomena—the dhammas of the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere—extends.”

‘Vicinanto’ means testing and investigating. ‘Pubbakehi’ means by previous Bodhisattas. ‘Anuciṇṇaṃ’ means constantly practiced and cultivated. ‘Samādiya’ means perform the undertaking; it is the undertaking: “From today, I must fulfill this first Perfection of Generosity.” ‘Dāna pāramitaṃ gaccha’ means go to the perfection of giving, i.e., fulfill it. ‘Yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi’ means if you wish to approach the foot of the Bodhi tree and attain the peerless Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi). ‘Yassa kassaci’ refers to a pot filled with any liquid, whether water or milk. Because it is used with the word ‘sampunṇa’ (full), experts in grammar desire the genitive case (chaṭṭhī vibhakti). Or, the genitive should be understood in the sense of the instrumental. ‘Adho kato’ means turned downwards. ‘Na tattha parirakkhati’ means it does not protect (the water) while pouring it out, but pours it out completely. ‘Hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhime’ refers to the low, the high, and the middle. The letter ‘ma’ performs the function of joining words (sandhi). ‘Kumbho viya adhokato’ means that upon seeing beggars arrive, like an overturned pot, one fulfills the Perfection of Generosity by giving away all wealth without leaving anything for oneself, and the Higher Perfection of Generosity (dāna upapāramī) by giving away limbs...
130:
Experts in grammar desire [this]. Or, it is the use of the genitive case in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is 'by any means whatsoever.' 'Adho kato' means turned downward. 'Na tattha parirakkhati' means he does not protect [the water] in that vomiting, meaning he vomits out the water completely. 'Hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhime' refers to the low, the middle, and the excellent. The letter 'ma' is a euphonic conjunction (padasandhikara). 'Kumbho viya adho kato' means like a pot turned upside down. Seeing the supplicants approaching, he admonished himself thus: "Sumedha, fulfill the Dāna Pāramī (Perfection of Giving) by sacrificing all your wealth without leaving anything for yourself, the Upapāramī (Minor Perfection) by sacrificing your limbs, and the Paramattha Pāramī (Ultimate Perfection) by sacrificing your life."

Then, as the hermit Sumedha investigated further, thinking, "The factors for becoming a Buddha cannot consist of only these Perfections of Giving," he saw the second, the Sīla Pāramī (Perfection of Virtue), and thought: "Wise Sumedha, from this day forward, you should fulfill the Sīla Pāramī. Just as the Camarī deer protects its tail hair without even regarding its own life, in the same way, from this day forward, you shall become a Buddha by protecting your virtue alone, without even regarding your life." Thus, he made a firm determination for the second, the Sīla Pāramī. Therefore, it was said:

"These are not the only factors for becoming a Buddha; I will search for other factors that ripen the state of Awakening (bodhipācanā).

Searching then, I saw the second, the Sīla Pāramī, practiced and cultivated by the Great Sages of the past.

121. While searching thus, I saw the second, the Sīla Pāramī, which was repeatedly practiced and cultivated by the former Great Sages.

122. If you desire to reach Awakening, first take up this second Sīla Pāramī very firmly and fulfill it.

123. Just as the Camarī deer, when its tail hair is caught in something, would rather face death there than damage its tail hair,

124. In the same way, you should fulfill the virtues in the four planes; always protect your virtue as the Camarī deer protects its tail hair." (Thus he admonished himself).

In those verses, 'na hete' means these Perfections of Giving alone are not the factors for becoming a Buddha. 'Bodhipācanā' refers to the factors that ripen the Path-knowledge or Omniscient Knowledge. 'Dutiyam sīla pāramim' means that virtue is the foundation of all wholesome states; one who is established in virtue does not fall away from wholesome states and can obtain all mundane and supramundane qualities.
131:
One can obtain all mundane and supramundane qualities. Therefore, the Sīla Pāramī should be fulfilled; this is the meaning of 'he saw the second Sīla Pāramī.' 'Āsevitani-sevitaṃ' means that which is repeatedly developed and frequently practiced. 'Camarī' refers to the Camarī deer (yak). 'Kismiñci' means in any place such as trees, creepers, thorns, and so on. 'Paṭilaggitaṃ' means being entangled. 'Tattha' means staying and facing death in the very place where it is entangled. 'Na vikopeti' means not breaking or cutting. 'Vāladhiṃ' means it does not go away by cutting its tail hair, but meets death right there; this is the meaning. 'Catūsu bhūmīsu sīlāni' refers to the fourfold virtue: Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla (virtue of restraint regarding the Patimokkha), Indriya-saṃvara-sīla (virtue of restraint of the senses), Ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla (virtue of purity of livelihood), and Paccaya-sannissita-sīla (virtue concerning the use of requisites). Although by way of planes they are included in only two planes, they are still the fourfold virtue. 'Paripūraya' means fulfill it completely without holes, tears, or spots. 'Sabbadā' means at all times. 'Camarī viya' means like the Camarī deer. The remaining words here have clear meanings.

Then, as that wise Sumedha investigated further, thinking, "The factors for becoming a Buddha cannot be completed by only these factors," he saw the third, the Nekkhamma Pāramī (Perfection of Renunciation), and thought: "Wise Sumedha, from this day forward, you should also fulfill the Nekkhamma Pāramī. Just as a man who has lived in prison for a long time has no affection for that prison but is weary and only desires to leave, in the same way, you should look upon all existences as being like a prison; being weary of all existences and desiring to be liberated, be one who is directed only towards renunciation. In this way, you will become a Buddha." Thus, he made a firm determination for the third, the Nekkhamma Pāramī. Therefore, it was said:

These are not the only factors that cause one to become a Buddha; I will search for other factors that ripen the state of Awakening. Then, while searching, he saw the third, the Nekkhamma Pāramī, practiced and cultivated by the former Buddhas. If you wish to obtain Omniscient Knowledge, first take up this third Nekkhamma Pāramī firmly and reach the pinnacle of the Perfection of Renunciation. Just as a man who has reached suffering by living in prison for a long time does not develop attachment to that prison but only searches for a way to be liberated.
132:
"Likewise, you should look at all existences as if they were a prison; be one who is inclined towards renunciation for the sake of liberation from existence." (Thus he admonished himself). In that verse, 'andughare' means in a prison. 'Ciravuṭṭho' means one who has lived there for a long time. 'Dukhaṭṭito' means one who is oppressed by suffering. 'Na tattha rāgaṃ janeti' means he does not produce attachment or affection in that prison. It means he does not produce attachment in that prison, thinking, "Once I am free from this prison, I will not go anywhere else," but rather he seeks only liberation, only release. 'Nekkhammābhimukho' means being inclined towards renunciation. 'Bhavato' means from all existences. 'Parimuttiyā' means for the sake of complete liberation. There is also a reading: "Being inclined towards renunciation, you will attain supreme enlightenment." The remaining words are clear in meaning.

Then, as he was further investigating, thinking, "There cannot be only this many Buddha-making factors," he saw the fourth, the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā-pāramī), and this thought occurred to him: "O wise Sumedha, from this day forward, you must also fulfill the Perfection of Wisdom. Without bypassing anyone among the low, middle, or high, you should approach all wise people and ask questions. Just as a monk wandering for alms, not bypassing any family among the low and so on, but wandering for alms in order, quickly receives enough for his sustenance; even so, if you approach and question all wise people, you will become a Buddha." Thus, he firmly resolved upon the fourth, the Perfection of Wisdom. Therefore, it was said:

"These are not the only Buddha-making factors;
I will search for other factors that mature enlightenment.

Searching then, I saw the fourth, the Perfection of Wisdom,
practiced and cultivated by the Great Sages (Mahesi) of the past.

If you wish to reach enlightenment, first undertake this fourth
Perfection of Wisdom firmly and fulfill it.

Just as a monk begging for alms, not avoiding families
of low, high, or middle status, thus obtains sustenance,

In the same way, by always inquiring of wise people and
reaching the perfection of wisdom, you will attain supreme enlightenment."
133:
In that verse, 'bhikkhanto' means wandering for alms. 'Hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhime' means families that are low, high, and middle. Here, a change of gender (inflection) is made. 'Na vivajjento' means not avoiding; avoiding is called wandering while skipping the sequence of houses; the meaning is wandering without doing so. 'Yāpanaṃ' means obtaining food just enough for the maintenance of life, for sustenance. 'Pariပုစ္ဆံ' (paripucchaṃ) means approaching and inquiring of well-known wise people in various places in this manner: "Venerable sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless?" and so on. 'Budhaṃ janaṃ' means a wise person. There is also a variant reading 'budhe jane'. 'Paññāya pāramiṃ' means reaching the end of wisdom. There is also a variant reading 'paññāpāramitaṃ gantvā'. The remaining words here are clear.

Then, as he was further investigating, thinking, "There cannot be only this many Buddha-making factors," he saw the fifth, the Perfection of Energy (Viriya-pāramī), and this thought occurred to him: "O wise Sumedha, from this day forward, you must also fulfill the Perfection of Energy. Just as a lion, the king of beasts, has firm energy in all postures, even so, if you have firm energy and unsluggish energy in all existences and in all postures, you will become a Buddha." Thus, he firmly resolved upon the fifth, the Perfection of Energy. Therefore, it was said:

"These are not the only Buddha-making factors;
I will search for other factors that mature enlightenment.

Searching then, I saw the fifth, the Perfection of Energy,
practiced and cultivated by the Great Sages of the past.

If you wish to reach enlightenment, first undertake this fifth
Perfection of Energy firmly and fulfill it until you reach the end of the Perfection of Energy.

Just as a lion, the king of beasts, has unsluggish energy
in sitting, standing, and walking, and always has an uplifted mind,

In the same way, you should exert firm energy in all existences;
reaching the end of the Perfection of Energy, you will attain supreme enlightenment."

In those verses, 'alīnaviriyo' means having unsluggish energy. 'Sabbabhave' means in every single existence that arises, in all existences. There is also a variant reading 'āraddhaviriyo hutvā sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi'. The remaining words here are clear.
134:
Then, as the wise Sumedha further reflected, 'It is not possible for there to be only these many qualities that make one a Buddha,' he saw the sixth perfection, the Perfection of Patience (Khanti Pāramī), and thought: 'O wise Sumedha, from this day forward, you shall fulfill the Perfection of Patience. Be one who is patient in both praise and honor, as well as in blame and contempt. Indeed, just as the earth remains indifferent when both clean and unclean things are cast upon it, and does not feel affection or resentment but simply endures, bears, and accepts them; even so, if you remain patient in all instances of honor and contempt, you will become a Buddha.' Thus, he firmly resolved upon the sixth perfection, the Perfection of Patience. Therefore, it was said:

'These are not all; there must be other Buddha-qualities.
I shall search for other qualities that mature toward Enlightenment.

Searching then, I saw the sixth perfection, the Perfection of Patience,
Which was practiced and cultivated by the Great Sages of old.

First, undertake this sixth perfection and hold it firmly;
With an undivided mind in that perfection, you will reach Supreme Enlightenment.

Just as the earth endures everything that is cast upon it,
Both clean and unclean, and feels no resentment toward the thrower;

Even so, you must be patient under all honor and contempt;
Having reached the Perfection of Patience, you will reach Supreme Enlightenment.'

In those verses, 'tattha' means in that Perfection of Patience. 'Advejjhamānaso' means having a mind that is absolutely singular (undivided). 'Sucimpi' refers to clean things such as sandalwood, eaglewood, perfumes, and flowers. 'Asucimpi' refers to unclean things such as the carcasses of snakes, dogs, and humans, as well as excrement, urine, saliva, and snot. 'Sahati' means endures or tolerates. 'Nikkhepaṃ' means that which is cast down. 'Paṭighaṃ' means anger (resentment). 'Tayā' means because of that casting or because of being cast down. There is also a variant reading 'paṭighaṃ dayaṃ,' which means it does not produce resentment or affection because of that casting. 'Sammānāvamānakkhamo' means 'May you also be one who can endure all honor and contempt.' Some also recite 'tatheva tumpi sabbabhave, sammānanavimānakkhamo.' There is also a variant reading 'khantiyā pāramiṃ gantvā,' meaning having gone by way of fulfilling the Perfection of Patience. The remaining words here are clear. From this point on, I shall not repeat such explanations but will only mention specific differences and variant readings where they occur.

Thereafter, as he further reflected, 'It is not possible for there to be only these many qualities that make one a Buddha,' he saw the seventh perfection, the Perfection of Truthfulness (Sacca Pāramī), and thought: 'O wise Sumedha, from this day forward, you shall also fulfill the Perfection of Truthfulness. Even if a thunderbolt were to fall upon your head, do not speak a deliberate lie for the sake of wealth or due to the power of desire and such. Just as the Morning Star (Osadhī-tārakā) in all seasons never deviates from its path to travel another way but follows only its own course; even so, if you do not abandon the truth and do not speak lies, you will become a Buddha.' Thus, he firmly resolved upon the seventh perfection, the Perfection of Truthfulness. Therefore, it was said:

'These are not all; there must be other Buddha-qualities.
I shall search for other qualities that mature toward Enlightenment.'
135:
Then, as the wise Sumedha further reflected, 'It is not possible for there to be only these many Buddha-making qualities,' he saw the seventh perfection, the Perfection of Truthfulness (Sacca Pāramī), and thought: 'O wise Sumedha, from this day forward, you shall also fulfill the Perfection of Truthfulness. Even if a thunderbolt were to fall upon your head, do not speak a deliberate lie for the sake of wealth and property or due to the power of desire and such. Just as the Morning Star (Osadhī-tārakā) in all seasons never abandons its own path to travel another way but follows only its own course; even so, only if you do not abandon the truth and do not speak lies will you become a Buddha.' Thus, he firmly resolved upon the seventh perfection, the Perfection of Truthfulness. Regarding this, it was said:

'These qualities alone cannot be the only Buddha-dhamma;
I shall search for other qualities that mature toward Enlightenment.'

'Searching then, I saw the seventh perfection, the Perfection of Truthfulness,
Which was repeatedly practiced and cultivated by the Great Sages of old.'

'First, undertake this seventh perfection and hold it firmly;
Being one whose word is undivided in that truth, you will reach Supreme Enlightenment.'

'Just as the Morning Star, which is the standard for the world including the devas,
Does not deviate from its path during the seasons or the rains;'

'Even so, do not deviate from your path regarding truths;
Having reached the Perfection of Truthfulness, you will reach Supreme Enlightenment.'

In those verses, 'tattha' means in the Perfection of Truthfulness. 'Advejjhavacano' means having a word that does not fail (unerring speech). 'Osadhī' refers to the Morning Star; it is called 'Osadhī-tārakā' because people gather medicinal herbs only after seeing the Morning Star rise. 'Tulābhūtā' means being a standard or measure. 'Sadevake' means of the world including the devas. 'Samaye' means in the rainy season. 'Utuvasse' means in the winter and summer seasons. There is also a variant reading 'samaye utuvaṭṭe.' In that reading, 'samaye' means the summer season, and 'utuvaṭṭe' means the winter and rainy seasons. 'Na vokkamati vīthito' means not deviating or departing from its own path in those respective seasons; it means it travels to the west for six months and to the east for six months. Alternatively, 'osadhī' refers to medicinal plants such as ginger, long pepper, and black pepper. 'Na vokkamati' means that whatever medicinal plant is capable of bearing fruit, it reaches that fruit-bearing state...
136:
It does not turn back without giving its fruit, which is its own effect. Vīthito means from the usual path of travel. Medicine that removes bile indeed removes bile; medicine that removes wind indeed removes wind; medicine that removes phlegm indeed removes phlegm. The rest of the phrasing here is also quite clear.

Then, as that Sumedha Paṇḍita reflected further, thinking, "The qualities that make one a Buddha should not be only these many," he saw the eighth, the Perfection of Determination (Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī), and this thought occurred to him: "Sumedha Paṇḍita, from now on, you must also fulfill the Perfection of Determination. Whatever matter you determine upon, be unshakable in that determination. Just as a mountain does not shake or move even when struck by storms from all directions, but remains in its own place, even so, you too, by being unshakable in your determination, shall become a Buddha." Thus, he firmly made his determination, having established the eighth, the Perfection of Determination. Therefore, [the Buddha] said:

"These are not all the qualities that make one a Buddha; I shall search for other qualities that mature toward Enlightenment.

While searching then, I saw the eighth, the Perfection of Determination, which was practiced and cultivated by the Great Sages of the past.

First, take up this eighth perfection, making it firm; by being immovable in that determination, you shall reach Supreme Enlightenment.

Just as a mountain made of stone, well-established and immovable, does not shake due to fierce storms but remains in its own place.

Even so, you too, be always immovable in your determination; having reached the culmination of the Perfection of Determination, you shall reach Supreme Enlightenment."

In those verses, selo means a mountain made of stone. Acalo means an immovable mountain. Suppatiṭṭhito means a mountain well-established because of its immovability. There is also a reading: "Yathāpi pabbato acalo, nikhāto suppatiṭṭhito." Bhusavātehi means because of powerful storms. Sakaṭṭhāneva means only in its own place, meaning in the very place where it stands. The rest of the phrasing here is also quite clear.

Then, as that Sumedha Paṇḍita reflected further, thinking, "The qualities that make one a Buddha should not be only these many," he saw the ninth, the Perfection of Loving-kindness (Mettā-pāramī), and this thought occurred to him: "Sumedha Paṇḍita, from now on, you must fulfill the Perfection of Loving-kindness. Toward those who work for your welfare and those who work for your harm..."
137:
...you must be one of equal mind. For example, just as water pervades both the wicked and the virtuous, making coolness equal for both, even so, you too, by having a mind of equal loving-kindness toward all beings, shall become a Buddha." Thus, he firmly made his determination, having established the ninth, the Perfection of Loving-kindness. Therefore, it was said:

"These are not all the qualities that make one a Buddha; I shall search for other qualities that mature toward Enlightenment.

While searching then, I saw the ninth, the Perfection of Loving-kindness, which was practiced and cultivated by the Great Seers of the past.

First, take up this ninth perfection, making it very firm; if you wish to reach Enlightenment, be unequaled in loving-kindness.

Just as water pervades both the virtuous and the wicked equally with coolness, and washes away dirt, dust, and sweat,

Even so, you should develop loving-kindness equally toward those who benefit you and those who do not; having reached the culmination of the Perfection of Loving-kindness, you shall reach Supreme Enlightenment."

In those verses, "asamo hohi" means be unequaled in the development of loving-kindness. There is also a variant reading: "tvaṃ samasamo hohi," which has a clear meaning. "Samaṃ" means equally. "Pharati" means pervades or touches. "Pavāheti" means cleanses or carries away. "Rajo" means adventitious dust. "Malaṃ" means impurities such as sweat produced in the body. There is also a reading "rajamalaṃ," which has the same meaning. "Hitāhite" means toward those who benefit and those who do not benefit, toward friends and enemies. "Mettāya bhāvaya" means develop loving-kindness, make it increase. The rest of the words here also have clear meanings.

Then, as that Sumedha the Hermit reflected further, thinking, "The qualities that make one a Buddha should not be only these many," he saw the tenth, the Perfection of Equanimity (Upekkhā-pāramī), and this thought occurred to him: "Friend Sumedha Paṇḍita, from now on, you must also fulfill the Perfection of Equanimity. Be neutral in both pleasure and pain. For example, just as the earth is neutral whether clean or unclean things are cast upon it, even so, you too, by being neutral in pleasure and pain, shall become a Buddha." Thus, he firmly made his determination, having established the tenth, the Perfection of Equanimity. Therefore, it was said:
138:
"These are not all the qualities that make a Buddha; I shall search for other qualities that ripen into Enlightenment."

"While searching, he saw the tenth, the Perfection of Equanimity (Upekkhā pāramī), which was practiced and cultivated by the Great Sages (Mahesī) of the past."

"First, undertake this tenth Perfection of Equanimity very firmly. Being firm like a scale that remains level and upright amidst pleasure and pain, you shall attain Omniscience."

"Just as the earth remains indifferent, free from anger or attachment, toward both impure and pure things cast upon it, so too should you always be like a scale, level and upright amidst pleasure and pain. Reaching the end of the Perfection of Equanimity, you shall attain Omniscience," he exhorted.

In that verse, "tulābhūto" means remaining in a neutral state. Just as the needle of a scale, when weighed evenly, stands straight without tilting down or up, so too shall you attain Omniscience by being like a scale amidst pleasure and pain. "Kopānunayavajjitā" means being free from aversion and attachment. There is also a reading "dayākopavivajjitā," which has the same meaning. The remaining meanings should be understood as stated in the Perfection of Patience (Khanti pāramī).

Then, the wise Sumedha, having searched for these ten Perfections, thought further: "In this world, these are the only qualities to be fulfilled by Bodhisattas, which ripen into Buddhahood and make one a Buddha; there are no others beyond these. These Perfections do not exist in the sky above, nor in the earth below, nor in the directions such as the East. Indeed, they are established within my very heart." Seeing that they were established in his heart, he undertook all of them firmly and contemplated them repeatedly, in forward and reverse order. He took them from the end to the beginning, from the beginning to the end, from the middle to both ends, and from both ends to the middle.

The sacrifice of external possessions is called Pāramī; the sacrifice of limbs is called Upapāramī; the sacrifice of life is called Paramattha pāramī. Thus, he contemplated the thirty varieties of Perfections—the ten Perfections, the ten Higher Perfections, and the ten Ultimate Perfections—like one turning a mill for oil. While he was contemplating the ten Perfections...
139:
Due to the power and majesty of the Perfections, this vast Great Earth (Mahāpathavī), which is two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, shook, trembled, and quaked violently in all directions—up and down, left and right—roaring loudly like a bundle of reeds stepped on by an elephant, or like a sugarcane press being squeezed. It revolved like a potter's wheel or an oil-mill wheel. Therefore, it was said:

"In the world, these are the only qualities that ripen into Enlightenment.
Beyond these, there is no other quality; stand firm in these qualities.

While contemplating these qualities together with their individual essences and characteristics,
By the power of the Dhamma, the earth in the ten-thousandfold world system trembled.

The earth moves and roars like a squeezed sugarcane press;
Like the wheel in an oil-mill, so the earth quakes."

In those verses, "ettakāyeva" is said to show that the ten Perfections pointed out are neither less nor more. "Tatuddhaṃ" means beyond those ten Perfections. "Aññatra" means another meaning (the characteristic should be taken from grammatical treatises); it means there is no other quality that makes a Buddha apart from these ten Perfections. "Tattha" means in those ten Perfections. "Patiṭṭhaha" means stand firm while fulfilling them.

"Ime dhamme" refers to the qualities of the Perfections. "Sammasato" refers to one who is contemplating (here, the genitive case should be noted in the sense of disregard). "Sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇe" means while contemplating with the characteristic of function (rasa) known as individual essence (sabhāva). "Dhamma-tejena" means due to the power and majesty of the knowledge that investigates the Perfections. "Vasudhā": wealth/treasure is called "vasu"; because it bears that treasure, it is called "Vasudhā." What is that Vasudhā? It is the earth (Medanī). "Pakampatha" means it trembled. It means that while the wise Sumedha was searching for the Perfections, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled due to the power of his knowledge.

"Calati" means shaking in six ways. "Ravati" means roaring or crying out. "Ucchuyantaṃva pīဠitāṃ" means like a sugarcane press being squeezed. There is also a reading "guဠayantaṃva pīဠitāṃ," which has the same meaning. "Telayante" means in an oil-pressing machine. "Yathā cakkaṃ" means like the great mechanical wheel of the bell-strikers. "Evaṃ" means just as an oil-pressing wheel revolves and shakes, so this earth quakes. The remaining words are clear.
140:
When the great earth shook in this manner, the people living in the city of Rammanagara, while they were attending to the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, were unable to remain steady and fell down in a swoon like great sal trees struck by the winds of Mount Yugandhara. Pottery such as jars and vessels rolled and struck against each other, being crushed into powder. The great multitude, terrified and trembling, approached the Teacher and asked: "Blessed One, is this the whirling of Nagas, or the whirling of some spirit, ghost, or deity? We do not know the cause. Indeed, all these people are afflicted by fear. Will there be evil or good for this world? Please tell us the reason for this."

Then the Teacher, hearing their words, said: "Do not be afraid, do not worry. There is no danger to you from this cause. Today, I have given the prophecy to the wise Sumedha that 'In the future, he will become a Buddha named Gotama.' He is now contemplating the Perfections (pāramīs). Due to the power of the Dhamma of his contemplation, the entire ten-thousandfold world system is simultaneously shaking and roaring." Therefore, [the ancient teachers] said:

The entire assembly that was present at the attendance of the Buddha trembled there and lay in a swoon upon the ground.

Many thousands of jars and hundreds of water-pots were crushed and smashed there, having struck one another.

Terrified, trembling, and fearful, with agitated minds, the great multitude gathered together and approached Dīpaṅkara.

O One with the Eye of Wisdom, will there be good or evil for the world? The whole world is afflicted; please dispel that danger.

Then the Great Sage Dīpaṅkara informed them: "Be confident, do not fear this earthquake.

The one to whom I gave the prophecy today that 'He will become a Buddha in the world,' he is contemplating the Dhamma practiced by former Conquerors (Jinas)."
141:
While that wise Sumedha was contemplating without remainder the Perfections which are the ground for Buddhahood, this ten-thousandfold earth, together with the devas, shook because of the power of that contemplation.

In that verse, 'yāvatā' means 'as many as'. 'Āsi' means 'there was'. There is also a reading 'yā tadā parisā āsi', which means the assembly that was present at that time. 'Pavedhamānā' means 'trembling'. 'Sā' refers to that assembly. 'Tattha' means in that place of attendance. 'Seti' means they lay down.

'Ghaṭā' refers to jars; it is a nominative used in the sense of a genitive, meaning 'many thousands of jars'. 'Sañcuṇṇamathitā' means being crushed into powder and as if being churned. 'Aññamaññaṃ paghaṭṭitā' means striking one another. 'Ubbiggā' means having a terrified heart. 'Tasitā' means being filled with dread. 'Bhītā' means fearful due to danger. 'Bhantā' means having a trembling mind or a spinning mind. All these terms are synonyms for one another. 'Samāgammā' means having come together.

'Upadduto' means afflicted. 'Taṃ vinodehi' means 'dispel that approaching danger', meaning 'destroy it'. 'Cakkhumā' refers to the Blessed One who is endowed with the five eyes. 'Tesaṃ tadā' refers to those people at that time. 'Saññāpesi' means he informed them or made them understand. 'Visatthā' means those with a mind free from hesitation. 'Mā bhāthā' means 'do not be afraid'. 'Yamahaṃ' means 'the one to whom I (gave the prophecy), the wise Sumedha'. 'Dhammaṃ' refers to the practice of the ten Perfections. 'Pubbakaṃ' means 'of old'. 'Jinasevitaṃ' means 'practiced by the Buddhas during their time as Bodhisattas'. 'Buddhabhūmi' refers to the practice of the ten Perfections itself. 'Tena' means 'because of that reason of contemplation'. 'Kampitā' means 'shaken'. 'Sadevake' means 'in the world together with the devas'.

Then the great multitude, hearing the words of the Tathāgata, became joyful and delighted. Taking flowers, scents, unguents, and so forth, they departed from the city of Rammanagara, approached the Bodhisatta, honored him with flowers and scents, paid homage, circumambulated him, and re-entered the city of Rammanagara. Then the Bodhisatta also, having contemplated the ten Perfections and having made his energy firm and determined, rose from his seat. Regarding this, it was said:

Upon hearing the words of the Buddha, their minds became peaceful at that very moment. All of them approached me and paid homage to me once again.
142:
"I, having undertaken the ten perfections (pāramīs) which are the virtues to be practiced by the Bodhisattas, and having made my mind firm, paid homage to the Buddha Dīpaṅkara and then rose from my seat."

In that verse, "mano nibbayi" means that the multitude of people, whose hearts were terrified by the earthquake, heard the cause of that earthquake and thus their hearts became calm and reached peace. There is also a variant reading "jano nibbayi," the meaning of which is quite clear. "Samādiyitvā" means having well-taken or undertaken. "Buddhaguṇaṃ" refers to the perfections (pāramīs). The meaning of the remaining words is clear.

Then, the deities and Brahmas from the entire ten thousand world systems gathered and honored the Bodhisatta—who has compassion for all beings and was rising from his seat—with divine flowers, scents, and so forth, and spoke these auspicious words of praise: "O Noble Sumedha the Hermit, today you have made a great aspiration for Buddhahood at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the One of Ten Powers. May that aspiration of yours be fulfilled without any obstacles. May you have no fear or trepidation in that quest. May not even a slight illness arise in your body. Quickly fulfill the perfections and realize the Supreme Self-Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). Just as trees laden with flowers and fruits bloom and bear fruit when the season arrives, so too, without passing that time, may you quickly attain Enlightenment (Sambodhi)." After speaking such words, they paid homage to the Bodhisatta and returned to their respective celestial abodes. The Bodhisatta, being highly praised by the deities, made a firm resolve and effort, thinking, "I shall fulfill the ten perfections and become a Buddha at the end of four incalculables and a hundred thousand eons." Then, he ascended into the sky and went to the Himalayas, where the company of hermits resided. Therefore, it was said:

"As I rose from my seat, both deities and humans scattered divine and human flowers upon me in worship.

Both deities and humans wished for your well-being: 'May you obtain that great aspiration you have made, according to your wish.

May all calamities be averted; may sorrow and disease perish. May there be no obstacles for you; quickly reach the supreme Enlightenment.

Just as flowering trees bloom when the season arrives, so too, O Great Hero, may you bloom with the Buddha-knowledges.'"
143:
"Just as all the Buddhas fulfilled the ten perfections, so too, O Great Hero, may you fulfill the ten perfections.

Just as all the Buddhas awakened at the Bodhi-mandala, so too, O Great Hero, may you awaken to the Enlightenment of the Conqueror (Jina-bodhi) at the supreme site of victory.

Just as all the Buddhas turned the Wheel of Dhamma, so too, O Great Hero, may you preach the Wheel of Dhamma.

Just as the pure moon shines on the full moon day, so too, with your wishes fulfilled, may you shine throughout the ten thousand world systems.

Just as the sun, released from the mouth of Rāhu, shines intensely with its radiance, so too, being released from the world, may you shine with the glory of a Buddha.

Just as all rivers flow into and gather in the great ocean, so too, may the world together with its deities come to gather in your presence."

Then, Sumedha the Hermit, who was thus greatly praised by those deities and humans, undertook the ten perfections and, while fulfilling those perfections, entered the great forest.

In those verses, 'dibbaṃ' means the deities took divine flowers such as Mandārava, Pāricchattaka, Santānaka, and Kusesaya, while humans took human flowers. 'Samokiranti' means they scattered them over me in worship. 'Vuṭṭhahantassa' means of one who is rising from his seat. 'Vedayanti' means they made it known or announced. 'Sotthiṃ' means the state of safety and well-being. Now, to show the manner in which they made it known, the words beginning with 'mahantaṃ patthitaṃ tuyhaṃ' were spoken. It means: "O Wise Sumedha, you have aspired to the great state of Omniscience; may you obtain it as aspired." 'Sabbitiyo': 'itiyo' are those that approach and oppress; 'sabbitiyo' means all calamities or obstacles. 'Vivajjantu' means may they not occur. 'Soko rogo vinassatu' means may sorrow, known as grieving, and disease, known as pain, perish. 'Te' means your. 'Mā bhavantantarāyā' means may there be no obstacles. 'Phusā' means may you obtain or reach. 'Bodhiṃ' refers to the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (Arahatta-magga-ñāṇa); it can also refer to the Knowledge of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). 'Uttamaṃ' means noble or supreme; the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship is called 'uttama' because it bestows all the qualities of a Buddha.
144:
"Samaye" means reaching the flowering time of various trees. "Pupphino" means those (trees) that have the nature of blooming. "Buddhañāṇehi" means by the eighteen Buddha-knowledges. "Pupphatu" means "may it bloom." "Pūrayuṃ" means "they have fulfilled." "Pūrayā" means "please fulfill." "Bujjhare" means "they have awakened/realized." "Jinabodhiyaṃ" means in the Enlightenment of the Victorious Buddhas, meaning at the foot of the Bodhi tree where Omniscience is attained. "Puṇṇamāya" means on the full moon day. "Puṇṇamano" means one whose heart's desire is fulfilled.

"Rāhumutto" means like the moon freed from the Asura Rahu named Sobbhānu. "Tāpena" means by majesty, power, and light. "Lokā muccitvā" means being unstained by the worldly conditions (lokadhamma). "Virocā" means "please shine forth." "Siriyā" means by the glory of a Buddha. "Osarantī" means "they enter the great ocean." "Osarantu" means "may they arrive." "Tavantike" means "near you." "Tehi" means "by those devas." "Thutappasattho" means both extolled and praised, or called "Thutappasattho" because of being praised by Buddhas such as Dīpaṅkara. "Dasa dhamme" means the ten perfections (pāramīs). "Pavanaṃ" means the great forest, meaning he entered the great forest at the foot of Mount Dhammika. The remaining verses are very clear in their meaning.

## Thus, the Explanation of the Aspiration of Sumedha
## in the Commentary on the Buddhavamsa, Madhuratthavilāsinī, is finished.
## 3. Chronicle of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara

Those lay devotees living in the city of Rammavatī also gave a great gift (mahādāna) to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha. After the meal, when the Blessed One had removed his hand from the bowl, they honored him with flowers, scents, and so forth, and sat down nearby, wishing to hear the words of appreciation (anumodanā) for their gift. Then the Teacher delivered this extremely sweet and heart-touching appreciation of the gift to those lay devotees:

"Giving (dāna) is known to be the supreme cause of happiness and so forth. It is like a stairway for ascending to Nibbāna and is said to be a foundation.

Giving is the protection of humans. Giving is a kinsman and a refuge. Giving is the supreme destination for beings who have fallen into suffering.

In the sense of crossing over from suffering, giving is shown to be a ship. Because it protects from danger, giving is also praised as a city."
145:
Giving is said to be like a venomous cobra because of the sense that it is difficult for (defilements) to approach; and it is like a Paduma lotus because it is not smeared by the stains of greed and so forth.

In the world, there is no refuge for humans equal to giving. Therefore, practice that giving with a heart's desire to perform it.

In this world, for the wise, gifts are the causes for reaching the heavenly realm. Indeed, what person in the world, delighting in welfare, would not give?

Having heard of the prosperity and happiness in the heavenly realms that arise from giving, what person would not give the gift that bestows happiness and greatly delights the heart?

Because of the gift practiced, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, one delights for a very long time in the Nandana Grove, which is the delight of the devas.

The giver finds noble joy. In this world, the giver attains respect. The giver also attains boundless fame and becomes one who is trustworthy.

By giving a gift, that person attains the fulfillment of wealth and long life. He also finds a sweet voice and a beautiful form, and plays together with the devas in heaven,

Abiding in various mansions filled with the cries of intoxicated peacocks.

Giving is wealth that is not shared with thieves, enemies, kings, water, or fire. It bestows the stage of Disciple-knowledge (Sāvaka-bodhi), the stage of a Private Buddha (Pacceka-bodhi), and the stage of a Buddha (Buddhabhūmi).

After delivering the appreciation of the gift in this and other ways and revealing the advantages of giving, he immediately preached the discourse on virtue (sīlakathā). This virtue is the root of prosperity in this present world and the world beyond.

"Virtue is the supreme cause of happiness. Through virtue, one who is virtuous goes to the heavenly realm. Indeed, for one who has entered the round of rebirth (saṃsāra), virtue is the protection, the shelter, and the refuge."
146:
In this present world or in the world beyond, what other refuge is there for all people like virtue? Just as the earth is the support for both stationary and moving things, virtue is the supreme support for all good qualities.

Virtue alone is truly auspicious; virtue is supreme in the world. Because of which practice, a person of noble conduct and behavior is called 'virtuous.'

There is no ornament equal to the ornament of virtue; there is no scent equal to the scent of virtue; there is no purification of the stains of defilements equal to virtue; there is no quelling of feverish heat equal to virtue; there is no producer of fame equal to virtue; there is no stairway for ascending to heaven equal to virtue; and in entering the city of Nibbāna, there is no gate equal to virtue. As it was said:

Kings adorned with pearls and jewels do not shine in such a way
as monks shine when adorned with the ornament of virtue.

Where indeed could there be a scent equal to the scent of virtue,
which wafts equally with the wind and against the wind?

The scent of flowers does not go against the wind, nor does sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine.
Only the scent of the virtuous goes against the wind; the good person wafts in all directions.

Whether it be sandalwood, tagara, blue lotus, or jasmine,
among these various kinds of scents, the scent of virtue is supreme.

The waters of the Ganges, Yamunā, Sarabhū, Sarasvatī,
the Aciravatī, or the Mahi, the great river,

Are not able to wash away that stain of beings here in this world.
Only the water of virtue can truly wash away the stains of beings.

Neither the cool winds with rain, nor yellow sandalwood,
nor pearls, nor gems, nor the rays of the moon..."
147:
In this world, this virtue (sīla), which is well-guarded, pure, and exceedingly cool, can extinguish the fever of beings such as passion (rāga). Neither cool winds with rain, nor yellow sandalwood, nor pearls, nor gems, nor the rays of the moon can extinguish that fever of passion and so forth.

Virtue always and in every way destroys all fears for the virtuous person, such as the fear of self-reproach (attānuvāda-bhaya). It also always generates fame and joy for the one endowed with virtue.

Where else is there a stairway like virtue for ascending to heaven? Or where else is there a gate like virtue for entering the city of Nibbāna?

Know thus the incomparable benefit of virtue, which is the root of all mundane and supramundane qualities and the destroyer of the power of faults known as defilements.

Having thus shown the benefits of virtue, the Blessed One, in order to show that "by depending on this virtue, one can attain this heaven," gave a discourse on heaven (saggakathā) immediately after that discourse on virtue. This so-called heaven is desirable, lovely, pleasing, and exclusively pleasant; therein they always enjoy play and always obtain prosperity. The devas born in the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) obtain divine happiness and divine prosperity for nine million years. The devas born in the Tāvatiṃsā realm obtain divine happiness and divine prosperity for thirty-six million years. Thus he gave a discourse connected with the qualities of heaven. Having thus enticed them with the discourse on heaven, he again declared the danger (ādīnava), the meanness, and the defilement of sensual pleasures, saying, "This heaven too is impermanent, not lasting; one should not conceive desire and lust for it," and he showed the benefit of renunciation (nekkhamma), giving a Dhamma discourse ending in the Deathless Nibbāna. Having thus preached the Dhamma to that great multitude, he established some in the Refuges, some in the Five Precepts, some in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), some in the Fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-phala), some in the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), some in all four Fruits, some in the Three Knowledges (vijjā), some in the Six Supernormal Powers (abhiññā), and some in the Eight Attainments (samāpatti). Then, rising from his seat, he departed from the city of Rammavatī and entered the Sudassana Mahāvihāra. Therefore, it is said in the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi:

"Then, having fed the World Leader together with the Saṅgha, the people of Rammavatī approached that Teacher Dīpaṅkara for refuge.

The Tathāgata established some in the Refuges, some in the Five Precepts, and others in the Ten Precepts."
148:
"To some he gives the Noble Path and the four supreme Fruits; to some the Peerless Dhamma, the Analytical Insights (paṭisambhidā).

To some that Best of Men gives the eight excellent Attainments (samāpatti); to some he bestows the Three Knowledges (vijjā) and the Six Supernormal Powers (abhiññā).

In that manner, the Great Sage (Mahāmuni) admonishes the multitude; because of that, the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the World Leader became widespread and prosperous.

The one named Dīpaṅkara, who has a jaw like a great lion and shoulders like a noble bull, delivers many people and releases them from woeful states (duggati).

Seeing a person ready for awakening (bodhaneyya), even if they are a hundred thousand yojanas away, the Great Sage approaches in a moment and awakens them to the Four Noble Truths."

In those verses, "te" refers to the lay followers (upāsakas) living in the city of Rammavatī. In this word "saraṇaṃ", one should understand the refuge (saraṇa), the act of going for refuge (saraṇagamana), and the person who goes for refuge. It is called "saraṇa" because it crushes, harms, and destroys (dangers). What is that? It is the Triple Gem (Ratanattaya). That Triple Gem, for those who have gone for refuge, through that very act of going for refuge, removes, harms, and destroys fear, trembling, suffering, woeful states, and defilements; therefore, it is called "saraṇa". Thus it was also said:

"Whoever have gone to the Buddha for refuge,
They will not go to a woeful state;
Having abandoned the human body,
They will fill the heavenly hosts."

"Whoever have gone to the Dhamma for refuge,
They will not go to a woeful state;
Having abandoned the human body,
They will fill the heavenly hosts."

"Whoever have gone to the Saṅgha for refuge,
They will not go to a woeful state;
Having abandoned the human body,
They will fill the heavenly hosts."
149:
The arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that occurs in the manner of taking the Triple Gem as one's mainstay is called 'Taking Refuge' (saraṇagamana). The person endowed with that arising of consciousness is called 'one who goes for refuge' (saraṇassa gantā). Thus, first, these three—the refuge (saraṇa), the taking of refuge (saraṇagamana), and the one who goes for refuge (saraṇassa gantā)—should be understood together.

'Tassa' refers to that Blessed One Dīpaṅkara; the genitive case should be understood in the sense of the accusative. There is also a reading 'upagacchuṃ saraṇaṃ tattha'. 'Satthuno' means the Teacher (the Buddha). 'Saraṇāgamane kañci' means establishing a certain person in the taking of refuge. Although it is spoken in the present tense, the meaning should be taken according to the past tense. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. There is also a reading 'kassaci saraṇāgamane', and its meaning is the same.

'Kañci pañcasu sīlesu' means establishing a certain person in the five precepts of abstinence (virati-sīla). The reading 'kassaci pañcasu sīlesu' also has the same meaning. 'Sīle dasavidhe paraṃ' means establishing another person in the ten precepts. If there is the reading 'kassaci kusale dasā', it means making some persons undertake the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakamma-patha).

In the phrase 'kassaci deti sāmaññaṃ', in the ultimate sense, the Noble Path (ariya magga) is called 'sāmañña' (the state of a recluse). As it is said: "And what, bhikkhus, is recluseship (sāmañña)? It is just this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view ... right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called recluseship" (SN 5.36).

'Caturo phalamuttame' means the four supreme fruits (phala). The letter 'ma' is a euphonic junction (sandhi). It is spoken with a change of gender. It means that according to their strong supporting conditions (upanissaya), he gave the four paths and the four fruits of recluseship to some. 'Kassaci asame dhamme' means he gave the four incomparable analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) to some.

'Kassaci vara-samāpattiyo' means he gave the eight supreme attainments (samāpatti) through the removal of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) to some. 'Tisso kassaci vijjāyo' means he gave the three knowledges (vijjā)—namely, the divine eye, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and the knowledge of the destruction of taints—to some according to their supporting conditions. 'Chaḷabhiññā pavecchati' means he gave the six higher powers (abhiññā) to some.

'Tena yogena' means by that method and in that sequence. 'Janakāyaṃ' refers to the multitude of people. 'Ovadati' means he admonished (in the past). It should be understood that this is spoken with a change of tense. In subsequent expressions of this kind, the meaning should also be taken according to the past tense.
150:
The meaning should be taken (as past tense). 'Tena vitthārikaṃ āsi' means that through the advice and instruction of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the Dispensation (sāsana) became widespread, extensive, and prosperous.

'Mahāhanu' means that the two jaws of Great Men are full, appearing like the moon on the twelfth day of the fortnight. Because he has such great jaws, he is called 'Mahāhanu'; it means having jaws like those of a lion king. 'Usabhakkhandha' refers to one whose shoulders are like those of a noble bull (usabha). It means having shoulders that are as beautiful as a well-turned golden drum, being evenly rounded and lovely. 'Dīpaṅkarasānāmaka' means the one named Dīpaṅkara. He rescued many beings who were capable of being enlightened by a Buddha; he liberated them. 'Duggatiṃ' is used in the sense of the ablative, meaning from the woeful states.

Now, to show the manner of rescuing and liberating, the verse beginning with 'bodhaneyyaṃ janaṃ' is spoken. There, 'bodhaneyyaṃ janaṃ' refers to the multitude of beings who are capable of being enlightened (realizing the Four Noble Truths), or it is simply the reading as it stands. 'Disvā' means seeing with either the Buddha-eye or the All-seeing eye. 'Satasahassepi yojane' refers to beings situated even at a distance of many hundreds of thousands of yojanas. However, it should be understood that this is said with reference to ten thousand yojanas.

It is said that the Teacher Dīpaṅkara, having attained Buddhahood and spent seven weeks (forty-nine days) at the foot of the Bodhi tree, accepted the request of Mahābrahmā to teach the Dhamma in the eighth week. Having set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma at Sunandārāma, he made a hundred crores of devas and humans drink the nectar of the Dhamma (the Deathless). This was the first realization (abhisamaya).

Then the Teacher, knowing the maturity of knowledge of his own son named Usabhakkhandha, who had evenly rounded shoulders like a noble bull, placed that son at the head and taught a discourse similar to the Rāhulovāda Sutta, making ninety crores of devas and humans drink the nectar of the Dhamma. This was the second realization.

Again, the Blessed One, having performed the Twin Miracle at the foot of a great Sirīsa tree (Albizia lebbeck) by the gate of the city of Amaravatī, and having released a great multitude of people from their bonds, surrounded by a host of devas, ascended to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, a realm of radiance exceeding that of the sun. There, seated on the extremely cool Paṇḍukambala stone at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, he caused joy to the entire host of devas...
151:
The Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, placing his mother Queen Sumedhā at the head, being the God of Purity well-known in all the worlds, the God above gods, preached the Abhidhamma Piṭaka consisting of seven books—which performs the welfare of all beings, is exceedingly deep and subtle, and clarifies wisdom—and gave the nectar of Dhamma to ninety billion devas and brahmas. This was the third realization of the Truths (abhisamaya). Therefore, it was said in the Pali:

“In the first realization, the Buddha awakened one hundred crores;
In the second realization, the Protector awakened ninety crores.
And when the Buddha preached the Dhamma in the celestial abode,
There was the third realization of ninety billion [devas and brahmas].”

There were three assemblies of disciples for the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara. Among them, the first assembly of one hundred thousand crores [of Arahants] took place at the Sunandārāma monastery. Therefore, it was said in the Pali:

“There were three assemblies of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara;
The first gathering was of one hundred thousand crores.”

Then, on another occasion, the Blessed One, the Possessor of Ten Powers, surrounded by four hundred thousand monks, while wandering for the benefit of the great multitude through villages, market towns, and cities in succession, reached a most delightful mountain named Nāradakūṭa. This mountain had peaks where the great multitude performed offerings, was famous in the world, was possessed by non-humans (yakkhas), was extremely terrifying, had peaks kissed by hanging clouds, had peaks perfumed with various fragrant tree blossoms, and had peaks frequented by various herds of wild animals. That mountain, it is said, was possessed by a yakkha named Nārada. On that mountain, the great multitude had to offer human sacrifice (bali) to that yakkha every year.

Then, the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, seeing the fulfillment of the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of those people, sent the community of monks to the four directions and, being alone and without a companion, with a heart imbued with great compassion, ascended Mount Nārada to tame that yakkha. Then that yakkha, who was a consumer of human flesh, indifferent to his own welfare, and skilled in killing others, being unable to endure the Buddha's presence and with a mind overcome by anger, shook that mountain, wishing to frighten the Possessor of Ten Powers and make him flee. That mountain...
152:
Although that yakkha Nārada shook Mount Nāradakūṭa, by the power of the Blessed One, it was as if the mountain was falling onto the yakkha's own head.

Then, being frightened, the yakkha thought, “Now I shall burn this ascetic with fire,” and created a massive and terrifying mass of fire. That mass of fire, like fire thrown against the wind, caused suffering only to himself and was not able to burn even a single thread of the Blessed One's robe. The yakkha, looking to see whether the ascetic was burnt or not, saw the Blessed One sitting like the moon—which is free from impurities in the autumn season and brings delight to all people—or like one sitting on the pericarp of a lotus in a cool body of water. He then thought: “Oh, this ascetic has great power! Whatever harm I do to him, that very harm falls back upon me. Apart from this ascetic, I have no other refuge or resort. Just as those who have slipped on the ground must rise by depending on the ground itself, I shall go to this very ascetic for refuge.”

Having thought thus, the yakkha fell with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, which were adorned with the wheel marks, and said, “Venerable Sir, a transgression has overcome me,” and went to the Blessed One for refuge. Then the Blessed One preached the Gradual Instruction (Anupubbīkathā) to him. At the end of the discourse, he, together with ten thousand yakkhas, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). On that day, the people living throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa brought one man from each village for the purpose of sacrifice to that yakkha. They also brought many sesame seeds, rice, kidney beans, green grams, black grams, and so on, as well as ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses. Then the yakkha gave all the rice and other items brought on that day to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, and handed over those men brought for sacrifice to the Blessed One.

Then the Teacher ordained those men with the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination and, within seven days, established them all in the Fruit of Arahantship. On the full moon day of Māgha, in the midst of one hundred crore monks, he recited the Pātimokkha in an assembly endowed with four factors. The four factors are: all the monks were 'Ehi Bhikkhus', all were possessors of the six higher powers (abhiññā), all had come without being invited, and it was the Uposatha day of the fifteenth. This was the second assembly. Therefore, it was said in the Pali:

Verse 11. Again, at Mount Nāradakūṭa,
While the Victorious Buddha was in seclusion,
One hundred crores of monks, taintless and stainless,
Assembled together.
153:
“Again, when the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara approached a secluded spot at Nāradakūṭa, one hundred crores of Arahants, who were free from the stains of defilements, assembled.”

In that verse, ‘pavivekagate’ means having gone away from the group. ‘Samiṃsu’ means they assembled.

At the time when the Leader of the World, the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, entered the rains-retreat at the mountain named Sudassana, it is said that the inhabitants of Jambudīpa held an annual mountain-top festival (giraggasamajja). The people who gathered at that festival, upon seeing the Possessor of Ten Powers and hearing the Dhamma, gained faith and went forth as monks. On the day of the Great Pavāraṇā, the Teacher taught a discourse on Vipassanā (insight) suited to their inclinations. Having heard that teaching, all those monks contemplated conditioned phenomena and attained Arahantship through the stages of insight and the stages of the Path. Then, the Teacher performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony together with ninety thousand crores of Arahants. This was the third assembly. Therefore, it is said:

“At the time when the Great Hero, the Great Sage, performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony at the Sudassana mountain with ninety thousand crores of Arahants.

At that time, I was the ascetic Sumedha, of fierce austerity, who could travel through the air and had reached the far shore of mastery in the five supernormal knowledges.”

Although this verse is written in the Dīpaṅkara Buddhavamsa within the introductory explanation (Nidāna-vaṇṇanā) of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Commentary named Atthasālinī, it is not found in this Buddhavamsa text. Its absence in this text is actually more appropriate. Why? Because it has already been mentioned in the stories of Sumedha below.

When the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was teaching the Dhamma, there was indeed the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) by ten thousand and twenty thousand beings. However, there is no end to the count of those who realized the Dhamma individually, such as one, two, three, or four persons. Therefore, the dispensation of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was widespread and popular, becoming a refuge for many. Thus, it is said:

“There was the realization of the Dhamma by ten and twenty thousand beings;
The realizations of the Dhamma by individuals, one or two at a time, were beyond counting.”

In that verse, ‘dasavīsatasahassānaṃ’ refers to ten thousand and twenty thousand beings. ‘Dhammābhisamayo’ means the penetration of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. ‘Ekadvinnaṃ’ refers to individuals one by one and two by two.
154:
It means they were countless, following the method of 2, 3, 4... up to 10 and so on. Because of such countless realizations of the Dhamma, and because it was known by many wise devas and humans as the way leading out of suffering (niyyānika), the dispensation reached greatness, being prosperous through the training of higher virtue (adhisīla) and flourishing through concentration (samādhi) and other qualities. Therefore, it is said:

“At that time, the dispensation of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was widespread, popular, prosperous, flourishing, and well-purified.”

In that context, ‘suvisodhitaṃ’ means it was made pure because it was well-cleansed by the Blessed One. It is said that four hundred thousand monks, who possessed the six supernormal powers and great psychic power, always surrounded the Teacher Dīpaṅkara. At that time, if those who were still trainees (sekha) passed away, they were reproached. The implication is that everyone attained Parinibbāna only after becoming Arahants. Therefore, the dispensation of that Blessed One was well-blossomed and well-accomplished, shining greatly with Arahant monks. Thus, it is said:

“Four hundred thousand monks, possessing the six supernormal powers and great psychic power,
Always surround Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World.

Whoever leaves the human life at that time,
Those trainees who have not reached the goal of the mind (Arahantship) are reproached.

The well-blossomed Word of the Buddha (pāvacanaṃ) always shines,
With such Arahants who are free from stains.”

In those verses, “four hundred thousand” is shown by way of counting, and the phrase “possessing the six supernormal powers and great psychic power” is said to show that these monks were of such a nature; this is how the meaning should be understood.
