Alternatively, “possessing the six supernormal powers and great psychic power” should be seen as the nominative case used in the sense of the genitive, meaning “of the four hundred thousand monks who possess the six supernormal powers.” “Always surround” means they surround the Possessor of Ten Powers at all times; the meaning is that they do not go anywhere leaving the Blessed One. In the phrase “at that time,” the word ‘samaya’ is found in nine meanings, such as concourse (samavāya) and others. How was it taught? It is as follows:
155: "The word 'samaya' is seen in the sense of a combination of causes, an opportunity, a time, a group, a cause, a view, an attainment, an abandonment, and the nature of penetration or the knowledge of penetration." (DN-a 1.1, etc.). In this text [tena samayena], this word 'samaya' should be understood as 'time'; it means 'at that time'. 'Mānusaṃ bhavaṃ' means human existence. 'Appattamānasā' refers to those whose minds (the fruit of Arahatship) have not yet reached, attained, or been realized. The word 'mānasa' is a designation for passion (rāga), the mind (citta), and the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala). Indeed, in the Pali verse, 'That snare of passion (mānasa) which moves in the sky...', 'mānasa' is said to be passion. In the Pali, 'Citta, mano, mānasa, hadaya, paṇḍara...', 'mānasa' is said to be the mind. In the Pali, 'Why should a trainee (sekha) who has not yet reached the mānasa (Arahatship) die among people?', 'mānasa' is said to be Arahatship. Here too, only Arahatship is intended. Therefore, it means those who have not yet reached the fruit of Arahatship. For what reason are they called 'sekhas' (trainees)? They are called 'sekhas' because they have attained the qualities of a trainee (sekha-dhamma). For it is said: 'To what extent, venerable sir, is one a trainee? Here, monks, a monk is endowed with the Right View of a trainee... endowed with the Right Concentration of a trainee. To this extent, monks, a monk is called a trainee.' (SN 5.13). Furthermore, they are called 'sekhas' because they are training (sikkhanti). For it is said: 'He trains, he trains, monk; therefore he is called a trainee. In what does he train? He trains in higher virtue (adhisīla), he trains in higher mind (adhicitta), and he trains in higher wisdom (adhipaññā). Monk, therefore he is called a trainee.' (AN 3.86). 'Supupphitaṃ' means well-blossomed (vikasita). 'Pāvacanaṃ' means the sublime word, or the word that has reached growth (pavacana); 'pavacana' itself is 'pāvacana', meaning the Dispensation (sāsana). 'Upasobhati' means it is very beautiful and radiant, it shines intensely. 'Sabbadā' means at all times. There is also a reading, 'It is beautiful in the world together with devas.' For that Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, there was a city named Rammavatī. A khattiya named Sudeva was his father. A queen named Sumedhā was his mother. Two elders, Sumaṅgala and Tissa, were his chief disciples (aggasāvaka). An elder named Sāgata was his attendant. Two female elders, Nandā and Sunandā, were his chief female disciples (aggasāvikā). The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One was a Pipphalī tree. His height was eighty cubits. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years. If it is asked, 'What is the purpose of showing these details such as the city of birth?', the answer is: If the city of birth, the father, and the mother of a Buddha were not known, there would be reason to think this Buddha might be a deva. The city of birth of this Buddha is also not well-known...
156: ...if the city of birth, the father, and the mother were not known, people would think, 'This is surely a deva, or Sakka, or a yakkha, or Māra, or Brahmā.' Thinking that such a miracle is not surprising for devas, they would not think that he should be listened to or believed. If they do not think so, the realization (abhisamaya) of the Four Noble Truths would not occur. If there is no realization, the arising of a Buddha would be fruitless, and the Dispensation would be one that does not lead out [of suffering]. Therefore, the specific details such as the city of birth of all Buddhas must be shown. Thus, it was said: 'The city was named Rammavatī; a khattiya named Sudeva was the father, and Sumedhā was the mother of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara. Sumaṅgala and Tissa were the chief disciples; Sāgata was the attendant of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara. Nandā and Sunandā were the chief female disciples; the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Pipphalī. Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage (Mahāmuni), was eighty cubits in height; he was as beautiful as a lamp-tree or a blossoming Sal king. The lifespan of that Great Seer was one hundred thousand years; remaining for that long, he saved many people. Having illuminated the True Dhamma and saved the great multitude, that Blessed One, together with his disciples, attained Nibbāna like a great mass of fire being extinguished. That power, that fame, and those wheel-marks on the feet—all have vanished. Are not all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) indeed empty?' Among those verses, 'Sudeva named khattiya' means the khattiya named Sudeva was the father. 'Janikā' means the mother. 'Pipphalī' is the Bodhi tree, which is a Pilakkha tree (Ficus infectoria). 'Asītihatthamubbedho' means eighty cubits in height. 'Dīparukkho vā' means like a lamp-tree crowded with intensely glowing garlands of lamps, he was endowed with the perfection of height, girth, and form, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor marks, like the sky shining with a multitude of stars through a spreading net of rays...
157: The Blessed One was beautiful while he lived. Like a sal king tree in full bloom, or like the Pāricchattaka tree a hundred leagues high in full bloom, the Blessed One, eighty cubits in height, was exceedingly beautiful. 'Satasahassavassāni' means his lifespan was a hundred thousand years. 'Tāvatā tiṭṭhamāno' means remaining for that length of time. 'Janataṃ' means the multitude of people. 'Santāretvā mahājanaṃ' means having saved the great multitude. There is also a reading 'santāretvā sadevakaṃ', which means having saved the world together with the devas. That psychic power and success, and that fame and retinue—all those various kinds of attainments have vanished and disappeared. Are not all conditioned things empty? They are devoid of permanent substance and so forth. In this context, the definition of the city and so forth appears in the Pali text itself. However, the section on various details (sambahulavāra) does not appear; it should be brought in and explained. These are: the section on children, the section on wives, the section on palaces, the section on household life, the section on dancing women, the section on the great renunciation, the section on the great struggle (dukkharacariyā), the section on the monastery, and the section on the attendant. The reason for explaining these sections has been stated below. That Buddha Dīpaṅkara had three hundred thousand wives. His chief queen was named Padumā, and his son was named Usabhakkhandha. Thus it is said: "The wife of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara was named Padumā, with a face like a blooming lotus; his son was named Usabhakkhandha. There were three palaces known as Haṃsā, Koñcā, and Mayūrā; it is said he lived in the household for ten thousand years. Departing by an elephant vehicle, the Conqueror lived in the Nandārāma monastery; his attendant was named Nanda, who brought joy to the world." Among all Buddhas, there are five variations (vematta): variation in lifespan, variation in height, variation in caste, variation in the struggle (striving), and variation in radiance. Among these, variation in lifespan means some...
158: ...are long-lived, while some are short-lived. This is indeed true. For the lifespan of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was a hundred thousand years, while our Blessed One's lifespan was a hundred years. Variation in height (pamāṇa-vematta) means some Buddhas are tall, while some are short. For Dīpaṅkara was eighty cubits in height, while our Blessed One was eighteen cubits in height. Variation in caste (kula-vematta) means some Buddhas are born in the Khattiya (warrior-noble) caste, while some are born in the Brāhmaṇa (brahmin) caste. For Dīpaṅkara and others were born in the Khattiya caste, while Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and others were born in the Brāhmaṇa caste. Variation in the struggle (padhāna-vematta) means for some Buddhas the struggle is very brief, as it was for the Blessed One Kassapa, while for others it is long, as it was for our Blessed One. Variation in radiance (rasmi-vematta) means the bodily radiance of the Blessed One Maṅgala stayed pervading ten thousand world systems, while our Blessed One's radiance was only a fathom. That variation in radiance is connected to their inclination (ajjhāsaya). To whatever extent they wish to pervade with their bodily radiance, it pervades that far. The Blessed One Maṅgala always had the inclination, "May it pervade ten thousand world systems." However, regarding the qualities of a Buddha that are penetrated (realized), there is no variation among any of the Buddhas. Likewise, for all Buddhas, there are four unrenounced (fixed) locations. The place where the Bodhi-throne (Bodhi-pallaṅka) stands is in the same location and is never renounced. The place where the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion in the Deer Park at Isipatana is also never renounced. The place where the first step was taken at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa at the time of the descent from the deva world is also never renounced. The locations of the four bedposts in the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) at Jetavana are also never renounced. The monastery itself is also an unrenounced location; whether it be small or large, it is not renounced. Furthermore, the details of the co-natals and the asterisms of our Blessed One are unique. It is said that together with our Bodhisatta, the mother of Rāhula, the Elder Ānanda, Channa the courtier, Kaṇṭhaka the king of horses, the four great pots of treasure, the Great Bodhi tree, and Kāဠuဒāyī the courtier—these seven were co-natals. The Great Being entered his mother's womb under the asterism of Uttarāsāḷha; his great renunciation...
159:
The Blessed One went forth; He turned the Wheel of Dhamma; He performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire. His birth, His attainment of Buddhahood through the realization of the Four Noble Truths, and His Parinibbāna occurred under the Visākha constellation. The assembly of that Blessed One's disciples and the relinquishing of His life-principle occurred under the Māgha constellation. His descent from the celestial realm occurred under the Assayuja constellation—this much should be brought forth and explained. This is the definition of the various occurrences. The remaining verses are clear in their meaning.

Thus, the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, having lived for the full duration of His life and having performed all the duties of a Buddha, gradually attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna-element without remainder.

In the same Sāramaṇḍa-kappa in which the Dīpaṅkara Ten-Powered One arose, three other Buddhas named Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, and Saraṇaṅkara also arose. Our Bodhisatta did not receive a prophecy in the presence of those three Buddhas. Therefore, they are not shown here. However, in the Commentary, this was said to show all the Buddhas who arose from the beginning of that aeon:

“Taṇhaṅkara and Medhaṅkara, and also Saraṇaṅkara,
Dīpaṅkara the Fully Enlightened One, and Koṇḍañña, the supreme among men.

Maṅgala and Sumana, Revata and Sobhita the Sage,
Anomadassī, Paduma, Nārada, and Padumuttara.

Sumedha and Sujāta, Piyadassī of great fame,
Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, and Siddhattha, the leader of the world.

Tissa and Phussa the Fully Enlightened One, Vipassī, Sikhī, and Vessabhū,
Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa the leader.

These were the Fully Enlightened Ones, free from passion and well-concentrated,
They arose like the hundred-rayed sun, dispelling the great darkness,
Having shone like great masses of fire, they have been extinguished along with their disciples.”

## Thus, in the Commentary on the Buddhavaṃsa named Madhuratthavilāsinī,
## composed in a manner neither too concise nor too detailed,
## the explanation of the Chronicle of Dīpaṅkara Buddha is finished.
## The first Chronicle of the Buddha is finished.
160:
## 4. Commentary on the Chronicle of Buddha Koṇḍañña

It is said that after the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara attained Parinibbāna, his dispensation lasted for one hundred thousand years. Then, with the disappearance of the disciples who had followed the Buddha, his dispensation also disappeared. Thereafter, after one incalculable period (asankheyya) had passed, in a certain aeon, the Teacher named Koṇḍañña arose in the world. That Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections for sixteen incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons, and having matured his knowledge of enlightenment, remained in a state of existence similar to that of King Vessantara. Passing away from there, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Having remained there for the full span of his life and having accepted the request of the deities, he passed away from the Tusita heaven. He took conception in the womb of Queen Sujātā, in the family of King Sunanda, in the city of Rammavatī. At the moment of his conception, the thirty-two miracles as described in the Chronicle of Buddha Dīpaṅkara also appeared. Protected by the deities, after ten months had passed, he emerged from his mother's womb. Being supreme among all beings, he faced the north, took seven steps, and surveying all directions, he uttered these noble words: “I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world. This is my final birth; now there is no further rebirth.”

Then, on the day of naming the prince, they gave him the name “Koṇḍañña.” Indeed, that Blessed One belonged to the Koṇḍañña clan. He had three most delightful palaces named Rāma, Surāma, and Subha. In those palaces, three hundred thousand dancing women, skilled in dancing, singing, and music, were always present to serve him. His chief consort was named Rucidevī. His son was named Vijitasena. He lived the household life for ten thousand years.

Having seen the four signs—an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a monk—he departed on a noble chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses and went forth into homelessness. He practiced the life of austerities for ten months. When Prince Koṇḍañña went forth, ten crores of people followed him into homelessness. Surrounded by them, he practiced austerities for ten months. On the full moon day of Visākhā, in the village of Sunanda, he partook of the most delicious honey-milk rice offered by the merchant's daughter named Yasodharā, who was of equal fortune and had firm breasts. He then spent the day in a grove of Sal trees adorned with fruits, tender leaves, and sprouts...
161:
The Bodhisatta, having passed the day, left his companions in the evening. Taking the eight handfuls of grass offered by Sunandaka the Ājīvaka, he circumambulated the Sāla-kalyāṇī tree three times. Facing the East and with his back to the Bodhi tree, he spread the grass over an area fifty-eight cubits wide. Sitting cross-legged and resolving with fourfold effort, he defeated the forces of Māra. In the first watch of the night, he purified the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa). In the middle watch, he purified the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). In the last watch, he contemplated the factors of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Emerging from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, he directed his mind to the five aggregates. Seeing the fifty characteristics by way of rise and fall, he developed insight up to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). He then realized the four path knowledges, the four fruition knowledges, the four analytical insights, the knowledge of defining the four types of birth, the knowledge of defining the five destinations, the six uncommon knowledges, and all the attributes of a Buddha. With his aspiration fulfilled, while still seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, he uttered this inspired solemn utterance:

“Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I wandered, seeking but not finding the builder of this house. Sorrowful is repeated birth.
O house-builder, you are seen! You shall build no house again. All your rafters are broken, your ridge-pole is shattered. My mind has attained the unconditioned; I have reached the end of craving.”

“Just as the destination of a blazing fire, struck by a smith's iron hammer and gradually extinguished, is not known;
Even so, there is no way to describe the destination of the Arahants, who are well-released, who have crossed the flood of the bond of sense-pleasures, and who have reached the unshakable bliss of Nibbāna.”

Having uttered this inspired solemn utterance, he spent seven weeks (satta-sattāha) at the foot of the Bodhi tree, experiencing the bliss of the attainment of fruition. In the eighth week, in response to the request of the Great Brahmā, he reflected, “To whom should I first preach the Dhamma?” He saw the ten koṭis of monks who had renounced along with him. “These noble sons have well-accumulated roots of merit. They renounced following my example, practiced austerities with me, and attended to me. I shall preach the Dhamma to them first.” Having reflected thus, he looked to see where they were living and saw: “They are living in the Devavana forest near the city of Aruṇdhavatī, eighteen leagues from here.” Thinking, “I shall go to preach the first sermon to them,” he took his bowl and robes. Just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, he disappeared from the foot of the Bodhi tree and appeared in the Devavana forest. At that time, those ten koṭis of monks were residing in the Devavana forest, depending on the city of Aruṇdhavatī. When those monks saw the Blessed One approaching from afar, with clear and confident minds, they went out to meet him. They took the Blessed One's bowl and robes, prepared a seat for the Buddha, showed respect to the Teacher, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side surrounding him.
162:
(The Blessed One) saw: “They are living in the Devavana forest near the city of Aruṇdhavatī, eighteen leagues from here.” Thinking, “I shall go to preach the first sermon to them,” he took his bowl and robes. Just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, he disappeared from the foot of the Bodhi tree and appeared in the Devavana forest.

At that time, those ten koṭis of monks were residing in the Devavana forest, depending on the city of Aruṇdhavatī. When those monks saw the Blessed One approaching from afar, with clear and confident minds, they went out to meet him. They took the Blessed One's bowl and robes, prepared a seat for the Buddha, showed respect to the Teacher, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side surrounding him. While they sat surrounding him, the Blessed One named Koṇḍañña, seated on the Buddha's seat and surrounded by the assembly of sages, shone brilliantly like the thousand-eyed Sakka surrounded by the host of gods, like the moon shining in a cloudless sky, or like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars.

Then the Teacher preached to those monks the incomparable Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which is practiced by all Buddhas and has three rounds and twelve modes. He gave the ambrosia of the Dhamma to a hundred thousand koṭis of devas and humans, headed by the ten koṭis of monks. Therefore, it is said (in the Pali):

“After Dīpaṅkara, there was a leader named Koṇḍañña, of infinite power, immeasurable fame, incomparable, and difficult to approach.

He was like the earth in patience, like the ocean in virtue, like Mount Meru in concentration, and like the sky in knowledge.

The Buddha always preached the Dhamma that reveals the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, the path, and the truths, for the benefit of all living beings.

When Koṇḍañña, the leader of the world, set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, the first realization of the Four Noble Truths occurred for a hundred thousand koṭis (of devas and humans).”

In those verses, “Dīpaṅkarassa aparena” means in the period after the Teacher Dīpaṅkara. “Koṇḍañño nāma” is the name he acquired according to his lineage. “Nāyako” means the leader (the Buddha). “Anantatejo” means having infinite power due to his own power of virtue, knowledge, and merit. Between Avīci below and the highest point of existence (Bhavagga) above, and across the infinite world systems horizontally, even a single person...
163:
There is no one who is able to stand looking at the face of that Blessed One. Therefore, he is called 'Anantatejo' (The One of infinite power). 'Amitayaso' means having an infinite retinue. Indeed, for that Blessed One, until the time of his Parinibbāna during the hundred thousand years, there was no limit to the number of the assembly of monks within this interval. Therefore, he is called 'Amitayaso'. He is also called 'Amitayaso' because of his immeasurable fame and reputation. 'Appameyyo' means immeasurable because he cannot be measured by the extent of his collection of qualities. As it was said:

Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of another Buddha,
Speaking nothing else for an entire aeon,
The aeon would reach its end in that long interval,
But the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.

Therefore, because he is endowed with an immeasurable collection of qualities, he is called 'Appameyyo'. 'Durāsado' means difficult to approach; he is called Durāsado because he cannot be approached by way of assault or harassment; it means he is difficult to overcome.

'Dharaṇūpamo' means being like the earth. Because of his patience (khanti), like the great earth which is two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, he is unshaken by natural winds, gain and loss, desirable and undesirable objects, and so forth. Thus he is called 'Dharaṇūpamo'. 'Sāgarūpamo' by virtue of his morality means he is like the ocean because he does not overstep the shore through the restraint of morality. For it was said: "Monks, the great ocean is of a stable nature and does not overstep the shore."

'Merūpamo' by virtue of concentration means he is like Mount Meru, the king of mountains, because he is free from the shaking caused by states that are opposed to concentration. Or it can be said that he has a body as firm as Mount Meru. 'Gaganūpamo' by virtue of knowledge means that here, an analogy is made with the infinite sky because the Blessed One's knowledge is infinite. The Blessed One spoke of four infinite things:

The collection of beings and the sky,
The universes are infinite,
The Buddha's knowledge is immeasurable,
It is not possible to fully know these four.

Therefore, his infinite knowledge is compared to the infinite sky.
164:
The manifestation of the faculties (indriya), powers (bala), factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), path factors (magga), and truths (sacca) means that by taking these faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path factors, and truths, the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), right efforts (sammappadhāna), and bases of power (iddhipāda) are also included. Therefore, by way of the four summaries such as the faculties, he manifested and taught the Dhamma that clarifies the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma). 'Hitāya' means for the sake of welfare. 'Dhammacakkaṃ pavattente' means while setting in motion the knowledge of the teaching.

Thereafter, at the assembly of the Great Blessing (Mahāmaṅgala), deities from the ten thousand universes created subtle forms and gathered in this very universe. There, it is said, a certain son of the gods asked the Buddha Koṇḍañña the question on blessings. To that son of the gods, the Blessed One taught the blessings. In that Maṅgala Sutta, nine hundred billion deities attained Arahantship. There was no limit to the number of those who became Stream-enterers and so forth. Therefore, it was said: 'Thereafter, while teaching in the assembly of humans and gods, there was the second realization for nine hundred billion [beings].'

In that verse, 'tato parampi' means thereafter. 'Desente' means while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma. 'Naramarūnaṃ' means of humans and gods. When the Blessed One performed the Twin Miracle (yamakapāṭihāriya) in the sky to subdue the pride of the heretics and taught the Dhamma, eight hundred billion deities attained Arahantship. Those established in the lower three fruits were beyond counting. Therefore, it was said: 'Subduing the heretics, when he taught the Dhamma, there was the third realization for eight hundred billion [beings].'

In that verse, the meaning should be understood by bringing in the word 'tadā' (then). When the Blessed One taught the Dhamma, then there was the realization of the Dhamma for eight hundred billion humans and gods.

It is said that the Teacher Koṇḍañña, after attaining supreme enlightenment, stayed at the Candārāma monastery near the city of Candavatī during the first rainy season. There, the young man Bhadda, son of the wealthy Brahmin Sucindhara, and the young man Subhadda, son of the Brahmin Yasodhara, heard the Dhamma teaching in the presence of the Buddha Koṇḍañña. With confident hearts, they went forth in the presence of that Blessed One along with ten thousand young men and attained Arahantship.
165:
At that time, the Blessed One Koṇḍañña, on the full moon day of Jeṭṭha, recited the Ovādapātimokkha surrounded by one hundred thousand crores of Arahants led by the Elder Subhadda; that was the first assembly (sannipāta). Later, when the son of the Blessed One Koṇḍañña, named Vijitasena, attained Arahantship, the Blessed One recited the Ovādapātimokkha in the midst of one thousand crores of Arahants led by him; that was the second assembly. At another time, the Dasabala, while wandering through the countryside, caused King Udena, who had a retinue of ninety crores of people, to go forth into monkhood along with his followers. When that king attained Arahantship, the Blessed One, surrounded by ninety crores of Arahants led by him, recited the Ovādapātimokkha; that was the third assembly. Regarding this, it was said in the Pali:

“There were three assemblies of the Great Sage Koṇḍañña,
Of the Arahants whose taints were exhausted, who were stainless,
Of peaceful minds, and possessed of the quality of Tādi.

The first gathering was of one hundred thousand crores,
The second was of one thousand crores, and the third was of ninety crores.”

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) named Vijitāvī, residing in the city of Candavatī. That Universal Monarch, surrounded by many noble men, ruled the earth—bounded by the four oceans, including Mount Meru and Mount Yugandhara, and bearing immeasurable treasures—righteously, without punishment or weapons. At that time, the Buddha Koṇḍañña, also surrounded by one hundred thousand crores of Arahants, while wandering through the countryside, arrived at the city of Candavatī in due course.

When King Vijitāvī heard, “The Fully Enlightened One has arrived at our city,” he went out to welcome Him, prepared a place for the Blessed One to reside, and invited Him along with the Saṅgha of monks for the following day. On the next day, having prepared excellent food and offerings, he gave a great alms-giving (Mahādāna) to the Saṅgha of one hundred thousand crores of monks with the Buddha at their head. After the Bodhisatta had offered the meal to the Blessed One, at the conclusion of the appreciation (anumodanā) discourse, he requested, “Venerable Sir, please reside in this very city for the three months of the rainy season, showing favor to the many people.” He then gave the incomparable great alms-giving (asadisa-mahādāna) to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at their head continuously for three months.

Then the Blessed One gave the prediction to the Bodhisatta, saying, “In the future, he will become a Buddha named Gotama,” and preached the Dhamma to him. The Bodhisatta, having heard the Dhamma discourse of the Blessed One...
166:
Having heard that Dhamma discourse, he handed over the kingdom, went forth as a monk, learned the Tipiṭaka, and developed the eight attainments and five superknowledges. With his jhānas unimpaired, he was reborn in the Brahma realm. Therefore, it was said:

"At that time, I was a khattiya named Vijitāvī,
I exercised sovereignty over the entire world, with the ocean as its boundary.

I satisfied one hundred thousand crores of stainless Great Sages,
Along with the Lord of the World, with the most excellent food.

That Buddha Koṇḍañña, the Leader of the World, also predicted of me:
'In an immeasurable aeon from now, he will become a Buddha in the world.'

'Having exerted great effort and performed difficult austerities (dukkara-cariyā),
That one of great fame will attain Enlightenment at the foot of an Assattha tree.'

'The mother who gives birth to him will be a queen named Māyā,
His father will be a king named Suddhodana; he will be known as Gotama.'

'Kolita and Upatissa will be his chief disciples,
An attendant named Ānanda will serve that Conqueror (Jina).'

'Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā will be his chief female disciples,
The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Assattha.'

'Citta and Hatthāḷavaka will be his chief male lay attendants,
Nandamātā and Uttarā will be his chief female lay attendants.
The lifespan of that famous Gotama will be one hundred years.'

Having heard this word of the incomparable Great Sage,
Humans and Devas rejoiced, saying: 'This is indeed a Buddha-seed!'

Shouts of applause arose; they clapped their hands and laughed;
Ten thousand world-systems of deities saluted him with joined palms."
167:
## 
“If we should miss the teaching of this Lord of the World, Koṇḍañña Buddha, may we be in the presence of this [Gotama Buddha] in the future.

“Just as people crossing a river, if they miss the opposite landing place, take the lower landing place to cross the great river;

“In the same way, if we all miss this Conqueror, may we be in the presence of this [Gotama Buddha] in the future,” so they prayed.

Having heard the words of that Buddha, I felt even greater devotion. Wishing to fulfill the perfections for that purpose of Buddhahood, I offered my great kingdom to the Conqueror. Having offered the great kingdom, I ordained in the presence of that Buddha.

Having mastered the Suttanta, the Vinaya, and the ninefold teaching of the Teacher, I adorned the Conqueror's Dispensation.

Living there diligently in sitting, standing, and walking, and having reached the perfection of higher knowledge (abhiññā), I went to the Brahma realm.

In that text, 'ahaṃ tena samayena' means 'I, the Bodhisatta, at that time was a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch) named Vijitāvī.' In the phrase 'samuddaṃ antantena,' it means exercising sovereignty by making the ocean, which is bounded by the Cakkavāḷa mountains, the limit. This much is not yet clear; I shall explain in detail.

It is said that the Cakkavatti King, by the power of the Wheel Treasure, keeping Mount Sineru on his left, travels over the ocean to the Eastern Island (Pubbavideha), which is eight thousand yojanas in extent. In that Eastern Island, the Cakkavatti King gives this advice: 'Do not kill living beings, do not take what is not given, do not commit sexual misconduct, do not tell lies, do not drink intoxicants, and enjoy only the rightful taxes.' After giving such advice, the Wheel Treasure rises into the sky and enters the Eastern Ocean. As it enters, the waves subside and sink, and the water of the Great Ocean recedes by one yojana, standing on both sides like walls of beryl, most wonderful to behold. Thus, having reached the edge of the Eastern Ocean, the Wheel Treasure returns. As it returns...
168:
## 
That retinue is in the front, the Cakkavatti King is in the middle, and the Wheel Treasure is at the end. The water, as if unable to bear separation from the edge of the water, reaches the shore while touching the rim of the wheel.

In this way, the Cakkavatti King, having conquered the Eastern Island bounded by the Eastern Ocean, and wishing to conquer Jambudīpa bounded by the Southern Ocean, proceeds toward the Southern Ocean by the path shown by the Wheel Treasure. Having conquered Jambudīpa, which is ten thousand yojanas in extent, he rises from the Southern Ocean and proceeds in the same manner as mentioned above to conquer the Western Island (Aparagoyāna), which is seven thousand yojanas in extent. Having conquered that island bounded by the ocean, he rises from the Western Ocean and proceeds in the same way to conquer the Northern Island (Uttarakuru), which is eight thousand yojanas in extent. Having made the ocean its boundary and conquered that Northern Island, he rises again from the Northern Ocean. By thus traveling through all four islands, the Cakkavatti King attains sovereignty over the earth bounded by the four oceans. Therefore, the Buddha said, 'exercising sovereignty by making the ocean the limit.'

'Koṭisatasahassānaṃ' means one hundred thousand crores. Or, this very reading is the correct one. 'Vimalānaṃ' refers to the Arahants who are free from taints (āsavas). 'Saha lokagganāthena' means together with the Buddha and one hundred thousand crores of Arahants. 'Paramannena' means with excellent food. 'Tappayiṃ' means satisfied. 'Aparimeyyito kappe' means after passing through three incalculable periods (asaṅkheyyas) and one hundred thousand aeons (kappas) from this aeon, in a single Bhadda-kappa.

'Padhānaṃ' means effort or energy. 'Tam eva atthaṃ sādhento' means fulfilling and completing the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī), which is the cause of achieving Buddhahood. 'Mahārajjaṃ' means the sovereignty of a Cakkavatti. In the word 'jine,' the locative case should be understood in the sense of the dative (to the Buddha). 'Adāṃ' means gave. The connection should be understood with the phrase 'evam-atthaṃ sādhento.' Some teachers read 'mahārajjaṃ jine dadiṃ.' 'Daditvāna' means having renounced. 'Suttantaṃ' refers to the Suttanta Piṭaka, 'Vinayaṃ' to the Vinaya Piṭaka, and 'navangaṃ' to the ninefold scriptures starting with Sutta and Geyya. 'Sobhayiṃ jinasāsanaṃ' means adorned the teaching through the acquisition and realization of the mundane scriptures. 'Tattha' means in the teaching of that Buddha. 'Appamatto' means being endowed with mindfulness. 'Brahmalokamagañchahaṃ' means I went to the Brahma realm.

For that Koṇḍañña Buddha, the city was named Rammavatī. King Sunanda was the father, and Queen Sujātā was the mother. The Elders Bhadda and Subhadda were the pair of chief disciples (aggasāvaka). The attendant was the Elder named Anuruddha. The Elders Tissā and Upatissā were the pair of chief female disciples (aggasāvikā). The Bodhi tree where he realized the Four Noble Truths was the Salala (Napai) tree. His body was eighty-eight cubits high. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years. The chief queen of that Koṇḍañña Buddha was named Rucidevī. His son was named Vijitasena. The king named Canda was his attendant. He resided in the Candārāma monastery. Therefore, the Buddha said in the Pali: 'The city was named Rammavatī... all conditioned things.'
169: There were two chief disciples, an attendant named Anuruddha, and two chief female disciples named Tissā and Upatissā. The Bodhi tree was a Sālakalyāṇī (Napai) tree. His body was eighty-eight cubits high. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years. That Blessed One had a chief queen named Rucidevī. His son was named Vijitasena. The attendant king was named Canda. It is said that he resided in the Candārāma monastery. Therefore, it was said: ## "The city was named Rammavatī, the king was named Sunanda. The mother of Koṇḍañña the Great Sage was named Sujātā. ## "Bhadda and Subhadda were the chief disciples. The attendant of Koṇḍañña the Great Sage was named Anuruddha. ## "Tissā and Upatissā were the chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of Koṇḍañña the Great Sage was the Sālakalyāṇī. ## "That Great Sage was eighty-eight cubits high; he shone like the moon, or like the sun at midday. ## "At that time, the lifespan was one hundred thousand years. Remaining for that long, he saved many beings. ## "The earth was adorned with Arahants who were free from taints and pure. Just as the sky is adorned with stars, so did he shine. ## "Those Arahants, immeasurable in virtue, unshakeable and difficult to approach, having shown themselves like a flash of lightning, attained Parinibbāna, those of great fame. ## "That incomparable power of the Conqueror, and the concentration developed through wisdom—all that has disappeared. Are not all conditioned things indeed empty?" In that verse, 'Sālakalyāṇiko' means the Sālakalyāṇī tree. That tree appears only during the time of a Buddha and the time of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch), and not at other times. It is said that it grows in a single day. 'Khīṇāsavehi vimalehi vicitṭā āsi medanī' means that this earth was adorned and extremely beautiful to behold, shining with the single color of the robes of the Arahants. 'Yathā hi' is a particle used in the sense of a simile. 'Uḷūbhi' means by the stars.
170:
The meaning is that just as the sky is beautiful with the host of stars and constellations, so too this earth where the Buddha appeared was beautiful, adorned with Arahants.

“Asaṅkhobha” means being unshakeable and unchangeable by the eight worldly conditions. “Vijjupātaṃva dassetvā” means having shown like a flash of lightning; there is also a reading “Vijjupātavā”. It is said that in the time of Koṇḍañña Buddha, the bhikkhus who were attaining Parinibbāna ascended into the sky to the height of seven palm trees, and like a flash of lightning entering the gap of a dark rain cloud, they shone all around, entered the fire-element (tejo-dhātu), and like a fire without fuel, they attained Parinibbāna. Therefore, it was said, “Vijjupātaṃva dassetvā”. “Atuliyā” means incomparable or peerless. “Ñāṇaparibhāvito” means developed or increased by knowledge. The remaining verses are clear as they follow the same method mentioned below.

“The Fully Enlightened One named Koṇḍañña attained Parinibbāna at the delightful Candārāma monastery.
A stupa seven yojanas high was built for that Blessed One.

The relics of that Teacher did not disperse,
But remained as a single mass, like a golden statue.”

People living throughout the entire Jambudīpa came together and completed the stupa, which was seven yojanas high and made of the seven kinds of jewels, using orpiment (haritāla) and realgar (manosilā) for the plastering work, and using ghee and oil for the liquid requirements.

## The explanation of the Chronicle of Koṇḍañña Buddha is finished.
## The second Chronicle of the Buddha is finished.
## 5. Explanation of the Chronicle of Maṅgala Buddha

It is said that when the Teacher Koṇḍañña attained Parinibbāna, His Dispensation (Sāsana) lasted for one hundred thousand years. With the passing away of the disciples who were enlightened after the Buddha, His Dispensation disappeared. After Koṇḍañña Buddha, having passed over one incalculable period (asankheyya), four Buddhas named Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita arose in a single aeon. Among them, the Blessed One Maṅgala, the leader of the world, fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for sixteen incalculable periods and one hundred thousand aeons, was reborn in the Tusita heaven, and stayed there for the full duration of His life. When the five preliminary signs appeared, the Buddha-uproar (Buddha-kolāhala)...
171:
The tumultuous proclamation (Buddha-kolāhala) that a Buddha was about to arise occurred. At that time, the deities and Brahmās of the ten thousand world systems gathered in a single world system and made this request: “O Great Hero, the time has come for you to become a Buddha; please arise in the womb of a mother. Saving the world together with the devas, may you realize the Deathless state (Nibbāna).”

Having been thus requested by the deities and Brahmās, and having performed the five great investigations, the Bodhisatta passed away from the Tusita heaven and took rebirth in the womb of Queen Uttarā, the consort of the peerless King Uttara, in the city of Uttara, the most excellent of all cities. At that moment, many miracles appeared. These miracles should be understood in the same manner as described in the Chronicle of Dīpaṅkara Buddha. From the moment the Bodhisatta Maṅgala, the blessing of the entire world, was conceived in the womb of Queen Uttarā, his bodily radiance spread throughout an area of eighty cubits day and night, remaining unsubdued by the light of the moon or the sun. The Queen, without the need for any other light, moved about dispelling the darkness solely by the emergence of his bodily radiance, attended by sixty-eight nurses.

After ten months had passed while under the protection of the deities, the Queen gave birth to the auspicious Great Man in the auspicious garden named Uttaramadhura, a most delightful place frequented by herds of various deer such as the ruru, lion, tiger, elephant, gavaya, buffalo, and spotted deer, adorned with lotuses and lilies, and possessing branches and foliage laden with most fragrant flowers and fruits. As soon as he was born, the Great Being looked towards all directions, took seven steps towards the north, and uttered a noble speech. At that instant, the deities and Brahmās throughout the entire ten thousand world systems appeared with visible bodies, their forms adorned with divine garlands and the like, and standing here and there, they chanted words of victory and auspicious praise. The miracles were as previously described. On the day of his naming, the fortune-tellers, seeing that he was born with the fulfillment of all auspicious blessings, named him “Prince Maṅgala.”

For Prince Maṅgala, there were three palaces: Yasavā, Rucimā, and Sirimā. There were thirty thousand dancing women and attendants, headed by Queen Yasavatī. There, the Great Being enjoyed happiness similar to divine bliss for ninety thousand years. After his chief consort Yasavatī gave birth to a son named Sīlavā, he saw the four omens, mounted the noble and beautiful horse named Paṇḍara, and departed on the Great Renunciation to become an ascetic. Following the Bodhisatta Maṅgala into the homeless life, thirty million people also became ascetics. Surrounded by those thirty million monks, the Great Man practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for eight months.

Then, on the full moon day of Vesākha, he accepted and partook of the honeyed milk-rice containing divine essence offered by Uttarā, the daughter of the merchant Uttara in the village of Uttara. He spent the day in a delightful Sal grove of dark green hue, adorned with fragrant flowers. In the evening, taking the eight handfuls of grass offered by the ascetic named Uttara, he approached the Nāga-Bodhi tree (Ironwood tree), which resembled Mount Asitañjana, was as beautiful as the pinnacle of a golden net, possessed cool shade, was free from the disturbance of wild animals, was adorned with thick branches swaying in the gentle breeze, and shone as if dancing with joy...
172:
(The Bodhisatta Maṅgala) renounced the world and became an ascetic. When he renounced, thirty million people followed him into the homeless life. Surrounded by them, the Great Man practiced austerities for eight months.

Then, on the full moon day of Vesākha, he partook of the honeyed milk-rice infused with divine essence offered by Uttarā, the daughter of the merchant Uttara in the village of Uttara. He spent the day in a delightful Sal grove of dark green hue, adorned with fragrant flowers. Then, taking the eight handfuls of grass offered by the ascetic named Uttara, he approached the Nāga-Bodhi tree, which resembled Mount Asitañjana, was as beautiful as the pinnacle of a golden net, possessed cool shade, was free from the disturbance of wild animals, and was adorned with branches and trees swaying in the gentle breeze, appearing as beautiful as if dancing with joy. Approaching with the gait of a noble elephant in rut, he circumambulated the Bodhi tree and stood on the northeastern side. He spread the grass mat, fifty-eight cubits wide, and sat there in a cross-legged posture, resolving with fourfold energy. Having conquered the King of Māras together with his army, he attained the Knowledge of Past Lives (Pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) and the Divine Eye (Dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa). After contemplating Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) in forward and reverse order, and meditating on the five aggregates as impermanent and so forth, he gradually attained the peerless Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi) and uttered this verse of exaltation (Udāna):

“Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I wandered, seeking but not finding the builder of this house. Sorrowful is repeated birth.
O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build the house again. All your rafters are broken, the ridge-pole is shattered. My mind has reached the Unconditioned; I have attained the destruction of craving.”

The bodily radiance of Maṅgala Buddha was far more extraordinary than that of other Buddhas. While the bodily radiance of other Buddhas normally extends eighty cubits or one fathom around them, it was not so for this Blessed One. The bodily radiance of that Blessed One constantly pervaded the ten thousand world systems. Trees, mountains, houses, walls, pots, and door-leaves appeared as if they were overlaid with gold plates. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. During all that time, there was no light from the moon, sun, or stars. The distinction between night and day was not apparent. Just as beings move about by sunlight during the day, they constantly performed all their activities and moved about solely by the Buddha’s radiance. They distinguished night from day only by the flowers that bloomed in the evening and the songs of the birds that sang in the morning.

If it is asked whether other Buddhas do not have such power, the answer is that it is not that they lack it. Those Buddhas, if they so desire, can also pervade the ten thousand world systems or even further with their radiance. However, for Maṅgala Buddha, due to the power of a past aspiration, his radiance constantly pervaded the ten thousand world systems, just as the one-fathom radiance of other Buddhas remains constant. To elaborate, when this Buddha Maṅgala was a Bodhisatta, in a life similar to that of King Vessantara, he lived with his wife and children on a mountain resembling Mount Vaṅka. While living there, a powerful ogre named Kharadāṭhika, who was known for harassing and eating humans, heard of the Great Man’s desire to practice generosity...
173:
(Beings) went about performing all their tasks. People of the world marked the distinction between night and day by the power of flowers that bloom in the evening and by the power of birds and such that sing in the morning.

If it is asked whether other Buddhas do not have such power, it is not that they do not. For those Buddhas, if they so desired, could also pervade ten thousand world systems or even more with their radiance. However, due to the power of a past aspiration of the Blessed One Mangala, his bodily radiance—like the fathom-wide radiance of other Buddhas—constantly pervaded and remained throughout ten thousand world systems. It is said that when he was a Bodhisatta, in a life similar to that of King Vessantara, he lived with his wife and children on a mountain similar to Mount Vaṅka. At that time, a powerful yakkha named Kharadāṭhika, who was a harasser of all people and a consumer of human flesh, heard of the Great Being’s disposition toward giving. Approaching in the guise of a Brahmin, he asked the Bodhisatta for his two young children. The Great Being, saying, "I give my children to the Brahmin," was exceedingly delighted and joyful, and he gave the two children while causing the earth, bounded by the ocean, to tremble. Then, while the Great Being was looking on, the yakkha discarded his Brahmin guise and—having eyes as red as flames, uneven, crooked, and terrifying tusks, a flat and ugly nose, and tawny (or brownish-grey), coarse, long hair, with a body like a freshly burnt palm trunk—he seized those children like a bunch of lotus stalks and devoured them. Although the Great Being saw the yakkha’s mouth wide open, with streams of blood flowing out like flames, not even a hair’s breadth of displeasure arose in him. Instead, as he thought, "My gift was indeed well given," great rapture and joy (pīti-somanassa) arose in his body. He made an aspiration: "By the result of this gift of mine, in the future, let rays of light emerge in this same manner." Relying on that aspiration, when he became a Buddha, rays of light emerged from his body and pervaded this much space.

There is also another ancient practice of this Buddha Mangala. It is said that when he was a Bodhisatta, seeing the cetiya of a Buddha, he thought, "It is fitting for me to sacrifice my life for this Buddha." He had his entire body wrapped in the manner of a torch, filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand with scented ghee, lit a thousand wicks in it, and placing it on his head, he let his whole body be set ablaze and spent the entire night circumambulating the Stupa of the Conqueror. Although he strove in this way until dawn, he did not feel even a hair's breadth of heat. It was as if he had entered the interior of a lotus...
174:
...it was as if he had entered the interior of a lotus. Indeed, this thing called Dhamma protects the one who protects himself (by practicing it). Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“The Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by the Dhamma,
Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness.
This is the benefit of Dhamma well-practiced:
The one who lives by the Dhamma does not go to a state of woe.”

Due to the result of this wholesome deed as well, the bodily radiance of that Blessed One Mangala pervaded and remained throughout ten thousand world systems. Therefore, it was said:

“After the Buddha Koṇḍañña, there was a leader named Mangala.
Having dispelled the darkness in the world, he held aloft the torch of Dhamma.

“His radiance was incomparable, surpassing that of other Conquerors.
Overpowering the light of the moon and sun, he shone throughout ten thousand worlds.”

In those verses, ‘tamaṃ’ refers to the darkness of the world and the darkness of the heart. ‘Nihantvāna’ means having overcome or dispelled. In this term ‘dhammokkaṃ’, the word ‘ukkā’ is found in various senses, such as the crucible of a goldsmith and others.

Indeed, in the passage, “Taking the gold with tongs, one should drop it into the mouth of the ukkā (furnace/crucible),” ‘ukkā’ should be understood as the crucible of goldsmiths. In the passage, “One should bind a torch (ukkā); having bound the torch, one should smear the mouth of the furnace,” it refers to the charcoal pan of artisans. In the passage, “Just as the torch (ukkā) of smiths burns within and not without,” it refers to a blacksmith's forge. In the passage, “There will be a falling of a meteor (ukkā-pāta) with such a result,” the force of wind is called ‘ukkā’. In the passage, “While torches (ukkā) were being carried,” a lamp or torch is called ‘ukkā’.

Here too, ‘ukkā’ is intended as a torch. Therefore, in this context, “he held aloft the torch made of Dhamma” means he held the torch of Dhamma for the world which was covered and overcome by the darkness of ignorance (avijjā).

‘Atulāsi’ means it was incomparable. Or, this itself is the reading, meaning it was unlike that of other Buddhas. ‘Jinehanyehī’ means with the Buddhas who are Conquerors...
175:
He became unlike other Buddhas. "Canda-sūriyappabhaṃ hantvā" means having surpassed and dispelled the radiance of the moon and the sun. "Dasa-sahassī virocati" means that the ten thousand world systems shine by the radiance of the Buddha alone, without the need for moonlight or sunlight.

After attaining the Knowledge of the Arahat Path and Omniscient Knowledge, the Mangala Buddha spent seven weeks (forty-nine days) at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Having accepted the Brahma's request to teach the Dhamma, He reflected, "To whom should I first teach this Dhamma?" and saw three koṭis of monks who had gone forth with Him and were possessed of the sufficiency of supporting conditions (upanissaya). Then the thought occurred to the Buddha: "These sons of noble families who followed Me into the homeless life are possessed of the supporting conditions. On the full moon day of Vesākha, I, desiring seclusion, left them; they are now residing in the Sirivana forest, depending on the city of Sirivaḍḍhana. I shall now go there and teach them the Dhamma." Having taken His bowl and robes, He rose into the sky like a king of swans and descended in the Sirivana forest.

Those monks paid homage to the Blessed One, performed the major and minor duties of disciples, and sat down surrounding the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught them the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which is practiced by all Buddhas. Subsequently, the three koṭis of monks attained Arahatship. There was the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) for one hundred thousand koṭis of devas and humans. Therefore, it is said:

"That Buddha also proclaimed the four supreme noble truths;
Having drunk the essence of the truths, those various beings dispelled the great darkness.

Having reached the incomparable supreme enlightenment, in the first teaching of the Dhamma,
There was the realization of the Dhamma for one hundred thousand koṭis of devas and humans."

In those verses, "caturo" means four. "Saccavaruttame" means the noble truths and the supreme truths; the meaning is the supreme noble truths. There is also a reading "cattāro saccavaruttame," which also means the four supreme noble truths. "Te te" refers to those various devas and humans who were disciplined by the Blessed One. "Saccarasaṃ" means having drunk the deathless nectar of the penetration of the Four Truths. "Vinodenti mahātamaṃ" means they dispel or destroy the darkness of delusion that is to be abandoned by the respective Paths. "Patvāna" means having penetrated. Regarding the word "Bodhi" in this context—
176:
The word "Bodhi" is used in the sense of the Path, the Fruit, Nibbāna, the tree, a designation, and also Omniscient Knowledge.

Indeed, this word "Bodhi" appears in the sense of the Path in such passages as: "Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four Paths." It appears in the sense of the Fruit in: "It leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to supreme enlightenment (sambodha)." It appears in the sense of Nibbāna in: "Having reached the deathless, unconditioned Bodhi." It appears in the sense of the Assattha tree in: "Between Gaya and the Bodhi tree." It appears as a designation (name) in: "Prince Bodhi pays homage to the feet of the Blessed Gotama with his head." It appears in the sense of Omniscient Knowledge in: "The Buddha of noble and vast wisdom reaches Bodhi." In this context as well, it should be understood as Omniscient Knowledge. It is also appropriate as the Knowledge of the Arahat Path. "Atula" means incomparable, beyond measure, or immeasurable. The meaning should be taken as the occasion of the first teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One after reaching supreme enlightenment (sambodhi).

Furthermore, while residing near the city of Citta, at the foot of a Champaka tree and a Kaṇḍamba mango tree, He performed the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya) to humble the pride of the heretics, just as our Blessed One did. Then, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, in the delightful abode of gold and silver that is the joy of the maidens of devas and asuras, He sat on the Paṇḍukambala stone throne at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree and taught the Abhidhamma. At that time, one hundred thousand koṭis of deities realized the Dhamma. This was the second realization (abhisamaya).

Again, a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) named Sunanda, having fulfilled the duties of a Cakkavatti in the city of Surabhi, obtained the Wheel Treasure. It is said that when the Mangala Buddha appeared in the world, King Sunanda, seeing the Wheel Treasure shift from its place, became distressed and asked the brahmins: "This Wheel Treasure arose due to my merit; why has it shifted from its place?" Then they explained the reason for its shifting to the king. They said: "The Wheel Treasure shifts from its place upon the end of a Cakkavatti king's life, or his renunciation, or the appearance of a Buddha. For you, Great King, there is no end of life; you are very long-lived. However, the Mangala Buddha has appeared in the world; therefore, your Wheel Treasure has shifted." Hearing this, King Sunanda, the Universal Monarch, along with his retinue, paid homage to the Wheel Treasure with his head and requested: "O Wheel Treasure, do not disappear as long as I have not yet paid respects to the Mangala Buddha." Then the Wheel Treasure remained in its original place.

Thereafter, King Sunanda, filled with joy and surrounded by a retinue thirty-six leagues wide, approached the Mangala Buddha, the blessing of the whole world. Having satisfied the Buddha and His community of monks with a great offering, he donated robes made in the Kāsī country to one hundred thousand koṭis of Arahats. Furthermore, he offered all the requisites to the Buddha and the entire world...
177:
King Sunanda, the Universal Monarch, together with his retinue, paid homage to the Wheel Treasure (Cakkaratana) with his head and made a request: "By your power, as long as I am performing acts of veneration and honor to the Mangala Buddha, may you not disappear." Then, the Wheel Treasure remained stationary in its original position.

Thereafter, the inspiring King Sunanda, the Universal Monarch, surrounded by a retinue spanning thirty-six yojanas, approached the Mangala Buddha, who is the blessing of the entire world. Having satisfied the Buddha and the Saṅgha of disciples with a great offering (mahādāna), he offered Kāsika cloth to one hundred thousand crores of Arahats. He also offered all the necessary requisites to the Blessed One and performed a worship that caused the entire world to marvel. Then, approaching the Mangala Buddha, the Refuge of the World, he placed his hands—which were radiant with ten fingernails and resembled a pure lotus bud—upon his head in salutation, and sat in a suitable place to listen to the Dhamma. His son, Prince Anurāja, also sat in the same manner.

At that time, the Blessed One delivered a graduated discourse (anupubbikathā) to them, headed by King Sunanda. King Sunanda, along with his retinue, attained Arahatship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Then, the Teacher, observing their past conduct and seeing their strong supporting conditions for possessing miraculous bowls and robes, stretched out his right hand, adorned with the wheel-pattern network, and said, "Come, monks (Etha, bhikkhavo)." At that very moment, they all became endowed with the proper appearance of elders of sixty years' standing, possessing miraculous bowls and robes and with hair two finger-breadths long, and they stood surrounding the Blessed One. This was the third realization of the Truths (abhisamaya). Therefore, it was said:

"In the abode of the King of Devas, the Buddha preached the Dhamma;
There was the second realization for one hundred thousand crores of beings.

When King Sunanda, the Universal Monarch, approached the Fully Enlightened One,
The Fully Enlightened One then beat the most excellent drum of Dhamma.

The multitude of people following King Sunanda then numbered ninety crores;
All of them, without exception, became 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks."

In those verses, "Surindadevabhavane" means in the palace of the King of Devas. "Dhammaṃ" refers to the Abhidhamma. "Āhani" means he beat or struck. "Varuttamaṃ" means the Noble Buddha (beat) the excellent drum of Dhamma. "Anucarā" refers to the followers who constantly serve and follow. "Āsuṃ" means they became. "Tadāsi..."
178:
There is also a variant reading "navutikoṭiyo." If one asks how many followers King Sunanda had, the meaning is ninety crores.

At that time, while the Mangala Buddha, the Refuge of the World, was residing in the city of Mekhala, two youths named Sudeva and Dhammasena, each with a retinue of ten thousand youths, went forth as 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks in the presence of the Blessed One. On the full moon day of Māgha, when the two chief disciples together with their retinues attained Arahatship, the Teacher recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha in the midst of an assembly of one hundred thousand crores of monks; this was the first assembly. Again, at the peerless gathering of relatives at the place called Uttarārāma, he recited the Pātimokkha in an assembly of one hundred thousand crores of monks who had gone forth; this was the second assembly. In the gathering of the group of monks from King Sunanda's retinue, he recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of nine thousand crores of monks; this was the third assembly. Therefore, it was said:

"There were three assemblies for Mangala, the Great Sage;
The first gathering was of one hundred thousand crores.

The second was of one hundred thousand crores, and the third was of ninety crores;
That was the gathering of the stainless ones whose taints were exhausted (khīṇāsava)."

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Brahmin named Suruci in the Brahmin village of Suruci. He was a master of the three Vedas, proficient in the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha treatises, along with phonology (Akkharappabheda) and the Itihāsas as the fifth; a philologist and grammarian, fully versed in Lokāyata and the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa). Having approached the Teacher and heard the sweet Dhamma discourse of the Ten-Powered One, he gained faith in the Blessed One, took refuge, and invited the Blessed One along with the Saṅgha of disciples, saying, "Venerable Sir, please accept my alms-food tomorrow."

The Blessed One asked, "Brahmin, how many monks do you require?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, how many monks are in your retinue?" Since it was only the time of the first assembly, the Buddha replied, "There are one hundred thousand crores of monks." He then invited them, saying, "Venerable Sir, if that is so, please accept my alms-food together with all the monks." The Teacher accepted.

After inviting the Blessed One for the next day, the Brahmin, while returning to his home, thought: "I am able to provide gruel, rice, robes, and so forth to this many monks, but how can there be enough space for them to sit?" It is said that the thought of that Bodhisatta Brahmin heated the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone throne of the thousand-eyed Sakka, the King of Devas, which is situated on the summit of Mount Meru, eighty-four thousand yojanas in height. Then, Sakka, the King of Devas, seeing that his emerald stone throne had become hot, wondered, "Who wishes to displace me from this seat?" and looked upon the world of men with his divine eye...
179:
"Where will the seating place be?" he thought. That thought of the Bodhisatta caused the Pandukambala stone seat of Sakka, the King of Devas with a thousand eyes, situated on the summit of Mount Meru which is eighty-four thousand yojanas in height, to become hot. Then, the King of Devas, seeing the heat of his seat, wondered, "Who wishes to displace me from this position?" Having such a reflection, he looked down at the human world with his divine eye and saw the Great Being. He thought, "This Bodhisatta has invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and is thinking of a place for them to sit. It is proper for me to go there and take a share of the merit." He then disguised himself as a carpenter and, holding an adze and an axe in his hands, appeared before the Great Being. The carpenter asked, "Is there any work to be done for anyone for wages?"

The Great Being, seeing him, asked, "What work are you able to do?" "There is no craft I do not know. Whatever pavilion, palace, or any other dwelling anyone desires, I am capable of making it for them," he replied. "If so, I have work for you," said the Great Being. "What is it, sir?" he asked. "For tomorrow, I have invited one hundred thousand crores of monks. Can you build a seating pavilion for those monks?" "I can indeed build it, if you are able to give me wages," he said. "My dear, I can give them," he replied. "If so, very well, I shall build it," he said and looked at a certain area. That area, twelve yojanas in extent, became as level as a kasina-disk and extremely delightful. Again, the carpenter thought, "Let a pavilion made of the seven jewels, with a visible essence, arise in this place," and he looked. At that very moment, a structure like a pavilion emerged from the earth, splitting the ground. In the golden pillars of that pavilion, there were silver pot-shaped capitals; in the silver pillars, there were golden pot-shaped capitals; in the ruby pillars, there were coral pot-shaped capitals; in the coral pillars, there were ruby pot-shaped capitals; and in the pillars made of the seven jewels, there were pot-shaped capitals made of the seven jewels.

Then he looked, thinking, "Let networks of small bells hang in the intervals of the pavilion." As soon as he looked, the networks of small bells hung down. When stirred by a gentle breeze, they emitted a sweet and extremely delightful sound like that of a five-piece musical ensemble; it was like the time of a divine musical performance. He thought, "Let divine garlands of fragrance, garlands of flowers, garlands of leaves, and garlands of the seven jewels hang in the intervals." As soon as he thought, the garlands hung down. For the one hundred thousand crores of monks, the seats...
180:
...and allowable, highly valuable rugs and bowl-rests, he thought, "Let them arise, breaking through the earth." They arose at that very moment. He thought, "In every corner, let a large water jar arise." At that very instant, large water jars arose, filled with exceedingly cool, sweet, pure, fragrant, and allowable water, with their mouths covered with banana leaves. That thousand-eyed Sakka, having created these many things, went to the Bodhisatta brahmin and said, "Come, sir, look at your pavilion and give me my wage."

The Great Being went and looked at the pavilion. Even as he was looking, his entire body was suffused without interval by the five-fold joy.

Then, as he was looking at the pavilion, this thought occurred to him: "This pavilion was not made by a human being. Surely, because of my intention and my virtues, the abode of Sakka, the king of devas, became hot; therefore, this pavilion must have been created by Sakka, the lord of devas." Again, he thought, "It is not proper for me to give alms for only one day in such a pavilion; I shall give alms for seven days."

What is called external alms (bāhira-dāna), even if it is that much, is not able to satisfy the hearts of Bodhisattas. Only at times such as when they cut off their decorated heads and give them, or pluck out their anointed eyes and give them, or extract the flesh of their hearts and give them, does satisfaction arise for Bodhisattas based on their renunciation. Indeed, for our Bodhisatta in the Sivi Jātaka, although he spent five hundred thousand pieces of money daily and gave alms at the four city gates and in the center of the city—at five places—that almsgiving was not able to produce satisfaction in renunciation. But when Sakka, the king of devas, came in the guise of a brahmin and begged for his eyes, then he plucked out those eyes and gave them. Even while giving, joy and gladness arose, and there was not even a hair's breadth of alteration in his mind. Thus, for the omniscient Bodhisattas, there is no satisfaction based on external alms. Therefore, that Great Being also thought, "It is proper for me to give alms to the one hundred thousand crores of monks," and having them sit in that pavilion, he gave the alms called 'Gavapāna' for seven days.

In this context, 'Gavapāna' refers to food prepared by filling large jars with milk, placing them on hearths, boiling the milk until it is thick, then adding a little rice, and seasoning it with honey, powdered sugar, and ghee. This is also called 'Catumadhura' food. Human beings alone were not able to serve, so the devas also took turns helping to serve. Although that area of twelve yojanas was not sufficient to contain the monks, those monks resided there by their own psychic power. On the final day of the almsgiving, he had all the monks' bowls washed and filled them with ghee, fresh butter, honey, molasses, and so on for the sake of medicine, and donated them along with sets of three robes. Among that assembly of monks, even the cloth for robes received by the youngest monk was worth one hundred thousand. Then, while the Blessed Mangala Buddha was performing the appreciation (anumodanā), he reflected, "This Great Being has given such a great gift; what kind of result and power will arise?" and he saw that in the future, beyond a hundred thousand aeons...
181:
The deities also served by taking turns (or one by one). Although that place, measuring twelve yojanas, was not sufficient to accommodate those monks, they sat there by their own psychic power. On the final day, he had the bowls of all the monks washed and filled them with ghee, fresh butter, honey, molasses, and so on for medicinal purposes, and offered them along with the three robes. Among that assembly of monks, even the robe-cloth received by the most junior monk (saṅghanavaka) was worth a hundred thousand.

Then, while giving the talk of appreciation (anumodanā), the Teacher reflected: "This noble man has given such a great gift; what will he become in the future?" He saw: "In the future, at the end of two incalculable periods (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa), he will become a Buddha named Gotama." Then, addressing the Great Being (Mahāsatta), he gave the prophecy: "After this much time has passed, you will become a Buddha named Gotama." Upon hearing the Buddha's prophecy, the Great Being was filled with joy and thought: "It is said that I shall become a Buddha. There is no use for me in the household life; I shall go forth." He abandoned such wealth as if it were a glob of spit, went forth in the presence of the Teacher, mastered the Word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana), attained the supernormal powers (abhiññā) and the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti), and with his meditative absorptions (jhāna) undiminished, he remained for the rest of his life and was reborn in the Brahma realm at the end of his lifespan. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:

"At that time, I was a Brahmin named Suruci, a reciter of the mantras, a master of the three Vedas."

"Having approached that Teacher and gone to him for refuge, I honored the Sangha headed by the Buddha with perfumes and garlands. After honoring them with perfumes and garlands, I satisfied them with a milk-drink (milk-rice porridge)."

"That Buddha Mangala, the supreme among bipeds, also gave me the prophecy: 'In an immeasurable aeon from now, this person will become a Buddha.'"

"Having exerted effort in striving... we shall be in the presence of this [Gotama Buddha]." -
These eight verses should be expanded.

"Hearing his words, I gladdened my heart even more. I undertook a superior practice for the fulfillment of the ten perfections (pāramī)."
182:
"Then, increasing my joy for the sake of attaining the noble supreme enlightenment, I gave my house to the Buddha and went forth in his presence."

"Having mastered the Suttanta, the Vinaya, and the nine-fold teaching (navaṅga) of the Teacher, I graced the Dispensation of the Conqueror."

"Dwelling there without negligence, having developed the meditation of the Brahma-vihāras and reached the pinnacle of supernormal powers, I went to the Brahma realm."

In those verses, "gandhamālena" means with perfumes and with garlands. "Gavapānena" is as already mentioned. Some teachers also read it as "ghatapānena". "Tappayiṃ" means I satisfied them. "Uttariṃ vatamadhiṭṭhāsiṃ" means I undertook an even more superior practice. "Dasapāramipūriyā" means for the purpose of fulfilling the ten perfections. "Pītiṃ" means the joy of the heart. "Anubrūhanto" means increasing. "Sambodhivara-pattiyā" means for the sake of attaining Buddhahood. "Buddhe datvāna" means having given to the Buddha. "Maṃ gehaṃ" means having renounced all the wealth in my house for the sake of the four requisites and giving it to the Blessed Buddha. "Tattha" means in that Dispensation of the Buddha. "Brahmā" means having developed the meditation of the Brahma-vihāras.

The city of the Blessed One Mangala was named Uttara. His father was the kshatriya king named Uttara, and his mother was named Uttarā. Sudeva and Dhammasena were the two chief disciples. The attendant was named Pālita. Sīvalā and Asokā were the two chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree was the Nāga tree (Ironwood). His body was eighty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years. His wife was named Yasavatī, and his son was named Sīvala. He renounced the world using a horse-carriage and stayed at the Uttarārāma monastery. The attendant was named Uttara. After the Blessed One had remained for ninety thousand years and entered Parinibbāna, the ten thousand world systems simultaneously became a single mass of darkness. There was great weeping and lamentation among the people in all the world systems. Therefore, it was said:

"The city was named Uttara, the kshatriya [king] was named Uttara, and the mother of the Great Sage Mangala was named Uttarā."

"Sudeva and Dhammasena were the chief disciples; Pālita was the name of the attendant of the Great Sage Mangala."
183:
“Sīvalā and Asokā were the chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Nāga tree (Ironwood).

The Blessed One Mangala, who was a Great Sage (Mahāmuni), was eighty-eight cubits tall. From that Blessed One, hundreds of thousands of rays radiated forth.

At that time, the lifespan was ninety thousand years. Remaining for that long, he saved many beings.

Just as the waves in the ocean cannot be counted, so too the disciples of that Blessed One cannot be counted.

As long as the Fully Enlightened One, Mangala, the Leader of the World, remained, there was no death accompanied by defilements in his dispensation during that time.

Having held aloft the torch of Dhamma and saved the great multitude of beings, having shone like a flame, that highly renowned one attained final peace (nibbāna).

Having shown the nature of impermanence of conditioned things (saṅkhāra) to the world including the devas, having blazed like a great mass of fire, he set like the sun."

In those verses, "tato" means from the body of that Mangala Buddha. "Niddhāvatī" should be understood as "niddhāvanti" (they radiate/flow out), noting the grammatical variation. "Raṃsī" means rays. "Anekasatasahassiyo" means many hundreds of thousands. "Ūmī" means waves or ripples. "Gaṇetuye" means to count or calculate. Just as it is impossible to count the waves in the ocean, so too it is impossible to count the disciples of that Blessed One; indeed, they have transcended the path of counting. "Yāva" means for as long a time. "Sakilesamaraṇaṃ tadā" means there was no death accompanied by defilements. It is said that at that time, in the dispensation of that Blessed One, all disciples attained final peace (parinibbāna) only after reaching Arahantship. The meaning is that they did not pass away while still being worldlings (puthujjana) or those in the lower stages of awakening like Stream-enterers (sotāpanna). Some teachers read "sammohamāraṇaṃ tadā" (death in delusion). "Dhammokkaṃ" means the torch of Dhamma. "Dhūmaketū" refers to fire, but here it should be understood as a lamp; therefore, the meaning is that he blazed like a lamp and then attained final peace. "Mahāyaso" means...
184:
He had a great retinue and great fame. Some teachers recite, "That Blessed One attained Nibbāna together with his disciples." 'Saṅkhārānaṃ' means of the conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma) or of the things that arise with their four causes. 'Sabhāvattaṃ' refers to the common characteristics such as impermanence (anicca). "Sūriyo atthaṅgato yathā" means: just as the sun, the day-maker with a thousand rays, dispels the entire mass of darkness, illuminates the whole world, and then sets; likewise, the Sun-like Mangala Buddha, who caused the lotus-grove of veneyya beings to bloom, dispelled all internal and external darkness of the world, shone with the radiance of his own body, and then attained Parinibbāna. The remaining verses are clear in meaning in all places.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of Mangala Buddha is finished.

## The Third Chronicle of the Buddha is finished.

## 6. The Commentary on the Chronicle of Sumana Buddha

In this way, having turned the ten-thousand world systems into a single mass of darkness at once when that Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, in the period after that Mangala Buddha, among humans whose lifespan was 90,000 years, the lifespan gradually decreased to ten years, then increased again to an incalculable (asankheyya) age, and then decreased again to 90,000 years. At that time, the Bodhisatta named Sumana, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he took rebirth in the womb of Queen Sirimā, in the family of King Sudatta in the city of Mekhala. The miracles were the same as previously described.

When he gradually reached maturity, he lived in three palaces named Sirivaḍḍhana, Somavaḍḍhana, and Iddhivaḍḍhana, attended by 6,300,000 dancing women. Like a celestial youth attended by celestial maidens, he enjoyed sensual pleasures similar to divine bliss for 9,000 years. After Queen Vaṭaṃsikā gave birth to an incomparable son named Anupama, he saw the four omens and renounced the world, departing on an elephant. Thirty crores of people followed him and renounced the world.

Surrounded by them, he practiced asceticism (dukkara-cariyā) for ten months. On the full moon day of Visākha, he accepted milk-rice mixed with divine essence offered by the merchant's daughter named Anupamā, the daughter of Anoma Seṭṭhī in the village of Anoma. Having spent the day in a Sal grove, he took eight handfuls of grass offered by the Ājīvaka Anupama and approached the Nāga-bodhi tree. He circumambulated the Bodhi tree to the right, made a grass seat thirty cubits wide with the eight handfuls of grass, and sat down cross-legged on that seat. Then, having conquered the hosts of Māra, he realized Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and uttered the solemn utterance: "Aneka-jāti-saṃsāraṃ... taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā." Therefore, the Buddha said in the Pali text: "After Mangala... the supreme of all beings." After the time of Mangala Buddha, the Buddha named Sumana, the supreme of gods and men, appeared. That Buddha was incomparable in all dhammas and was superior to all beings.
185:
Having partaken of the thick milk-rice infused with divine essence, and having spent the day-rest in the Sal grove, He took the eight handfuls of grass offered by Anupama the Ājīvaka and approached the Nāga-Bodhi tree. Having circumambulated the Bodhi tree to the right, He prepared a grass mat thirty cubits wide with those eight handfuls of grass and sat there cross-legged.
