"Enduring patience is the highest austerity; the Buddhas say Nibbāna is supreme. One who injures others is not a renunciant (pabbajita); one who harms others is not an ascetic (samaṇa).

Not doing any evil, the undertaking of what is wholesome, the purification of one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Not reviling, not harming, restraint in the Pātimokkha, moderation in eating, dwelling in a secluded place, and devotion to the higher mind (samāpatti)—this is the teaching of the Buddhas."

It should be understood that these verses are the Pātimokkha exhortations of all Buddhas. That was the first assembly. Again, after seeing the Twin Miracle, a second assembly of one hundred thousand monks who had entered the monkhood took place. When the three half-brothers of Vipassī Buddha had pacified the border regions and received the boon of serving the Blessed One, they invited Him to their city and, after hearing the Dhamma while serving Him, they entered the monkhood. Sitting in the midst of those eight million monks, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha at the Khema Deer Park; that was the third assembly. Regarding this, it was said:

"There were three assemblies of the great sage Vipassī, consisting of Arahants who were free from taints, stainless, peaceful in mind, and possessed of the quality of 'Tādi' (equanimity).

The first gathering consisted of six million eight hundred thousand Arahants. The second gathering consisted of one hundred thousand monks.

The third gathering consisted of eighty thousand monks. In the midst of that group of monks, the Perfectly Enlightened One shone brilliantly."

In those verses, 'aṭṭhasaṭṭhisatasahassānaṃ' refers to six million eight hundred thousand monks. 'Tattha' means in that Khema Deer Park. 'Bhikkhugaṇamajjhe' means in the midst of the assembly of monks.

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Naga King named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and majesty. Surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of crores of nagas, with a heart cooled by compassion and incomparable power...
282:
In those verses, 'aṭṭhasaṭṭhisatasahassānaṃ' means six million eight hundred thousand (or one hundred sixty-eight thousand) Arahants. 'Tattha' means in that Khema Deer Park. 'Bhikkhugaṇamajjhe' means in the midst of the assembly of monks. There is also a variant reading 'tassa bhikkhugaṇamajjhe', which also means in the midst of that assembly of monks.

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a Naga King named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and majesty. Surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of crores of nagas, he desired to pay homage to the Blessed One who possessed the Ten Powers, incomparable strength and virtue, and a heart cooled by compassion. He had a pavilion (maṇḍapa) constructed, adorned with the seven gems, resembling the lunar disc, and possessing a delightful essence. Having invited the Buddha to stay there, he offered a great gift suitable for divine wealth for seven days. He then offered the Blessed One a golden throne (pīṭha) of great value, encrusted with the seven gems and brilliant with the radiance of various jewels. At the conclusion of the appreciation (anumodanā) for the gift of the throne, the Buddha prophesied: 'This Naga King, in the ninety-first aeon from now, will become a Buddha.' Therefore, in the Buddhavamsa, the Blessed One said:

"At that time, I was a Naga King of great psychic power, named Atula, meritorious and possessing radiance.

Surrounded then by many crores of nagas, and making offerings with divine musical instruments, I approached the Buddha, the Foremost of the World.

Having approached the Perfectly Enlightened One, Vipassī, the Leader of the World, and having invited the King of Dhamma, I offered a golden throne encrusted with jewels and pearls and adorned with all kinds of ornaments.

That Buddha also, sitting in the midst of the Sangha, prophesied of me: 'In the ninety-first aeon from this one, he will become a Buddha.'

Leaving the delightful city named Kapila, the Tathāgata, having exerted the Great Effort and performed the difficult austerities (dukkarakārikā), [will become a Buddha].

Sitting at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree, the Tathāgata, having accepted milk-rice (pāyāsa) there, will approach the Nerañjarā River.

Having consumed the milk-rice on the banks of the Nerañjarā River, that Conqueror (Jina) will approach the foot of the Bodhi tree by the excellent path prepared by the devas."
283:
Then, having circumambulated the Bodhimaṇḍa, the peerless one of great fame will realize the Supreme Enlightenment at the foot of the Assattha tree.

The biological mother of this Blessed One will be the queen named Māyā, and the father will be the king named Suddhodana. This [Blessed One] will be Gotama.

Kolita and Upatissa, who are free from taints, free from lust, of peaceful mind and concentrated, will be the chief disciples. The monk named Ānanda will be the attendant and will serve this Victorious One (Jina).

Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā, who are free from taints, free from lust, of peaceful mind and concentrated, will be the chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Assattha... etc...

Having heard the words of that Blessed One, I felt even greater devotion in my heart. I undertook the superior practice to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).

In those verses, 'puññavanto' means one who has merit, one who has a well-accumulated store of merit. 'Jutiandharo' means one endowed with radiance. 'Nekānaṃ nāgakoṭīnaṃ' means by many crores of Nagas; here the genitive case should be understood in the sense of the instrumental. 'Parivāretvāna' means surrounding the Blessed One. 'Ahaṃ' refers to oneself. 'Vajjanto' means playing, beating, or striking [musical instruments]. 'Maṇimuttaratanakhacitaṃ' means adorned with various jewels such as rubies and pearls. 'Sabbābharaṇabhūsitaṃ' means decorated with all kinds of ornaments made of jewels, such as animal figures. 'Suvaṇṇapīṭhaṃ' means a golden bench or chair. 'Adāsahaṃ' means I gave.

The city of that Blessed One Vipassī was named Bandhumatī. The father was the king named Bandhumā, and the mother was named Bandhumatī. The two chief disciples were Khaṇḍa Thera and Tissa Thera. The attendant was named Asoka. The two chief female disciples were Candā Therī and Candamittā Therī. The Bodhi tree was the Pāṭali tree. His body was eighty cubits in height. The radiance of his body always spread and remained for seven leagues. His lifespan was eighty thousand years. The chief queen was named Sutanu. His son was named Samavaṭṭakkhandha. He renounced the world in a noble chariot. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the Pali:

The city of the Blessed One named Vipassī was Bandhumatī. The king who was the father was named Bandhumā. The mother was the queen named Bandhumatī.

That Bodhisatta reigned over the kingdom for eight thousand years. That Bodhisatta had three noble palaces: Nanda, Sunanda, and Sirimā.

There were forty-three thousand well-adorned court ladies. The queen was named Sudassanā. The son was named Samavaṭṭakkhandha.

Having seen the four omens, he renounced the world by chariot. The Victorious Blessed One practiced the meditation for eight full months.
284:
The city was named Bandhumatī; the king was a Khattiya named Bandhumā. The mother of the Blessed One Vipassī was named Bandhumatī.

Khaṇḍa Thera and the one named Tissa were the chief disciples (aggasāvaka) of the Blessed One Vipassī. The Thera named Asoka was the attendant of the Blessed One Vipassī.

Candā Therī and Candamittā Therī were the chief female disciples (aggasāvikā). The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Pāṭali tree.

Vipassī, the Leader of the World, was eighty cubits high. The radiance of that Buddha spread and shimmered for seven leagues all around.

At that time, the lifespan of the Buddha was eighty thousand years. Remaining for that long a period, he saved a great multitude of beings.

He liberated many devas and humans from bonds (such as sensual lust). He also taught the remaining worldlings (puthujjana) what is the path and what is not the path.

Having shown the light and preached the Deathless state (Nibbāna), that Blessed One, together with his disciples, attained Parinibbāna like a great mass of fire being extinguished.

The noble psychic power, the noble merit, and all the blossomed marks have disappeared. Are not all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) indeed empty?

In those verses, 'bandhanā' means liberating devas and humans from bonds such as the fetter of sensual lust; it means causing them to blossom. 'Maggāmaggañca ācikkhi' means he preached to the remaining worldlings: 'This Middle Way, free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism, is the only true path for the attainment of the Deathless; this practice such as self-mortification is not the path.' 'Ālokaṃ dassayitvāna' means showing the light of Path-knowledge and the light of Insight-knowledge. 'Lakkhaṇañca kusumitaṃ' refers to the body of the Blessed One, which was blossomed and adorned with the marks of a great man. The meaning of the remaining verses is clear.

## The Commentary on the Chronicle of Buddha Vipassī is finished.
## The nineteenth Chronicle of Buddhas is finished.
285:
## 22. Sikhībuddhavaṃsavaṇṇanā

In the period after the Buddha Vipassī, when that aeon had disappeared, for fifty-nine aeons thereafter, no Buddhas appeared in the world. The world remained devoid of the light of Buddhas. The sole sovereignty of the Māra of defilements (Kilesa-māra) and the Māra of the celestial son (Devaputta-māra) prevailed, free from any obstacles.

Thirty-one aeons prior to this Bhadda Kappa, two Fully Enlightened Ones, the Buddha Sikhī and the Buddha Vessabhū, appeared in the world. Like a smokeless flame (sikhī) fueled by smooth, dry heartwood and poured with abundant ghee, the Buddha Sikhī appeared. Among those two Buddhas, the Buddha Sikhī, having fulfilled the Perfections (pāramīs), was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of Queen Pabhāvatī, the chief consort of King Aruṇavā (also known as Aruṇa), who was endowed with supreme virtues, in the city of Aruṇavatī, also called Kusalakaraṇavatī. The Queen possessed a delightful radiance like a statue made of red gold. After ten months had passed, he was born from his mother's womb in the Nisabha Grove. When the fortune-telling brahmins were bestowing a name upon the prince, they named him "Sikhī" because his cranial protuberance (uṇhīsa) rose up like a flame (sikhā).

That Bodhisatta Sikhī lived in the household life for seven thousand years. There were three palaces named Sucandaka, Sirigiriyasa, and Narivasabha. Twenty-four thousand female attendants, headed by Queen Sabbakāmā, waited upon him.

After seeing the four omens, and when a son named Atula, who was a peerless collection of virtues, was born to Queen Sabbakāmā, the Bodhisatta Sikhī departed for the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana) on an elephant, mounted upon the noble elephant's shoulder, and became an ascetic. Seven million men followed him into the ascetic life. Surrounded by those monks, he practiced the ascetic struggle (dukkaracariyā) for eight months. On the full moon day of Visākha, leaving his followers, he partook of the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of the merchant Piyadassī in the village of Sudassana. After spending the day's rest in a young Khadira grove, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by the ascetic named Anomadassī and approached the Puṇḍarīka (White Mango) Bodhi tree. The size of that Puṇḍarīka Bodhi tree was equal to that of a Pāṭali tree. On that very day, the trunk of that White Mango tree rose up to fifty cubits, and its branches also extended to fifty cubits. It was covered with divine scents and divine flowers. Not only was it covered with flowers, but it was also covered with fruits. On one side of the White Mango tree, tender fruits hung; on another side, medium-sized fruits; on another, fruits that were not overripe; and on another, fruits that were delicious as if infused with divine essence, endowed with perfect color, fragrance, and taste, hanging from various parts. Just as it was with that White Mango tree, so too in the ten thousand world systems, the flowering trees were adorned with flowers and the fruit-bearing trees were adorned with fruits.

The Bodhisatta Sikhī spread a carpet of grass twenty-four cubits wide at the foot of that White Mango Bodhi tree, sat in a cross-legged posture, and resolved with fourfold effort. While sitting thus, he conquered the army of Māra together with Māra himself, which extended thirty-six leagues, and attained Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). He then uttered the solemn utterance (udāna): "Through many a birth in saṃsāra... [etc.] ...I have attained the destruction of craving."
286:
Just as it was at the foot of that White Mango Bodhi tree of the Bodhisatta Sikhī, so too in the ten thousand world systems, the flowering trees were adorned with flowers and the fruit-bearing trees were adorned with fruits. That Bodhisatta Sikhī spread a carpet of grass twenty-four cubits wide at the foot of that White Mango Bodhi tree, sat in a cross-legged posture, and resolved with fourfold effort. While sitting thus, he blew away and destroyed the army of Māra together with Māra himself, which extended thirty-six leagues, and attained Supreme Enlightenment. Having uttered the solemn utterance: "Through many a birth in saṃsāra... [etc.] ...I have attained the destruction of craving," he spent seven weeks (forty-nine days) in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree. Accepting the request of the Great Brahma to teach the Dhamma, and seeing the spiritual potential (upanissaya-sampatti) of the seventy thousand monks who had gone forth with him, he traveled through the air and descended at the Migācī Grove near the royal capital of Aruṇavatī, also known as Vividhāvaraṇavatī. Surrounded by that assembly of sages, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion (Dhammacakkappavattana) in their midst. At that time, the first realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisamaya) occurred for one hundred billion beings. Therefore, it was said in the Buddhavaṃsa:

"After the time of Vipassī, the Fully Enlightened One, the Supreme among bipeds,
The Conqueror named Sikhī arose, peerless and without equal.

Having crushed the army of Māra, he attained the supreme Enlightenment,
And set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion out of compassion for living beings.

While the Conqueror, the Bull among Men, Sikhī, was setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion,
The first realization occurred for one hundred billion beings."

Again, near the royal capital of Aruṇavatī itself, he taught the Dhamma to the two princes, Prince Abhibhū and Prince Sambhava, along with their retinues, and let ninety billion beings drink the nectar of Dhamma. That realization was the second abhisamaya. Therefore, it was said:

"Furthermore, while the Supreme among Men, the Best of the Group, was teaching the Dhamma,
The second realization occurred for ninety billion beings."

At the time when the Blessed One was performing the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) at the foot of a Campaka tree at the gate of Suriyavatī city, for the purpose of crushing the pride and arrogance of the heretics and for the purpose of liberating all people from their bonds, he taught the Dhamma. At that time, the third realization occurred for eighty billion beings. Therefore, it was said:

"When the Buddha performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire in the world including the devas,
The third realization occurred for eighty billion beings."

While residing in the midst of one hundred thousand Arahants who had gone forth together with Prince Abhibhū and Prince Sambhava, he recited the Pātimokkha. That event was the first assembly (sannipāta). While residing in the midst of eighty thousand monks who had gone forth during the assembly of his relatives in the city of Aruṇavatī, he recited the Pātimokkha. That event was the second assembly. At the time of disciplining the Naga king Dhanapāla in the city of Dhanañjaya, those who had gone forth...
287:
When the Blessed One preached the Dhamma, there occurred the third realization (abhisamaya) of eighty billion human and celestial beings. Therefore, it is said in the Pali:

''When He displayed the Twin Miracle to the world including the devas, there occurred the third realization of eighty billion beings.''

Sitting in the midst of one hundred thousand Arahants who had gone forth together with the princes Abhibhū and Sambhava, He recited the Pātimokkha; that was the first assembly. Sitting in the midst of eighty thousand monks who had gone forth at the gathering of relatives in the city of Aruṇavatī, He recited the Pātimokkha; that was the second assembly. In the city of Dhanañjaya, at the time of taming the elephant king Dhanapāla, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha in the midst of seventy thousand monks who had gone forth; that was the third assembly. Therefore, it is said:

''There were three assemblies of the great sage Sikhī, consisting of Arahants who were stainless, of peaceful mind, and possessed of the quality of steadfastness (tādi).

The first gathering was of one hundred thousand monks; the second gathering was of eighty thousand monks.

The third gathering was of seventy thousand monks; like a lotus grown in water that is unsullied by water (so too was that assembly unsullied by worldly conditions).''

In those verses, 'unsullied like a lotus' (anupalitto padumaṃva) means that just as a lotus born in water and grown in water is not smeared by water, so too that assembly of monks, though born in the world, was not smeared (not shaken) by the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma) such as gain and loss.

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a king named Arindama in the city of Paribhutta, not associating with anyone else. When the Teacher Sikhī arrived at the city of Paribhutta, the King, together with his retinue, went out to welcome the Blessed One. With his heart, eyes, and ears filled with increasing devotion, he paid homage with his head at the stainless lotus-like feet of the Possessor of Ten Powers. Having invited the Possessor of Ten Powers, he gave a great alms-giving for seven days in accordance with his sovereignty, lineage, wealth, and faith. He ordered the doors of the cloth storehouses to be opened and offered expensive garments to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. He offered a noble elephant, endowed with strength, beauty, auspicious marks, and swift speed, adorned with golden nets and garlands, beautiful with a pair of yak-tail fly-whisks with handles made of new gold, having broad and soft ears, and a face as radiant as the moon's rays...
288:
...He offered expensive garments to the Saṅgha of monks. He offered a noble elephant, a subduer of enemies like the elephant Erāvaṇa, endowed with strength, beauty, auspicious marks, and swift speed, adorned with golden nets and garlands, beautiful with a pair of yak-tail fly-whisks with handles and cases made of new gold, having broad and soft ears, and a face as radiant as the moon's rays. He also gave allowable articles (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) equal to the value of that noble elephant. That Teacher also prophesied: "In the thirty-first kappa from now, he will become a Buddha." Concerning this, it was said:

"At that time, I was a khattiya named Arindama, and I satisfied the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with food and drink.

Having given many excellent garments and many crores of cloths, I gave a decorated elephant-vehicle to the Buddha.

Having matched the value of the elephant-vehicle, I offered allowable articles. I filled my mind, which was always firmly established, with the joy of giving.

That Buddha Sikhī, the Chief Leader of the World, also prophesied to me: 'In the thirty-first kappa from now, this person will become a Buddha.'

Departing from the delightful city named Kapilavatthu... may we be among those who realize (Nibbāna) in the presence of this Buddha."

Hearing the words of that Buddha, I gladdened my heart even more. I undertook a superior practice to fulfill the ten perfections."

In that verse, 'nimminitvā' means by comparing with the value of that noble elephant. 'Kappiyaṃ' refers to allowable articles (kappiya-bhaṇḍa); the articles that are allowable for monks to receive are called kappiya-bhaṇḍa. 'Pūrayiṃ mānasaṃ mayhaṃ' means I filled my mind with the joy of giving; it means I was able to generate joy within myself. 'Niccaṃ daḷhamupaṭṭhitaṃ' means a mind firmly established through the power of giving, with the thought "I shall always give alms."

The royal city of that Blessed One was named Aruṇavatī. King Aruṇa was His father, and Pabhāvatī was His mother. Abhibhū and Sambhava were the two chief disciples (aggasāvaka). The attendant was named Khemaṅkara. Sakhilā and Padumā were the two chief female disciples (aggasāvikā). The Bodhi tree was the Puṇḍarīka (White Mango) tree. The height of His body was seventy cubits.
289:
(His height was seventy cubits.) The aura of the Buddha Sikhī constantly spread and remained for three yojanas. His lifespan was seventy thousand years. His chief queen was named Sabbakāmā, and his son was named Atula. He renounced the world using an elephant vehicle. Therefore, it was said:

"The city was named Aruṇavatī, and the king was named Aruṇa. The mother of the Great Sage Sikhī was named Pabhāvatī.

Abhibhū and Sambhava were the chief disciples, and Khemaṅkara was the attendant of the Great Sage Sikhī.

Sakhilā and Padumā were the chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Puṇḍarīka.

Sirivaḍḍha and Nanda were the chief male lay attendants, and Cittā and Suguttā were the chief female lay attendants.

In height, that Buddha rose seventy cubits; he resembled a golden sacrificial post and was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

From the body of that Blessed One, rays of a fathom's length continuously issued day and night; the light spread in all directions for three yojanas.

The lifespan of that Great Sage was seventy thousand years; remaining for that long, he saved many people.

Having showered the rain of Dhamma, having moistened the world including the devas, and having led them to the state of safety, he attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.

That entire body, endowed with the secondary characteristics and the thirty-two excellent marks, has disappeared. Are not all formations indeed empty?"

In those verses, 'Puṇḍarīka' refers to the white mango tree. 'Aura for three yojanas' means that the rays of light issued forth for three yojanas. 'Rain of Dhamma' refers to the Buddha-cloud that rains down the Dhamma. 'Having moistened' means having sprinkled and poured with the water of Dhamma discourse. 'Including the devas' means the beings including the devas. 'State of safety' means the state of safety...
290:
...which is Nibbāna. "Endowed with the secondary characteristics" means the body of the Blessed One was adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics, such as copper-colored nails, a prominent nose, and rounded fingers, as well as the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. It is said that the Buddha Sikhī attained Parinibbāna at the Assārāma monastery in the city of Sīlavatī.

"Like a fire (sikhī) he shone in the world through his practice;
Like a peacock (sikhī) he cried out at the coming of the clouds;
That Great Sage Sikhī, having abandoned the fuel of defilements,
That Sugata has gone to peace like a fire that has gone out."

It is said that the relics of the Blessed One Sikhī remained as a single mass and were not dispersed. The people of the entire Jambudīpa built a stupa three yojanas high, made of the seven jewels, and as beautiful as the Himālaya mountains. The rest of the words in these verses are clear.

## The Chronicle of the Buddha Sikhī is finished.
## The twentieth Chronicle of the Buddha is finished.
## 23. The Chronicle of the Buddha Vessabhū

After the passing of the Buddha Sikhī and the disappearance of his dispensation, the lifespan of humans, which was seventy thousand years, gradually decreased to ten years. After increasing again to an incalculable age, it gradually decreased to sixty thousand years. At that time, the Teacher named Vessabhū, who had conquered the five Maras, who surpassed the whole world, and who possessed self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū), appeared in the world. Having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) and being reborn in the Tusita heaven, he passed away from there and took conception in the womb of Queen Yasavatī, the virtuous chief queen of King Suppatīta in the city of Anoma. After ten months, he was born from his mother's womb in the Anupama Grove. At the moment of his birth, he delighted the people and uttered a roar like that of a bull. Because of that bull-like roar, on the day of his naming, they gave him the name "Vessabhū." Prince Vessabhū lived in the household life for six thousand years. There were three palaces named Ruci, Suruci, and Rativaḍḍhana.
291:
Thirty thousand court ladies, headed by Queen Sucittā, attended to that prince.

Having seen the four omens, and when the prince named Suppabuddha was born to Queen Sucittā, the prince departed on a golden palanquin to view the park. He took the dyed robes offered by a Brahma and entered the monkhood. Thirty-seven thousand people followed the Bodhisatta and ordained. Then, surrounded by those monks, the Bodhisatta practiced asceticism (dukkharacariyā) for six months. On the full moon day of Visākha, in the market town of Sucitta, he partook of the delicious milk-rice (madhupāyāsa) offered by the Naga maiden named Sirivaḍḍhanā, who had manifested her physical form. After spending the day-rest in a Sal grove, in the evening, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by the Naga King Narinda and approached the Sal Bodhi tree, circling it clockwise. The dimensions of that Sal tree were the same as those of the Pāṭali tree. Likewise, its splendor of flowers, fruits, and other riches should be understood similarly.

Approaching the foot of the Sal tree, the Bodhisatta spread a carpet of grass forty cubits wide and sat cross-legged. Attaining the Unobstructed Knowledge (Anāvaraṇañāṇa), which is free from hindrances and blocks all intoxication of sensual pleasures, he uttered the solemn exclamation: 'Through many a birth in saṃsāra... I have reached the end of cravings.' He spent seven weeks in that very place. Seeing the sufficiency of the supporting conditions (upanissaya-sampatti) for the attainment of the Paths and Fruits in his younger brothers, Prince Soṇa and Prince Uttara, he traveled through the air and descended at Aruṇa Park near the city of Anoma. He had the park keeper summon the princes, and in the midst of those princes and their retinue, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. At that time, the first realization of the Four Noble Truths occurred for eighty thousand koṭis (eight hundred billion) devas and brahmas.

Again, while the Blessed One was wandering through the countryside and preaching the Dhamma in various places, the realization of the Dhamma occurred for seventy thousand koṭis (seven hundred billion) beings; this was the second awakening. In the city of Anoma itself, while destroying the net of false views, humbling the banner of pride of the heretics, crushing their conceit, and hoisting the banner of Dhamma, he performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) for a human assembly ninety leagues wide and an immeasurable assembly of devas. Having inspired faith in devas and humans, he satisfied sixty koṭis (six hundred million) beings with the deathless nectar of Dhamma; this was the third awakening. Therefore, it was said:

'In that same Maṇḍa-kappa, the peerless one, the incomparable person,
The leader of the world named Vessabhū, appeared in the world.'
292:
'The fire of passion was indeed burning; then the realm of cravings was conquered. Like a great elephant breaking its bonds, he reached the supreme Enlightenment.

While Vessabhū, the Leader of the World, was setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, the first awakening occurred for eighty thousand koṭis beings.

While the Best of the World, the Bull among Men, was wandering through the kingdoms, the second awakening occurred for seventy thousand koṭis beings.

Dispelling great false views, he performed a miracle. Devas and humans from the ten-thousandfold world system, along with the world of devas, assembled.

Seeing the great wonder, marvelous and hair-raising, sixty koṭis of devas and humans realized the Four Noble Truths.'

In those verses, 'ādittaṃ' means this entire triple world is intensely burning. 'Rāgagginā' means (burning) with passion. 'Taṇhānaṃ vijitaṃ' means having known thus: the realm of cravings, the place that follows the will of cravings. 'Nāgo va bandhanaṃ chetvā' means having broken the bonds like a great elephant breaking a bond of rotten creepers, he reached (adhigato) Enlightenment. 'Dasasahassī' means in the ten-thousandfold world system. 'Sadevake' means in the world together with devas. 'Bujjhare' means they realized (bujjhisu).

Furthermore, on another occasion, at the assembly of the two chief disciples named Soṇa and Uttara, he recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha in the midst of eighty thousand arahants who had ordained; this was the first assembly. At the time when thirty-seven thousand monks, who had ordained together with Vessabhū, the Conqueror of all worlds, had remained behind from the group, they heard of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma by Vessabhū the Perfectly Enlightened One and came to the city of Soreyya to see the Blessed One. The Blessed One preached the Dhamma to them, ordained them all with the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination, and recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha in the assembly endowed with the four factors; this was the second assembly.

At the time when a prince named Upasanta was reigning in the city of Nārivāhana, the Blessed One went there out of compassion for him. When the prince heard of the Blessed One's arrival, he went out with his retinue to welcome him, invited him, and gave a great gift. After hearing the Dhamma, his heart was filled with faith, and he ordained. Following his example, sixty thousand men...'
293:
Men followed and went forth as monks. Together with that Venerable One, they attained Arahantship. Surrounded by those monks, the Blessed One Vessabhū recited the Ovadā Pātimokkha; that was the third assembly. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:

“There were three assemblies of the Great Sage Vessabhū, of those who had destroyed the taints, the stainless ones, those with peaceful minds, the poised ones.

The first gathering was of eighty thousand monks; the second gathering was of seventy thousand monks.

The third gathering was of sixty thousand monks, who had transcended the fear of old age and so forth, the spiritual sons of the Great Sage.”

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a king named Sudassana, of exceeding beauty, in the city of Sarabhavatī. When the Leader of the World, the Blessed One Vessabhū, arrived at the city of Sarabha, the king heard his Dhamma and, with a heart full of faith, placed his hands—shining with the meeting of ten fingernails and resembling a pure lotus bud born in water—upon his head. He gave a Great Gift (Mahādāna) of robes and other requisites to the Sangha headed by the Buddha. Right there, he built a Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) for the Blessed One to reside in, and surrounding it, he caused a thousand monasteries to be built. Having renounced all his wealth in the Dispensation of the Blessed One, he went forth in his presence. Endowed with the virtue of conduct, delighting in the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutanga), and devoted to seeking the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra), he lived delighting in the Buddha's Dispensation. That Blessed One also made a prediction regarding him: “In the future, thirty-one aeons from now, this person will become a Buddha named Gotama.” Regarding this, the Blessed One said:

“At that time, I was a kshatriya named Sudassana. Having invited the Great Hero and given a costly gift, I honored the Victor together with the Sangha with food, drink, and robes.

Having heard the noble Dhamma-cakka (Wheel of Dhamma) turned by that peerless Buddha, I took great delight in the going forth.

Having bestowed a great gift, untiring day and night, I went forth in the presence of the Victor into the virtuous state of a monk.

Endowed with the virtue of conduct, composed in duties and morality, seeking omniscience, I delight in the Victor's Dispensation.”
294:
“Approaching with faith and joy, I pay homage to the Buddha, the Teacher. Joy arises within me because of the very cause of Enlightenment.

Knowing my unwavering mind, the Fully Enlightened One said this: ‘Thirty-one aeons from now, this person will become a Buddha.’

Leaving the delightful city named Kapilavhaya... they made the aspiration: ‘May we be in the presence of this [Gotama Buddha].’

I heard the words of that Blessed One and gladdened my heart even more. I undertook a superior practice for the fulfillment of the ten perfections.”

In those verses, “Cakkaṃ vattitaṃ” means the Wheel of Dhamma was turned (taught). “Paṇီtaṃ dhammaṃ” means the Dhamma of the path, fruit, and jhāna which is superior to the ten courses of wholesome action of humans, or the Dhamma of the noble ones who have attained jhāna. “Pabbajjaṃ guṇasampannaṃ” means knowing that the state of a monk is endowed with virtue, I went forth. “Vattasီlasamāhito” means being composed in duties and in morality; it means being composed in the fulfillment of various duties and moralities. “Ramāmi” means I greatly delighted. “Saddhāpီtiṃ” means having approached with faith and joy. “Vandāmi” means I paid homage with great respect; it should be noted that the present tense is used in the sense of the past. “Sattharaṃ” means the Buddha who is the Teacher. “Anivattamanasaṃ” means a mind that does not retreat.

The city of that Blessed One Vessabhū was named Anoma. His father was a kshatriya named Suppatီta, and his mother was named Yasavatီ. Soṇa and Uttara were the two chief disciples. The attendant was named Upasanta. Rāmā and Samālā were the two chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree was a Sāla tree. His body was sixty cubits in height. His lifespan was sixty thousand years. His wife was named Sucittā, and his son was named Suppabuddha. He departed for the great renunciation by a golden palanquin. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“The city was named Anoma; the kshatriya father was named Suppatီta; the mother of the Great Sage Vessabhū was named Yasavatီ.

Soṇa and Uttara were the chief disciples of the Great Sage Vessabhū; the attendant was named Upasanta.

Rāmā and Samālā were the chief female disciples; the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Mahāsāla (Great Sāla tree).”
295:
The lay followers Sotthika and Ramma were the chief male attendants; the lay followers Gotamī and Sirimā were also the chief female attendants.

That Blessed One was sixty cubits in height and resembled a golden pillar. At night, rays radiated from his body like a fire burning on a mountain peak.

The lifespan of that Great Sage (Mahesi) was sixty thousand years. Remaining for that long, he rescued a great multitude of beings from the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra).

Having spread the Dhamma far and wide, and having categorized the great multitude [according to their attainments], he left behind the boat of Dhamma and attained Parinibbāna together with his disciples.

All those people worthy of being seen (the Buddha and his disciples) have vanished, and the monastery which was the place for his postures has also vanished. Are not all conditioned things indeed empty?

In those verses, 'hemayūpasamūpamo' means resembling a golden pillar. 'Nissarati' means streaming or radiating here and there. 'Rasmi' means the light of the rays. 'Rattiṃva pabbate sikhī' means the radiance of rays shining from his body like a fire on a mountain top at night. 'Vibhajitvā' means having made a division, either by the type of person such as the ugghaṭitaññū (one of quick intuition) or by the stages such as the sotāpanna (stream-enterer). 'Dhammanāvaṃ' means having established the boat of Dhamma, known as the Eightfold Path, for the purpose of crossing the four floods (ogha). 'Dassaneyyaṃ' means worthy of being seen. 'Sabbajanaṃ' means all people, referring to the Perfectly Enlightened One together with the Community of Disciples. 'Vihāraṃ' means the monastery. In all these instances, the accusative case (upayogavacana) should be understood in the sense of the nominative case (paccatta).

The Blessed One Vessabhū, it is said, attained Parinibbāna in the Khema Deer Park in the city of Usabhavatī. His relics were scattered in various places.

'In the supreme city of Usabhavatī, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Bull of Conquerors (jinavasabha), attained the Nibbāna element without remainder in the delightful Upavana monastery.'

The meaning of the remaining verses is clear in every respect.

## The Explanation of the Chronicle of the Buddha Vessabhū is Finished.
## The Twenty-first Chronicle of the Buddha is Finished.
296:
## 24. The Explanation of the Chronicle of the Buddha Kakusandha
After the Blessed One Vessabhū attained Parinibbāna and that Maṇḍa-kappa had passed, for twenty-nine kappas, no Buddhas, who are like suns, appeared. In this Bhadda-kappa, however, four Buddhas have appeared. Which four? Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Buddha. The Blessed One Metteyya will appear in the future. Thus, this kappa is praised by the Blessed One as a 'Bhadda-kappa' (Auspicious Aeon) because it is adorned by the appearance of five Buddhas. Among those five, the Blessed One Kakusandha, having fulfilled the perfections, was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of the brahmin woman named Visākhā, the chief consort of the royal chaplain named Aggidatta, who was the advisor on temporal and spiritual matters to King Khemaṅkara in the city of Khemavatī. At a time when kings respect, revere, honor, and worship brahmins, Bodhisattas are born into brahmin families. At a time when brahmins respect, revere, honor, and worship kings, they are born into khattiya (warrior-noble) families. At that time, it is said, brahmins were respected and revered by kings. Therefore, the Bodhisatta Kakusandha, who was true to his word, was born into a pure and undisturbed brahmin family, abundant with wealth and glory, causing the ten thousand world systems to echo and tremble. Miraculous signs as described previously occurred. Then, after ten months, he emerged from his mother's womb in the Khemavatī park like a flame of fire from a golden creeper.

That Bodhisatta lived the household life for four thousand years. He had three palaces named Kāma, Kāmavaṇṇa, and Kāmasuddhi. There were thirty thousand female attendants led by the brahmin woman Rocinī. Having seen the four signs, and when a son named Uttara was born to the brahmin woman Rocinī, he departed on the Great Renunciation by a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses and became an ascetic. Forty thousand people followed him and became ascetics. Surrounded by those monks, he practiced austerities for eight months. On the full moon day of Visākha, having eaten the honey-rice porridge given by the daughter of the brahmin Vajirindha in the village of Sucirindha, and having spent the day in a Khadira grove, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a barley-field guard named Subhadda in the evening and approached the Sirīsa Bodhi tree. At the foot of that Bodhi tree, which was filled with divine fragrances, he spread the grass covering an area of thirty-four cubits, sat cross-legged, and attained Omniscience. He then uttered the solemn utterance beginning with 'Aneka-jāti-saṃsāraṃ'. After seven weeks had passed, seeing that the forty thousand monks who had renounced with him were capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths, he entered the Isipatana Deer Park near the city of Makila in a single day and taught the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta in the midst of those monks. At that time, the first realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) occurred for forty thousand crores of humans, devas, and brahmās.
297:
Approaching the Sirīsa Bodhi tree (Acacia tree) of the aforementioned size, while divine scents were wafting, he spread a mat of grass thirty-four cubits wide, sat in the cross-legged posture, and attained Supreme Enlightenment. Having uttered the solemn utterance (udāna), "Through many a birth in saṃsāra... [etc.] ...I have attained the destruction of cravings," he spent the seven weeks (forty-nine days). Seeing that the forty thousand monks who had gone forth with him were capable of penetrating the Four Noble Truths, he entered the deer park named Isipatana near the city of Makila in a single day, and in the midst of those monks, the Blessed One set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. At that time, the first realization of the Truth (Dhammābhisamaya) occurred for forty thousand crores of humans, devas, and brahmās.

Again, at the foot of a great Sal tree at the gate of the city of Kaṇṇakujja, he performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) and caused the Eye of Dhamma (Dhammacakkhu) to arise in thirty thousand crores of humans, devas, and brahmās. That was the second realization of the Truth. At another time, in a certain shrine near the city of Khemavatī, a yakkha named Naradeva, who was esteemed by kings, appeared with a visible human body in the middle of a wilderness. Standing near a lake of cool, extremely sweet, and refreshing water, fragrant to all people and adorned with red, blue, and white lotuses, he would entice beings with the lotuses and devour humans. When that road fell into ruin and became deserted, he entered the great forest and devoured the beings who arrived there. That place became famous in the world as the great wilderness road.

It is said that a great multitude of people gathered at both entrances of the wilderness and stood waiting to cross it. At that time, the Teacher Kakusandha, who had freed himself from the bonds of existence, arose from the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) at dawn and, surveying the world, saw the powerful yakkha Naradeva and that multitude of people who had come within the net of his knowledge. Having seen them, the Blessed One traveled through the air and, while that multitude of people was watching, performed various miracles, descended to the abode of the yakkha Naradeva, and sat upon his auspicious throne.

Then, that man-eating yakkha, seeing the Sun-like Sage who came through the path of the sky like the sun surrounded by a rainbow, emitting the six-colored rays, felt a clear and confident heart, thinking, "The One of Ten Powers (Dasabala) has come here out of compassion for me." Together with his retinue of yakkhas, he went to the Himavanta mountains, which abound with many herds of deer, and gathered various colored and scented flowers from both water and land that were extremely delightful and fragrant. Having brought them, he worshipped the Lord of the World, Kakusandha, the Flawless One, who was seated on his throne, with flowers, scents, and fragrant ointments. While performing praises and unison chanting, he stood with his hands raised in salutation (añjali) upon his head. Then, the people, seeing that miracle...
298:
Worshipping the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Lord of the World, who was seated on his throne and was free from all flaws, with flowers, scents, and ointments, and while performing songs of praise, he stood with his hands raised in salutation upon his head. Then, the people, seeing that miracle, with clear and confident hearts, came together and stood surrounding the Blessed One in worship.

Then, the Blessed One Kakusandha, for whom there is no more rebirth, encouraged the highly-honoured yakkha Naradeva by showing the connection between kamma and its results, terrified him with talk of hell, and then taught the discourse on the Four Noble Truths. At that time, the realization of the Truth occurred for an immeasurable number of beings. This was the third realization of the Truth. Regarding this, it was said:

"After Vessabhū, the Buddha, the best of bipeds,
Kakusandha by name, incomparable and difficult to approach.

Having uprooted all existence, he reached the end of the practice of perfections;
Like a lion breaking a cage, he reached the supreme Enlightenment.

While the Lord of the World, Kakusandha, was setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion,
The realization of the Truth occurred for forty thousand crores.

Performing the Twin Miracle in the open sky,
He enlightened thirty thousand crores of devas and humans.

In the proclamation of the Four Noble Truths to the yakkha Naradeva,
His realization of the Truth was beyond counting."

In those verses, "ugghāṭetvā" means having uprooted or removed. "Sabbabhavaṃ" means all nine types of existence, or kamma which is the cause of the arising of existence. "Cariyāya pāramiṃ gato" means reaching the further shore by way of fulfilling all perfections. "Sīho va pañjaraṃ bhetvā" means that just as a lion breaks a cage, the Great Elephant among Sages destroyed the cage of existence.

There was only one assembly of disciples for the Blessed One Kakusandha, who had destroyed the bonds of existence. Surrounded by forty thousand Arahants who had gone forth with him, at the Isipatana deer park in the city of Kaṇṇakujja, on the full moon day of Māgha, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha. Regarding this, it was said:
299:
...having destroyed. The assembly of the disciples of the Blessed One Kakusandha, who had destroyed the bonds of sensual existence and the like, occurred only once. Surrounded by forty thousand Arahants who had gone forth with him, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha on the full moon day of Tabodwe (Māgha) in the Isipatana Deer Park near the city of Kaṇṇakujja. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Kakusandhassa... Āsavārigaṇakkhayā."

The assembly of the Arahants of the Blessed One Kakusandha, who were free from the taints of defilements, possessed peaceful minds, and were endowed with the quality of tādi (equanimity), occurred only once. At that time, there was an assembly of forty thousand Arahants who had reached the stage of the disciplined (dantabhūmi) due to the destruction of the dangers of the taints (āsavas).

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a king named Khema. Having offered a great gift of bowls, robes, and so forth to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he also offered all kinds of medicines such as eye-ointment (añjana). Having also offered other requisites for monks and heard the Dhamma teaching of that Buddha, his heart was filled with faith, and he went forth as a monk in the presence of the Blessed One. That Teacher also prophesied: "In the future, in this very Bhadda Kappa, this person will become a Buddha." Therefore, the Blessed One said this:

I was then a king named Khema, and I gave a great gift to the Tathāgata and the sons of the Conqueror (the Saṅgha).

Having given bowls, robes, eye-ointment, and honey-balls (liquorice), I prepared and offered all these desired and most excellent things.

That Buddha Kakusandha, the Leader who disciplines beings, also prophesied to me: "In this Bhadda Kappa, this person will become a Buddha."

Departing from the delightful city of Kapilavatthu... they prayed, "May we be in the presence of this Buddha."

Having heard the words of that Blessed One, I made my mind very clear and faithful. I undertook the supreme practice to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).

The city of that Blessed One was named Khemavatī. At that time, I was named Khema. Seeking omniscience, I went forth in the presence of that Blessed One.

In those verses, 'añjanaṃ' refers to the well-known eye-ointment. 'Madhulaṭṭhikaṃ' means honey-balls (liquorice). 'Imetaṃ' should be analyzed as 'imaṃ etaṃ'. 'Patthitaṃ' means that which is desired. 'Paṭiyādemi' means I give or I have given. 'Varaṃ varaṃ' means the most excellent. There is also a reading "yadetaṃ patthitaṃ"; according to that reading, it means all that was desired was given. This reading is better.

The city of the Blessed One Kakusandha, who possessed unsluggish wisdom, was named Khema. The Brahmin named Aggidatta was his father, and the Brahmin woman named Visākhā was his mother. The Elders Vidhura and Sañjīva were the two chief disciples. The monk named Buddhija was the attendant. The female Elders Sāmā and Campā were the two chief female disciples. The Sirīsa tree was the Bodhi tree. His body was forty cubits in height. The radiance of his body spread for ten yojanas all around. His lifespan was forty thousand years. The Brahmin woman named Rocinī was his wife, and he had a son named Uttara. He renounced the world in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. Therefore, the Blessed One said this:

14. The Brahmin Aggidatta was the father of that Buddha. The woman named Visākhā was the mother of the Teacher Kakusandha.
300:
The radiance of his body shines forth; his lifespan is forty thousand years; his wife is the Brahmin woman named Rocinī; his son is named Uttara; he renounced the world in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. This was said as follows:

"The Brahmin Aggidatta was the father of the Buddha; Visākhā was the mother of the Teacher Kakusandha.

The noble family of the Buddha, who was the best and most excellent among men, of noble birth and great fame, lived in that city of Khema.

Vidhura and Sañjīva were the chief disciples; the one named Buddhija was the attendant of the Teacher Kakusandha.

Sāmā and Campā were the chief female disciples; the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Sirīsa.

The Great Sage was forty cubits tall; a golden radiance shines forth for ten yojanas all around.

The lifespan of that Great Seer was forty thousand years; remaining for that long, he saved many people.

Having spread the Dhamma-market for men and women in the world including the devas, and having roared the lion's roar (preached the Dhamma), he attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.

The Buddha, endowed with speech of eight factors, and the disciples, whose virtue was constantly flawless, have all vanished. Are not all conditioned things indeed empty?"

In those verses, the verse beginning with "Vasate tattha kheme pure" should be understood as being spoken to show the birthplace of the Buddha Kakusandha. "Mahākulaṃ" refers to the renowned family of the Blessed One's father. "Narānaṃ pavaraṃ seṭṭhaṃ" means the most excellent and praised among all humans by virtue of birth. "Jātimantaṃ" means one of noble birth. "Mahāyasaṃ" means one with a great retinue. To the question "What is the noble family of the Buddha?", the word "Mahākulaṃ" should be seen in connection with the words "Kheme pure vasate".

"Samantā dasayojanaṃ" means that the golden radiance constantly emitted from his body spreads for ten yojanas all around.
301:
"Dhammāpaṇa" means the market-stall (or shop) known as the Dhamma. "Pasāretvā" means having spread out the Dhamma-market, like a market-stall filled with various goods for the purpose of selling merchandise. "Naranārīnaṃ" is for the purpose of the attainment and realization of the special jewels of jhāna, meditative attainments, paths, and fruits by the men and women who are beings to be tamed (veneyya). "Sīhanādaṃ" means having uttered a fearless roar (abhayanāda) like the roar of a lion king. "Aṭṭhaṅgavaca-nasampanno" refers to the Teacher who possesses a voice endowed with eight qualities. "Acchiddāni" refers to virtues that are free from defects such as being broken, and are unspotted and unblemished. Alternatively, "acchiddāni" refers to the pairs of disciples and others who are without gaps (incessant). "Nirantaraṃ" means constantly, at all times. "Sabbaṃ tamantarahitaṃ" means that both the Teacher and the pairs of disciples and others—all those persons—having reached the state of an Arahant, have reached the state of being no longer seen (attained Parinibbāna).

The Kakusandha Buddha, who is free from bonds, possessed of swift wisdom,
Who is free from all flaws (or has reached the opening called Nibbāna),
Who is connected with the three worlds, and is truly joined with truthful speech,
He indeed made his dwelling in the forest called Khema.

In the remaining verses, the meaning is entirely clear.

## The Description of the Chronicle of Kakusandha Buddha is finished.
## The Twenty-second Chronicle of the Buddhas is finished.
## 25. The Chronicle of Koṇāgamana Buddha

After the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha, when his dispensation had disappeared and when the lifespan of beings had reached thirty thousand years, the Teacher named Koṇāgamana, who brings welfare to others, appeared in the world. Alternatively, the Teacher named Koṇāgamana appeared in the world because of the arrival of gold (kanakāgamana). In that name "Koṇāgamana," by substituting "Ko" for the letter "ka," "ṇā" for the letter "na," and eliding one "ka," according to the method of linguistics (nirutti), he is called "Koṇāgamana" because at the time of that Blessed One’s appearance, there was a raining down (arrival) of ornaments made of pure gold. Here, although the lifespan seems to have decreased in order, it should be understood that it did not decrease directly like that, but increased again and then decreased. How? In this very Bhadda-kappa, the Blessed One Kakusandha was born at the time when the lifespan was forty thousand years.
302:
That lifespan, gradually decreasing, reached ten years, then reached an incalculable period (asaṅkheyya), and then decreasing from there, it stood at the time of a thirty-thousand-year lifespan. It should be understood that at that time, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana appeared in the world.

He too, having fulfilled the perfections, was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of the Brahmin woman named Uttarā, who was unsurpassed in qualities such as beauty and was the wife of the Brahmin Yaññadatta in the city of Sobhavatī. After ten months had passed, he was born from his mother's womb in the Subhavatī park. While he was being born, the rain-deity caused a rain of gold to fall throughout the entire Jambudīpa. Because of that reason—the arrival of gold—they gave him the name "Kanakāgamana." That name, through gradual transformation, became "Koṇāgamana." He lived in the household life for three thousand years. He had three palaces named Tusita, Santusita, and Santuṭṭha. There were sixteen thousand ladies, headed by the Brahmin woman Rucigattā.

Having seen the four omens, and when a son named Satthavāha was born to the Brahmin woman Rucigattā, he mounted the back of a noble elephant and departed for the Great Renunciation by elephant-vehicle to become a monk. Thirty thousand men followed him into monkhood. Surrounded by those monks, he practiced asceticism for six months. On the full moon day of Visākha, having consumed the thick milk-rice offered by the daughter of the Brahmin Aggisoṇa, the young Brahmin lady Aggisoṇā, and having spent the day in the Khadira forest, in the evening he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by a barley-field watchman named Jaṭātinduka. He approached the Udumbara Bodhi tree, which was endowed with the splendor of fruits and flowers of the size previously mentioned, from the south. Having spread the grass-mat twenty cubits wide and sitting in the cross-legged posture, he defeated the host of Māra and attained the Knowledge of the Ten Powers (dasabala-ñāṇa). Having uttered the solemn utterance: "Through many a birth in saṃsāra... I have attained the destruction of craving," he spent the seven weeks (satta-sattāha). Seeing the maturity of the supporting conditions (upanissaya-sampatti) of the thirty thousand monks who had ordained with him, he traveled through the air and descended at the Isipatana Deer Park near the city of Sudassana. In the midst of those monks, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. At that time, there was the first realization of the Truths by thirty thousand crores of beings.

Again, at the gate of the city of Sundara, at the foot of a great Sal tree, he performed the Twin Miracle and caused twenty thousand crores of beings to drink the nectar of Dhamma. That was the second realization. Having placed his mother Uttarā at the head, while he was preaching the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to the devas and brahmas who had assembled from the ten thousand world-systems, the realization of the Truths by ten thousand crores of devas and brahmas was the third realization.
303:
While the Blessed One was preaching the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to the deities who had assembled from the ten thousand world systems, the third realization (abhisamaya) of the Four Noble Truths occurred for ten billion deities. Therefore, it was said in the Buddhavaṃsa:

“After the Buddha Kakusandha, there appeared the Buddha named Koṇāgamana, the Conqueror, the supreme among bipeds, the eldest in the world, and the bull among men.

“Having fulfilled the ten perfections, He crossed the wilderness of rebirth; having washed away all stains, He attained the supreme Enlightenment.

“While the Leader Koṇāgamana was turning the Wheel of Dhamma, the first realization occurred for three hundred billion humans and deities.

“And while He was performing miracles to crush the arguments of others, the second realization occurred for two hundred billion humans and deities.

“Thereafter, the Conqueror, having performed various psychic transformations, went to the city of the gods; there the Buddha resided on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat.

“That Sage resided there for the three months of the rainy season, preaching the seven books of Abhidhamma; the third realization occurred for one hundred billion humans and deities.”

In those verses, “dasa dhamme pūrayitvāna” means having fulfilled the ten perfections (pāramīs). “Kantāraṃ samatikkami” means He crossed the wilderness of existence known as rebirth (jāti). “Pavāhiya” means having washed away. “Malaṃ sabbaṃ” refers to the group of three stains, such as lust (rāga) and so forth. “Pāṭihīraṃ karonte ca, paravādappamaddane” means while the Blessed One was performing miracles to crush the doctrines of other teachers. “Vikubbanaṃ” refers to the psychic power of transformation (vikubbana-iddhi); after performing the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya) at the gate of the beautiful city (Sundara), He went to the city of the gods and resided there on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat. How did He reside there? “Pakaraṇe satta desento” means He resided there while preaching the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, consisting of the seven books, to the deities. This means that while the Blessed One was preaching the Abhidhamma there, the realization of the Four Noble Truths occurred for ten billion deities.

For the Buddha Koṇāgamana, who came by fulfilling the pure perfections, there was also one assembly of disciples. While He was residing in the Surinda Park in the city of Surindavatī...
304:
...having preached the Dhamma to Prince Bhiyyasa and Prince Uttara, as well as to their thirty thousand followers, and having admitted them all into the Order through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination, He recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha in the midst of those monks on the full moon day of Māgha. Regarding that, it was said:

“For that Buddha, the God of gods, there was also only one assembly of Arahants who were free from stains, possessed of peaceful minds, and endowed with the quality of steadfastness (tādi).

“At that time, there was an assembly of thirty thousand monks who had crossed over the four floods (oghas) and had destroyed death.”

In that verse, “oghānaṃ” is a designation for the four floods, such as the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha). Those are called floods (oghas) because they sink or submerge the person in whom they exist into the cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭa). The genitive case here should be understood in the sense of the objective case; thus, it means those who have crossed the fourfold floods. The same method applies to the word “bhizzitānaṃ.” “Maccuyā” means of death (maccuno).

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a king named Pabbata in the city of Mithilā. Then, hearing that “the Buddha Koṇāgamana, the refuge of all beings, has arrived at the city of Mithilā,” the King went out with his retinue to welcome Him, paid homage, invited the Possessor of Ten Powers, and offered a great gift. He then requested the Blessed One to reside there for the rainy season and attended to the Teacher along with the community of disciples for the three months of the rains. He offered expensive and fine garments such as silk from the Pattuṇṇa country, Chinese silk, silk cloth, woolen cloth, white cloth, and cotton cloth, as well as golden sandals and many other requisites. That Blessed One also prophesied concerning him: “In this very Bhadda-kappa, this king will become a Buddha.”

Then, that Great Being, having heard the prophecy of the Blessed One, renounced his great kingdom and was ordained in the presence of that very Blessed One. Regarding that, it was said:

“At that time, I was a kshatriya named Pabbata, endowed with friends and ministers, and possessing an infinite army and vehicles.

“Having gone to see the Buddha and heard the unsurpassed Dhamma, I invited the Conqueror along with the Saṅgha and gave gifts according to their wishes.

“I offered garments of Pattuṇṇa silk, Chinese silk, silk cloth, woolen cloth, and golden sandals to the Teacher and his disciples.

“That Blessed One, seated in the midst of the Saṅgha, also prophesied to me: ‘In this very Bhadda-kappa, this king will become a Buddha.’

“At that time, having departed from the delightful city of Kapilavatthu... they made the aspiration: ‘May we be in the presence of this Buddha Gotama.’

“Having heard the words of that Blessed One, I made my mind very confident. I undertook a superior practice to fulfill the ten perfections.

“Seeking omniscience, I gave gifts to the Buddha, the supreme among men, renounced the great kingdom, and was ordained in the presence of the Blessed One.”

In those verses, “anantabalavāhano” means one who has an infinite and vast army and vehicles such as horses and elephants.
305:
That Blessed One also, seated in the midst of the Saṅgha, prophesied of me: "In this very Bhadda Kappa, this person will become a Buddha."

13. At that time, having come out from the delightful city of Kapilavatthu... they made the aspiration: "May we be in the presence of this Blessed One Gotama."

14. Having heard the words of that Blessed One, I gladdened my mind even more and undertook a superior practice to fulfill the ten perfections (pāramīs).

15. While seeking omniscience, I gave alms to the Buddha, the best of men, and having renounced the great kingdom, I went forth in the presence of the Conqueror (Jina).

In those verses, "anantabalavāhano" means having infinite forces and vehicles such as horses and elephants. "Sambuddhadassanaṃ" means for the purpose of seeing the Buddha. "Yadicchakaṃ" means giving as much as desired to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with the four types of food, even to the point of being told "enough, enough" and causing them to close their bowls with their hands. "Satthusāvake" means he gave to the Teacher and the disciples. "Naruttame" means to the Buddha, the best of men. "Ohāya" means having abandoned or renounced.

Furthermore, the city of that Blessed One Koṇāgamana was named Sobhavatī. His father was the Brahmin named Yaññadatta, and his mother was the Brahmin lady named Uttarā. Bhiyyasa and Uttara were the two chief disciples. The attendant was named Sotthija. Samuddā and Uttarā were the two chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree was the Udumbara (fig tree). His body was thirty cubits high, and his lifespan was thirty thousand years. His wife was the Brahmin lady named Rucigattā, and his son was named Satthavāha. He renounced using an elephant vehicle. Thus the Blessed One said, "The city named Sobhavatī," and so on.

16. The city was named Sobhavatī. There was a king named Sobha. In that city lived the great family of the Buddha.

17. The father of the Buddha Koṇāgamana, the teacher of gods and men, was the Brahmin Yaññadatta, and his mother was named Uttarā.

18. That Bodhisatta lived in the household for thirty thousand years. He had three magnificent palaces named Tusita, Santusita, and Santuṭṭha.

19. There were no less than sixteen thousand well-adorned court ladies. His wife was named Rucigattā, and his son was named Satthavāha.

20. Having seen the four omens, the Bodhisatta renounced using an elephant vehicle. He practiced the exertion of meditation for six months.

21. The Buddha Koṇāgamana, of great exertion and best of men, being requested by the Great Brahmā, turned the Wheel of Dhamma in the Migadāya (Deer Park).

22. The elders named Bhiyyasa and Uttara were the chief disciples of the Buddha Koṇāgamana. The attendant of that Blessed One was named Sotthija.

23. Samuddā and Uttarā were the chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Udumbara.
306:
The Elder nuns Samuddā and Uttarā were the pair of chief female disciples. The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called the Udumbara.

In height, that Buddha rose to thirty cubits. Like pure gold in a smith's furnace, he was likewise adorned with rays of light.

At that time, the lifespan of the Buddha was thirty thousand years. Remaining for that long, he saved many beings.

Having raised the Dhamma-cetiya (shrine of Dhamma) adorned with the banner of the four truths, and having woven the garland of Dhamma flowers, that Blessed One attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.

The great splendor of his disciples and that Blessed One who proclaimed the glorious supramundane Dhamma—all that has disappeared. Are not all conditioned things indeed empty?

In those verses, 'ukkāmukhe' means in a smith's furnace. 'Yathā kambū' means like pure gold. 'Evaṃ raṃsīhi maṇဒိတော' means thus equally adorned with rays of light. 'Dhammacetiṃ samusseitvā' means having established a shrine made of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma). 'Dhammadussavibhūsitaṃ' means adorned with the banner of the four truths. 'Dhammapupphaguဠံ katvā' means having made a garland of Dhamma (the fruit of Arahantship). The meaning is that after establishing the Dhamma-cetiya for the purpose of worship by the multitude of beings standing on the courtyard of the shrine of insight (vipassanā), the Teacher together with the assembly of disciples attained Parinibbāna. 'Mahāvilāso' means having reached the splendor of great psychic power. 'Tassa' means of that Blessed One. 'Jano' means the assembly of disciples. 'Siridhammapappakāsano' means that Blessed One who clearly showed the supramundane Dhamma, and all that has disappeared.

The Buddha Koṇāgamana, free from taints, detached from sensual pleasures, born of a noble lineage, seeker of the noble practice, dwelt happily in the secluded forest named Siri.

In the remaining verses, the meaning is clear throughout.

## The Explanation of the Chronicle of the Buddha Koṇāgamana is finished.
## The Twenty-third Chronicle of the Buddhas is finished.
307:
## 26. Kassapa Buddhavaṃsavaṇṇanā

After the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, when his dispensation had disappeared, the lifespan of beings, which was thirty thousand years, gradually decreased until it reached ten years. From there, it increased again to an immeasurable age, and then gradually decreased once more. When the lifespan reached twenty thousand years, the Teacher named Kassapa, who protects many multitudes of people, appeared in the world. Having fulfilled the perfections, that Bodhisatta was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of the Brahmin lady named Dhanavatī, who was endowed with abundant virtues, and the Brahmin named Brahmadatta in the city of Bārāṇasī. When ten months had passed, he was born from his mother's womb in the Isipatana Migadāya forest. By virtue of his lineage, they named him "Kassapa Kumāra."

That Kassapa Kumāra lived in the household life for two thousand years. He had three palaces: Haṃsavā, Yasavā, and Sirinanda. There were forty-eight thousand female attendants, headed by the Brahmin lady Sunandā.

Having seen the four signs, and when a son named Vijitasena was born to the Brahmin lady Sunandā, the Bodhisatta felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and thought, "I shall depart for the Great Renunciation." Immediately after that thought, the palace revolved like a potter's wheel and flew up into the sky. Like the moon of the month of Kattika surrounded by a host of stars with exceeding radiance, like decorating the sky while surrounded by hundreds of people, as if manifesting the power of his merit, as if drawing the eyes and hearts of the multitudes, and as if making the treetops exceedingly beautiful, the palace traveled and settled on the ground, placing the Nigrodha Bodhi tree in the center. Then the Bodhisatta, the Great Being, standing on the ground, took the monastic robes—the banner of Arahantship—offered by the Brahma King and renounced the world. The dancing women of that Bodhisatta descended from the palace, traveled a distance of about half a gāvuta, and sat down where the army had gathered with their attendants. Then, leaving behind the female servants, all those who had come along renounced the world.

The Great Being, surrounded by those monks, practiced the exertion of meditation for seven days. On the full moon day of Visākha, having partaken of the milk-rice offered by the Brahmin lady named Sunandā, he spent the day in the Khadiravana (Acacia grove). In the evening, he accepted eight handfuls of grass offered by the barley-field guard named Soma and approached the Nigrodha Bodhi tree. Having spread a mat of grass fifteen cubits in length and breadth, he sat at the foot of that Nigrodha Bodhi tree and attained the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship and Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), and then uttered the solemn utterance: "Aneka jāti saṃsāraṃ... taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā." After passing the seven weeks (forty-nine days), he saw the potential (upanissaya) for the attainment of the Paths and Fruits of the ten million monks who had renounced with him. He then traveled through the sky and descended at the Isipatana Migadāya forest in the city of Bārāṇasī, and surrounded by those monks...
308:
Having spread a mat of grass fifteen cubits in length and breadth and sitting there, he attained Supreme Enlightenment (Abhisambodhi). He then uttered the solemn utterance: "Aneka jāti saṃsāraṃ... taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā," and passed the seven weeks (forty-nine days). Seeing the perfection of the supporting conditions (upanissaya-sampatti) for the attainment of the Paths and Fruits of the ten million monks who had renounced with him, he traveled through the sky and descended at the Isipatana Migadāya forest in Bārāṇasī. Surrounded by those monks, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhamma-cakka) there. At that time, the first realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) occurred for twenty thousand koṭis of beings. Regarding that, it was said:

"After the time of Koṇāgamana, there appeared the Fully Enlightened One, the Supreme among bipeds, the King of Dhamma, the Maker of Light, known by his lineage as Kassapa.

Having abandoned his ancestral home which was filled with many kinds of food and drink, and having given gifts to beggars to fulfill his heart's desire, he reached the supreme Enlightenment, just as a bull breaks out of its pen.

While Kassapa, the Leader of the World, was setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, the first realization occurred for twenty thousand koṭis of beings."

In those verses, 'sañchaddita' means abandoned, discarded, or relinquished. 'Kulamūla' refers to the ancestral home, which is a mass of immeasurable wealth, an accumulation of many thousands of koṭis of riches, similar to the palace of the Thousand-Eyed One (Sakka), which is extremely difficult to give up; the meaning is that he discarded it like grass. 'Yācake' means giving to beggars. 'Āḷaka' means a cattle pen. Just as a bull breaks the pen and reaches its desired place at ease, so too the Great Being broke the bond of the household and reached Supreme Enlightenment; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, while the Teacher was wandering for four months on a journey through the countryside, the second realization occurred for ten thousand koṭis of beings. When he performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) at the foot of an Asana tree at the gate of the city of Sundara and preached the Dhamma, the third realization occurred for five thousand koṭis of beings. Again, after performing the Twin Miracle, he resided in the Sudhammā hall, the assembly of devas in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, which is difficult for the enemies of the devas (Asuras) to conquer. There, placing his mother, the goddess Dhanavatī, at the head, he preached the seven books of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka for the benefit of the deities from the ten thousand world systems. At that time, three thousand koṭis of deities drank the ambrosia of the Dhamma. Regarding that, it was said:
309:
In that Tāvatiṃsa heaven, the Blessed One sat and, placing the goddess Dhanavatī—who had been his mother—at the head, preached the seven books of the Abhidhamma, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, to the devas and brahmas who had arrived in unison from the ten thousand world-systems for their benefit, providing the nectar of the Dhamma to three billion devas and brahmas. Therefore, the Blessed One said this in the Pāḷi text:

“When the Buddha wandered for four months in the world,
There was the second realization of the Truth for ten billion veneyyas.

Having performed the Twin Miracle and proclaimed the nature of Omniscient Knowledge,
There was the third realization of the Truth for five billion veneyyas.

In the delightful Sudhammā assembly hall in the celestial city, the Victorious One preached the Dhamma,
And caused three billion devas to realize the Truth.

In another discourse to the yakkha named Naradeva,
The realizations of these devas and humans were beyond counting.”

In those verses, “catumāsaṃ” means for four months. This is also a textual reading. “Carati” means he wandered and practiced. “Yamakaṃ vikubbanaṃ katvā” means having performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire. “Ñāṇadhātuṃ” refers to the nature of Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Some also say “sabbaññāṇadhātu.” “Pakittayī” means he manifested clearly to the great multitude. “Sudhammā” refers to the assembly hall named Sudhammā in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; it means having sat in that place. “Dhammaṃ” refers to the Abhidhamma.

At that time, there was a powerful yakkha named Naradeva, who was conquered by [the Buddha’s] majesty, and who was as mighty as the Naradeva yakkha mentioned below. That Naradeva yakkha, in a city in Jambudīpa, created a form, appearance, and voice similar to the king’s, killed and ate the real king, and then took over the kingdom along with the harem, becoming one who consumed an immeasurable amount of human flesh. It is said that he was also a lustful man. When the clever and skillful women of the palace realized, “This is not our king, this is a non-human,” the yakkha, out of shame, ate all those women and went to another city. In this very way, while that Naradeva yakkha was consuming humans and heading toward the city of Sundara, the citizens, terrified by the fear of death, fled from their city in various directions.

Seeing those people fleeing, the Kassapa Buddha, the Possessor of Ten Powers, stood before that Naradeva yakkha. When Naradeva saw the God of gods standing there, he let out a terrible and horrific roar, but being unable to frighten the Blessed One, he went to him for refuge and asked questions. After answering the questions and taming him, while the Dhamma was being preached, the countless devas and humans who had arrived realized the Truth. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke the Pāḷi beginning with “Naradevassa yakkhassa.” In that text, “apare dhammadesane” means in another teaching of the Dhamma. “Etesānaṃ” means of those devas and humans.

Furthermore, for that Kassapa Buddha, there was only one assembly of disciples. In the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a young man named Tissa, the son of the chaplain. That Tissa, seeing the perfection of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks on the body of the Bodhisatta Kassapa, and hearing his father’s words, thought: “Undoubtedly, this person will go forth in the Great Renunciation and become a Buddha; I shall ordain in his presence and free myself from the suffering of the round of rebirth (saṃsāra).” He then went to the Himalayas, where there were groups of pure sages, and became an ascetic. That ascetic Tissa had twenty thousand ascetics as his followers. Later, when he heard that “the youth Kassapa has gone forth and attained the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship and Omniscient Knowledge,” ...
310:
The realization of the Truth (abhisamaya) for the devas and humans, who were beyond the path of counting, occurred. Thus, it was said: “Naradevassa yakkhassa,” and so on. In that text, “apare dhammadesane” means in another teaching of the Dhamma. “Etesānaṃ” means of those [devas and humans]. Or, this reading “etesaṃ” is the correct one.

For that Blessed One Kassapa, there was only one assembly of disciples. In the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a young man named Tissa, the son of the chaplain. That Tissa, seeing the perfection of the major and minor marks on the body of the Bodhisatta Kassapa and hearing his father’s words, thought: “Undoubtedly, this one will go forth in the Great Renunciation and become a Buddha. I shall ordain in this noble one’s presence and free myself from the suffering of the round of rebirth.” He went to the Himalayas, where there were groups of pure sages, and became an ascetic. He had twenty thousand ascetics as his followers. Later, hearing that “the youth Kassapa has gone forth and attained Omniscient Knowledge,” he came with his followers to the presence of the Blessed One Kassapa, ordained through the “Ehi Bhikkhu” ordination, and attained the fruit of Arahantship. In that assembly, the Blessed One Kassapa recited the Pātimokkha on the full moon day of Māgha. Therefore, the Blessed One said this:

“For that God of gods, there was also one assembly of Arahants, who were stainless, of peaceful mind, and steadfast (tādi).”

“There was then an assembly of twenty thousand monks, who had transcended existence, and were steadfast in shame and virtue.”

In those verses, “atikkantabhavantānaṃ” means those who have transcended the states of worldlings, stream-enterers, and so on—meaning only Arahants. “Hirisīlena tādinaṃ” means those who are equal in shame (hiri) and virtue (sīla).

At that time, our Bodhisatta was a young man named Jotipāla, who had reached the far shore of the three Vedas, was famous on earth and in the sky, and was a friend of Ghaṭīkāra the potter. That young man Jotipāla visited the Teacher along with Ghaṭīkāra, and having heard the Dhamma, he ordained in the presence of the Buddha. He was one of exerted effort, mastered the three Piṭakas, and adorned the Buddha’s Dispensation (Sāsana) with his major and minor duties. That Teacher also delivered the prophecy to the monk Jotipāla. Therefore, the Blessed One said this:

“I was then the young man known as Jotipāla,
A student and bearer of mantras, who had reached the far shore of the three Vedas.”
311:
